articles.title: CGI Animated Movie ‘Juul,’ Featuring Lenny Henry, Joins Studio 100 Film’s Toronto Sales Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 25, 2026 1:57am PT CGI Animated Movie ‘Juul,’ Featuring Lenny Henry, Joins Studio 100 Film’s Toronto Sales Slate (EXCLUSIVE) By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Seth Rogen, Colman Domingo, Danny Boyle Join Speakers Lineup at Toronto Market Summit 4 days ago The Freyas, a New Awards Ceremony Celebrating Nordic Film and TV Talent, to Launch in Helsinki (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago See All Courtesy of Fabrique Fantastique Studio 100 Film has added CGI animated feature “Juul” to its international sales slate and will introduce the project to buyers at the Toronto Film Festival . The English-language voice cast features Lenny Henry , while five-time Grammy Award-winners Michael League and Bob Lanzetti of Snarky Puppy contribute to the original score. The film is directed by Tom Van Gestel and written by An De Gruyter. “Juul” is in production and is scheduled for delivery in Q4 2026. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller Set in the 1950s, Juul follows 17-year-old circus acrobat Juul, whose life changes forever after a tragic accident leaves her in a coma and declared brain-dead. Facing financial ruin, her magician father takes a desperate and morally complicated decision: he steals her body from the hospital and presents her as a “living puppet” to revive the failing circus. But Juul is still conscious, trapped inside a body she no longer controls. As her anger and resistance grow, her body begins to transform into porcelain, becoming a powerful symbol of her silent rebellion and her fight to reclaim her own identity. Popular on Variety Van Gestel said, “‘Juul’ dares to go where most animated films don’t. It tackles a dark, raw and difficult subject, but does so by keeping every character deeply human. At its heart, ‘Juul’ is the story of a young girl who is constantly being pulled down by the world around her. Yet, no matter how hard she is pushed, she finds a way to fight back.” The film is produced by Fabrique Fantastique (Belgium) in co-production with M.A.R.K.13 (Germany), Keplerfilm (The Netherlands), Mr Miyagi (Spain) and Avalon Films (Ireland). Studio 100 Film handles worldwide sales, excluding Belgium, Germany, Spain and The Netherlands. Lorena Booth, senior manager sales and acquisitions at Studio 100 Film, said, “’Juul’ represents the kind of ambitious animated storytelling we are increasingly looking to bring to international audiences. articles.title: ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’
articles.full_text: Aug 25, 2026 2:00am PT ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race 17 minutes ago ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ 30 minutes ago Epstein Files Documentary ‘Diabolical’ Lands at HBO Max in International Deal 38 minutes ago See All Manuel Harlan “ Pride ,” the joy-filled British musical based on the true story of Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners (LGSM), will transfer to London’s Bridge Theatre from Nov. 12, following sold-out seasons at Cardiff’s Sherman Theatre and the National Theatre’s Dorfman space. The production will mark the inaugural show at the Bridge Theatre, a 900-seat venue on the Thames near Tower Bridge, under its new ownership by Trafalgar Entertainment. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller “Pride” reunites the creative team behind the acclaimed 2014 film of the same name: director Matthew Warchus (“Matilda the Musical”) and writer Stephen Beresford (“The Last of the Haussmans”), who wrote the musical’s book and lyrics. Set during the 1984 U.K. miners’ strike, the show follows 24-year-old activist Mark Ashton as he rallies LGSM to form an alliance with a striking mining community in South Wales. Popular on Variety The musical features an original score by Christopher Nightingale, Josh Cohen and DJ Walde, drawing on protest anthems, pop, rock, disco and the Welsh choral tradition. The transfer cast includes Samuel Barnett as Jonathan, Matthew Durkan as Mike, Gillian Elisa as Gwen, Chris Jenkins as Gethin, Darren Lawrence as Cliff, Kirsty Malpass as Hefina, Madeleine Morgan, Sarah Pugh as Siân, Caroline Sheen as Maureen, Courtney Stapleton as Steph and Matthew Woodyatt as Dai, with further casting to be announced. Speaking with Variety ahead of the transfer, Warchus says he always treats a remount as a chance to “get access to it again and make little fiddly improvements and changes.” He never approaches an opening night as a finished product, he says: “The opening night is a record, a document of where you got to in the amount of time you had and with the resources that you had.” The move to a bigger house, he says, will also change how the production’s comedy and sound design land. “The difference between 800 people laughing and 400 people laughing is more than double,” Warchus says. “I think the comedy will really benefit from more people watching.” He points to the show’s layered sound design – the birds of Wales, chapel bells, the chants of striking miners, the cheers of the Pits and Perverts benefit concert – as an element he expects to intensify rather than dilute in a larger room. “Sound design always works better in larger spaces,” he says. Warchus adds that the production’s essential character, built on simplicity rather than spectacle, will not change with the move. “It’s still going to be a story that’s got a handmade feel to it,” he says. “Very basic props, no glitzy automation or hydraulics or anything like that.” The “Pride” film bowed at Cannes – where it won the Queer Palm – and went on to be distributed globally. Beresford draws a parallel to audience reactions when the film was first released. “There were reports in cinemas all over the world that at the end of the screening people would applaud as though it were a stage production,” he says, adding that theater audiences have taken to hugging strangers and sharing tissues by the end of a performance. Asked whether the story, set 40 years ago, has taken on new relevance, Beresford points to a line from a review of the film that has stayed with him: “Prejudice cannot survive proximity.” He says the story’s emphasis on LGSM members physically showing up for a community unlike their own still resonates. “It’s the proximity that matters,” he says. Warchus recalls watching a performance alongside recently appointed U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and noticing how the audience responded whenever the word “hope” appeared in the lyrics. “It was like a bell being rung,” he says. The stage adaptation followed two decades after Beresford first tried to get the story told on screen. “It took me 20 years to get the film made,” he says. “Nobody would touch it, the film, with a bargepole.” Warchus says the pair spent a couple of years weighing whether to attempt a musical version at all, wary of tampering with a project both are proud of. “You have a strong sense of why what kind of idiot messes with something,” he says. “But then, on the other hand, it’s quite painful if some other putz messes it up and you don’t get a chance to do it.” Warchus credits Beresford’s writing as the reason he has anything to direct in the first place. “I wouldn’t have known the story if Stephen hadn’t written it up and added his own angle to it,” he says. Beresford, in turn, says what drew him to Warchus was an aversion to visual spectacle for its own sake. “Directors who say, ‘I’m going to CGI this and the camera’s going to swing underwater and then it’s going to’ I just it’s white noise to me. I’m not really interested,” he says, adding that their work together on the film centered on character. “We talked about who they were and what they wanted and what they didn’t want,” he says. “And in making a musical – Matthew has made a lot of musicals – but he has a fantastic detailed eye. And I think we complement each other very well and have the same taste, largely,” Beresford adds. Asked how the show balances the AIDS crisis and the defeat of the strike against its comedy, Beresford says the two are inseparable. “One of the most subversive and powerful weapons at our disposal is humor and cheerfulness and the particular black humor that comes from living through adversity,” he says. He recalls a 2015 Pride march where Anne Scargill, then the wife of former National Union of Mineworkers president Arthur Scargill, approached him. “She said, ‘You’ve made the truest film about the miners’ strike that’s ever been made,'” Beresford says. “And I said, ‘Anne, we both know that is not true.’ And she said, ‘It is. Because it’s funny.'” On the decision to commission an original score rather than build the musical around existing songs, as the film’s beloved soundtrack had done, Warchus says jukebox musicals tend to interrupt their own storytelling. “The songs stop the story every single time they turn up, because they can’t carry the story,” he says. “A true musical is a completely different thing, and that’s what we wanted to do.” Designer Bunny Christie’s set, built around the idea of a touring production that has “come out the back of a minibus,” was a deliberate choice, according to Warchus, who says he grew up watching similar scratch-built touring shows in the 1980s. “That’s definitely in my blood,” he says, adding that the production also layers in “a rock-and-roll lighting rig” to give the show the feel of a live concert during its Pits and Perverts sequence. Warchus says he gave Christie a physical brief during an early workshop, taping off a square around a crowd of test performers to demonstrate how much stage space the show’s crowd scenes would require. “I need it to be this crowded when we’re doing the Pride march or an event happening,” he recalls telling her. “Therefore, I need the stage to be this small, this size.” Beresford and Warchus also address criticism that the musical understates the role of LGSM’s lesbian members, a group that in real life numbered around 40 to 50 people, some of whom broke away to found the support group Lesbians Against Pit Closures. Beresford says the real-life group had to be condensed for the stage, with composite characters like Reggie and Steph standing in for several real activists. Warchus says the show’s small ensemble size, which has to account for understudies across both the Welsh and LGSM characters, further limited how many roles could be written. “We worked out we could have seven people,” he says. Beresford notes the production made a point of casting an all-female band. “They’re the lesbian band,” he says. “They represent the lesbians.” Asked what Ashton, who died of an AIDS-related illness in 1987, might make of the musical, Beresford describes him as a natural showman. “He was a huge, huge theatric,” Beresford says. “He loved camp … his whole political process was about making things fabulous.” He adds that Ashton would likely have one specific complaint. “He would be frustrated that I do not have a song which literally is the entire Communist Manifesto set to music, perhaps to a samba beat,” Beresford says. Warchus says he expects Ashton’s reaction would mirror those of LGSM members who have already seen the show. “I hope that he would laugh uproariously, and I’m sure that he would cry,” he says. “Pride” previewed to sold-out houses at the Sherman Theatre before opening at the National Theatre’s Dorfman in June, where it runs through Sept. 12. The musical is produced by P&P Productions in association with the National Theatre, Pathé, Calamity Films and David Binder Productions. articles.title: Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race
articles.full_text: Aug 25, 2026 2:13am PT Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race 7 minutes ago ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ 21 minutes ago Epstein Files Documentary ‘Diabolical’ Lands at HBO Max in International Deal 29 minutes ago See All Netflix The Korean Film Council (KOFIC) has selected “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong , as South Korea ‘s official entry for the international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards. “Possible Love” marks Lee’s first feature in eight years, following “Burning,” “Poetry” and “Secret Sunshine.” The film centers on two married couples whose lives intersect after a funeral: Mi-ok and her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who live quietly with their young son Cheol, and Ye-ji, a filmmaker making a documentary about workers who lost their jobs, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed by Ye-ji, the two women grow close, while Mi-ok finds herself unsettled by an attraction to Sang-woo. As the two couples’ worlds overlap, cracks begin to surface in both marriages. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller A 15-member selection committee, chaired by film critic Jung Sung-il, made the choice. Other committee members included Kang Myung-chan, Kim So-young, Kim Jae-joong, Kim Tae-sung, Kim Hyun-chul, Moon Young-hwa, Song Kyung-won, Won Dong-yeon, Yoo Hyun-taek, Yoon Sung-eun, Lee Han, Lim Dae-hyung, Jung Yi-jun and Cho Hwa-sung. Popular on Variety In its evaluation, the committee cited the film’s polished craftsmanship and the clarity of its directorial vision, pointing to the tone and mise-en-scène that sustain a sense of pressure throughout the story. The drama was described as prompting reflection on gentle forms of violence, incomplete freedom and the nature of true happiness, alongside a labor movement sequence that the committee said captured layered social undercurrents. The committee also highlighted the film’s humanism and delicate direction, its dense, multidimensional character relationships, and its meditation on love, desire and original sin. Members called it the culmination of Lee’s perspective and preoccupations as a filmmaker, praising what they described as nearly flawless performances from the four leads. The committee pointed to the international feature category’s track record of favoring auteur-driven dramas, noting that Lee’s 2018 film “Burning” became the first Korean title to advance to the Academy’s foreign language film shortlist. Members also flagged strong anticipation from North American press and said a Netflix awards team is preparing a campaign for the film that extends to a best picture push. The film’s world premiere will be at the Venice Film Festival and North American Premiere at the Toronto Film Festival. Under Academy international feature film category rules, “Possible Love” must complete its local theatrical release in South Korea by Sept. 30. The film will open in Korean theaters Sept. 23, followed by select theatrical releases in Australia Oct. 22 and in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Ireland and Japan Oct. 23, before streaming globally on Netflix starting Nov. 6. South Korea has submitted films in the category since 1962 without a nomination for decades, until Lee Chang-dong’s “Burning” became the first Korean film to make the shortlist in 2018. Bong Joon Ho’s “Parasite” then won the category and best picture in 2020 – the first non-English-language film to do so – and Park Chan-wook’s “Decision to Leave” (2022) and “No Other Choice” (2025) both reached the shortlist without landing a nomination. The 99th Academy Awards are scheduled for March 14, 2027. articles.title: Field Of Vision Debuts Ukraine War-Themed ‘When It Started To Burn’ On Ukrainian Independence Day
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Six Finalists To Vie For 2026 Library of Congress Lavine/Ken Burns Prize for Film, With Winner To Receive $200,000 ‘Vultures’ Swoops To Top Award At Oscar-Qualifying HollyShorts Film Festival: Winners List HollyShorts Festival Set To Propel Documentary Jury Award Winner Into Oscar Race View All August 24, 2026 4:29pm 'When It Started to Burn' Field of Vision EXCLUSIVE: On the 35 th anniversary of Ukrainian Independence Day, Field of Vision is launching a new documentary on Ukraine’s valiant fight to maintain its freedom. When It Started to Burn debuted on the Field of Vision platform Monday, the third in a trilogy of short films from director Anders Hammer that examine “conflicts and civilian resilience across the globe.” His 2023 film The Takeover centered on the Taliban’s return to power in Afghanistan after the U.S. military withdrawal; Do Not Split , a chronicle of pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong, earned an Academy Award nomination in 2021. Related Stories Documentary Wendy Williams Docuseries Set At Peacock News WildBrain Buys Personality AI In Deal Worth Up To $70 Million We understand Hammer immediately traveled to Kyiv after Russia embarked on its “special military operation” in Ukraine (as Russian President Putin euphemistically put it) in February 2022. Four years’ worth of filming have gone into the making of When It Started to Burn . Watch on Deadline The documentary short “focuses on the civilians making great efforts to contribute to the resistance [against Russian aggression] in every possible way,” notes a synopsis. “As the fighting continues with no end in sight, the mental impact of war becomes clearer, and lives are changed forever. “Following the journey of Kseniia, a Kyiv local who sets up a volunteer center while her children seek refuge abroad, we witness as landscapes are rendered unrecognizable and neighborhoods are abandoned in the Ukrainian capital. Yet as years pass and the war rages on, Kseniia must choose between fleeing herself to reunite with family or staying behind to protect what’s left of what she once called home.” The film not only documents the brutality of war, but also “the kindness of humans finding solidarity in the face of extreme danger.” Ukrainian Independence Day marks the day in 1991 when Ukraine achieved its freedom from a collapsing Soviet Union. (Putin, in his attempt to capture Ukraine, appears intent on trying to reestablish Russian hegemony over not only Ukraine but potentially all Eastern Europe.) Filmmaker Anders Hammer in 2021 Francisco Seco-Pool/Getty Images Hammer’s additional credits include the documentary series Our Allies , set in Syria and Iraq, for Field of Vision. Escape from Syria: Rania’s Odyssey , published by The Guardian , won a Webby Award and a One World Media Award for Best Refugee Reporting in 2018; it has gained more than 10 million views and 100,000 shares on social media. In Hammer’s native Norway, he has directed nine documentaries for the Norwegian investigative journalism program NRK Brennpunkt. Field of Vision, founded in 2015, is a “filmmaker-driven non-profit organization that commissions and supports films, filmmakers, journalists and artists that use innovative and artistic ways to explore contemporary global issues through a cinematic lens, and push the boundaries of nonfiction storytelling.” Its impressive slate includes American Factory , winner of the 2020 Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature, and the Oscar-nominated features Soundtrack to a Coup d’État , Ascension , Strong Island , and Hale County This Morning, This Evening ; and the Oscar-nominated shorts A Night at the Garden , In the Absence , and Do Not Split . You can watch When It Started to Burn here . articles.title: ‘Hangover’ Architects Jon Lucas & Scott Moore On Keeping Comedy In Theaters With ‘Spa Weekend’ – Crew Call Podcast

Pure original comedies. Why did studios give up? Why did the genre jetison to streaming? Did Lucas and Moore’s original screenplay for The Hangover set the bar so high back in 2009 (near $470M global gross in what became a trilogy) that all subsequent comedies would fall short? The duo also got another comedy franchise off the ground back in 2016 and 2017, Bad Moms, and we talk with them about the current state of that feature series. articles.title: ‘Not Suitable For Work’ Canceled By Hulu After One Season
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Disney Offering Voluntary Early Retirement Packages To Executives Kit Harington Joins ‘Harry Potter’ Season 2 As Gilderoy Lockhart In Recasting, Reprising Voice Role Michael Wright Dies: ‘The Five Heartbeats’ Star Was 70 View All August 24, 2026 7:21pm 'Not Suitable For Work' Hulu Hulu has opted not to renew Mindy Kaling ‘s Not Suitable For Work for a second season. The news comes two months after the 20somethings romantic comedy ended its Season 1 run on the Disney streamer. It is the latest casualty in the YA arena at Hulu, which also recently passed on its pilots Buffy: New Sunnydale , Foster Dade and Don’t Get High. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals 2026 TV Cancellations Photo Gallery: Series Ending This Year & Beyond Cancellations and Renewals 2026 TV Series Renewals Photo Gallery Not Suitable For Work ‘s cancellation leaves multiple storylines up in the air for the professionally driven — and romantically entangled — quintet at the center of it, AJ (Ella Hunt), Josh (Jack Martin), Abby (Avantika), Kel (Nicholas Duvernay) and Davis (Will Angus), as the two-episode finale ended on a big cliffhanger and a couple of smaller ones . By the end of the closer, all five characters found themselves in love triangles, (AJ, Josh & Davis), (Abby, Kel & Kel’s theater colleague), with Davis and AJ’s employment also in limbo after they stood up to their arrogant boss Bill (Jay Ellis). The Warner Bros. TV-produced ensemble comedy, whose original title Murray Hill was changed by Hulu, was not a breakout but had done respectable business attracting viewers and creating buzz, leaving series creator/executive producer Kaling hopeful about a renewal when Deadline spoke with her at the time of the finale. Watch on Deadline “Our writers room has been up for Season 2, which is wonderful,” she revealed in June . “Of course, the big question is whether we’ll get an official pickup for production, I keep my fingers crossed. I love the show so much, I’m so glad that it’s doing well. One of the things that has made me so happy is how much the cast loves the show, and the writing staff loves the show, and the way that the cast expresses their love through all the social content that they’ve been doing.” The cancellation of Not Suitable for Work raises questions about the viability of series that bet on largely unknown young actors and do not follow the conventional YA romantic tropes. It may discourage streamers from taking a shot at such shows that are not as easy to market and may develop devoted following that is deemed not big enough. While it drew mixed reactions from critics with 54% on Rotten Tomatoes, the comedy was another crowd pleaser from Kaling scoring 82% with viewers on the platform. Not Suitable For Work completed Kaling’s trilogy loosely based on her life, which started with Never Have I Ever , which chronicles the teen experience, continued through college with The Sex Lives Of College Girl s, and ended with post-college life in New York on NSFW . The main cast of Season 1 included Hunt, Avantika, Angus, Martin, Duvernay and Ellis. Kaling executive produced with Charlie Grandy, Howard Klein and Greg Mottola. The news of the series’ cancellation was first reported by Variety. articles.title: Taylor Swift On Writing “I Knew You Were Trouble” As A “Really Sad Ballad” & Why She Wants To Honor Her Country Roots The “Further Along This Path I Get”

In a new interview with Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. as part of the Icon Sessions , Swift opened up that she originally wrote “I Knew You Were Trouble” as a “really sad piano ballad.” “It can either be compelling to make a song sound exactly how it feels or to flip it, which the people that really taught me the most about that are Max Martin and Shellback,” Swift said. Related Stories News Taylor Swift Goes Inside Capturing 'The Eras Tour: The Final Show' With Director Glenn Weiss On Emmy Campaign Trail News Taylor Swift To Be Inducted Into Nashville Songwriters Hall Of Fame She continued, “I was really excited to bring it in, and I played them this really, really sad ballad, and I was like I think just no drums and they’re like, ‘What if it’s dubstep?’ I was like I don’t know, guys. Let’s give it a run. I don’t know.” Watch on Deadline Swift said that it “ended up being the best thing for it, and I think as a collaborator, my favorite people to be in the room with are ‘Yes, and?’ people. So why not try it? If they heard it and they thought dubstep, and I came to them specifically because I didn’t want to be making lateral moves creatively, why wouldn’t we go down that path? Why wouldn’t we? I really think that enthusiasm in the studio, it can really make or break what you end up creating.” During the same conversation, Swift opened up about why she seems to want to honor her country music origins. “I love my country roots more and more the further along this path I get, and I want to honor them more and more,” Swift said. “I feel more tied to them, more loyal to them… The people that shaped who I am as an artist and as a writer, that all happened in Nashville.” Watch Taylor Swift’s full interview in the video below. articles.title: Bitters End International Chief Sayaka Ito Talks Japan’s New Generation, Indie Spirit & Expanding Into Sales
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Bitters End International Chief Sayaka Ito Talks Japan’s New Generation, Indie Spirit & Expanding Into Sales Prime Video To Adapt CJ ENM Reality Format ‘EXchange’ In Brazil As ‘Love Transit’ Lav Diaz’s Venice Title ‘Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors’ Boarded By Heretic For Sales View All August 25, 2026 12:05am All Of A Sudden CineFrance, Bitters End EXCLUSIVE : Amid the resurgence of Japanese cinema on the international festival circuit over the past few years, one resolutely indie banner, Bitters End , has been quietly growing its profile across production, distribution and international sales. Founded three decades ago by producer-distributor Yuji Sadai, the company is more of a highly-regarded veteran than a snappy startup, but has managed to stay at the forefront of bringing international arthouse cinema to Japanese audiences – as well as taking new and established Japanese filmmakers to the world. Related Stories News Cannes Heats Up As Ryusuke Hamaguchi's 'All Of A Sudden' Gets 11-Minute Standing Ovation Festivals 'All Of A Sudden' Review: Oscar Winner Ryusuke Hamaguchi's Humane 3-Hour-Plus Exploration Of French Health Care Too Often Feels Like A Lecture - Cannes Film Festival The company had two films in Cannes official selection this year – Ryusuke Hamaguchi ’s competition title All Of A Sudden , which it co-produced and split sales duties with Cinefrance Studios, and Yukiko Sode’s Un Certain Regard title All The Lovers In The Night , which it both produced and sold. All Of A Sudden , which was Hamaguchi’s first film made in France, extends a long association between Bitters End and the filmmaker stretching back to his early Cannes title Asako I & II, and his Best International Feature Oscar winner Drive My Car . Watch on Deadline In addition, as the company expands its international sales activities under Head of International Business, Sayaka Ito, it has also picked up In My Father’s Room , the directing debut of celebrated writer Maha Harada, which has been selected for main competition at the upcoming San Sebastian International Film Festival. In My Father’s Room Speaking to Deadline on Zoom from Tokyo, Ito describes the expansion into sales as a “natural and organic move” for the company, “as we were already involved in the life cycle of a film, from production and financing to domestic distribution and marketing.” She adds that there’s also a solid business motivation behind the move as Japan’s arthouse market has “become increasingly challenging, making it more difficult to recoup production costs through the domestic market alone”. Of course, this is an experience shared by many Japanese specialist producers and distributors. Japan may be one of the few international territories to recover to pre-pandemic box office levels, but most of the spoils are going to local anime and franchise content, while the country’s storied arthouse cinema circuit, once the envy of the region, continues to contract. But at the same time, Japan is in the fortunate position of having a lot more to offer the international arthouse circuit these days. “We’ve seen a new generation of highly talented Japanese filmmakers emerging over the past few years, and we believe it’s important to ensure that their work reaches international audiences,” Ito says. Japan’s new generation has been one of the sensations of the festival circuit since it booted up again in real life following the pandemic. After years in which just a handful of established names – Hirokazu Kore-eda, Naomi Kawase, Takeshi Kitano and Kiyoshi Kurosawa – were appearing at major festivals, a host of new filmmakers have recently broken through. Cannes selected seven new Japanese films for last year’s edition, and around the same number this year, while other major festivals including Berlin, Locarno, Venice, Toronto and San Sebastian are also paying attention to Japanese cinema, with directors including Hamaguchi, Koji Fukada and Sho Miyake leading the charge. Sayaka Ito, Head of International Business, Bitters End Bitters End has been involved in many of these titles in different capacities – producing or taking part in the production committee behind the film; handling international sales for films it has produced, as well as third-party pick-ups; and also distributing films in Japan. In some cases, it handles Japanese distribution for films produced by other companies, with recent examples including Wim Wenders’ Perfect Days , Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Wife Of A Spy and Neo Sora’s Happyend . Increasingly, the company takes on all three roles, as was the case with All The Lovers In The Nigh t and the three films it had playing in San Sebastian in 2025 – Miyake’s Two Seasons, Two Stranger s, which won Locarno’s Golden Leopard before playing in San Sebastian’s Zabaltegi-Tabakalera section; serial killer fable Sai: Disaster, co-directed by Yutaro Seki and Kentaro Hirase, which premiered in main competition; and Yukari Sakamoto’s White Flowers And Fruits in New Directors. Ito explains the company is not completely new to international sales – as it has handled a few titles it also produced over the years, including Shinji Aoyama’s Helpless and Nobuhiro Yamashita’s cult classic rock film Linda Linda Linda – but expanded this activity when she rejoined the company after a brief hiatus with streamer U-Next in 2023. While acknowledging that it’s a tough time for the international arthouse market, Ito says the company has managed to leverage the relationships it has built with distributors, sellers, producers and festivals around the world over the past three decades, as well as to tap into the buzz around the Japanese new wave. “There’s now a growing number of people who are interested in Japanese cinema, so we’re seeing more representation at an international level of both new talent and auteurs. We’re also seeing more companies that don’t usually buy Japanese films reaching out to us, or at least being more open to acquiring Japanese titles. So we think that’s a good sign.” Among recent sales successes, Hamaguchi’s All Of A Sudde n was pretty much sold out worldwide by Cinefrance and Bitters End (which handled Asian territories) before it even played in Cannes. Sode’s All The Lovers In The Night , based on Mieko Kawakami’s novel about first love and false appearances, has so far been sold to 12 territories including Several Futures for the US and Ritual Films for Canada. “We believe Sode is also one of the most important filmmakers working in Japan today. With All The Lovers In The Night , we were able to combine her distinctive artistic voice with recognizable elements such as leading actors Yukino Kishii and Tadanobu Asano, and Kawakami’s novel,” Ito says. All The Lovers In The Night Two Seasons, Two Strangers has been sold to 15 territories, including Several Futures in the US. “Miyake had previously presented films at festivals including Berlin, but we felt that his international profile still did not fully reflect his importance as a filmmaker,” Ito says. “The Locarno win allowed his name and work to reach a much broader global audience.” Staying Indie In A Corporate World What’s also unusual about Bitters End is that the company has managed to retain its independent status over three decades, without accepting any major outside finance – no small feat in a market where smaller companies tend to get swallowed up by studios or slowly fade away. Sadai, who prefers to keep a low profile and let the films do the talking, founded the company in 1994 after working in curation and distribution, naming it after the 1972 Roxy Music song (with the name also encapsulating the spirit of striving to the “bitter end”). The company started out distributing international films in Japan – the Dardenne brothers say Sadai was the first buyer to pick up their films – and has since released around 300 titles, working with a ‘who’s who’ of international arthouse cinema, including Jia Zhangke, Bong Joon Ho, Fatih Akin, Nuri Bilge Ceylan, Bela Tarr, Otar Iosseliani, Roy Andersson, Gianfranco Rosi, Mikhael Hers and Alice Rohrwacher. Bong’s Oscar winner Parasite is the company’s biggest ever release, grossing more than $40M in early 2020. Ito says it could have gone even bigger if the pandemic hadn’t hit. The company also works with Universal Pictures on its more specialist titles, including Manchester By The Sea , Anora and Oppenheimer – with the latter film resulting in a relationship with director Christopher Nolan that extended to also releasing The Odyssey this year. Sadai stepped into co-producing and investing in both local and international films back in the ‘90s, at a time when few Japanese companies got involved in international co-production. In addition to working with Japanese filmmakers such as Shinji Aoyama, Nobuhiro Yamashita and Naomi Kawase, he also co-produced the early titles of filmmakers including China’s Jia Zhangke, Iran-born filmmaker Amir Naderi and Kyrgyz director Aktan Arym Kubat. Bitters End was also a co-producer on anthology film Tokyo! , with sections directed by Bong, Leos Carax and Michel Gondry. Ito describes Bitters End’s taste as “director rather than genre-driven” and explains that the company tends to work with the same filmmakers over many years, patiently introducing their body of work to Japanese audiences: “We place great importance on a filmmaker’s individual voice and consider artistic quality, social and cultural significance, and the commercial potential all at the same time. “We rarely select films because a particular genre or trend is currently popular. We don’t specialize in genre cinema, although we’re open to genre films when they have a strong and distinctive directorial vision. Many of the films we handle are human dramas. They may address social or political subjects, but they tend not to present their messages in an overly explicit or didactic way.” Those choices can be seen in the company’s current and upcoming release slate in Japan, which in addition to The Odyssey , All Of A Sudden and All The Lovers In The Night , also includes Fatih Akin’s Amrum , Gianfranco Rosi’s Below The Clouds and The World Of Love from Korean filmmaker Yoon Ga-eun. The company is also leaning into classics with current releases including 4K restorations of Ryusuke Hashiguchi’s All Around Us and Hush! Meanwhile, on the sales front, Ito is getting ready to launch In My Father’s Room at San Sebastian, a festival that has become an important launchpad for the company’s productions and acquisitions. Based on Harada’s short story An Unnecessary Man , the film revolves around a young woman working in a museum who is handed a key to a room she wasn’t aware of following her father’s death. While retracing the steps of a man mostly written off by society, she discovers his deep appreciation of art, antiques, poetry and Japanese tea ceremony. Yu Aoi ( Wife Of A Spy ), Issey Ogata ( Silence ), Eita Nagayama ( Monster ) and Eri Watanabe ( Shall We Dance? ) head the cast. “The film has strong authentic Japanese elements, but also features the paintings of Mark Rothko, so it combines Western and Japanese culture in a way that resonates visually and spiritually,” Ito says. “We feel it’s a perfect fit for European festival audiences.” Without giving too much away, Ito also shares that the company’s upcoming slate includes a film from an acclaimed French director shooting in Japan, as well as some features based on original stories from debut Japanese filmmakers. “We also have an international co-production project with Asian partners currently in development. We hope to support both established directors taking on new challenges, as well as talented emerging filmmakers,” Ito says. articles.title: ‘Strictly Come Dancing’ Star Giovanni Pernice Felt Suicidal After Being Dropped By BBC Over Amanda Abbington Complaint: “They Hung Me Out To Dry”
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Netflix Renews ‘House Of Guinness,’ ‘Being Gordon Ramsay’ & ‘Legends’ Billie Piper Says ‘Doctor Who’ Fans Need To “Chill Out” After Sci-Fi Show’s “Rough Time” Jo Gardiner Dies: ‘Race Across The World’ Star Passes A Year After Son’s Death View All August 25, 2026 12:57am Giovanni Pernice BBC Professional dancer Giovanni Pernice has vented his fury at the BBC over its handling of his Strictly Come Dancing exit following a clash with Sherlock star Amanda Abbington . In an interview with The Daily Telegraph , Pernice said he was left feeling suicidal after being “hung out to dry” by the BBC, arguing that the broadcaster’s duty of care did not extend to him. Pernice has not appeared on Strictly (the format on which Dancing with the Stars is based) since 2023, when he clashed with dance partner Abbington, who later filed a complaint. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News BBC Files New Motion To Dismiss Donald Trump's $10 Billion Lawsuit, Challenges Claims Of U.S. Viewership Via VPN News Billie Piper Says 'Doctor Who' Fans Need To "Chill Out" After Sci-Fi Show's "Rough Time" Abbington alleged that her Italian dance partner was “nasty” and accused him of inappropriate, bullying behavior during her five weeks on Strictly . The BBC’s subsequent investigation partially upheld some of her concerns , though the corporation was never specific about the nature of the allegations it deemed credible. The BBC apologized to Abbington for her experience on Strictly , which remains one of the UK’s most-watched shows. “I feel they hung me out to dry to cover their backs. I was devastated by that,” Pernice said in an excerpt from his memoir, Gio: Taking the Lead , published by The Telegraph . He added that Abbington’s apology “made it seem like all of the stories in the newspaper[s] were real, when most of them had been found to be totally untrue. Her claims had ruined my life and my career. Where was my apology?” The Italian told The Telegraph : “I had made concerted efforts to be positive and supportive to Amanda, in both the training room and our text conversations.” He claimed that most of the upheld complaints related to him swearing: “They found that I threw my arms up and said ‘f***’ on one occasion.” Pernice said he should never have been paired with Abbington. “I’m a taskmaster,” he said. “But I know that I can take you to the final, and that I can take you to win the show – if you want to be pushed.” Pernice found himself “spiralling mentally” following the controversy. “I’m a very work-oriented person,” he said. “I really dedicate my life to work. It wasn’t even the financial [side]. It’s more, I have to do something. I always wanted to be something. “I was thinking, ‘There’s no place for me any more in this industry. So what’s the point?’ That’s when I thought, ‘Well, let’s end this. There’s no point. Let’s end it. I’m never going to have back what I had.’” On the BBC’s repsonse, he added: “They didn’t look after me. ‘Well, you’re not contracted with us, your contract finished in December.’ Yeah, but I’ve been with you for nine years, so you can look after me. If I’m sending an email saying that I’ve got myocarditis and depression, you can’t even reply to me and say, ‘Oh, sorry if you feel a bit down’?” The BBC has been approached for comment. articles.title: Hannah Einbinder Supports Mark Ruffalo & Describes Antisemitism Accusations As “Ludicrous”
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac René Malo Dies: Veteran Québécois Filmmaker & ‘The Decline Of The American Empire’ Producer Was 84 Woody Allen To Start Shooting Next Project In Spain In October San Sebastián Adds David Ayer’s ‘Heart Of The Beast’ Starring Brad Pitt To Lineup View All August 25, 2026 1:17am Hannah Einbinder attends the 32nd Actor Awards Presented by SAG-AFTRA on March 1, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Gilbert Flores/PMC Hannah Einbinder shared a lengthy Instagram story post on Monday evening supporting Mark Ruffalo after he was accused of being antisemitic by a Paramount spokesperson for highlighting the Ellison family’s connection to the Israeli state and its military apparatus. “I’m so grateful that Mark Ruffalo drew a connection between the Ellisons providing military technology to Israel during a genocide and their unprecedented media takeover–and pointed out that this is a dangerous consolidation of power that could ultimately be used against us,” Einbinder posted. Related Stories News Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo For "Antisemitism" & "Demonization" News Mark Ruffalo Blasts Paramount For Calling Him "Antisemitic" Over Merger Criticism: "Appalling And Fundamentally Dishonest" “The idea that he only said these things because the Ellisons are Jewish is LUDICROUS. Is it also antisemitic to point out that Safra Catz, the Oracle executive vice chair who boasted about the ‘profoundly scary technology’ provided to the IDF, also sits on Paramount’s board? Or that Larry Ellison has been buying favor with Trump by donating tens of millions to his political efforts for years? Or that he once offered Netanyahu a lucrative Oracle post?” Einbinder continued to write that Ruffalo’s comments are, in fact, criticisms of “right-wing technofeudalist oligarchs who are in the process of carrying out the largest media acquisition in history.” Watch on Deadline Einbinder ended her post by noting that opposition to the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger is also about “fighting for the working class of Hollywood: the crews and other workers that we artists claim to care so much about, who could lose thousands of jobs if it goes through.” She added: “All of us artists could stand to be more like Mark, willing to speak out for oppressed people everywhere.” Ruffalo has also dismissed Paramount’s antisemitism accusations with a lengthy X post. “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest,” he began on X . “Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people.” He continued: “To be clear, my views come from my own political convictions and should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect.” Ruffalo had initially shared a video online that showed Oracle executive vice chair Safra Catz discussing how the company had made some “really profoundly scary technology” available to the Israeli military during its violent onslaught in Gaza. “This is the company that Larry Ellison is using to fund his son David’s Warner Bros acquisition,” Ruffalo wrote with the clip on his Instagram Story. articles.title: John Gore Studios CEO Hilary Strong Steps Down
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Lux Angeles Studios Assembles Exec Team To Lead On Indie Pics Up To $20M Fremantle Global Formats Boss Vasha Wallace Exiting ‘Got Talent’ Firm After Two Decades Sky Arts Slates ‘The Handel Scandal’ & ‘Dangerous Debussy’ Docs View All August 25, 2026 1:42am John Gore andHilary Strong John Gore c/o John Gore Organization / John Gore Studios - photo by Sean Gleason Hilary Strong is stepping down from her CEO post at John Gore Studios. This comes as theater and screen producer John Gore moves to bring the UK company and its U.S. sister, The John Gore Organization , together under a single holding company. Gore himself will now lead both operations. Gore, who has won more 25 Tony Awards, is framing the restructure as allowing for both companies to better coordinate their respective film, TV and theatrical businesses under on strategic vision. As we revealed back in January 2025, Gore fulfilled a long-held ambition to launch a British studio, with veteran TV producer Hilary Strong taking on the CEO post to oversee a slate that included Joan Collins-starring Wallis Sampson biopic. Related Stories Documentary 'Hunt: We Need To Talk About James': Feature Doc On Legendary Late Formula 1 Driver Goes Into Production Festivals Breaking Baz: From Stage To Screen, Broadway's John Gore Discusses His Royal Film With Joan Collins & Why He Sat On Sean Connery's Sofa With Ted Sarandos - Cannes Market “Hilary and the team took the business from zero to seven feature films in 18 months, which must be a record – all the while burnishing the legacy of Hammer Films and expanding into new technologies and complementary businesses to pave a path for the future,” said Gore. “I am extremely grateful to Hilary for the significant role she has played in the launch of John Gore Studios and excited about this next chapter.” Watch on Deadline Strong was exec producer on each of John Gore Studios’ first six pictures. She is know as the founder and CEO of International Literary Properties, where she managed the estates of several authors, and as Chief Exec for The Anthology Group and Agatha Christie Limited, as well as Managing Director of Acorn Productions. Further back, she worked at Chorion and Hat Trick Productions. No word on her next move, but she exits as a “friend and supporter of John Gore Studios as she explores exciting new opportunities,” according to the company. “I have adored my time working with John and the wonderful team we have put together to create John Gore Studios, and I will always be grateful to John for the opportunity, but we have both agreed that, with the reshaping of the global business, my work here is done. I wish the team every success for the future.” Gore’s credits include Oklahoma! , Dear Evan Hansen and Hello, Dolly! , and he owns the likes of Broadway Across America, Broadway.com and The Broadway Channel through The John Gore Organization. In the UK, John Gore Studios has acquired the likes of AI production specialist Deep Fusion, Hilary Bevan Jones’ Hilltop Screen and Angel Costumes. articles.title: Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo’s Paramount Remarks: “Obsession and Demonization”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 23, 2026 9:44am Mark Ruffalo and Paramount. Amy Sussman/Getty Images; Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center , is defending Paramount after the studio called Mark Ruffalo’s anti-merger comments “antisemitic.” “Words matter, and so does the willingness to draw a line when legitimate debate gives way to antisemitic tropes,” Berk wrote. “We commend Paramount for speaking clearly and refusing to allow prejudice to masquerade as political or corporate criticism. At a time when antisemitism is too often minimized, rationalized or repackaged in more socially acceptable language, this kind of moral clarity matters.” “Invoking Israel in an issue where it is completely irrelevant is a textbook case of obsession and demonization. Paramount was right to call it out. More leaders and institutions should have the courage to call antisemitism what it is, regardless of who is spreading it,” his statement concluded. Earlier this week, the Oscar-nominated actor, who has been an outspoken opponent of Paramount’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros., highlighted Larry Ellison’s (Paramount CEO David Ellison’s father) Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military amid the Israel-Gaza war. Ruffalo resurfaced a clip from 2024 of former Oracle chief Safra Catz talking about “profoundly scary technologies” the tech company had built in relation to Israel’s war effort in Gaza. The actor also described the war as a “genocide” that “was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” In response, Paramount clapped back , calling the Marvel star’s remarks “antisemitic.” The studio’s spokesperson’s statement read in part, “We are, as always, troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute. Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.” Creative Community for Peace, a Hollywood-based pro-Israel advocacy organization, has also called for Hollywood to boycott Ruffalo until the actor “retract[s] these remarks and apologize[s],” the group’s executive director, Ari Ingel, wrote in a statement. “ Mark Ruffalo ’s rhetoric has increasingly crossed the line from criticism of Israel into extremist and antisemitic messaging,” Ingel also wrote, adding, “Point blank, he has been warned before about the consequences of this rhetoric, yet continues contributing to the toxic antisemitic atmosphere we are witnessing today. That makes him culpable. His argument increasingly fuses hostility toward Israel and Zionism with Jewish-associated wealth, media ownership, oligarchic power and ominous warnings about concentrated control into a single narrative. Those echoes are impossible to ignore.” On Saturday, Ruffalo took to X to dismiss Paramount’s claims that his comments were “antisemitic” as well as offer a distinction between his criticism of the Israeli military and his views about Jewish people. He wrote in part, “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest. Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people. This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel.” THR

articles.title: ‘Tucci in Italy’ Cinematographer Matt Ball on Making Italy Look Delicious
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Matthew Jacobs Plus Icon Matthew Jacobs thrnews@thr.com View All August 23, 2026 11:00am Says director of photography Matt Ball: “The work of making Tucci in Italy look beautiful has been done for me already.” National Geographic/Matt Holyoak (3) Tucci in Italy is swarming with handsome images: a mouthwatering dollop of spaghetti and clams inspired by a Neapolitan chef’s 94-year-old mother, majestic Renaissance-era palaces and quaint villages where the show’s host, Stanley Tucci , enlists locals to expound on Italian culture. But director of photography Matt Ball isn’t always looking for polish — he wants candor. “It’s not necessarily a show about how beautiful everything looks,” Ball says. “The primary goal is to get authenticity. And then we shoot around it and try to make it look as nice as we can.” Related Stories Hollywood Flashback Before 'The Pitt,' There Was 'St. Elsewhere' 'Awards Chatter' Podcast Emmy Nominee Patrick Ball on His Rollercoaster Journey to 'The Pitt' and How His Own Addiction Battle Has Informed His Performance Ball’s cinematography led to one of the three Emmy nominations that Tucci in Italy received this year, alongside a sound mixing citation and outstanding hosted nonfiction series or special. He met Tucci as a camera operator on Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy , which ran for two seasons on CNN. When National Geographic picked up the retitled version, Ball was brought on as DP. They’re currently in production on another spinoff, this time set in Great Britain. Before shooting, Tucci, producer Lottie Birmingham and their research team map out a roughly seven- to 10-day stint in each city being featured that season. They find cooks, farmers, food producers and culinary experts to show off the region’s cuisine and landscapes. Ball, who collaborated with two camera operators and two assistants on Tucci in Italy , then designed shots as unobtrusive as possible so the contributors could feel comfortable. “The work of making it look beautiful has been done for me already,” Ball says, downplaying his aptitude for capturing the vistas of Sicily, Tuscany or Sardinia so elegantly. If Searching for Italy prioritized major destinations such as Rome and Milan , Tucci in Italy sought out less touristy locales, like Ball’s personal favorite stop, Le Marche. There, at the seaside restaurant Da Emilia, Tucci tried a spaghetti and mussels dish the chef’s eponymous grandmother had taught her to make years earlier. The Devil Wears Prada actor dined with the chef at a long outdoor table overlooking the Adriatic Sea — an example of the charisma that Ball encountered everywhere he went. “It looked fantastic,” he says. “The light was coming off the water, and it was a beautiful day. It was really lovely.” Ball, for his part, gets to sample many of the dishes, too. Some of that intake depends on how much offal, for example, he’s willing to eat. Ball’s food-oriented résumé is accidental, though. It started with a gig as a camera operator on the long-running Barefoot Contessa , where he met his wife. He’s since shot Be My Guest With Ina Garten as well as shows with celebrity chefs Jamie Oliver and Lorraine Pascale. He says he’ll stay on with Tucci as long as Tucci wants to continue his savory travels. “Everywhere we go,” he says, “you’ll always hear somebody whisper, ‘That’s Stanley Tucci!’ ” This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.
