articles.title: There Are Scores of Great New Animated Shows. The Emmys Won’t Nominate Them.
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All August 23, 2026 11:30am From left: Long-running shows like The Simpsons, South Park and Bob’s Burgers dominate the Emmys’ animated category. Illustrated by Brian Taylor One of the great creative innovations America has given the world in the past 30 years is TV animation. That sounds like hyperbole, but it’s true. The Simpsons changed how we look at the American family (and current events). Rick and Morty changed how we looked at comedy and the tragedy behind it. (“Wubba lubba dub dub.” Also, current events.) South Park changed how we looked at each other (and current events). The problem is that those shows all started doing that a very long time ago. Rick and Morty is nine seasons in. South Park is 28. The Simpsons is 37 damn seasons deep. There are children who weren’t born when the series debuted who now have children who themselves are old enough to think Bart has got this whole life thing figured out. Related Stories Hollywood Flashback Before 'The Pitt,' There Was 'St. Elsewhere' 'Awards Chatter' Podcast Emmy Nominee Patrick Ball on His Rollercoaster Journey to 'The Pitt' and How His Own Addiction Battle Has Informed His Performance All three of those shows are nominated for outstanding animated program this year. So is Bob’s Burgers , which just completed its 20th season. Now, a charitable view would hold that such shortlisting reflects the durability of these shows — how they manage to maintain their creative spark through so many changing winds. There is something to that — it’s not easy to do anything well for three decades, let alone maintain character freshness. But I fear the fact that animated characters don’t age — and that they’re basically money-minting machines for a few networks (especially Fox) — has led us to a pretty calcified place. No show should so regularly take a place on the Emmys stage. The Simpsons and Bob’s Burgers have been nominated every year since the Obama days. Nothing is that good for that long. What isn’t on the animated shortlist this year? Dark sci-fi like Owen Dennis’ Among Us on Paramount+. The acquired taste but still bold stylings of Raphael Bob-Waksberg’s time-jumping family series Long Story Short on Netflix. Joe Cappa’s Adult Swim single-dad delight Haha, You Clowns . These are all newish shows from the past year or two with great energy and original takes. But to look at the Emmys noms is to not even know they exist (and indeed, many viewers won’t without the exposure). A little breath of fresh air in the category comes via Smiling Friends , Adult Swim’s truly wacky take on a nonprofit and what it means to do good/be happy. And while I would hardly call anything in the George Lucas-verse fresh in 2026, Star Wars: Visions at least uses varied artists and styles in a way that feels original. But these shows seem token-y amid the Simpsons and South Park oak trees and probably won’t win anyway. What can the Emmys do to fix this? Fortunately, there are a few things. For starters, stop with just nominating a single episode. Unlike TV Academy convention elsewhere, the Emmys don’t award a show — they award an episode. That means that the kind of newer, zanier material that takes months to really settle into is completely disadvantaged — you’re not going to appreciate something weird and new if you just try to watch one episode. You’re just going to go back to something you know and like, such as The Simpsons or South Park . Of course, the irony is that The Simpsons and South Park were themselves once oddball and required a multi-episode commitment to appreciate. But now that they are appreciated, voters just keep rubber-stamping them. I mean, Rick and Morty hasn’t really been good in several years. But voters just keep checking the box without thinking there might be a new Rick and Morty waiting out there. The other irony is that many of the characters on these very shows would hate this kind of lazy legacy thinking and would balk at it. A category that is literally designed to celebrate subversiveness champions the sclerotic. Another fix: Stop with the international ghettoizing. My colleague David Canfield just covered this on the live-action side, but it applies on the animated side, too. Bluey is one of the best shows on television these past 10 years. And many people in America watch it. Find a way to make it eligible for the primetime Emmy. While we’re on the topic of Bluey , get rid of the “Eligibility in animation is for programming that targets an audience age 13 and above” rule. This is just not how people watch television anymore. And finally, open up the Phase II voting beyond just the animation branch to the whole TV Academy. Animation is one of two realms that has this limitation. And it’s having a bad effect. People in the animation branch work in the field, which means they tend to vote for the shows of folks they know or have worked with. So we get the 30-year veterans. I get why this exclusionary voting rule was first drafted: Animation is a specialized craft, and specialists should vote on their specialty. Also, there is a fear that the, ahem, unwashed masses who don’t work in animation won’t really know the shows because they’re too busy watching the live-action stuff. But if that was ever true, it’s not anymore. Everyone watches everything. All of these might seem like big changes, hard to implement, but they’re really not. They’re possible and would make a world of difference. And if you doubt it, there’s a group you can ask that will help. A group that looked at the world as it is and said, “Maybe there’s another, more daring way to view it.” They are, of course, called animators. This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. To receive the magazine,

articles.title: Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert Call for Protection of Child Actors After Hayden Panettiere’s Death: “Where Is the Collective Outrage?”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 23, 2026 12:55pm Hayden Panettiere Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Anna Paquin , Christy Carlson Romano and Melissa Gilbert are calling on Hollywood to protect child actors following the deaths of Hayden Panettiere , Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase . Panettiere’s death at age 36 last Sunday prompted the three actresses, who were child stars themselves, to take their concerns public. Trachtenberg died at 39 in February 2025, while Chase died in July at age 35. “It’s not a coincidence that so many former, specifically pre-sexualized female, child ‘stars’ have profoundly sad lives and untimely ends. We were not as protected by the ‘systems’ that look great on paper, as we are supposed to be,” Paquin wrote on Instagram Friday. She rose to fame at 11 years old with her film debut in 1993’s The Piano , which earned her an Oscar for best supporting actress. Related Stories Movies Busan Film Festival Sets 23 Titles for Vision Korea, Vision Asia Sections General News Hayden Panettiere's Mom Blasts Gayle King and Megyn Kelly's Criticisms of Her in Wake of Daughter's Death “RIP HP, MT, DC and too many others. It’s a strange small club we belong to and you are worthy of support no matter how our industry makes us feel,” Paquin continued. “Literally DM me. I believe you and I will stand by your side. You aren’t alone. Let’s have each other’s backs. It might make public disclosure less terrifying.” The True Blood alum added in a separate post , “One more thing– As an adult I’ve had the pleasure of working on productions where the welfare and mental health of young performers was handled incredibly carefully. Especially around material that was intense. It is possible to holistically look after the kids on set and tell complex and sometimes upsetting stories. It just has to be the top priority of the production.” Earlier in the week, Elle published an essay by Romano — who appeared in 1996’s Everyone Says I Love You as a child before becoming a teen Disney star with her role in Even Stevens and voicing Kim Possible — where she compared child stardom to the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). “The former child actor exists in a category the world does not know how to hold. We are children when the public wants to feel protective of us, professionals when the industry wants to profit from us, and spoiled celebrities when we eventually show symptoms of having been both,” Romano wrote in part. “Early fame is like CTE. Not as a diagnosis. As a way of thinking about repeated impact. We now have language for youth sports: protocols, helmets, parents worried about concussions. But we have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood. She added, “Young performers are still treated as exceptions. Lucky exceptions. Cute exceptions. Talented exceptions. Exceptions whose labor powers one of the most profitable storytelling machines in the world, while their mental needs are treated as inconvenient or irrelevant. Social work be damned.” Gilbert also shared a lengthy post on Substack Saturday, where she asked, “Why are these three sweet, wildly talented, vibrant, vital young women gone?” Gilbert landed her breakout role at just nine years old, playing Laura Ingalls Wilder on Little House on the Prairie from 1974 to 1983. “I did not know Hayden personally and only worked briefly with Mishy and Daveigh. It feels personal because I was them,” Gilbert wrote. “We are all members of the same tribe; Female Former Child Performers, and when one of us dies, it runs through all of us like an electrical current. When three of us die so close together, something is very, very wrong. We all know the stories of how the entertainment industry uses, abuses, exploits and then throws away it’s youngest, but for some reason, this trend is getting worse.” She later added, “Where is our Union in all of this? Where is the collective outrage? Where are the regulations? Where is the protection of privacy?” “It really seems like no one cares enough to enact real change. At least, not until the next death and everyone talks about how sad they are and how we must do something and then they forget and get on with their lives until it happens again and again and again,” Gilbert continued. “Yes, addiction is a real disease. Family dysfunction is real. PTSD is real. In actors, all those things are assets. They enable us to access emotion and share it with an audience. But when it comes through children, it should be treated tenderly, protectively, respectfully and in a way that is as limited as possible.” Gilbert’s post comes as her husband, Timothy Busfield, awaits trial in Albuquerque, New Mexico, after being accused of child sex abuse on the set of the former Fox/Warner Bros. Television series The Cleaning Lady . Gilbert has defended Busfield , who has denied the allegations. Panettiere started working in Hollywood at a young age, appearing in the soap opera One Life to Live at just four years old before starring in 2000’s Remember the Titans at 10, among other projects. As for Trachtenberg, she appeared in the Nickelodeon series The Adventures of Pete & Pete as a child, as well as 1996’s Harriet the Spy and 1999’s Inspector Gadget . Chase was known for voicing Lilo in 2002’s Lilo & Stitch when she was younger as well as starring in the 2002 horror film The Ring . THR

articles.title: Shelley Fabares, Star of ‘The Donna Reed Show’ and ‘Coach,’ Dies at 82
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Cheryl Cheng , Duane Byrge August 23, 2026 1:27pm Shelley Fabares Michael Buckner/Getty Images Shelley Fabares, the wholesome daughter on The Donna Reed Show who went on to star opposite Elvis Presley in three movies and as Craig T. Nelson’s independent wife on Coach , has died. She was 82. Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles after a brief illness, her family announced. Survivors include her husband, M*A*S*H actor Mike Farrell, whom she married in 1984. “To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter and comfort,” they said in a statement. “She was a devoted wife, cherished stepmother, daughter, sister, niece, aunt, family member and loyal friend whose warmth, generosity, humor and grace made an enduring difference in the lives of everyone who knew her. She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued and cared for.” Related Stories Movies Nick Glennie-Smith, Composer on 'The Rock,' 'The Man in the Iron Mask' and 'Secretariat,' Dies at 74 Movies Leslie Parrish, Actress in 'Li'l Abner' and 'The Manchurian Candidate,' Dies at 90 On the original One Day at a Time , Fabares played against her prim, good-girl persona as Francine Webster, a nasty business rival of Bonnie Franklin ‘s Ann Romano. (Her late aunt, Caesar’s Hour and The Band Wagon star Nannette Fabray , also appeared on the CBS sitcom, playing the mother of Franklin’s character.) Fabares also portrayed the wife of doomed Chicago Bears running back Brian Piccolo ( James Caan ) on the landmark 1971 ABC telefilm Brian’s Song . On The Donna Reed Show , which aired on ABC for eight seasons, from September 1958 through March 1966, Fabares played high schooler Mary Stone opposite Reed as her mom, homemaker Donna Stone; Carl Betz as her pediatrician dad, Dr. Alex Stone; and Paul Petersen as her younger brother, Jeff. When Mary left for college at the start of the sixth season, the Stones adopted a daughter, Trisha (Patty Petersen, real-life sister of Paul). Capitalizing on her national fame, Fabares — backed by Darlene Love and the Blossoms and Glen Campbell on guitar — recorded a version of “Johnny Angel,” which went to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in April 1962. She had debuted the song on a Donna Reed episode a couple months earlier. “I literally cannot sing. So there’s a lot of overdubbing,” she admitted in a 1983 interview. “The girls in the back — ‘Could you sing a little louder please?’ It was unusual. But [ The Donna Reed Show ] was very successful at that time, so [the song] had a built-in audience.” During “live” performances — in “the days when they would play the record and you would lip sync” — she recalled, “my worst experience was [when] I did a live local television show and, needless to say, the record stuck. I think I went into a coma.” Fabares starred on the ABC comedy Coach for eight seasons while earning a pair of Emmy nominations for playing Christine Armstrong, a TV newscaster and the girlfriend and then wife of Nelson’s college football coach, Hayden Fox. “Clearly, Christine is a very successful woman and firmly entrenched in her career and loves her work. And she loves this man,” she said . “It’s a difficult problem in life to find your balance. We’re all going through the same things. I have a wonderful relationship with my husband, but I’m still a career woman.” In 2015, NBC developed a Coach revival in which Nelson’s character returns to coaching and Fabares’ character is killed off, but the reboot did not emerge beyond the pilot stage. Michele Ann Marie Fabares was born in Santa Monica on Jan. 19, 1944. Her mother, Elsa, got her into modeling at age 3, and that led to TV appearances. By the time she was 9, Frank Sinatra was singing “Young at Heart” to her on an NBC special. She also appeared on a 1955 NBC adaptation of Our Town that starred Sinatra, Paul Newman and Eva Marie Saint and with Rock Hudson in Never Say Goodbye (1956). In 1958, she was on the ABC series Annette , which starred lifelong friend Annette Funicello . Fabares said Reed “was not given credit for being the head of her own series, the guiding force behind the series,” she said in 1994. “She produced the series, had an enormous part in writing it and also had four children at home. Having been there, I knew the amazing strength of that woman.” During a 2011 reunion of the show’s surviving castmembers, Fabares remembered when she was feeling nervous about having to dance during a scene. Reed tried to calm her down. “Shelley, there are three things I can’t do: I can’t swim, I can’t dance, and I can’t act.” But she had to do all three for a film scene. “Oh yeah, that movie I was talking about was It’s a Wonderful Life .” After several years as Mary Stone, Fabares concentrated on the big screen and appeared in the fun-in-the-sun movies Ride the Wild Surf (1964) with Fabian and Hold On! (1966) with Peter Noone of Herman’s Hermits. She then co-starred with Presley in Girl Happy (1965), Spinout (1966) — Betz played her dad in that one too — and Clambake (1967). “The first day of shooting [ Girl Happy ], I’m on the set. Something was happening, and I didn’t know what it was,” she said . “And I looked over, and it was Elvis. He was walking in. He wasn’t doing anything. He was just walking in. The presence that this man had … you couldn’t talk. Nobody did anything. You just sort of stopped. And I remember thinking, ‘Oh, my God. It’s Elvis Presley. I’m never going to be able to open my mouth around him.’ ” In the late 1960s, during a time of protest and rebellion, her good-girl appeal fell out of sync with the cultural zeitgeist. It wasn’t until Brian’s Song that she regained her career momentum. Buoyed by that role, Fabares rebounded to work on such popular series as The Brian Keith Show , The Practice with Danny Thomas and Highcliffe Manor . In the late ’70s and early ’80s, she starred on One Day at a Time , then showed a saucier dimension as the tart-tongued Eleanor Major on the syndicated soap opera spoof Forever Fernwood . Fabares also had guest-starring roles on Mannix ; Love, American Style ; Daniel Boone ; McCloud ; Mork & Mindy ; and Hello, Larry (as McLean Stevenson’s ex-wife). She had a liver transplant in October 2000 after spending nearly two years on the waiting list to receive one. In 1984, she married Farrell at Aunt Nanette’s Pacific Palisades home. The two had first met in 1970 when she was a guest star on Farrell’s series The Interns , but it was not until they reunited 12 years later during a CBS press tour that they started to date. (Earlier, Fabares had been married to record producer Lou Adler, while Farrell’s first wife was actress Judy Farrell , who played Nurse Abel on M*A*S*H .) Farrell, known to be a serious human rights activist, said his wife made him a bit more light-hearted. “People talk about how much more fun I am,” he said in 1991. “Shelley has allowed people to understand I’m not this unapproachable doomsayer.” Added Fabares: “Nothing in Mike’s life is casual. He’s very serious. Mike grounds me, and I think I pull him out sometimes. It’s a nice mix.” Shelley Fabares and Mike Farrell. Courtesy Fabares/Farrell family Survivors also include her stepchildren, Erin and Michael. THR

articles.title: Hayden Panettiere’s Mom Blasts Gayle King and Megyn Kelly’s Criticisms of Her in Wake of Daughter’s Death
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 23, 2026 2:31pm Hayden Panettiere, Jansen Panettiere and Lesley Vogel in 2019. Amanda Edwards/Getty Images Lesley Vogel, Hayden Panettiere ’s mom, is slamming both Gayle King and Megyn Kelly for their recent criticisms in the wake of her daughter’s death . “I was very, very hurt and deeply disappointed in the lack of professionalism, the lack of compassion in slamming someone who’s lost two children, without even a modicum of consideration,” Vogel said during a recent interview with the Daily Mail regarding the CBS Mornings host and podcaster’s separate comments. “No one reached out to me before,” she added. “It’s shameful. It’s unconscionable to me.” Related Stories Movies Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert Call for Protection of Child Actors After Hayden Panettiere's Death: "Where Is the Collective Outrage?" News Hayden Panettiere's Boyfriend Gave Her Narcan Before Death, Brother Says The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to CBS Mornings for comment, but did not hear back at the time of publication. Panettiere, an actress known for her roles in Heroes , Nashville and the Scream franchise, died last Sunday at age 36. Following her death, Vogel spoke to NBC News on Tuesday, where she criticized her daughter’s on-again-off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson and felt her daughter “lost her way.” “This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death and that was Brian Hickerson,” she said at the time. “I think Hayden was an amazingly talented person in so many departments and I think young people who grow up in the entertainment industry — it is a struggle and it’s a very challenging industry and it’s not unusual for them to sadly find the wrong path.” Vogel added, “I think Hayden sadly lost her way and I wish it were different. I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes.” The following day, during Wednesday’s CBS Mornings broadcast , King criticized Vogel for focusing too much on her daughter’s struggles amid her death. “You know, guys, you read this and all I can think is, ‘Thanks, mom, for nothing,'” the host said. “It makes me so sad of the opportunity that you have after your daughter’s death that that’s what you choose to leave us with,” King added. As for Kelly, the former Fox News reporter went on The Megyn Kelly Show and declared, “You failed at your job… You got an F as a parent,” referring to Vogel. “You made a bunch of money off of your daughter,” Kelly added. “You probably have a super nice car and a big house. You failed. You raised someone to the age of majority who doesn’t feel safe, loved, or cherished. You’re a loser.” Panettiere had been open about her estranged relationship with her mother , who also served as her manager when she was growing up in the industry. In her memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning , the actress detailed the pressure she felt from Vogel. During an interview with THR in May , Panettiere also opened up about the challenges of delving into her childhood and relationship with her mom when writing This Is Me . “Having to touch on everything about my relationship with my mother, that was one of the harder things to talk about,” Panettiere said. “While writing it, I realized even more so how much of a toll it took on me.” Page Six reported in May that Vogel had chosen the “no-contact route” with Panettiere after “20 years of trauma” and on the advice of professionals. Her son and Panettiere’s younger brother also died in February 2023 at the age of 28. THR

articles.title: John Oliver Takes a Close Look at Sean Duffy’s “God-Awful” New Reality Show: “We’ve All Been Taken for a F***ing Ride”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All August 23, 2026 9:47pm 'Last Week Tonight With John Oliver' Courtesy of HBO John Oliver took a close look at what he called a “less-covered story from this week” on Sunday’s Last Week Tonight : a reality show from U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy called The Great American Road Trip. Duffy debuted a trailer for the show in May. At the time, a press release stated that the series “asks: Who are we? Following U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and his family, this five-part journey encourages Americans to step away from their screens for a vital civic experience. From small towns to iconic landmarks, the series captures the unscripted moments and shared values that prove to love America, you have to see America. The series will be released for free on YouTube, allowing every American family to follow along.” The show was timed to debut during this year, the nation’s 250th anniversary. Related Stories News Did Alex Vindman Just Get Burned by the Larry David Curse? Lifestyle Abdul El-Sayed's Watch Collection Has Drawn Scrutiny -- Is It Luxury or Simply Geek Chic? “So the motto is to love America is to see America,” Duffy explains to President Donald Trump in the trailer. He continues in voice-over: “It’s more than a road trip. It’s a civic experience. It’s one of the most powerful ways to understand the vast, beautiful, complicated place we call home.” (Watch it below.) Said Oliver of the trailer: “OK, lots not to like there — from the generic ‘hey ho’ folk rock to Trump giving insane grandma’s new boyfriend vibes to the very conspicuous close up of the Toyota logo to the seemingly AI-generated images of cars, which makes sense. No one’s ever thought to film a real car before.” At the time the show was announced, Duffy’s wife, Fox News Channel host Rachel Campos Duffy, “even claimed it was a solution to what ails us as a nation,” Oliver said. “I’m going to be really honest, we live in a Pornhub world,” Rachel said in a Fox News clip shown by Oliver. “This is really wholesome, good family stuff. This is what families need to do is just get together. That’s what our kids want from us.” Replied Oliver: “Is it? Because I think what every kid really wants is for their mum not to say the word ‘Pornhub’ on national TV. Also, she clearly hasn’t spent a lot of time on that site, or she’d know, families getting together is very much its own category.” However, the road-trip series drew controversy for a few reasons: the high cost of gas, the fact that Sean was out filming a reality series when he had an important government job to do, and who was paying for the show. Regarding the latter, Sean said that it wasn’t funded by taxpayer money; instead the series was funded through a nonprofit production company called Great American Road Trip Inc. However, that organization’s website lists 17 sponsors, many of which are companies that the Department of Transportation oversees and regulates. “Yeah, that’s not great,” said Oliver. “The only worse answer to who pay for this than ‘the American taxpayer’ is ‘a bunch of companies I oversee and regulate.’ Actually, I suppose an even worse answer would be a bunch of companies I oversee and regulate, and also my close personal friend Jeffrey Epstein.” The show was supposed to be released in June, but “all the scrutiny seemed to delay it,” Oliver noted, and all six episodes were “quietly dumped on YouTube” last week. Oliver said that it’s no surprise that Sean, a former star of MTV’s The Real World : Boston , wanted to return to reality TV. (He also met his wife on Road Rules: All Stars .) But Oliver pointed out some discrepancies in how Duffy recalled his time on those shows over the years. For example, in Road Trip, he visits the house that the Real World: Boston cast stayed in while filming and “tries to rewrite some history,” the Last Week Tonight host said. During the segment, Sean reflects on the tension between him and housemate Kameelah Phillips, denying he called her a “bitch.” But Oliver showed a clip from The Real World in which Duffy says, “I walked up ahead of the group and I called her a bitch.” “You did call her that,” Oliver said. “Call me CVS, Sean, because I will always bring the receipts.” As for Sean’s claim that the show is “a nationwide storytelling movement that invites Americans to explore the open road, connect with their communities,” Oliver said, “That’s not really what it is at all, because it turns out it’s basically just an expensively produced test run of a Duffy family reality show with each episode featuring a bare minimum about travel or America, but a ton of manufactured reality TV drama around the Duffys doing stuff like planning a family party or over the course of several episodes watching their daughter decide which college she’ll attend.” As for that lattter point, Sean and Rachel are seen talking to their daughter about her desire to go to Harvard, which they evidently don’t support because they believe Harvard has “professionalized figuring out how they can take good young girls like you and I think corrupt their minds,” Sean tells his daughter in the show while the two are chatting in their kitchen. Replied Oliver: “What the fuck are you talking about? First, this was supposed to be a road trip. Why are we still in your kitchen? Second, is there anything less relatable than a family whose conflict is, how do I tell my daughter she can’t go to Harvard because we did too good a job raising her?” He continued: “And finally, please don’t be worried that Harvard’s going to corrupt your daughter’s mind. Be worried that if she goes there, like every other Harvard grad, she’s never gonna shut the fuck up about it. One of this show’s writers went to Harvard and guess how I know that? Exactly . I don’t know where any of the others went.” Oliver then said that it’s no surprise that “hardly anyone” seems to have watched the show, based on the number of viewers available on YouTube. It also received very little promotion. “I don’t really give a shit if Sean Duffy and his wife want to become the next Duggars or Jon and Kate [Gosselin] or Alec and Hilaria Baldwin,” Oliver said, citing other families who’ve starred in reality TV shows. “What’s concerning is them doing it on the back of the Department of Transportation because it feels ethically dubious on so many levels, which may be why at this point everyone involved in The Great American Road Trip seems like they’d rather just sweep it under the rug.” He continued: “[H]aving watched all three hours of this god-awful show, from gender reveals to the Duffys renewing their vows for no clear reason, it feels less like the country’s been taken on a road trip by Sean Duffy and a lot more like we’ve all been taken for a fucking ride.” THR

articles.title: Busan Film Festival Sets 23 Titles for Vision Korea, Vision Asia Sections
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All August 23, 2026 11:53pm Shashank Walia's 'Birds in the Dark' Courtesy of the Busan International Film Festival The Busan International Film Festival has unveiled 23 features for its Vision Korea and Vision Asia sections, filling out its showcase for Korean and Asian independent cinema ahead of the reveal of this year’s main competition slate. BIFF selected 12 films for Vision Korea and 11 for Vision Asia. The two strands were introduced last year, part of a broader overhaul that also saw Busan launch its first formal main competition section. The festival describes its Vision program as a showcase for new Korean and Asian independent cinema. The section grew out of Korean Cinema Today – Vision, which traditionally focused on emerging Korean filmmakers. When Busan expanded Visions’ remit to cover all of Asia, it also broadened the section to include mid-career directors alongside newcomers. Related Stories Movies Sandra Wollner's 'Everytime' Wins Best Film in Sarajevo, Ana Urushadze Crowned Best Director Movies 'Voice of Hind Rajab' Director Slams Israeli Military Investigation Into 5-Year-Old Girl's Death as a "Smokescreen" Among the Korean selections, Park Kun-young returns with Things I Left at the Theater , a drama about a film journalist searching for an old friend’s short film. Jang Woojin brings Cosmic Trace , centered on two people reflecting on love, loss, chance and fate at the boundary between life and death. Kim Miyoung, whose A Lonely Island in the Distant Sea won Busan’s DGK Megabox Award in 2023, is back with Some Detective , about a writer confronted by figures from her past. Both Some Detective and Shin Dongmin’s Not For You received post-production support from BIFF’s Asian Cinema Fund this year. (The full Visions lineup is below.) On the broader Asian side, Vietnamese filmmaker Nguyễn Hoàng Điệp returns with 1982 , about a bankrupt filmmaker searching for her missing mother and uncovering family secrets. Her first feature, Flapping in the Middle of Nowhere , premiered in Venice Critics’ Week in 2014 before screening at Busan. Filipino filmmaker Arvin Belarmino brings Ria , a folk-punk drama about a musician fighting to preserve her home and music, while Mongolia’s Sakhya Byamba, winner of Busan’s New Currents Award in 2013 for Remote Control , returns with Zogsool , a satire set around an isolated gas station during the early days of COVID-19. Thai actor Inthira Charoenpura makes her directing debut with Bua , co-directed by feature newcomer Phensiri Klangsurin. BIFF earlier named Kim Jong-kwan’s The Table: Day and Night as its 2026 opening film. The Seoul cafe-set romance, a loose follow-up to his 2016 feature The Table , will world premiere at the Busan Cinema Center on Oct. 6, with star Kim Minha hosting the opening ceremony. Michelle Yeoh will receive the Asian Filmmaker of the Year honor, Hong Kong auteur Ann Hui the Chanel-backed Camellia Award and festival founder Kim Dong-ho the Korean Cinema Award. The festival’s full competition lineup is still to come. BIFF will unveil its complete official selection in Seoul on Sept. 1 at its official opening press conference. The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs Oct. 6-15, with the Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13. Vision Korea BALER , dir. Oh Sehyeon Beyond Love’s Horizon , dir. Park Songyeol The Birds , dir. Sohn Hyun-lok Cosmic Trace , dir. Jang Woojin Earbug , dir. Kim Hyomi The Flower , dir. Kim Si-jin FULL MOON , dir. Jeong Jihye Not For You , dir. Shin Dongmin Nothing Has Happened Yet , dir. Shin Sun Some Detective , dir. Kim Miyoung Space , dir. Park Hong-min Things I Left at the Theater , dir. Park Kun-young Vision Asia 1982 , dir. Nguyễn Hoàng Điệp (Vietnam) After the Song , dir. Ryohei Kumamoto (Japan) Birds in the Dark , dir. Shashank Walia (India) Bua , dirs. Inthira Charoenpura, Phensiri Klangsurin (Thailand) The Cord , dir. Darkhan Tulegenov (Kazakhstan) Dead End , dir. Isabella Lam Lok-hin (Hong Kong, China) Hinotama: Ball of Fire , dir. Takenoshin Yaza (Japan) Ria , dir. Arvin Belarmino (Philippines, Netherlands, Norway, Saudi Arabia, Japan) SELVI , dir. Sailesh Rathnakumar (India, Saudi Arabia) Slumber , dir. Mani Moghaddam (Iran) Zogsool , dir. Sakhya Byamba (Mongolia, Germany) THR

articles.title: ‘I Plant My Hand in the Garden’ Blurs the Line Between Autobiography and Fiction to Explore Identity and Family (Exclusive Venice Trailer)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 24, 2026 1:00am ‘I Plant My Hand in the Garden’ Courtesy of DFFB Hoda and Boris are in love and are expecting a child. So, they decide to marry and officially form a family together. But as the wedding draws nearer, it starts to dawn on them that becoming a family may require them to reinvent what it means to be a couple. After all, Hoda is an Iranian refugee living in Berlin, and Boris is a queer man from Serbia. They are the protagonists of I Plant My Hand in the Garden from co-writers and co-directors who share – no coincidence, you’ll see! – their first names: Hoda Taheri and Boris Hadžija. The film, marking the debut feature-length movie for the duo, will get its world premiere in the competition of Venice Days , or Giornate degli Autori, the independent section within the Venice Film Festival promoted by the Italian filmmaker associations Anac and 100autori. Related Stories Movies Busan Film Festival Sets 23 Titles for Vision Korea, Vision Asia Sections Movies Sandra Wollner's 'Everytime' Wins Best Film in Sarajevo, Ana Urushadze Crowned Best Director “Together, they decide to marry and raise the child, imagining a future built on their own terms,” reads a synopsis for I Plant My Hand in the Garden . “As they prepare for the wedding and enter more deeply into each other’s worlds, their relationship is unsettled by bureaucracy, family expectations and histories neither of them can leave behind. Surrounded by relatives, memories and inherited ideas of love and parenthood, Hoda and Boris begin to question the roles they are about to take on. What starts as a plan to become a family gradually opens into a more intimate and uncertain question: can they reinvent what it means to be a couple without losing what brought them together?” Taheri and Hadžija star in the movie, along with Branka Hadžija, Jahandokht Taheri and Hadi Khanjanpour. The cinematography comes courtesy of Lithuanian camera wiz Vytautas Katkus . Boris Hadžija also handled editing. The 2026 edition of the Venice Days competition takes place Sept. 2-12, with I Plant My Hand in the Garden debuting on Sept. 3. The filmmaking duo previously worked together on the short film trilogy Mother Prays All Day Long (2022), As If Mother Cried That Night (2023), and Mother Is a Natural Sinner (2024), which all premiered at the Locarno Film Festival. Their short Yugotransport – We Are All on the Same Bus (2023) premiered at Rotterdam. “ I Plant My Hand in the Garden grows out of the same questions that have shaped our earlier films: how identity, family and belonging are formed, contested and reinvented,” Taheri and Hadžija share about their new film. “By placing a queer Serbian man and an Iranian refugee with a German passport at the center of a fictional marriage, we explore how institutions, such as marriage, nationality and gender, assign roles that feel both real and constructed. Casting members of our own families intensifies this tension, blurring the line between autobiography and invention.” They conclude: “We are less interested in defining what a ‘real’ family or relationship is than in asking what might emerge when we step outside inherited forms. The title suggests claiming ground, but for us, planting a hand is about testing whether something unfamiliar can take root at all.” I Plant My Hand in the Garden is produced by Maximilian Feldkamp for DFFB in Germany, with co-production by Taheri and Hadžija’s Cruising in Germany, Čarna Vučinić and Ena Bajraktarević for Naked in Serbia, and Tyler Hill for Mala Productions LLC in the U.S. Square Eyes is handling world sales. THR can exclusively premiere a trailer for the movie. We won’t spoil much beyond saying: get ready for wedding conversations, music, a lost condom – and talk of cake, among other things. Watch the exclusive trailer for I Plant My Hand in the Garden right here. THR

articles.title: Meet Tuide, Your New Favorite Girl Group (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content K-pop girl group Tuide in exclusive photos for The Hollywood Reporter. ABD/Hybe As the girl-group renaissance continues globally, K-pop giant Hybe is ready to add a strong new entry into the mix — Tuide . The seven-member group, hailing from Hybe’s new girl group-centric sub-label ABD, officially debuted Monday (Aug. 24) with their first EP, Tune & Play , led by the single “Sun Kiss.” The young group, with members ranging in age from 15 to 19, uses the album to introduce their signature sound as a group, Soultronic — a genre that mixes soulful R&B vocals with electronic music . Tuide, whose name was inspired by the phrase “turn the tide,” is comprised of seven members — Seohee, Seoyeon, Elena, Jia, Saki, Seah and Yi Hani — and serves as ABD’s first group. The label is led by Jiwon No, the former head of artist planning at another Hybe label, Pledis Entertainment, known for groups such as Seventeen and TWS. Sung Soo Han, the head of Pledis, known as the master professional, has led the group’s overall production for music, visual concepts and their performances. Related Stories Music Madonna Tops U.K. Dance Charts a Record Fifth Time in 15 Weeks Next Big Thing 'The Last Sunrise' Star Maia Reficco Is Finally Facing Her Fears With Tuide, it feels like a new generation of K-pop is emerging — the world of K-pop is separated by years-long generations of groups that debuted in the same several years span. The group is already polished, global-facing and poised to take up the mantle of popular girl groups before them. The girls of Tuide, despite their young age, have been preparing for this debut for a while, with some members training for as little as eight months, while others trained for over four and a half years. For most of the group, a career as an idol is a childhood dream come to life, and for some in the group it’s not even their job. “I got to do some kids modeling, and that led me to be naturally exposed to a lot of singing and dancing,” Seah, 15, tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom from Seoul. “I became fascinated and naturally came to dream of becoming an idol.” As their debut date nears, Tuide speaks with THR all about their debut EP and how they learned to work together as a team. We’re getting really close to your debut date. How are you feeling? YI HANI We all have a mix of excitement, joy, gratefulness and just overall nerves and butterflies in our stomachs. But overall it’s a good feeling. It’s good butterflies, good nerves. Yi Hani, 15, of Tuide in an exclusive photo for THR . How have you been preparing for your debut together? SEOHEE We’ve been practicing together for quite a while. We spent a lot of time trying to get to know each other — each other’s strengths and just as people. I think all the time that we spent together brought us a lot closer and tighter as a group. After we became more tight-knit as a team, I think our performances have become better quality. We’re able to truly feel that we are one complete team. Has there been a moment lately that made you realize you were ready to debut? YI HANI When I was practicing with the members, I always felt ready as a team. We’re so ready, but we didn’t really have a chance to really test that out until we did an exclusive preview, Playground, [for an audience]. When I was performing on stage with all [my] wonderful members, I really felt like we are so ready to begin. We are super duper ready. ELENA I agree with Yi Hani. We were finally able to perform the songs that we were practicing for so long in front of so many people, I realized, oh yeah, we’re ready to debut. I could see each member shining so bright on stage, and I think we’re ready to show that to the world. Elena, 18, of Tuide in an exclusive photo for THR . ABD/Hybe During that preview, were there any songs that you appreciated more once you performed them live? JIA It’s so hard to choose, but I personally love “Sun Kiss.” [The song’s] about trusting our own voices and our rhythm and not worrying about what others think. I feel like the song really captures each of our individuality and voices. During the performance, in the outro, we all have freestyle moves. When it comes together as a whole, it really captures our bright and vibrant energy. After the preview or any of the teasers online came out, did anyone in your life say they saw you in a new light? SEOYEON My family and friends were telling me that when they saw pictures or videos of me smiling on stage, I looked happy. Really, really happy. That made me realize that I’m living my dream and that this is something that I’ve always wanted to do. Even though we didn’t have that many opportunities to really show off our chemistry with one another, people were already saying that we look so close and that the chemistry that we had on stage was so playful and bubbly. I think it really shines through. Seoyeon, 18, of Tuide in an exclusive photo for THR . ABD/Hybe Can you tell me a bit about your signature sound? YI HANI For our first EP, Tune & Play, we have set on the sound called soultronic. It’s a style that mixes groovy, warm R&B soul vocals with energetic and uplifting electronic music. I think the contrast and the blended sound of those two music elements is the key thing you should look out for in our first EP. ELENA I feel like each song on the album has its own charms. Some are super duper energetic. Some have a really soulful, R&B groove. You’re still very young but most of you have been training for a while. When did you decide this was the career you wanted? SEAH I got to do some kids modeling, and that led me to be naturally exposed to a lot of singing and dancing. I became fascinated and naturally came to dream of becoming an idol. At one point, I [realized] I wanted to be part of a group with girls around my age. ELENA I just loved to sing as a young child, so I always had the dream of becoming an artist, and I also really loved K-pop. I don’t know, I just naturally felt drawn to this job, and it was always a dream of mine. Being here is just a dream come true. Jia, 18, of Tuide in an exclusive photo for THR . ABD/Hybe SEOYEON I’ve always loved dancing, singing and performing in front of people and connecting with them. I realized at one point that being a singer ticked all my boxes and it became my dream. At the exclusive preview, it was so amazing to experience all of that firsthand. It was a true dream come true. JIA Ever since I was little, I really enjoyed watching videos of artists’ performances. I would sing or dance in front of my parents when I was little. I truly felt happy doing it and I think that’s when I started to dream of being a K-pop idol. SEOHEE I’ve also loved singing and dance since I was young. But one day, I got the opportunity to audience [for a K-pop company]. I got in, and I started the trainee life. After started training, I just realized, oh, I want to be an idol. SAKI I think it was four years ago when I came across a K-pop song by a senior group that really hooked me and got me into K-pop, and that’s when I started dreaming of becoming an idol. Saki, 15, of Tuide in an exclusive photo for THR . ABD/Hybe YI HANI Ever since I was little, I’ve loved music so, so, so much and loved performing on stage. Whenever I had the chance, at school or outside of school, I would always volunteer to be onstage. I’d always be singing. Or I’d always be listening to music and looking for more music. Naturally, growing up around music and holding onto my love of it, becoming a singer and performer came naturally. I got a great opportunity to audition as well. When I came in and met all these wonderful girls and started practicing with them, I really felt this is what I’ve been waiting for. It’s a really dream come true. Do you know what you want your debut day to look like? SAKI I’ve been imagining the seven of us standing onstage together on the day of our debut. I think I’ll be overwhelmed with joy. I’m already so grateful for our fans, who we met in early August at the exclusive preview. They’ve been waiting so much for our debut and counting down the days. I’m really thankful to them. What was the process like recording your first EP? ELENA When we were preparing this album, there were so many fun moments. Personally, it was my first time in the recording studio. I had so much fun recording and hearing my voice in the booth. We worked with [Korean producing duo] GroovyRoom on this album. Meeting them in real life was a crazy experience and being able to record with them was super fun. Seah, 15, of Tuide in an exclusive photo for THR . ABD/Tuide When you were training, did you find that there were things that your teammates were really good at that made you better? SEAH We all have different strengths and personalities, so there was so much to learn from each other as we were practicing and becoming a group. Even when we were practicing our freestyle, we each had our distinct style of dancing. While we share the same energy, we’re able to learn from each other’s strengths. I also learned a lot from the other girls’ attitude on stage. I think we’re just rubbing off on each other in general. Being anxious or nervous about this big step in your career is very normal. What gives you confidence during moments of doubt? JIA Trusting my members. I knew that the music was amazing. The performance itself is amazing. Everyone is fully prepared for this. I trust the members the most because they were a comfort for me. I feel like if we don’t trust each other, then we’re not able to create the best output. When we come together as a team because we’re all unique, [we have] seven different colors, [we] shine the brightest. Seohee, 19, of Tuide in an exclusive photo for THR . ABD/Hybe How did you work through communicating as a team? SEOHEE From the get-go, we just promised that we would be 100 percent honest and open when it comes to our emotions and feelings, and we’ve really stuck to that. Those conversations that we had — honest, open conversations — brought us closer as a team. THR

articles.title: Erik Poppe Talks Haugesund Opener ‘Beloved,’ Written by Nobel Prize Winner Jon Fosse: ‘People Long for Something Honest and Truthful’
articles.full_text: Aug 23, 2026 11:15pm PT Erik Poppe Talks Haugesund Opener ‘Beloved,’ Written by Nobel Prize Winner Jon Fosse: ‘People Long for Something Honest and Truthful’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Erik Poppe Talks Haugesund Opener ‘Beloved,’ Written by Nobel Prize Winner Jon Fosse: ‘People Long for Something Honest and Truthful’ 4 hours ago ‘Sentimental Value’ Star Anders Danielsen Lie and Anne Marie Ottersen Inducted Into the Haugesund Walk of Fame: ‘It Feels Full Circle’ 18 hours ago Monica Bellucci Has ‘Never’ Done Anything Like ‘Ketticè’: ‘I Was on Set in My Pajamas With a Knife in My Hand and Slippers on My Feet’ 2 weeks ago See All Erik Poppe's 'Beloved' Courtesy of Reinvent Yellow Sales In “ Beloved ,” opening the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund , Erik Poppe takes on a script by Nobel Prize winner Jon Fosse. “It’s a project that has been on my desk for many, many years. Jon Fosse wrote it almost 20 years ago. After he received the Nobel Prize in Literature [in 2023], it felt like the whole world wanted to read it. But I always knew it was a powerful piece of work,” he tells Variety . Related Stories Ryan Murphy on Toning Down Sex in ‘The Shards’ and Why L.A. Mayor Karen Bass Could Do a ‘Much Better Job’ Bringing Productions Back to Hollywood 'Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story' Trailer: Ella Beatty Is an Axe Murderer in the Fourth Chapter of Ryan Murphy's Bloody Anthology Series “Beloved” follows a couple who meet in a small coastal town. They have a child, but Asle is drawn back to the sea while Gerd remains in the village. Popular on Variety The film, starring Leo Magnus de la Nuez and Kristi-Helene Giæver Engeberg, was produced by Paradox and SF Production. It’s sold by Reinvent Yellow Sales. One of Norway’s most acclaimed directors, Poppe is known for larger productions, from “The King’s Choice” to “Utøya: July 22,” “The Emigrants” and “Quisling: The Final Days.” But focusing on a more intimate story felt right this time. “Looking at the world as it is right now, I needed to hold onto some sense of hope – or at least something more human. I wanted to explore the relationship between two people, as well as between a father and son, because it’s a story of daily life I can relate to.” He adds: “We’ve all seen how well they perform in the cinemas, surprisingly enough. People long for something honest and truthful that they can just dive into.” The fact that Fosse is only growing in stature doesn’t hurt either. “He’s about to be named one of the most important living authors in the world today, and this isn’t based on his novels or plays. [The screenplay] is an original piece of work that he wrote with only one goal in mind: to make it into a movie.” Still more adaptations are likely on their way. “I’m quite sure more movies will be made from his novels. As a filmmaker, he’s opening up the space between the dialogue for me to fill in. His style is so simple yet deep. You connect with it, understand it, and it hits you right in the stomach. His novels are short, but when you read them, it feels like Dostoyevsky. I find it extraordinary.” Despite following only two characters and their son, Poppe didn’t change his approach to working with actors. “On all my movies, I insist on having at least eight or 12 weeks with them [prior to the shoot]. If I can establish a truthful, honest relationship with my actors, I can push them quite far,” he says. He also paid extra attention to their surroundings. “I spent a lot of time figuring out where to shoot this film. It’s almost like a mythical landscape, a mythical part of Norway. It’s the fourth character in the film.” Misty and melancholic, it mirrors their insecurities and growing estrangement. “It’s quite typical of many relationships. It’s so hard to talk to each other,” says Poppe. “I was raised by two parents who were almost exactly like these two. Except, it was my mother who left and my sister and I stayed home with my father. The film is about the language these two used to share, which is disappearing, it’s about where they are and what they’re longing for.” Which is why, despite that title, there is a darker side to ‘Beloved.’ “Based on our first screenings, people have been surprised, but they also really love that it’s not your regular love story,” he admits. “I think it’s a brave piece of work by Jon. I was tempted by the fact that he doesn’t follow the paths we are so used to. I wanted to explore how that could work in a movie.” ‘American Blue’ Pilot With Milo Ventimiglia Not Moving Forward at HBO Max Paula Reid, CNN’s Chief Legal Affairs Correspondent, Will Exit Ahead of Paramount Takeover HBO Max Leads the Emmy Drama and Comedy Races for the First Time Since 2017. articles.title: ‘Game of Thrones’ Star Kristofer Hivju Turns to Rom-Com With ‘True Love’ by ‘Little Did I Know’s’ Martina Haag (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 23, 2026 11:30pm PT ‘Game of Thrones’ Star Kristofer Hivju Turns to Rom-Com With ‘True Love’ by ‘Little Did I Know’s’ Martina Haag (EXCLUSIVE) By Annika Pham Plus Icon Annika Pham Latest Icelandic Producer Hlín Jóhannsdóttir Sets ‘Just a Kid’ With Alief Ahead of Haugesund and Reunites With ‘Driving Mum’ Team (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago Haugesund New Nordic Films Reveals Standout 36 Nordic Projects and 15 Fresh Pics Set to Woo 300 Industry Attendees 2 weeks ago Haugesund New Nordic Films Unveils French Focus Including a Case Study on ‘Ibelin,’ From ‘The Imitation Game’ Director Morten Tyldum (EXCLUSIVE) 3 weeks ago See All From left, Helen Ahlsson, Kristofer Hivju and Martina Haag Credit: Courtesy of Anna-Lena Ahlström/SF Studios Norwegian star actor Kristofer Hivju (“Game of Thrones,” “ Red One ”, “Beck”) will play opposite Frida Hallgren (from Oscar-nominated “As It Is in Heaven”) in the upcoming Swedish-Croatian rom-com “True Love” (working title). Helmed by actor-turned writer, director and best-selling author Martina Haag , the SF Studios project, now in pre-production, will be pitched Aug. 26. at Haugesund’s Nordic Co-Production Market. Related Stories Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities LISTEN: Amazon Courts Creators to Build Businesses and Scale the Attention Economy for Brands “True Love” marks Haag’s second collaboration with seasoned screenwriter Peter Arrhenius (“Clark,” “Welcome to Sweden,” “Beck”) after the seasoned actor’s directorial debut “ Little Did I Know ,” which landed a Best Film Award at the Monte-Carlo Television Festival in 2024 before turning into one of Sweden’s biggest box office draws of 2025. Popular on Variety As with ‘ Little Did I know ,” “True Love”’s starting point is deceit and divorce and how to bounce back when you’re over 50. According to the logline, when Ellinor (played by Hallgren) is dumped by her husband after 20 years of marriage, she loses faith in life. When she wins €40 million ($46 million) immediately after, she finds it even harder to trust anyone. But then she meets Henrik (Hivju). The latter grew up at the elite Lundsberg boarding school, where his mother worked as a cleaner. To fit in, he learned to lie, and became an irresistibly charming master of deception. Their relationship should never work, but what if they’re exactly what the other needs? “As both main characters are flawed and a bit extreme in the beginning of the film, it was important for us to find great actors that are warm and relatable: Real people in exaggerated situations, that we want to be with and see get better,” said Hivju and Hallgren Haag. They added: “Both Frida and Kristofer feel grounded and are capable of going from being extremely funny to super sensitive. And of course, the chemistry and dynamics between the actors is super important in a romantic comedy. If the spark isn’t there, it doesn’t matter how great the story is. We’re so happy to have Frida and Kristofer on board!” Added SF Studios producer Helen Ahlsson : “Frida is a wonderfully warm and talented actress, and one audiences have taken to their hearts over the years. Kristofer has never really played a romantic lead before, which was perhaps a new challenge he was very keen to take on. In this film, you’ll discover a new Hivju like you’ve never seen before,” she enthusiastically shared with Variety . Haag said catering for mature audiences came naturally. “I love stories about and for women – and men – over 50,” she said. “I really can’t understand why we don’t see more of them as a whole scope of relatable, life altering relationship questions appear after surviving Project Family and raising the kids. One being deceit and divorce – as in “Little Did I Know” – but also how to be able to trust and love again.” “This story is about that,” she added. “Who we were, who we are, who we try to present ourself as, and who we really want to be. How can anyone dare to let their guard down and risk being hurt once again? We take that premise to the extreme in this film.” Teaming up again with Arrhenius was a no-brainer. “It is rare to find a writing partner that both has a skillset that completes your own and at the same time can respect and see your own strengths, like the yin and the yang,” she said, pointing out that “Peter is very interested in structure and serves up a lot of drastic jokes and situations, while I tend to focus on grounding these ideas in character and ”what would a real person do in this situation.” “When that works, what you get is drastic, funny situations happening to characters that feels true. Real emotions without being kitchen-sink drama. We share that desire to both touch an audience, but in an entertaining way,” she observed. Seasoned producer Ahlsson who’s worked mostly on dramas for film and TV – from Alicia Vikander’s Swedish debut “Pure” to Rojda Sekersöz’s upcoming “Will You Care if I Die” – said she couldn’t resist boarding her first rom-com after reading the script. “It’s got the magic of British comedy hits such as “Bridget Jones’s Diary” or “Mamma Mia,” which balance believable, engaging characters with lightness, humor and emotions. It’s a tricky mix that you can’t take lightly,” she said. Filming between Sweden-Stockholm, Dalecarlia-and Croatia is due to start Oct. 8, with delivery pencilled for fall 2027. The feature is produced by Scandi giant SF Studios in co-production with Croatia’s Kinorama, SVT and NRK, with funding from the Swedish Film Institute, Film Stockholm, Film i Dalarna, and a Croatian tax rebate. Ahlsson said she will discuss global sales at the New Nordic Films market unspooling Aug. 25-28 at Haugesund, Norway. Warner Bros. It is another milestone in building Emomee into a global entertainment company. Every step we’ve taken – from growing a loyal audience to expanding onto streaming platforms – is helping us build a long-term franchise that will extend beyond content into consumer products, licensing and live experiences,” said Pooja Jauhari, founder and CEO of Emomee. articles.full_text: Aug 24, 2026 1:30am PT ‘An Oak Tree’ Casts Sacha Dhawan, Gemma Whelan for London Run (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Alia Bhatt’s Young-Adult Rom-Com ‘Don’t Be Shy’ Sets September Prime Video Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 37 minutes ago ‘An Oak Tree’ Casts Sacha Dhawan, Gemma Whelan for London Run (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘Emomee,’ Indian Kids Life-Skills Series, Lands on Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago See All (c) Joanne Warren Moore Francesca Moody Productions has unveiled the first wave of guest performers joining Tim Crouch’s “ An Oak Tree ” for its run at The Other Palace in London, with Sacha Dhawan , Gemma Whelan , Bessie Carter, Rosalie Craig, Hammed Animashaun, George Fouracres, Clare Perkins and Tom Mothersdale each taking on a single performance. Crouch performs alongside a different second actor at every show, none of whom read or rehearse the script in advance. “An Oak Tree” runs at The Other Palace from Oct. 7 through Nov. 15. Related Stories LISTEN: Amazon Courts Creators to Build Businesses and Scale the Attention Economy for Brands Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities The schedule of guest performers, in order, runs as follows: Craig on Oct. 9, Perkins on Oct. 13, Mothersdale on Oct. 14, Whelan on Oct. 15, Carter on Oct. 16, Dhawan on Oct. 23, Animashaun on Oct. 29 and Fouracres on Nov. 10. Popular on Variety Craig recently starred as Kitty Eckersley in Sally Wainwright’s “Riot Women” for BBC One and earned an Olivier nomination for “The Light Princess” at the National Theatre. Perkins appeared in Indhu Rubasingham’s “Bacchae” at the National Theatre and starred opposite Sadie Sink in “Romeo & Juliet” in the West End. Mothersdale’s stage credits include “A Doll’s House” and “Oil” at the Almeida Theatre, while his television work spans “Wolf Hall: The Mirror and the Light” and “Peaky Blinders.” Whelan is known for playing Yara Greyjoy in HBO’s “Game of Thrones” and has appeared across all three series of ITV’s “The Tower.” Carter currently plays Nancy Mitford in BritBox’s “Outrageous” and is also known for playing Prudence Featherington in Netflix’s “Bridgerton.” Dhawan has been announced for Netflix’s “Extraction” and plays the latest incarnation of the Master in BBC One’s “Doctor Who.” Animashaun, a BAFTA nominee for “Black Ops,” appeared in Sky’s “SNL U.K.” and the Donmar Warehouse’s “Dealer’s Choice.” Fouracres, another “SNL U.K.” cast member, is a regular at Shakespeare’s Globe, with credits including “Hamlet” and “Twelfth Night.” “An Oak Tree” premiered in 2005 and has since been performed hundreds of times across more than 19 countries, with more than 350 guest artists taking part over two decades. Past performers include Frances McDormand, Geoffrey Rush, Peter Dinklage, David Tennant, Jessie Buckley and Phoebe Waller-Bridge. The production is part of a new Francesca Moody Productions season at The Other Palace running from Oct. 5, 2026 through Jan. 10, 2027, bringing together three shows that originated at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. The season also includes “Garry Starr: Classic Penguins,” created by Damien Warren-Smith and running Oct. 22 through Jan. 3 with a press night of Oct. 23, and “Feeling Afraid As If Something Terrible Is Going to Happen,” written by Marcelo Dos Santos and starring Steven Webb, running Nov. 19 through Jan. 10. Francesca Moody, the season’s executive producer, originated two of the past decade’s most successful television adaptations, “Fleabag” and “Baby Reindeer,” both of which began as stage productions before moving to the screen. articles.full_text: Aug 24, 2026 1:54am PT Alia Bhatt’s Young-Adult Rom-Com ‘Don’t Be Shy’ Sets September Prime Video Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Alia Bhatt’s Young-Adult Rom-Com ‘Don’t Be Shy’ Sets September Prime Video Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago ‘An Oak Tree’ Casts Sacha Dhawan, Gemma Whelan for London Run (EXCLUSIVE) 54 minutes ago ‘Emomee,’ Indian Kids Life-Skills Series, Lands on Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago See All Prime Video Prime Video has set a September premiere date for “Don’t Be Shy,” a young-adult romantic comedy from Alia Bhatt and Shaheen Bhatt’s Eternal Sunshine Productions. Sreeti Mukerji wrote and directed the coming-of-age film, which is produced by Bhatt and Shaheen Bhatt under the Eternal Sunshine Productions banner, with Grishma Shah and Vikesh Bhutani serving as co-producers. The film introduces four newcomers – Aarushi Bajaj, Ansh Duggal, Bianca Arora and Piyush Khati – who headline a story centered on friendship, young love, heartbreak and the process of figuring out life as a young adult. Kunaal Roy Kapur, Anurag Basu, Neha Dhupia and Anju Alva Naik round out the cast in pivotal roles. Related Stories Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities LISTEN: Amazon Courts Creators to Build Businesses and Scale the Attention Economy for Brands “‘Don’t Be Shy’ is one of our most cherished films, and we’re thrilled to finally announce its global streaming premiere,” said Nikhil Madhok, director and head of originals, Prime Video (SVOD) and Amazon MGM Studios India. “This film introduces four extraordinary new actors – Aarushi, Ansh, Bianca, and Piyush – who bring an incredible freshness and authenticity to their roles. Led by Sreeti Mukerji and shaped by the creative vision of Alia and Shaheen Bhatt, ‘Don’t Be Shy’ is a joyful, heartfelt celebration of friendship, love, and the beautifully messy journey of growing up. We can’t wait for audiences to immerse themselves in Shy’s world.” Popular on Variety Alia Bhatt and Shaheen Bhatt, co-founders of Eternal Sunshine Productions, added in a joint statement: “‘Don’t Be Shy’ has been extremely special to us from the very beginning, and we couldn’t be prouder to see it come to life. It captures something so honest about being young – the friendships that shape you, the first loves that change you, the heartbreaks that stay with you, and the process of gradually figuring out who you are. What excites us most is this brilliant young cast; their energy, vulnerability, and chemistry are magnetic, and they bring such life and honesty to these characters. We can’t wait for audiences in India and around the world to meet Shy and get swept into her wonderful, chaotic world.” Eternal Sunshine Productions was founded in 2021 by Bhatt, one of the most celebrated actors in Indian cinema, and her sister Shaheen Bhatt, author of the mental health memoir “I’ve Never Been (Un)Happier” (Penguin Ebury Press, 2019). The company’s debut feature, “Darlings,” bowed in August 2022 as a Red Chillies co-production and marked Jasmeet K. Reen’s feature directorial debut. Eternal Sunshine’s slate also includes “Poacher,” the Prime Video series from Emmy winner Richie Mehta, and “Jigra,” an action-adventure from Vasan Bala co-produced with Dharma Productions. “Don’t Be Shy” will premiere exclusively on Prime Video in Hindi with English subtitles across India and more than 240 countries and territories worldwide on Sept. 25. articles.full_text: Aug 24, 2026 2:20am PT Venice Adds ‘Naza,’ Documentary From ‘No Other Land’ Directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to Competition By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Meghan Markle in Talks to Join ‘The Gentlemen’ Season 3 3 days ago Trump’s White House Blasts Rosie O’Donnell After ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Hosting Run: A ‘Nasty Woman’ and ‘Total Slob’ 3 days ago Edward Bluemel Suits Up as Detective Poirot in First Look at BBC and BritBox Series ‘Hercule’ 3 days ago See All Venice Film Festival The Venice Film Festival has made a last-minute addition to its competition lineup: “ Naza ,” a new documentary from “ No Other Land ” directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. The doc, which was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis. “Naza” is produced by The Guardian and James Wilson of JW Films, and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer. Wilson and Glazer also worked on 2023’s “The Zone of Interest” together, which won the Oscar for best international feature. Related Stories Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities LISTEN: Amazon Courts Creators to Build Businesses and Scale the Attention Economy for Brands Abraham and Szor are two of the four co-directors of 2025’s Oscar-winning doc “No Other Land.” That film, which premiered at Berlin Film Festival, showed the destruction and displacement of Masafer Yatta, a Palestinian community in the West Bank. Popular on Variety “Naza” will screen at Venice Film Festival on Sept. 10 at 5:15 p.m. in the Sala Grande at the Palazzo del Cinema, in the presence of the directors, producers, Guardian journalists and the official delegation. The film is the only documentary included in this year’s Venice competition section. It joins a starry lineup including Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” Casey Affleck’s “Company,” Werner Herzog’s “Bucking Fastard,” Hirokazu Kore-eda’s “Look Back,” Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” and more. It marks Abraham and Szor’s first time competing for Venice’s Golden Lion, which will be awarded at the closing ceremony on Sept. 12. Discovery Deal, Says He’ll Meet When They ‘Stop Playing Games’ By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest After U.K. Approval of Paramount-WBD Deal, European Media Leaders Rally Behind David Ellison: ‘The Industry Will Be Stronger’ 2 weeks ago Cannes Critics’ Week Film ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building’ Sells to Strand Releasing for North America (EXCLUSIVE) 3 weeks ago ‘White Lotus’ Swaps the Palais for a Castle: Season 4 Cast Laura Dern, AJ Michalka and Marissa Long Drop by Disneyland Paris 3 weeks ago See All Getty California Attorney General Rob Bonta has canceled planned settlement talks with Paramount over the state’s lawsuit seeking to block David Ellison ‘s proposed $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, accusing Paramount of acting in bad faith, according to The New York Times . Bonta is leading a coalition of 12 states in challenging the proposed merger and asking the court to block the deal, arguing the merger would give the company too much power across cable television and movie production. Related Stories LISTEN: Amazon Courts Creators to Build Businesses and Scale the Attention Economy for Brands Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities The two sides had been due to meet Monday for preliminary discussions for a possible settlement, but Bonta called off the meeting late Sunday, after accusing Paramount of misrepresenting details of an earlier meeting held on Friday. Popular on Variety “Not only did Paramount leak the alleged substance of settlement discussions, but they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” Bonta said in a statement sent to The New York Times. “As soon as Paramount stops playing games and engages sincerely, my office is happy to meet again.” Variety has reached out to the California AG office for comment. The canceled meeting had been perceived as a possible opening toward resolving the case, particularly after Paramount threatened to leave California. Bonta has so far insisted that any settlement would require “structural remedies,” likely involving asset sales, which Paramount may resist. Pressure to resolve the dispute is growing ahead of the antitrust trial scheduled for March. articles.title: ‘Vultures’ Swoops To Top Award At Oscar-Qualifying HollyShorts Film Festival (Full Winners List)
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Bonta Cancels Paramount Settlement Meeting; CA AG Accuses Ellison Of “Playing Games” In WBD Merger Talks Read the full story By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew HollyShorts Festival Set To Propel Documentary Jury Award Winner Into Oscar Race Doc Talk Podcast: Rebecca Miller On Her Emmy-Nominated ‘Mr. Scorsese’, A Journey Into The Mind And Mastery Of Martin Scorsese DOC NYC Set To Honor Documentary Visionaries Alex Gibney, JT Takagi, Stephen Maing, And Raney Aronson-Rath View All August 23, 2026 6:32pm HollyShorts Dian Weys’ drama Vultures clutched top honors at HollyShorts Sunday evening, winning the prestigious festival’s Grand Jury Prize for Best Short Film. The award qualifies the film for Oscar consideration and comes with a prize of a $60,000 Panavision camera package. Edwin van der Walt, Jill Levenberg, and Albert Pretorius star in the 15-minute-long short from the South African-born filmmaker. Logline: “In the volatile moments after a car crash, before the authorities arrive, a hot-headed yet desperate tow truck driver fiercely protects his tow. But the situation quickly spirals out of his control.” Related Stories Documentary HollyShorts Festival Set To Propel Documentary Jury Award Winner Into Oscar Race News 'Degree of Certainty' Filmmaker Simon Schneider Tackles The Ironic Origins Of Climate Change Data -- HollyShorts Film Festival ‘Vultures’ HollyShorts Vultures also won the festival’s Best International award. The film premiered at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival and has screened around the world since then, including at Tribeca Festival, the Red Sea International Film Festival in Saudi Arabia, and the Zagreb Film Festival in Croatia. Weys’ previous credits include the shorts Bergie (2022) and Versnel (2017), and the 50-minute-long thriller Koffie en Sigarette (2023). Watch on Deadline In addition to the Panavision package, the Grand Jury Prize for Best Short Film comes with three hours of complimentary legal consultation presented by Sheppard Mullin. Along with the Grand Jury Prize, HollyShorts is Oscar-qualifying in three additional shorts categories: Best Live Action, Best Animation, and Best Documentary. HollyShorts The Best Live Action Award was claimed by Pale Sun , directed by Adrian Moyse Dullin and Jawahine Zentar. Anass El Hmami, Baki Bousmaha, and Sylvie Fasano star in that film, the story of 12-year-old Abel, who while spending time on a beach in summer with his family finds himself “ashamed of his father’s body, marked by cancer.” HollyShorts Best Animation went to With Tapes and Toasts in the Car (Im Auto Tapes und Butterbrot) , directed by Kiana Naghshineh. Logline: “In the face of her body fading into stardust, Shari realizes what truly matters to her.” Naghshineh, a native of Mannheim, Germany, studied animation at the Filmakademie Baden – Württemberg. Her previous films incude Augenblicke (2018) and Don Pasquale (2018). Aspen Film The Time My Grandmother Was Held Hostage by Bank Robbers , directed by Rosella Tursi, won the Best Documentary jury award. The film’s title gives a very strong sense of the content: the director’s nonna (Italian for grandmother) was held hostage in her home in Montreal in 1983 after two men fleeing a bank holdup entered her dwelling through an open door. Archive footage shows how news crews descended on the home as the hostage drama unfolded. The documentary is built around memories of that day shared by members of nonna Rosa’s family, as well as recollections from one of the bank robbers/hostage takers himself – a man tracked down by filmmaker Rosella Tursi over 40 years after the crime. (I served on the jury in this category). The awards ceremony was held at the TCL Chinese Theatres at Ovation Hollywood. Scroll for the full list of winners for the 22 nd edition of HollyShorts. Russell Tovey in ‘I Am the Prize.’ Courtesy I Am the Prize New this year at HollyShorts is the Best Performance Award, recognizing outstanding acting in short-form filmmaking. The inaugural award was presented to Russell Tovey for his performance in “I Am the Prize.” In the film, the British actor plays a self-help guru whose “true identity is revealed in the midst of a lecture tour.” Other major winners at HollyShorts: Jessy Moussallem’s Faux Bijoux for Best Director, Alyssa Loh’s Copy, Save for Best Drama JJ Adler’s The Oracle for Best Comedy, Junxiong Zhu’s The Kalgan Horse for Best Cinematography Altay Ulan Yang’s HYENA for Best Editing Peter Vass’ Banshee for Best Horror The HollyShorts Film Festival + IMGN Short Film Fund was awarded to The Fiddler’s Stroke , directed by Braden Barton, with a prize package valued at $25,000. The package includes a $10,000 cash grant from IMGN, a Blackmagic Cinema 6K Camera from HollyShorts, and exclusive one-on-one mentorship opportunities with filmmakers and industry executives, including Oscar winners Guy Nattiv and Jaime Ray Newman.
