articles.title: Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ Idea From TV Writer’s Pitch
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 8:30pm Gil Birmingham as Chief Rainwater and Mo Brings Plenty as Mo in season 5B of 'Yellowstone.' Paramount Network Taylor Sheridan , Paramount and NBC Universal are all being sued by a writer who says Sheridan stole her idea for a TV show and used it to create Yellowstone . In the suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on Friday, TV writer and entertainment journalist Lauren J. Salkin claims she submitted a pilot script, show bible and pitch deck for a show called Sovereign Nation to Sheridan’s reps at his management company, Elevate Entertainment, which is also named as a defendant in the suit, in late 2016 and early 2017. Related Stories Business Mark Ruffalo Rejects Paramount's Claim His Anti-Merger Comments Were "Antisemitic": "My Views Should Never Be Interpreted as Hostility Toward Jewish People" Business Gavin Newsom Says Paramount Settlement Talks Happening in "Real Time," Signals He'd Like a Deal Sovereign Nation, which Salkin spent more than 10 years developing, is described in the complaint, which was viewed by The Hollywood Reporter , as a “dramatic television series centered on tribal governance, casino-driven economic power and a modern war over land and development.” Salkin alleges that she received a response from Elevate on Feb. 1, 2017 saying that Sheridan was “unavailable for TV projects.” “Within months, Paramount greenlit Sheridan’s Yellowstone ,” the complaint states. The show premiered on the Paramount Network on June 20, 2018 and later began streaming on Peacock. The suit says Yellowstone featured “specific expressive choices already embodied in Salkin’s materials” including “a tribal casino functioning as the institutional center of political and development power; a signature confrontation staged in the tribal chairman’s casino office over expansion beyond reservation boundaries; the use of trust land, the absence of zoning restrictions and a 99-year lease structure as the concrete mechanism for that expansion; and recurring master-plan imagery deployed to dramatize the struggle for territorial control.” Salkin also argues that Yellowstone followed several of her proposed casting recommendations for key roles in Sovereign Nation . “Copyright law does not protect the abstract idea of a Western, a land dispute, an Indian casino or a powerful family — and that is not Plaintiff’s claim,” the complaint states. “The infringement alleged here lies in the copying of Salkin’s particular expressive choices and their coordinated selection and arrangement.” The suit also notes that a senior HBO scripted TV executive who had reviewed materials for Sovereign Nation later told her he recognized similarities in Yellowstone . Salkin argues that the hit Kevin Costner-led series, which has spawned numerous spinoffs, “has generated billions of dollars” for the defendants, of which she “has received nothing.” Salkin is seeking damages and profits tied to alleged copyright infringement and injunctive relief preventing future infringement. “This is a classic David-versus-Goliath situation,” Salkin’s attorney Paul B. Lackey told THR . “She spent years putting together the specific and multi-layered framework for a story that has become the biggest streaming success of all time. She has watched the vast commercial success of this story that was stolen from her and decided that enough was enough. We will do everything in our power to get her justice.” Reps for Sheridan, Paramount, Elevate and NBCUniversal have not yet responded to THR ‘s request for comment. THR

articles.title: Why Do We Love Spider-Man So Much?
articles.full_text: Aug 22, 2026 11:02am PT Why Do We Love Spider-Man So Much? By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest Why Do We Love Spider-Man So Much? 15 hours ago ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher in a High-Concept Comedy Without the Comic Highs 1 day ago ‘Mutiny’ Review: Jason Statham Dies Hard on a Cargo Ship in a Thriller of Impeccable Bring-the-Pain Timing 4 days ago See All ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Why does everyone love Spider-Man so much? When “Spider-Man: No Way Home” came out at the end of 2021, it made an insane amount of money ($814 million in the U.S. alone), blasting away any vestige of that era’s comic-book-movie fatigue. I thought the reason for the film’s mind-boggling success was obvious: It had three Spider-Men in it — Tom Holland , Andrew Garfield, and the OG Tobey Maguire — and that made it a unique royal-family reunion of spider-veined spandex. Related Stories China Box Office: 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East' Dominates With $70 Million Weekend as Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Debuts Second China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to Massive $121 Million Five-Day Opening There was a perfect storm of happenstance to how that confluence came to be. “Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse” (an infinitely better movie) had come out two years before, and borrowing deeply from the comic books it did a brilliant job of injecting head-spinning multiverse madness into the Spider-Man saga. The makers of “No Way Home” said, in essence, “Let’s do the same thing — only in a pandering, overstuffed, how-many-movie-stars-can-dangle-from-the-end-of-a-web? way.” I thought it was the definition of a one-shot. Popular on Variety But “ Spider-Man: Brand New Day ” has rewritten the playbook again. The movie is a solid and well-executed adventure, no more and no less, in which Holland’s Peter Parker and his love, MJ (Zendaya), barely even get to talk (because she doesn’t remember who she is). No one is pretending that “Brand New Day” is as great as, say, “Spider-Man 2.” Yet despite that, it is now likely to become… the top-grossing movie of all time . At least until the next Spider-Man adventure comes along. Why Spider-Man, why now? Ever since his debut in 1962, he has been immensely popular (though Stan Lee had to fight a skeptical publisher to approve the character). But if you look back over 50 years of American comic-book-movie culture, it’s undeniable that the two reigning superheroes have been Superman and Batman. Christopher Reeve’s performance in the first two “Superman” films remains, to me (and many others) , the most perfect live-action embodiment of a superhero there has ever been. Those first two films loom mythologically. After that, it was Batman who ruled for decades as the comic-book-movie antihero of our age. Batman is, of course, the only superhero who possesses no superpowers, which makes him uniquely like us. (With a bit more attitude, we feel like we could be him.) He’s the brooding cool film-noir god of the existential night who speaks to our alienation, which is why Christopher Nolan’s “ The Dark Knight ” is the greatest comic-book movie ever made. And let’s not underestimate the original creationist jolt given to live-action superhero culture by the indelible “Batman” TV series of the late ’60s. In half-hour episodes shot on cruddy sets, that show achieved the uncanny sense of being a comic book come to life. Adam West’s performance conveyed gravitas with a wry wink that’s never been matched. Does sweet, genial, wholesomely sexy Tom Holland really compete with all of that? Holland has grown in confidence as an actor, and there’s no doubt that he now owns the role of Peter Parker even more than Tobey Maguire did (Garfield, stuck in a sub-par chapter of the franchise, always looked glum and a bit lost). A generation has grown up with Holland, and now that his Peter is a young adult, he seems poised to rule all the more. One reason that superhero fatigue is always lingering around the corner is that the very quality that attracts us to comic-book superheroes — their Olympian strength and majesty, their pumped iconography of invincibility — is also, in an underlying way, exhausting. More and more, they come at us jam-packed into teams: the Avengers, the X-Men, the Fantastic Four. How super can a hero really be when the world is lined with them? Spider-Man provides a cathartic relief from all that, coalescing around the keyword that almost everyone uses to describe him: relatability . Peter Parker, as we all know, starts off as an ordinary high schooler contending with the effects of a spider bite as if they were the onset of puberty. (He has to harness and control the act of shooting sticky webs out of his wrist.) He’s got bully problems, girlfriend problems, as well as secretly sensitive hidden-identity problems. He’s the James Dean of superheroes (the web-swinging crime fighter as misunderstood kid), and the way Holland embodies him, with a buff abashment just this side of shy, he’s like a boy-band star audiences want to cuddle up with. He also sticks to his home turf of New York City (he needs its canyons to swing), and to the comrades who surround him like family. In an all-superhero-politics-is-local way, that’s a crucial part of his relatability. Yet Peter, as a young adult, also strikes a special balance that speaks to us right now. In 1978, a scruffy but ultimately more optimistic time, the character of Superman kicked off comic-book-movie culture by being valiant, chiseled, indomitable, supreme. A decade later, as the glittery ’80s were starting to crash and burn, Batman arrived to take center stage: a wealthy player who had a hidden dark side, a gruff manner, and a “power” that was a grand illusion. His real power had to come from within. Spider-Man is the superhero for our time because he’s the perfect spiritual fusion of Superman and Batman. He wears all-American red-and-blue spandex and does an exhilarating version of flying around; he’s an Eagle Scout believer in his own destiny. But he’s also masked and furtive and traumatized. In “Brand New Day,” when his spidery abilities get discombobulated, he literally doesn’t know which end is up. And that makes him a mirror of how so many of us feel in these scary days of American turmoil: yearning to stand up to the darkness, yet also mired in it. In the “Spider-Verse” films, which are every bit as amazing (as cinema) as Spider-Man himself, he grapples with issues of identity that make Batman’s look like child’s cosplay. Who is Spider-Man? He’s the light and dark sides of comic-book culture poured into one. He’s the superhero who speaks to our anxieties and our dreams, the romantic teen idol who has to keep figuring out who he is. He makes us all feel like we’re hanging — thrillingly — by a thread. articles.title: Mark Ruffalo Fires Back After Paramount Slammed His Merger Attack as ‘Antisemitic’: ‘Appalling and Fundamentally Dishonest’
articles.full_text: Aug 22, 2026 12:22pm PT Mark Ruffalo Fires Back After Paramount Slammed His Merger Attack as ‘Antisemitic’: ‘Appalling and Fundamentally Dishonest’ By Jack Dunn Plus Icon Jack Dunn Latest Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ From 2016 Pitch in Copyright Lawsuit 13 hours ago Mark Ruffalo Fires Back After Paramount Slammed His Merger Attack as ‘Antisemitic’: ‘Appalling and Fundamentally Dishonest’ 14 hours ago ‘National Treasure 3’ Is ‘Happening,’ Says Franchise Director Jon Turteltaub 15 hours ago See All Getty Images for AFI Mark Ruffalo has fired back at Paramount after the company slammed the actor as “antisemitic” for accusing David and Larry Ellison of “powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world.” “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest,” Ruffalo wrote on X Saturday morning. “Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people. This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel. To be clear, my views come from my own political convictions and should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect. Everything I know about acting, activism, and humanism has been profoundly shaped by the Jewish friends, colleagues, and loved ones who have been integral and family throughout every point of my life.” Related Stories 'One Battle After Another' and 'Marty Supreme' Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards On Saturday, the actor posted a clip of a Paramount board member, Safra Catz, outlining “really profoundly scary technologies” that Oracle used to help the Israeli military after the Oct. 7 terror attack. Ruffalo likened the elder Ellison to a “classic oligarch” and warned of the consequences if Paramount and Warner Bros. are allowed to merge. Popular on Variety “This merger has real consequences for real people, and for the entire country,” Ruffalo added. “Scrutinizing the Ellisons, including Oracle’s business built on data, surveillance technology and government contracts, and the serious threat to editorial freedom and the loss of a livelihood for thousands of families, is fair and necessary. The $111 billion deal would hand one family control over CNN, HBO and Warner Bros., backed in part by foreign money whose influence on editorial decisions has never been fully explained to the public.” After Ruffalo’s initial post, a spokesperson for Paramount said in a statement that the company is “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute. Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.” ‘GTA 6’ to Debut ‘Extended Look’ on Netflix and YouTube on Aug. 27 ‘I Will Find You’ Becomes Netflix’s No. 10 Most-Popular English-Language TV Series of All Time Steven Yeun to Lead Netflix Series ‘Pagans’ From ‘Say Nothing’ Creator Joshua Zetumer ‘Beef’ Creator Lee Sung Jin on Abandoning His Tom Brady Heist Plot and the Finneas, Cailee Spaeny Emmy Snubs Netflix Hit With $105 Million Suit After Losing Copy of Nicolas Cage WWII Film Christian Metal Band Demon Hunter Sues Netflix Over ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ Citing Trademark Infringement Loading comments... articles.title: ‘Sentimental Value’ Sweeps Amanda Awards
articles.full_text: Aug 22, 2026 12:45pm PT ‘Sentimental Value’ Sweeps Amanda Awards ‘One Battle After Another’ was named best foreign film By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest ‘Sentimental Value’ Sweeps Amanda Awards 13 hours ago Monica Bellucci Has ‘Never’ Done Anything Like ‘Ketticè’: ‘I Was on Set in My Pajamas With a Knife in My Hand and Slippers on My Feet’ 2 weeks ago Olivia Wilde Calls ‘The Invite’ the ‘Most Incredible’ Experience of Her Life: ‘It Was the Highlight of My Career’ 2 weeks ago See All 'Sentimental Value'. Kasper Tuxen/Mubi Joachim Trier ’s Oscar winner “ Sentimental Value ” became this year’s biggest Amanda Awards winner, taking home eight statuettes, including the top prize for best Norwegian film. Trier was also awarded for directing, as well as his screenplay written with longtime collaborator Eskil Vogt. “There’s a lot of stuff going on when you make and release films, and we both like to go back to that safe space and rediscover that calm where it’s just our two voices. We are fortunate enough that our films generate more and more noise that we have to shut out, so when we work, we make it personal and small again,” they told Variety back in January. Related Stories China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to Massive $121 Million Five-Day Opening China Box Office: 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East' Dominates With $70 Million Weekend as Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Debuts Second “When I write alone, I procrastinate. When I’m procrastinating with Joachim, even if I haven’t done anything, at least I got to spend a day with my friend,” said Vogt, with Trier adding: “Eskil is my longest relationship outside of my parents. We don’t need to be silly romantic about it, but we have to be honest: it’s a real gift.” Popular on Variety Paul Thomas Anderson’s hit “ One Battle After Another ” tok home the Amanda For best foreign film. On the acting front, Pia Tjelta scored her second Amanda – this time for her performance in “Don’t Call Me Mama.” Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas won for “Sentimental Value,” while Anna Drakopoulou Sverrisdóttir was named Newcomer of the Year for “Brightly Shining.” “The Battle of Oslo” – last year’s opening film at the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund – won the People’s Amanda. It depicts the sinking of German cruiser Blücher, under the leadership of Colonel Birger Eriksen, and “is one of the most famous events in our history. Some people are calling it the single most important event during the WWII in Norway,” said director Daniel Fahre. “We kept it quite accurate, also because it’s such a thrilling story. But we had to look for its emotional side, because there’s no mention of that in military reports. I am sure Colonel Eriksen had doubts, that he was afraid. But nobody wrote about it. I wanted to follow the facts and see what was hiding behind them.” The Amanda Committee’s Honorary Award went to Per Christian Ellefsen, known for “Elling” and called by the jurors “one of Norway’s most beloved actors.” “The first film about Elling was released in 2001, meaning it celebrates its 25th anniversary this year, and Per Christian Ellefsen was nominated for an Amanda Award for the title role in the first film,” they recalled, saying that “few characters in Norwegian cinema have been as beloved.” “While he struggles through three successful films, Per Christian Ellefsen certainly masters the role of Elling to perfection,” they said. Finally, the Amanda Committee’s Golden Clapper went to casting directirs Mette Holme Nielsen and Jannecke Bervell for their contributions to Norwegian film over more than 30 years. “Casting is one of the most crucial elements in film and TV production, yet it is also one of the most underrated. It is in the casting process that the script meets the actors, and this is where the foundation for credibility, chemistry, and cohesion is laid,” argued the jury. “A good casting can elevate an entire production, while poor casting can bring a film down. Casting also plays an important role in promoting diversity, by opening the doors to new voices, new expressions and a broader range of people on screen. It is therefore a profession that requires instinct, an understanding of people, experience and the ability to see potential where others may not.” Mette Holme Nielsen is known for “Kitchen Stories” and “Utøya July 22,” which earned her a nomination for the International Casting Director Award. Jannecke Bervell worked on “Elling,” “Kon-Tiki” or “The Quake.” The Amanda Awards were hosted by Vegard Larsen and Linnea Myhre. The broadcast was produced by Monster for NRK. The full list of awards: Best Norwegian Film “Sentimental Value” Director: Joachim Trier Producers: Maria Ekerhovd and Andrea Berentsen Ottmar Best Director Joachim Trier for “Sentimental Value” Best Screenplay Eskil Vogt and Joachim Trier for “Sentimental Value” Best Performance in a Leading Role Pia Tjelta for “Don’t Call Me Mama” Best Performance in a Supporting Role Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas for “Sentimental Value” Newcomer of the Year Anna Drakopoulou Sverrisdóttir for “Brightly Shining” Best Childrens’ Film “A Mouse Hunt for Christmas” Director: Henrik Martin Dahlsbakken Producers: Martin Sundland, Thea B. Kevin Karlsen and Tor Markus Iden Best Documentary “Flophouse America” Director: Monica Strømdahl Producers: Siri Natvik and Beathe Hofseth Best Production Design Jørgen Stangebye Larsen for “Sentimental Value” The People’s Amanda “The Battle of Oslo” Director: Daniel Fahre Producer: Knut Inge Solbu Best Sound Design Johannes Dekko for “Rally from Paris to the Pyramids” Best Makeup Design Trine Morland for “Sentimental Value” Best Editing Olivier Bugge Coutté for “Sentimental Value” Best Cinematography Kasper Tuxen Andersen for “Sentimental Value” Best Original Score Ola Kvernberg for “Rally from Paris to the Pyramids” Best Visual Effects Fredrik Fottland, Andreas Hylander, Jonas Larsen and Simon Jansson for “A Mouse Hunt for Christmas” Best Costume Design Alva Brosten for “Brightly Shining” Best Short Film “Fata Morgana” Director: Aasne Vaa Greibrokk Producer: Ragna Nordhus Midtgard The Amanda Committee’s Honorary Award Per Christian Ellefsen The Amanda Committee’s Golden Clapper Mette Holme Nielsen and Jannecke Bervell Best Foreign Language Film “One Battle After Another” Director: Paul Thomas Anderson, distributed in Norway by Warner Bros. articles.title: Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ From 2016 Pitch in Copyright Lawsuit
articles.full_text: Aug 22, 2026 12:56pm PT Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ From 2016 Pitch in Copyright Lawsuit By Jack Dunn Plus Icon Jack Dunn Latest Mark Ruffalo Fires Back After Paramount Slammed His Merger Attack as ‘Antisemitic’: ‘Appalling and Fundamentally Dishonest’ 14 hours ago ‘National Treasure 3’ Is ‘Happening,’ Says Franchise Director Jon Turteltaub 15 hours ago Box Office: ‘Insidious: Out of the Further’ Takes First Place on Friday With $10.6 Million, but ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Will Win the Weekend 17 hours ago See All Getty Images for Paramount+ Writer Lauren J. Salkin has accused Taylor Sheridan of stealing his marquee series “ Yellowstone ” from her 2016 pitch in a lawsuit filed on Friday. 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment are also listed as defendants. Reps for Sheridan, 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment did not immediately respond to Variety ’s request for comment. In the court documents, obtained by Variety , Salkin alleges that she pitched her own sprawling Western drama, “Sovereign Nation,” to Sheridan’s management company, Elevate Entertainment, in 2016, only to be told: “Taylor thanks you very much for your interest. Unfortunately, he’s unavailable for TV projects.” The suit then claims that “Yellowstone” was greenlit at Paramount “within months” of her rejection. Related Stories China Box Office: 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East' Dominates With $70 Million Weekend as Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Debuts Second China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to Massive $121 Million Five-Day Opening “Sheridan, however, was not ‘unavailable for TV projects,’” the suit reads, “Instead, he and others used Salkin’s copyrighted works to develop Yellowstone. On June 20, 2018, Paramount Network aired its first episode.” Popular on Variety The lawsuit lists several “specific expressive choices” that “Yellowstone” allegedly lifted from Salkin’s “Sovereign Nation.” Those elements, the suit states, include “a tribal casino functioning as the institutional center of political and development power; a signature confrontation staged in the tribal chairman’s casino office over expansion beyond reservation boundaries; the use of trust land, the absence of zoning restrictions, and a 99-year lease structure as the concrete mechanism for that expansion; and recurring master-plan imagery deployed to dramatize the struggle for territorial control.” Salkin’s lawyers also claim that she “proposed” Danny Huston and Gil Birmingham for “Sovereign Nation” in her pitch deck. Both were later cast in “Yellowstone” and played “materially parallel structural roles: Birmingham as the tribal political leader whose authority and development strategy run through the casino, and Huston as the outside development power broker who supplies the political or commercial path for that expansion.” The suit later states, “When the works are objectively compared, the same coordinated design repeatedly appears: casino-centered institutions organize political power; the same unusual land-development mechanisms propel the conflict; parallel scenes perform the same dramatic functions; and the same actors appear in materially parallel roles. These are not merely convergences of a shared genre. articles.title: Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89
articles.full_text: Aug 22, 2026 2:00pm PT Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89 By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89 12 hours ago Olivia Rodrigo Releases ‘Handmaid’s Tale’-Inspired Song, ‘Serena Joy,’ in a Tiny Run of CDs, With Digital Drop to Follow 1 day ago The Hollies Officially Call It Quits, as Last Two Members of Classic 1960s Lineup Retire After Being in Band for 63 Years 2 days ago See All Rick Diamond Dale Morris, one of the leading names in the ranks of Nashville music managers, who helped build up superstar careers for the group Alabama and then Kenny Chesney nearly from scratch, died Friday at 89. A representative said Morris died in his sleep. “He lived a big, bold, beautiful, blessed life, and I’m holding onto that right now,” said his protege and eventually managerial partner of many years, Clint Higham, president of Morris Higham Management. “It’s the end of an era.” Related Stories China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to Massive $121 Million Five-Day Opening China Box Office: 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East' Dominates With $70 Million Weekend as Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Debuts Second Morris met the fledgling Alabama in 1979 while heading up Dale Morris & Associates and played a massive role in making the group the most successful band in the history of country music, with 33 No. 1 hits in the 1980s and ’90s, along with a huge touring career that led to their being named Entertainer of the Year three times by the Country Music Association and five times by the Academy of Country Music in the mid-’80s. Alabama’s meteoric rise saw the group being credited for being early in country music to adopt some of rock’s touring production values, finding rock-star-level success as well. Popular on Variety Lightning struck twice for Morris, as he oversaw the rise of Chesney from a country also-ran into the genre’s most reliable stadium-filler, who was named Entertainer of the Year four times in the 2000s by both the CMAs and ACMs, and who has enjoyed 32 No. 1 Billboard country smashes. Other artists Morris steered included Old Dominion, Ricky Van Shelton, Jerry Lee Lewis and his very first management client going back into the late ’60s, Bobby “Crash” Craddock. Said Higham, “He was larger than life, and never met a dream he couldn’t build. Dale Morris gave me my first internship, and I never wanted to go anywhere else. He saw things in people, in me, in Kenny, and inspired everyone to reach beyond what we thought possible. Maybe it’s how much he loved life, loved his family, loved us.” Chesney devoted significant passages in his 2025 book, “Heart Life Music,” to describing his relationship with Morris, which came about from him being a huge fan of Alabama and discovering there was a man behind the scenes making it happen. “By the time I came into Dale Morris’s orbit, he’d been to the top of the mountain with Alabama and redefined what was possible in country music,” Chesney wrote in his book, co-authored with Holly Gleason. “Alabama not only won all the awards, sold millions of albums, had iconic hit after iconic hit, they’d created a new mainstream country star who actually looked like their audience… Alabama was high energy, the drums were rock and roll; Jeff Cook played fancy guitars and Randy Owen’s voice had this believability.” Watching the band roll into town for a concert, as a fan, Chesney noticed “there had been a fifth person. A man with white hair, I figured might have been someone’s father. Over time, I realized their manager had been the one to see around corners, didn’t do business the way everyone else did, made a space for a band who’d shown up looking like their fans. He didn’t care about anything but getting the music to the fans—and that was me, standing in a field, waiting for Alabama to arrive.” Dale Morris Morris Higham Management When Chesney finally got the chance to meet with Morris as an aspiring artist, he said, the manager “also asked hard questions, really digging in on what it took… ‘How hard are you willing to work?’ ‘How far will you go when it’s so hard and it’s not happening?’ I would have said anything to get Dale Morris to manage me… “We talked about country music. Even more than Alabama, how songs and charisma were such a part of it, that spoke to country people,” Chesney continued. “He told me his story. The similarities emerged. He was from South Carolina, another small Southern town with heart and people who all knew one another. He worked hard, to build a life, to create something more. He’d been a salesman, and he had that used car salesman thing where he could slap you on the back, be a good ole boy like your best friend. “He loved music, made friends, some people thought he could be a manager. He started with Billy “Crash” Craddock, doing booking, picking up Jerry Lee Lewis. Successful, but he wanted something more. He’d seen a band in Myrtle Beach, who’d put out an independent record. They needed help. Dale applied himself. Once he and Alabama got going, they were in it together. When he realized arenas weren’t paying country acts like the rock bands, he took his band to the fields. Literally, set up a stage, charged a fair price for the fans, and tripled their money. … “Classy, grateful, and humble, he knew how to make deals and close. I had a friend who called him ‘Make a Deal Dale’,” Chesney wrote. “He was raw, too. No airs, just unfiltered honesty about how rough it could be. He had relationships with everybody: labels, radio stations, big promoters, TV people, and publishers, but also the fair buyers, the country bar owners, the folks out in America who held careers together. We were gonna need them even more. “I didn’t bother meeting with another manager. Dale loved the game, and he loved coming up with new ways to do it. If I was willing to work as hard as I said, maybe I was the kid who’d let him do it all over again. He didn’t believe in contracts. Didn’t have one with Alabama, didn’t need one with me. He said, ‘Let’s do it.'” Before taking on management, Morris began his career as a songwriter, reaching the top 5 in 1967 with a cut by Johnny Paycheck, “Don’t Monkey With Another Monkey’s Monkey.” He was inspired by that hit to move more into the business side, at first doing radio promo work for Little Darlin’ Records, before he joined producer Ron Chancey in starting Cartwheel Records. Their success with Billy “Crash” Craddock led resulted in ABC purchasing the label, which spurred Morris to move on to exploring management, starting International House of Talent, where he both managed and booked Craddock. It was a decade into his management career that he discovered Alabama, with an agency arm, Dale Morris & Associates, booking shows for the group and finding increasingly large venues that few country acts of the time were playing. As Alabama’s shows grew, Morris realized other needs created by the group’s growth and purchased Bob Seger’s sound system in order to found Morris Leasing, which later became Morris Lighting + Sound. In 2010, Morris was elected into the International Talent Buyers Association Hall of Fame. He received the T.J. Martell Foundation’s Tony Martell Lifetime Entertainment Achievement Award in 2014 (at which he is pictured holding his trophy alongside Chesney, at top). Higham rose to become Morris’ partner after starting as an intern. In 2018, the two of them sold their booking agency part of their company to Paradigm Talent Agency (now The-Team), while continuing to hold onto the management division. In an interview with Pollstar that year, Morris said, “We’ve elected to stay small rather than to try to sign every act in the world. That way we were able to do what we were able to do and book and manage. Everybody seemed to be happy. We never signed contracts with any of the acts we represented. You come with us and if you want to leave us tomorrow, pay us what you owe us and out the door you go. That’s been our policy for at least 45 years.” Morris was married to his wife, Earline, for 68 years. He was preceded in death by a son, Tim. Survivors include the couple’s daughter-in-law, Jennifer, grandchildren Zack, Colton (and wife Mary Blair), Nick (and wife Shelby) and Kendall, and great grandchildren Mary Dee and Gus. “We’re so blessed to have had 90 years with him as the patriarch of our family,” said Zack Morris. “Thank you to our music industry family and to his vast community of friends in Nashville, Boca and beyond for loving him all these many years.” A celebration of life is being planned for this fall, with details to be announced in the weeks ahead. articles.full_text: Aug 22, 2026 8:22pm PT ‘One Battle After Another’ and ‘Marty Supreme’ Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest Sonic the Hedgehog to Headline Fortnite’s ‘Override’ Season (Gaming News Roundup) 1 day ago Jaafar Jackson: ‘Michael’ Sequel Will Give ‘More Insight’ Into Child Abuse Allegations and ‘Let His Voice Be Heard’ 2 days ago CBS Sets ‘Daughters of 9/11’ Special for 25th Anniversary of Sept. 11 3 days ago See All ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection “One Battle After Another” and “Marty Supreme” took top honors at the Location Managers Guild International (LMGI) LMGI Awarda. The LGMI Awards were handed out on Saturday night and honor the use of filming locations across motion pictures, television, commercials, film commissions, and special achievement categories. Paul Thomas Anderson’s “One Battle After Another” won outstanding locations in a contemporary feature film. It was shot across California’s Humboldt County, Sacramento, Stockton, Eureka, Arcata, San Diego and El Paso, Texas. Josh Safdie’s “Marty Supreme” won outstanding locations in a period feature film for its work across New York City, greater New York, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey and Tokyo. Related Stories 'One Battle After Another' and 'Marty Supreme' Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards “Pluribus,” “Fallout” and “Black Rabbit” were the television winners. “Pluribus” was filmed in Albuquerque, New Mexico, Montana, Nevada, and Spain, and won outstanding locations in a contemporary television series. “Fallout,” shot in California’s Dumont Dunes, Mojave Desert, Antelope Valley and Santa Clarita,” won outstanding locations in a period television series. Filmed around New York City, including Brooklyn and Manhattan, “Black Rabbit” won outstanding locations in a tv anthology, movie or limited series. Popular on Variety Four-time Emmy-winning director and writer Vince Gilliga received the Eva Monley Award for his dedication to storytelling through location over his career and his most recent work on “Pluribus.” Mike Fantasia, location manager of films including “Top Gun: Maverick,” “Killers of the Flower Moon” and “Spider-Man: Homecoming” was presented the Lifetime Achievement Award. “Celebrating our LMGI winners was a truly remarkable experience,” Nancy Haecker, LMGI Awards Chair, said. “The ceremony was a powerful celebration of achievement, filled with inspiring moments and well-deserved recognition, beautifully capped by the genius of Vince Gilligan. Each of this year’s winners is incredibly deserving, and it was a distinct privilege to honor their talent, dedication, and outstanding contributions to our industry.” Winners list below. Varma’s Sequel Titled ‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Korean Esports Group DRX Launches Digital Entertainment Division, Signs Two K-Drama Projects and Game Publishing Business 2 days ago Sriram Raghavan Developing New Thriller in the ‘Johnny Gaddaar’ Zone for India’s Matchbox Shots as ‘Operation Safed Sagar’ Soars on Netflix Charts (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All People Media Factory Kannada cinema superstar Upendra has joined the cast of “ Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl,” the sequel to the hit “Zombie Reddy,” in a powerhouse role, India’s People Media Factory has confirmed. The announcement, made on star Teja Sajja ‘s birthday, also confirms the film’s cast and creative team. The adventure zombie action-comedy marks the South Indian cinema debut of “Tu Yaa Main” star Shanaya Kapoor . Teja Sajja returns as the franchise’s zombie-slaying lead. Related Stories 'One Battle After Another' and 'Marty Supreme' Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards Directed by Prasanth Varma, “Zombie Reddy” was released in 2021, and followed a game developer who must save his village after a scientist’s vaccine experiment unleashes a zombie outbreak. Popular on Variety Suparn S. Varma, known for Prime Video’s “The Family Man” Season 2, Netflix’s “Rana Naidu” and film “Haq,” directs the sequel from a story created by Prasanth Varma. Gowra Hari, whose scores powered “HanuMan” and “Mirai,” composes the music. Hussain Dalal, Prasanth Varma and Suparn S. Varma wrote the screenplay. T.G. Vishwa Prasad and Krithi Prasad produce for People Media Factory. The film will release in seven languages – Hindi, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam, Nepali and Japanese. “The biggest takeaway from my career is that cinema survives on audacity, not formulas,” Teja Sajja said. “When ‘Zombie Reddy’ was made, it was a calculated risk born out of a desire to break the monotony of conventional storytelling. I can’t thank the audience enough for embracing me as a zombie slayer and their unbridled curiosity and faith in what I do next. It’s the love that I’ve received over the years that pushes me to make brave choices. So here’s a promise to take the mayhem to a whole new scale in ‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl.’ As I turn a year older, the zombies turn deadlier. With the audience validating everyone associated with the film, I’m all set to fight the dead onscreen like never before. It makes me very proud to be part of a team that wants to give viewers a grand, immersive spectacle that feeds their appetite for the extraordinary.” Suparn S. Varma said the goal was to surprise both himself and the audience with something unlike anything seen before. “Zombies have always been a fascinating expression of our worst catastrophes, and with this film, we wanted to take that idea to the next level,” he said. “We’ve taken the foundational brilliance that Prasanth Varma created and blown it wide open, building a never-seen-before zombieverse. It’s been an absolute treat to explore a genre with such enormous creative possibilities and collaborate with stalwarts who bring their own seasoned finesse to the film. Here’s wishing one of them – the audience’s superstar and favourite zombie slayer, Teja Sajja, a very happy birthday!” T.G. Vishwa Prasad said People Media Factory has always aimed to push the boundaries of commercial cinema. “‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl’ is an epic adventure designed for a global audience, which is why we are releasing it from India to Japan,” he said. “Everything is next level right from the actors starring in it to the director, technicians, and music. articles.title: Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 23, 2026 1:35am PT Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE) By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Seth Rogen, Colman Domingo, Danny Boyle Join Speakers Lineup at Toronto Market Summit 2 days ago The Freyas, a New Awards Ceremony Celebrating Nordic Film and TV Talent, to Launch in Helsinki (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago Sundance Prizewinner Luke Lorentzen’s Documentary ‘Boatbuilders’ Boarded by Metfilm Sales Ahead of Venice World Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Haus Kino, Entre Acto MoreThan Films has acquired Colombian filmmaker Sebastián Múnera ‘s film “Meteorite,” which will have its world premiere in Venice Critics’ Week (Sept. 2-12). The film follows Tefa and Nia, who live in a small town near the Magdalena River, where they raise Nia’s young nephew. Nia persuades Tefa to join her in smuggling cellphones into the regional prison. Their journey leads them through an extravagant amusement park built on the grounds of a drug lord’s former estate. Related Stories 'One Battle After Another' and 'Marty Supreme' Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards “As they wander among water slides, verdant paths, and concrete dinosaurs, disquieting memories whisper in the summer heat. In a landscape where violence lingers beneath every surface, Tefa is drawn toward an inevitable encounter,” according to the synopsis. Popular on Variety Queralt Pons Serra, managing partner at MoreThan Films, said, “What excited us about ‘Meteorite’ from the beginning was the strength and singularity of Sebastián’s gaze. You can really feel his artistic background in the way he approaches images, spaces and textures, creating a world that is incredibly cinematic, beautiful and also deeply emotional. There is something very immersive and atmospheric about the film that stayed with us long after watching it.” Múnera is a Colombian visual artist and filmmaker. He was a resident at the Cité Internationale des Arts in Paris, invited by the Centre Georges Pompidou. His films have been selected at festivals such as IFFR Rotterdam, DOK Leipzig and FICCI Cartagena. He has received distinctions including the Humberto Solás Cine en Construcción Award and the International Symposium on Auteur Cinema Altiplano Incuba Award. “Meteorite,” his first fiction feature, was awarded at work-in-progress programs in Málaga and Cartagena. The producers are Sebastian Martinez, Mauricio S. articles.title: Rosie O’Donnell Ends ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Guest Run With Trump-Roasting Song: “Use That Stable Genius Brain”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Kid Cudi Preparing To Film “F*ckin Gnarly” Followup To Directorial Debut ‘Doe’, Both Set For 2027 Josh Brolin Says ‘Sicario 3’ “Is Happening” Mark Ruffalo Blasts Paramount For Calling Him “Antisemitic” Over Merger Criticism: “Appalling And Fundamentally Dishonest” View All August 22, 2026 9:44am Rosie O'Donnell sings to Donald Trump on 'Jimmy Kimmel Live'. ABC Although Rosie O’Donnell’s late-night hosting run has come to an end, she graced her biggest fan with a song in his honor. On Friday’s Jimmy Kimmel Live , the 12x Emmy-winning guest host let longtime foe Donald Trump have it in the opening monologue, which she ended with a song roasting the twice-impeached POTUS, who previously called her a “nasty woman” this week. “Welcome to Jimmy Kimmel Live . I am your guest host, ‘Nasty’ Rosie O’Donnell,” she began in the monologue . Related Stories News White House Derides Rosie O’Donnell As A “Nasty Woman” After She Skewers Trump During Jimmy Kimmel Guest Host Gig News Rosie O’Donnell Takes Aim At Donald Trump In Fiery ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live!’ Monologue: “Hi, I Know You’re Watching!” O’Donnell was referencing White House spokesperson Davis Ingle’s statement in response to her joke about Trump’s relationship with White House aide Natalie Harp. “Rosie O’Donnell is a nasty woman and a total slob whose brain has been completely destroyed by Trump Derangement Syndrome,” Ingle said. Watch on Deadline As O’Donnell marked the end of her four-night hosting stint on the ABC late-night talk show, she added, “But I’ve really enjoyed my time here, thanks to everyone who’s been watching here this week, especially the hungry, hungry hypocrite in the White House. Kinda weird to think he spent more nights with me this week than Melania. True fact. “Most of all, I’d like to thank Jimmy Kimmel for inviting me to do this and for reminding everyone that we have the right to free speech in this country, whether orange Voldemort likes it or not,” she said to roaring applause. Having previously teased a “ love song ” she wrote for Trump, O’Donnell finally serenaded the audience. “I would like to close my final monologue here with a traditional Irish song, dedicated to a very special boy,” she prefaced before launching into her version of “Danny Boy”. “Oh, Donny boy. It’s Rosie, Rosie calling / from Hollywood, the Jimmy Kimmel Show / Drop that Big Mac that we all know you’re holding / Because my dear, I worry for you so / Poor Donny boy, your polls, your polls are falling / Your Reflecting Pool is green as Mountain Dew / Your wig’s a mess, your ballroom is appalling / And with Iran, you bit off more than you can chew.” After another verse of jabs, O’Donnell finished the tune, “But there’s a way to end this drama. It’s time to use that stable genius brain. Since we all know you’ll never be Obama, why not resign and make this country great again?” In June, Kimmel announced O’Donnell as one of his talk show’s summer guest hosts , along with a lineup including Tiffany Haddish, Anthony Anderson, Ike Barinholtz, Colman Domingo, Jelly Roll and Matt Damon. On Friday, National Treasure (2004) director Jon Turteltaub revealed that a third installment in the Nicolas Cage adventure franchise is in the works with a script that Disney has approved. “I was thinking about mentioning this tonight, I’ll say it tonight,” he teased during a live recording of the National Treasure Hunt podcast in Philadelphia. “It’s happening. articles.title: Mark Ruffalo Blasts Paramount For Calling Him “Antisemitic” Over Merger Criticism: “Appalling And Fundamentally Dishonest”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Kid Cudi Preparing To Film “F*ckin Gnarly” Followup To Directorial Debut ‘Doe’, Both Set For 2027 Josh Brolin Says ‘Sicario 3’ “Is Happening” Mark Ruffalo Blasts Paramount For Calling Him “Antisemitic” Over Merger Criticism: “Appalling And Fundamentally Dishonest” View All August 22, 2026 12:20pm Mark Ruffalo responds to Paramount. Tommaso Boddi/PMC/Paramount As things continue to get ugly around the proposed merger, Mark Ruffalo has called out Paramount for calling him “antisemitic” over his criticism of the Warner Bros acquisition. On Saturday, the 4x Oscar nominee clarified his views “should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people,” following his comments about Paramount-WBD backer Oracle ‘s involvement in supplying technology amid the Israel-Hamas conflict. “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest,” he began on X . “Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people. This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel. To be clear, my views come from my own political convictions and should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect. Everything I know about acting, activism, and humanism has been profoundly shaped by the Jewish friends, colleagues, and loved ones who have been integral and family throughout every point of my life.” Related Stories News Paramount Accuses Mark Ruffalo Of Being “Antisemitic” After He Slams Ellisons’ Ties To Oracle, Calling Them “Really Profoundly Scary People” News Mark Ruffalo Assumes “I’m Already On A List” For Opposing Paramount-Warner Bros Merger: “Vindictive Motherf*ckers” Ruffalo continued, “This merger has real consequences for real people, and for the entire country. Scrutinizing the Ellisons, including Oracle’s business built on data, surveillance technology and government contracts, and the serious threat to editorial freedom and the loss of a livelihood for thousands of families, is fair and necessary. The $111 billion deal would hand one family control over CNN, HBO and Warner Bros., backed in part by foreign money whose influence on editorial decisions has never been fully explained to the public. Watch on Deadline “Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have called for serious national security review, and regulators still haven’t given the public a real answer. Until they do, the merger shouldn’t move forward. Now is the time to dive boldly into all these issues, not step back or concede,” he added. The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest. Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people. This critical and necessary dialogue… — Mark Ruffalo (@MarkRuffalo) August 22, 2026 After Ruffalo shared a video of Oracle’s executive vice chair Safra Catz discussing how they made some “ really profoundly scary technology ” available to the Israeli military in its attacks on Gaza, Paramount responded saying they are “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute.” “This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone,” a Paramount spokesperson said. Accusations of antisemitism have been leveled against several in Hollywood over recent years, in many cases, falsely used to describe those who criticize Israel’s attacks on Gaza. In February, Netflix threw in the towel on the Warner Bros. deal, refusing to raise its bid against Paramount Skydance’s “superior” $31-per-share offer , following the $82.7 billion deal Netflix signed with WBD in December before the Ellison-owned company launched its hostile takeover . Ruffalo previously teamed up with attorney Norm Eisen in April to urge state officials to enact antitrust laws and block the hostile takeover, accumulating more than 5,000 signatures on an open letter claiming the merger will “threaten the sustainability of the entire creative community.” The letter was organized by the Committee for the First Amendment, the Future Film Coalition, the Writers Guild of America and the Democracy Defenders Fund. articles.title: HollyShorts Festival Set To Propel Documentary Jury Award Winner Into Oscar Race
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Doc Talk Podcast: Rebecca Miller On Her Emmy-Nominated ‘Mr. Scorsese’, A Journey Into The Mind And Mastery Of Martin Scorsese DOC NYC Set To Honor Documentary Visionaries Alex Gibney, JT Takagi, Stephen Maing, And Raney Aronson-Rath Emmys Host Mariska Hargitay Shares Scoop On Help From Colbert Writers And Why Stars Could Make Cameos With ‘SUV’ Toe Tags View All August 22, 2026 2:23pm HollyShorts By the end of the weekend, another documentary short will have punched its ticket to the Oscar race. The 22nd HollyShorts , the prestigious film festival in Los Angeles, will announce jury award winners Sunday in multiple categories, with four of them qualifying for the Academy Awards: Best Short Film Grand Prize, Best Short Animation, Best Short Live Action, and Best Documentary Short. The nonfiction contenders constitute “one of its strongest documentary programs to date,” the festival notes, exploring a wide range of themes. Two of them center on stories of the formerly incarcerated: I Got My Brother , directed by Victor K. Gabriel, examines siblings Jarrett Harper and Baylon Harper, who were dealt a very tough hand of cards as infants. They were shuffled around L.A.’s foster care system, where they faced Dickensian conditions. Related Stories News 'Degree of Certainty' Filmmaker Simon Schneider Tackles The Ironic Origins Of Climate Change Data -- HollyShorts Film Festival News Renée Zellweger, Michael Keaton & Judi Dench Projects Make 2026 HollyShorts Lineup Jarrett Harper (right) and Baylon Harper in ‘I Got My Brother.’ L.A. Times/Breakwater Studios/Schultz Family Foundation Jarrett, the elder brother, was eventually taken in by a man who later abused him, a victimizer who then set his sights on Baylon. Fearing what would happen to his younger brother, Jarrett killed the man and was sentenced to life in prison without possibility of parole. Eventually, Gov. Jerry Brown of California commuted his sentence. I Got My Brother offers a surprisingly joyous portrait of the Harpers as their bond remains unshakeable after Jarrett’s release. Watch on Deadline Freddie Nole Sweet World Films The Second Life of Freddie Nole , directed by Dana Nachman, follows the titular Nole, who spent an astonishing 50 years in prison. When he ultimately got out, Nole was essentially dumped on the street by the prison system, without any resources. Determined not to let this happen to others in his circumstances, Nole founded Meeting at the Door, a nonprofit that offers free transportation, a restaurant meal, new clothes, a prepaid phone, and valuable advice to newly freed prisoners. (After watching the film, I immediately donated to Meeting at the Door). HollyShorts contender The Time My Grandmother Was Held Hostage by Bank Robbers , directed by Rosella Tursi, tells the extraordinary story of the filmmaker’s nonna (Italian for grandma), who was minding her own business one day in her home in Montreal in 1983 when two men fleeing after a bank holdup burst into her place and held her captive. Rosa Tursi in ‘The Time My Grandmother Was Held Hostage by Bank Robbers.’ Aspen Film The documentary interweaves the memories of family members – some alive at the time of the news making drama and others who heard it second hand as they grew up. Remarkably, after more than a 40-year interval, Tursi was able to track down one of the hostage takers to get his recollections of that fateful day. The film, which premiered at DOC NYC last November, is full of humor and wonderful details – like a historical disagreement over whether the bank robbers availed themselves of a beer from nonna Rosa’s refrigerator, or not a frosty brew but a Mountain Dew. What isn’t in dispute is that they graciously offered to reimburse Rosa for the beverage, perhaps out of their newly acquired wad of cash. Black Panther Party “cubs” in ‘When The Revolution Doesn’t Come.’ HollyShorts When The Revolution Doesn’t Come , directed by Aurora Brachman, takes a fascinating look at “Black Panther Party cubs” – that is to say, children of parents integral to the movement. Among them is the son of Fred Hampton, a senior leader of the Black Panther Party who was assassinated by the FBI in 1969, at the age of 21. Another figure in the film: Erika Brown-Abram, daughter of Elaine Brown, who was chairwoman of the Black Panther Party. The film examines how these children of Black Panther Party leaders – now adults – maintain the ideals and purpose of the movement when, as the title suggests, the revolution didn’t come as their parents had hoped. The documentary premiered in June at Tribeca Festival. Markus Füchtner with nutcracker in ‘The Chimney Sweeper.’ RiverRun International Film Festival The Chimney Sweeper , meanwhile, directed by Jack Raese, centers on Markus Füchtner, a woodcarver and descendant of William Füchtner, “known as the father of the nutcracker,” according to the Leavenworth Nutcracker Museum. The 19 th century Füchtner “made the first commercial production of nutcrackers” on a lathe, crafting “standing wooden nutcrackers in the form of soldiers and kings.” Why wouldn’t the film be titled The Nutcracker (or perhaps the German Nussknacker )? Well, it turns out Markus faced a bit of a crisis deciding whether to follow his great-great-great-grandfather into the nutcracker business, or head down a chimney with a brush. Those are just a few of the short docs in the HollyShorts lineup. It has also screened The Baddest Speech Writer of All , directed by two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot, and Emily and Dave Schuman’s The Baker’s Hotline , which “offers a heartwarming look inside King Arthur Flour’s renowned baking helpline, where expert bakers forge unexpected human connections one phone call at a time.” Among eye-catching sport documentaries, HollyShorts notes, is ZINA , produced by Serena Williams, “shining a light on tennis pioneer Zina Garrison, revealing the triumphs and personal struggles behind one of the sport’s most influential yet overlooked champions.” Set Pace introduces Britain’s first Black female motorsport official as she launches her own race team. Miles of Life chronicles a former Ugandan runner “who channels personal disappointment into transforming his community,” while The Angry Bird , follows “female stock car racer Georgie´s fight to reclaim her place on the track following a devastating crash.” The 22 nd edition of HollyShorts opened August 13 and concludes on Sunday. The festival takes place at the TCL Chinese Theatres and venues throughout Ovation Hollywood. articles.title: Josh Brolin Says ‘Sicario 3’ “Is Happening”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Josh Brolin Says ‘Sicario 3’ “Is Happening” Mark Ruffalo Blasts Paramount For Calling Him “Antisemitic” Over Merger Criticism: “Appalling And Fundamentally Dishonest” ‘National Treasure 3’ In Works, Franchise Director Reveals: “It’s Finally Real” View All August 22, 2026 2:56pm Josh Brolin in 'Sicario' (2015) Richard Foreman Jr./Lionsgate/Courtesy Everett Collection After nearly a decade, CIA officer Matt Graver is still waging his war against Mexican drug cartels in Taylor Sheridan ‘s Sicario cinematic universe. Josh Brolin , who starred as Matt Graver in Sicario (2015) and Sicario: Day of the Soldado (2018), recently revealed that a third installment in the Sheridan-penned action thriller franchise “is happening” in the near future. The Oscar nominee told ScreenRant that production is expected to commence “soon” on the threequel. articles.title: Bunny Levine Dies: Librarian Turned Actress Who Appeared In Everything From ‘Gilmore Girls’ To Adam Sandler Movies Was 97
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom Karoline Leavitt Announces Post-White House Job Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo For “Antisemitism” & “Demonization” Bunny Levine Dies: Librarian Turned Actress Who Appeared In Everything From ‘Gilmore Girls’ To Adam Sandler Movies Was 97 View All August 22, 2026 6:47pm Bunny Levine attends the L.A. Premiere of 'Thelma' in 2024 Getty Bunny Levine , a librarian who took early retirement and then began acting on such shows as Gilmore Girls and Shameless as well as two Adam Sandler films, has died, according to multiple reports. She was 97. Levine graduated from college in 1951 and became a school librarian in New Jersey, where she worked before deciding to try acting full time. Levine had wanted to perform since childhood. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries News Kid Cudi Preparing To Film “F*ckin Gnarly” Followup To Directorial Debut ‘Doe’, Both Set For 2027 “I don’t know why. I don’t know that many of us could explain why — it’s just something,” she told her alma mater’s student newspaper, The Daily Evergreen , in 2025. “Maybe it’s in the genes.” Whatever it was, the diminutive actress (she was 4’10”) worked steadily on network television for the better part of four decades, mostly in single episode appearances as a character called “Old Lady,” Kindly Older Woman” or “Grandma.” Among the titles: As the World Turns, Law & Order, Chappelle’s Show, Everybody Loves Raymond, Las Vegas, Private Practice, Ugly Betty, Community, Criminal Minds, 2 Broke Girls, The Mindy Project, Fuller House and Mayans M.C. In film, one of her first appearances came in 1990’s Cadillac Man , starring Robin Williams and Tim Robbins. She was cast opposite Adam Sandler in Don’t Mess With the Zohan (as “Older lady in the salon”) and in an uncredited role as the main character’s grandmother in Sandy Wexler. Also on the big screen, Levine played a movie theater cashier in La La Land , Mrs. Grossman in Let Go and Mona opposite June Squibb in 2024’s Thelma . articles.title: Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo For “Antisemitism” & “Demonization”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo For “Antisemitism” & “Demonization” Bunny Levine Dies: Librarian Turned Actress Who Appeared In Everything From ‘Gilmore Girls’ To Adam Sandler Movies Was 97 Disney Inks Creator Content Deal With Dhar Mann Studios View All August 22, 2026 8:18pm Mark Ruffalo attends the AFI Awards in 2026 JC Olivera/PMC Just hours after Mark Ruffalo responded to Paramount ‘s accusations of antisemitism, the CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center issued a statement to Deadline on the subject. “Words matter, and so does the willingness to draw a line when legitimate debate gives way to antisemitic tropes,” wrote Jim Berk. Related Stories News Mark Ruffalo Blasts Paramount For Calling Him “Antisemitic” Over Merger Criticism: “Appalling And Fundamentally Dishonest” News Mark Ruffalo Notes Many “Were Afraid” To Sign Letter Opposing Paramount-Warner Bros Merger: “Not Unjustified” “We commend Paramount for speaking clearly and refusing to allow prejudice to masquerade as political or corporate criticism. At a time when antisemitism is too often minimized, rationalized or repackaged in more socially acceptable language, this kind of moral clarity matters.” The corporate criticism to which Berk refers is Ruffalo’s initial assertion about Paramount and the finacial support it receives from CEO David Ellison’s father, Watch on Deadline “This is the company that Larry Ellison is using to fund his son David’s Warner Bros acquisition,” wrote Ruffalo alongside a clip of the tech company’s executive vice chair Safra Catz discussing how they made some “really profoundly scary technology” available to the Israeli military amid the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict. “These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you. Look how she revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” He continued, “Larry Ellison will own most of ‘Para Bros’. Larry is a classic Oligarch. They are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.” In response, Paramount said in part, “We are, as always, troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute,” said a spokesperson. “Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe.” Wiesenthal CEO Berk said Ruffalo was conflating two issues. “Invoking Israel in an issue where it is completely irrelevant is a textbook case of obsession and demonization. Paramount was right to call it out.” Deadline has reached out to Ruffalo for comment and this post will be updated when one is received. You can read Berk’s full statement below. “Words matter, and so does the willingness to draw a line when legitimate debate gives way to antisemitic tropes. We commend Paramount for speaking clearly and refusing to allow prejudice to masquerade as political or corporate criticism. At a time when antisemitism is too often minimized, rationalized or repackaged in more socially acceptable language, this kind of moral clarity matters. Invoking Israel in an issue where it is completely irrelevant is a textbook case of obsession and demonization. Paramount was right to call it out. More leaders and institutions should have the courage to call antisemitism what it is, regardless of who is spreading it.” — Jim Berk, CEO, Simon Wiesenthal Center Settlement Talks With State AGs Next Week; Newsom Weighs In On Merger Sony’s One-Two Punch Weekend: $35M For Spidey & $23M For ‘Insidious’ Meghan Markle Eyed For Role In Guy Ritchie’s Netflix Series ‘The Gentlemen’ Michael Showalter Helming ‘Serendipity’ Redo For Amazon MGM & Miramax Read More About: 5 Comments

articles.title: Paramount Sued by Ex-Distribution Chief Chris Aronson Over Millions of Dollars in Pay
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All August 21, 2026 3:22pm Chris Aronson Ethan Miller/Getty Images Logo text Chris Aronson, former domestic distribution chief at Paramount Pictures , has sued the studio, alleging he’s owed millions of dollars in compensation after being let go last September as part of a round of layoffs shortly after its merger with Skydance Media. Aronson’s attorney, Barry Kaufman, tells The Hollywood Reporter he filed the complaint with Superior Court of Los Angeles County on Aug. 20 but it hasn’t yet been formally processed yet before the document leaked online. “I have not even received back a conformed copy of the Complaint and the associated documents from the court confirming that it was accepted for filing,” Kaufman added. Aronson did not reply for comment. In the complaint, Aronson claims that on Sept. 29 of last year — months into a new contract agreement inked in July that would have kept him at Paramount until Dec. 1, 2028 — he was summoned to a meeting with new Paramount co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. The duo informed him that he was terminated “without cause,” the complaint states, and that Greenstein assured him that Paramount would “pay you everything you’re owed under your contract” and “added words to the effect that ‘you’re worth every penny.'” Aronson claims that he was also informed that Paramount intended to “downgrade the position” he was occupying. As to that pay, “the remaining salary and incentive compensation under the agreement had an estimate value approaching $3.9 million,” Aronson’s complaint states, per the unprocessed court document confirmed by Kaufman to THR that leaked without a case number to Deadline. “When the value of lost employment benefits and related compensation components is included, Aronson’s projected economic damages exceed $4 million.” Shortly after the timeline Aronson outlines, Paramount announced in November that it hired Shaun Barber, who spent 18 years at Lionsgate and Summit Entertainment handling such blockbuster franchises like John Wick , The Hunger Games and Twilight , as its new domestic distribution chief. Aronson stayed on until Dec. 1, when Barber took over that role. At the time of his layoff, Aronson was 69 years old. The executive’s complaint states that as part of his termination process, he received disclosure data related to broader layoffs at the company and his own independently commissioned analysis found a statistical pattern of age discrimination. That included layoffs of 62 employees aged 40 years or older and 30 staffers under the age of 40. Aronson claims that Paramount’s HR department was aware of age-related impacts of its employment moves made for business strategy reasons. Aronson, who had overseen the theatrical distribution efforts on titles like Top Gun: Maverick , as well as multiple Mission: Impossible , Sonic the Hedgehog and A Quiet Place installments, stayed with the studio through December of last year. He joined Paramount in 2019 after running distribution at 20th Century Fox prior to the Disney acquisition of Fox studio assets. His contract was renewed in 2022 by Paramount and again in 2025, months before he was terminated. At the time of the September meeting, Paramount execs had “suggested and dangled the prospect of a future consulting relationship” that never materialized. Aronson had subsequently taken on a consulting role to Rentrak Theatrical, the box office data platform formerly known as Comscore Movies, a division that he once founded. Aronson’s complaint says that Paramount not only terminated the role but “abruptly ended what reasonably appeared to be the final chapter of a distinguished career in theatrical distribution.” Paramount declined comment on the suit.
