articles.title: ‘The Girls’: Khloé Kardashian Wanted Her Friends to Have Their Own Show. Then Things Got Complicated
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All August 21, 2026 3:59pm From left: Natalie Halcro, Nicole Williams English, Olivia Pierson, Khloé Kardashian, Khadijah Haqq, Yris Palmer and Malika Haqq at Hulu’s Get Real House on April 22. Disney/Jonny Marlow Logo text Can you now keep up with The Girls? It’s been nearly 20 years since Keeping Up With the Kardashians premiered on E! and helped shift the reality TV genre. Now, after years of having her own life and family filmed, Khloé Kardashian is stepping behind the camera to put the spotlight on her closest group of friends with her new unscripted series, The Girls: A Khloé Kardashian Project . The cast includes six women: Nicole Williams English, Olivia Pierson, Khadijah Haqq-McCray, Natalie Halcro, Malika Haqq and Yris Palmer. While all have experience in front of the camera except Palmer, they bring different histories and relationships to the group. Malika and Khadijah are longtime friends of Kardashian’s, while Williams English, Pierson and Halcro previously starred together on WAGS , another E! reality series. Related Stories TV How to Watch 'The Girls: A Khloé Kardashian Project' Online TV 'The Drop' Trailer Sees 'Snowfall' Characters Go After "New Gold Rush" of West Coast Rap The show, which premiered Friday on Hulu and Disney+, follows the women as they navigate motherhood, marriage, dating, business and their friendships with one another. Kardashian serves as an executive producer , narrator and appears onscreen at times, but intentionally doesn’t position herself as a main castmember. Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter , Kardashian opens up about the drama that surprised her, balancing being a boss and a friend as an EP and why she doesn’t want The Girls to feel like another Kardashian spinoff. She also praises her sisters Kim Kardashian and Kylie Jenner’s acting era and what’s ahead for the third season of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land . THR can also exclusively reveal that season eight of The Kardashians will premiere in October. *** What made you feel like this group of women deserved their own show and spotlight? I knew they were comfortable in front of the camera. I also know that they genuinely like each other. At least some more than others, as I realized later. ( Laughs. ) So how we’ve all hung out, and what I didn’t really realize until we started filming was that there are definitely more little cliquey groups, or some hang out more one on one than others, and not all six have ever really hung out in depth this way. So if I’m having a birthday party or a kid’s birthday party, they’re always there. Also, them being in my family, meaning all these girls are friends with different sisters in different ways, and they’ve all been around for so many years — at least a decade. I felt like this would be a great show. It’s an extension of us. They really are friends. They know where all the bodies are buried. They’re all really good girls. They all get along really well, so I thought. ( Laughs. ) How they have their own dynamics within each of the six of them is also really fascinating. Whenever I post them, people always have questions, so I’m like, OK, let’s let people see who they are because they’re such great, phenomenal women who have so much to offer and so much to show. People should know who they are. You’ve spent so much of your life being filmed. What was it like to be on the other side of the camera and deciding what parts of your friends’ lives audiences get to see? I left what parts of their lives up to them. But I did say, “When you do a reality show, the best thing to do is to be as open and transparent as possible.” Although they’re friends or acquaintances, when you’re doing a show with other people that aren’t family, those other people will probably want to expose you. ( Laughs .) No matter how friendly you guys are. Because if someone feels like they are carrying more weight than the other, other people can get resentful. I film with my sisters and family, and when we go through that where we feel like we’re doing more work than someone else, we get resentful, we’re frustrated and say our piece on camera. And the grace that family gives one another is also very different. So I made that very clear from the start: Be open. Some girls took that advice. Some girls didn’t. And you will see that unfold on camera. These women are all been your close friends for years but not necessarily friends with each other. Some of them we’ve seen on reality TV before while others are being introduced for the first time. Did you feel responsibility for putting them back into the spotlight? I had moments in this where I sort of regretted doing any of this because of the fighting and drama and me being in the middle because I put them all together. I’m now the EP. I didn’t think I would be involved as much as I was trying to navigate them through certain things. I thought, Most of them are used to TV. They’re fine on camera. Some of them took so many years off that it was like they were starting over again. And the insecurities of when you watch, like, “Is this going to sound right?” Because they don’t get to watch the show before it airs, so everyone’s spiraling and freaking out. Also, because I am friends with them, they do feel like they can call me and be like, “So and so said this about me, and I didn’t like that and to get these cameras back up.” It was so fucking middle school. I was so shocked that these girls acted like that. Some of them are more cliquey than others, which is totally fine, but they never spent this much time with one another, and that didn’t go well for a few of them. I felt bad, like, did I ruin some friendships with one another? I don’t know. I thought it would be a much more seamless process, and it wasn’t. But with all that being said, I think that would make for great TV. Was there any particular friendship that had drama and surprised you? I didn’t think Natalie and Yris would not get along the way they did, and there’s some contention between those two, which surprised me. They would butt heads a lot throughout the season, and it would be more continuous. I wasn’t expecting that to happen. ( Laughs. ) Nicole Williams English, Olivia Pierson, Khadijah Haqq-Mccray, Natalie Halcro, Malika Haqq and Yris Palmer of The Girls . Cristian Lopez/Disney Were there any arguments or storylines that unfolded after cameras wrapped? Oh my gosh, there’s a trip to Vegas that they take on camera, and there’s moments of that, and I should have known that maybe there’s some tension with them taking them to Vegas, where they’re partying. I just should have known that probably wasn’t going to go well. I just thought it was going to go really well, and there was definitely fighting there. We got a lot of it on camera, but we missed some. But they do make up for it, and there’s a lot of them. You still know exactly what happened. But even after the fact, I think everyone’s in their own heads. I get it. Maybe the anxiety of not knowing what’s going to come out exactly, because you film so much and not knowing what’s going to make it air versus what won’t, that anxiety will probably eat away at anyone. So there’s a lot of phone calls, often like, “Are you sure I’m gonna look good, or did I say something like this? Did I do that?” I could never do that. So I empathize, but I really think everyone’s gonna love it. With you appearing on the show and being an EP, there’s obviously a huge draw to it and a Kardashian connection. But you aren’t a main castmember, so was it important to you to make sure this felt like their show rather than another Kardashian spinoff? Correct, and that’s exactly right. I’m in a certain amount of episodes, but I pop in and out because, in real life, I would be at those lunches, I would be doing those things. So I made sure to do what I would normally be doing with them, but I didn’t want to feel like a main character. I didn’t want it to feel like a Kardashian spinoff, like you said. I want them to have their own legs and to run with it. They’re that great of girls, and they can definitely carry the weight of the show. But I am also the narrator of the show, so it’s an extension of me for sure or my family. I don’t want people to get confused and think it’s another Kardashian spinoff — it’s definitely not. This is all them. But in reality I am their friend, so I would be spending time with them. I think we did a really good job of me being around but not dominating. Do any of your sisters or anyone in the family make an appearance on the show, or was it, like you said , that you wanted to keep it separate for this project? Yeah, they do. Kylie does because Kylie and Yris are really great friends, so it’s literally just our organic relationships. And Kim does, because Kim, Natalie and Olivia are really great friends. If I remember correctly, my mom does, too. I think it would be weird if they didn’t, because this is just how we interact with these girls. It could be as little as FaceTimes, but these are really people in our close circle that we speak to. I speak to some of them every single day. It’s not us dominating. We are very much in the background. It’s not like it’s going to be a Kylie episode. It’s more like her having a conversation with Yris — just a very natural type of thing. You’ve been doing reality TV for almost 20 years. What did you learn from being on the other side of the camera that you maybe wish you had known when you first started? I’ll be honest with you: I loved how green I was. In hindsight, I loved that we were told, You guys might not get a second season, so go big or go home. This probably won’t go anywhere. Kourtney and I specifically did not think about it. We just were like, “Fuck it, we’re gonna film whatever we want to do.” We were just goofs. We weren’t overthinking. We never thought we were gonna be famous or be a star — nothing like that. And that’s what made everything work the way it did because you could smell that stuff. You know when someone’s putting on. You know when someone’s contrived. We were just who we were. I was 22 years old. And to be green, naive and not overthink anything. What a blessing. I remember watching in season three of Keeping Up With the Kardashians that you took an acting class , and Kourtney went with you for support. With your sisters Kim and Kylie breaking into the acting world over the last couple of years, with American Horror Story , All’s Fair and The Moment , is acting something that still interests you? Is that something you still ever think about? I’m literally traumatized from that whole experience. ( Laughs. ) We can blame season three for why I am so traumatized when it comes to acting. But I get asked to act all the time and to do these roles. I’m never gonna say never, but currently it’s not something I feel like makes my heart happy. It’s not like where my passion is with anything. But, oh my God, do I remember that scene and that acting class and having to say the word “hat” in so many different tones. It was horrible! But I love Kim and Kylie’s acting era. Are there any projects you can say you were approached for? I don’t know anything specific, but I get asked all the time: “Would you ever do a movie?” People will say someone wants you for a movie, and I’m like, no, no, no. I have taken meetings with people who wanted to do a scripted series with me, and I just don’t know if it’s my thing. I’m so honored and so flattered. But I also don’t want to do something that I don’t feel like I could give 100 percent with. I don’t think it’s fair to any production, any people that are working their butts off. It would have to be something I take classes in, really study and try to be the best I can be at it. It’s not something I would ever do, like, OK, acting sounds cool today. That’s just not who I am. I would have to take it seriously, and right now, I don’t know if I have the bandwidth to do all that extra stuff to give another workplace what they deserve out of me. Do you see yourself producing more reality shows centered on outside your family? Is building a slate of shows something that you want to do? I do. I mean, again, I want to be very passionate and intentional with everything that I do. But I do see that. I really do enjoy it. I think with your friends, it’s a different level of work involved because it does get very personal. But I still really enjoy it. I like being a therapist in a way to people. ( Laughs. ) But businessly, I find it really cool, really creative. I like the ins and out of it all. So yeah, I could see myself doing more. Kardashian on her Khloé in Wonder Land podcast with guest Dolly Parton. Khloe Kardashian/YouTube/Screenshot Season three of Khloé in Wonder Land is releasing later this year. What are you excited about with that? And do you have any more dream guests to appear? You’ve had some really great ones. I’ve had some fabulous guests. I’m excited for this new season because it’s going to be longer, which means I have more room to diversify a bit and see what has stuck with my audience versus what has not. The biggest thing that I want to do is branch out a little bit more. Last season, I did a lot of family [episodes], which I still love doing. I think people love that with us. It may be nostalgic for them. But I want to branch out into a ton of different genres. I do love conspiracies. I love all that crazy stuff. I still love self-help-type things. Other doctors that know how to break down whatever issues are so fascinating. I did something with Dr. Amen, and the amount of people that got all this positive knowledge from him made me feel so good because it’s almost like I was giving back to people that couldn’t afford to see him themselves or didn’t have access to his clinics. So that makes me feel good when I’m able to provide real information to people where they have a takeaway. Those obviously aren’t in every podcast episode, but I love when I’m able to do things like that. I could go from a celebrity to a doctor to a conspiracy theorist, and I have more room to play. I love how all over the place it is, but that’s why it’s Khloé in Wonder Land because my brain is fascinated by anything and everything. *** All six episodes of The Girls are now streaming on Hulu and Disney+ . THR

articles.title: Hayden Panettiere’s Boyfriend Gave Her Narcan Before Death, Brother Says
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All August 21, 2026 4:13pm Hayden Panettiere at the amfAR Gala Los Angeles in 2022. Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images The brother of Hayden Panettiere ‘s boyfriend revealed that Brian Hickerson administered Narcan to the actor after both found her unconscious at a South Carolina townhouse on Sunday. Zach Hickerson wrote to TMZ on Friday, giving the outlet a detailed account of what he experienced the day that the Heroes and Nashville actor was found unresponsive in the Airbnb in Greenville, South Carolina, where the on-off couple had just arrived. Brian Hickerson dated Panettiere on and off since 2018; he was arrested several times in the subsequent years for domestic abuse and, at one point, pleaded no contest to two felony charges related to an assault against Panettiere. Related Stories General News Hayden Panettiere's Ex-Fiancé Wladimir Klitschko Shares Heartfelt Message on Late Star's 37th Birthday: "You Are Loved" News Hayden Panettiere's Boyfriend Breaks Silence on Her Death A heavily redacted incident report from the Greenville Police Department released this week reveals details of the brothers’ reaction to Panettiere’s death. After first responders attempted but failed to revive Panettiere, Brian Hickerson became very emotional, according to the report; he also showed authorities a bag containing medication he said she was taking. Zach Hickerson reached out to TMZ to clarify the public record on what he experienced on Sunday so that he can now “mourn without additional noise, chaos, and misinformation being created and propagated by the media as well as the public.” “There are a lot of assumptions, speculations and accusations currently swirling,” he said in his statement, which TMZ published on Friday. “The truth will come out as the authorities complete and release additional details from the investigation. And that is important because the people who loved and adored Hayden deserve the truth.” Zach said that on Sunday morning he attended a church service and, on his way, exchanged messages with Brian; they planned to get lunch and play indoor golf together after the service. When he left church, he called and texted both Panettiere and his brother. He said he assumed they had fallen back asleep, so he drove to the Airbnb where the two were staying in Greenville, where the brothers’ grandmother also lives. He said he did not have the door code and was unable to enter. A loud knock on the door woke his brother, he said; both Brian and Panettiere had been asleep on the fold-out couch in the townhouse’s living room. “When we went in and tried to wake Hayden up for lunch, we realized she was unconscious,” he recalled. “I immediately called 911 and Brian gave her Narcan. We then jointly performed CPR while 911 was on speaker until Fire and EMS arrived. At that point we watched as they tried every measure possible to save her life.” A Narcan bottle was reported to have been at the scene of the actor’s death, and reports emerged that first responders had discussed an “overdose.” The account from the younger brother of Panettiere’s boyfriend and longtime abuser confirms that Panettiere was potentially the victim of a drug overdose. Zach Hickerson expressed his deep sense of loss over Panettiere’s death . “I am beyond heartbroken and devastated by this tragic and traumatic loss,” he told TMZ. “Hayden was one of my dearest and closest friends that I loved and cared about for the last 8 years.” THR

articles.title: Madonna Tops U.K. Dance Charts a Record Fifth Time in 15 Weeks
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All August 21, 2026 4:23pm Madonna and Kylie Minogue Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images; John Phillips/Getty Images for Netflix Madonna is back on top of the U.K.’s Commercial Pop club chart — and this time she’s brought Kylie Minogue with her. Eight weeks after “Love Sensation” first topped the chart with Madonna in a solo capacity, the track soared back to the peak in its new After Hours mix, entering straight in at No. 1 with Minogue joining her on vocals. The remix, helmed by longtime Madonna and Kylie collaborator Stuart Price, got its live debut at WorldPride Amsterdam on Aug. 1, when Minogue made a surprise appearance at Madonna’s Club Confessions party. With Price assisting on the decks, the pair unveiled the track together from the DJ booth — “Are we in gay heaven?” Madonna asked the crowd — before the studio version rolled out in the days that followed, complete with lyric videos featuring behind-the-scenes footage from the Amsterdam event. The reworking unites two of pop’s most enduring dancefloor queens on a single record — a pairing fans of both artists have long dreamed about — and the U.K.’s club DJs have responded by sending it straight to the top. It caps a remarkable run: the mix is Madonna’s fifth No. 1 hit in just 15 weeks on the U.K. dance chart, an unprecedented tally. Since the beginning of May she has also topped it with “I Feel So Free,” the Sabrina Carpenter collaboration “Bring Your Love” and “Danceteria,” in addition to the original solo version of “Love Sensation.” THR

articles.title: Gavin Newsom Says Paramount Settlement Talks Happening in “Real Time,” Signals He’d Like a Deal
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All August 21, 2026 4:39pm California Gov. Gavin Newsom Heather Diehl/Getty Images Gavin Newsom signaled his support on Friday for settlement talks in the antitrust suit seeking to block the Paramount -Warner Bros. merger. When asked about his stance on the controversial merger and the antitrust suit from 12 states challenging it at a press appearance in San Francisco, the California governor gestured to remarks made by the state’s Attorney General Rob Bonta earlier in the week. “Look, I was appreciative, I think this week, earlier this week, you heard the attorney general himself say he’d prefer this settled in the boardroom, not the courtroom,” Newsom said. “So I think there’s some universal sentiment there, if that’s possible. The question is if that’s possible. And what’s the best deal, what’s the landing? And that has to be worked through.” The governor suggested that talks were already happening to determine a way forward for the parties. “That’s a process that’s unfolding, I assure you, in real time,” he said on Friday. “I know there are many meetings that are going on and there’s a lot of conversation about what that could look like, but the attorney general is not just representing the state of California, he’s also part of this coalition with a dozen other states. So we also have to be mindful of that coalition as well.” Newsom’s remarks followed a report in The Wall Street Journal on July 31 stating that the governor was concerned about the states‘ antitrust suit. The story reported that, wary of potential consequences for employment in California, Newsom had encouraged Bonta to find a solution out of court. At the time, the governor did not confirm or comment on the record about his stance. That changed on Friday. When asked about a recent threat made by Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison to take one or two of Hollywood’s remaining historic studios out of California if the antitrust suit isn’t resolved by October, Newsom said he was taking the remarks “seriously.” He said, “We’re hoping that doesn’t happen. And I’m of the belief that they don’t want to see that happen. It’s not, I don’t think, in the company’s long-term interest, but I take it seriously.” He added that he was talking to people on all sides of the debate, given the stakes for California. “I’m very mindful of what this means to the state, I‘m concerned about the state, our reputation,” the governor said. His support for settlement talks puts him in the same camp as Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor in this year’s elections. It also aligns him with L.A. Mayor Karen Bass , who expressed her desire for both parties to “come to the table” and “work urgently to find common ground” on Thursday. THR

articles.title: ‘Voice of Hind Rajab’ Director Slams Israeli Military Investigation Into 5-Year-Old Girl’s Death as a “Smokescreen”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All August 21, 2026 5:03pm 'The Voice of Hind Rajab' Willa The director of the Oscar-nominated docudrama The Voice of Hind Rajab has criticized the Israeli military investigation announced this week into the death of the 5-year-old Palestinian girl, who was killed after Israeli forces fired on her family’s car in Gaza City. “This announcement is a smokescreen,” Kaouther Ben Hania said on Instagram , questioning why it took so long to launch the investigation. “For more than two years, the evidence has been there: independent investigations, satellite imagery, ballistic analysis,” Ben Hania wrote. “And there was the most devastating evidence of all: Hind’s own voice, describing the Israeli tanks circling around her. What more did we need? Did we really have to wait for the accused to decide to investigate itself (yes, itself!) before these facts could finally be taken seriously?” Related Stories TV Meghan Markle in Advanced Talks to Join Guy Ritchie's 'The Gentlemen' After She and Prince Harry Move Back to the U.K. TV Edward Bluemel Is Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot in BBC, BritBox First-Look Image for 'Hercule' She added, “Look at the cases the Israeli military is choosing to speak about today: they are precisely the ones that international public opinion has made impossible to ignore. And what about all the others? Those whose names we will never know because their deaths never broke through the wall of international indifference? Meanwhile, the Israeli military continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza, while the occupation intensifies in the West Bank.” Suggesting that Israel’s move to launch a criminal investigation into Rajab’s death is a “public relations operation,” Ben Hania wrote, “What is needed is justice (delivered by an independent authority) for Hind and for all the victims of the genocide in Gaza.” Israel’s military this week said it fired at the Rajab family’s car and an ambulance dispatched to help them — all six people in the car and two paramedics were killed — as the family was trying to flee an Israeli invasion. The military has launched an investigation into its troops’ conduct. Like Ben Hania, Rajab’s mother Wesam Hamada has also called for an independent investigation and questioned the delay on Israel’s probe. “Why did the investigation and the acknowledgment of the shooting at Hind’s car and at the paramedics come only after more than two years?” Hamada told the Associated Press . “It’s an attempt to distract from what’s happening in Gaza and improve the (Israeli) army’s image to the world. That’s it.” The voices of Rajab and her 15-year-old cousin Layan Hamada calling for help from January 2024 were released by the Palestinian Red Crescent Society and excerpted in The Voice of Hind Rajab . The film received numerous accolades, including Oscar and BAFTA nominations and a Venice grand jury prize win. When asked earlier this year if she thought there would someday be justice for Rajab, Ben Hania told The Hollywood Reporter , “I hope so, because we can’t live in a world without accountability. … I don’t have a crystal ball, but my hope is that this film can be part of the change. Because we can’t live in a world where just because you have the biggest gun, you rule the world. “ THR

articles.title: Mark Ruffalo Links Paramount to Oracle’s Israeli Military Ties. The Studio Calls Remarks “Antisemitic”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All August 21, 2026 5:31pm Mark Ruffalo Ishika Samant/Getty Images Mark Ruffalo has been a consistent opponent of Paramount’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros., testifying against the merger to a Senate hearing, signing an open letter along with hundreds of actors opposing the buy and amplifying his message on social media consistently. His latest missive took aim at Larry Ellison, the Oracle founder worth about $200 billion who’s the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison. Larry’s billions are a key backstop to help his son’s merger of the two historic Hollywood studios cross the finish line. Ruffalo’s post on Instagram highlighted Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military, circulating a clip of former Oracle chief Safra Catz talking up Oracle’s tech at the Israeli-American Council National Summit in 2024 as it related to Israel’s war effort in Gaza. In the clip, which was resurfaced over the past week by several social media accounts, the executive spoke about “profoundly scary technologies” the company had built that could be deployed. The Marvel actor added his own commentary and described the war as a “genocide” that “was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” Ruffalo’s implication to his 20.5 million followers was to link Oracle, the Ellisons and their media empire all together, saying that the moguls “are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.” A spokesperson at Paramount took the normally unusual step of issuing a lengthy reply to Ruffalo, both calling for the temperature of the debate to be lowered while also deeming that actor’s remarks “antisemitic.” “We are, as always, troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute,” the Paramount rep stated. “Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.” The studio rep elaborated, “This brings us to a moment to lower the temperature, not raise it. We’d rather build than further engage in such rhetoric. This simply exposes the true motivation of some who have advocated opposition to this transaction. On the other hand, our commitment to great content is matched by our commitment to acceptance – to every story, every storyteller, and no blacklists, no exceptions, for anyone.” Paramount added, “We understand people feel strongly about this merger and are hopeful and expect that it will be judged based on the legal merits, not underlying bias. We’re asking for the same good faith we’re extending: less rhetoric, more understanding. Paramount’s future is being written for everyone who wants to make and watch great stories.” Oracle, the Austin-based tech conglomerate, increasingly has become an AI power player as well as a stakeholder in TikTok’s U.S. operations. The far-reaching applications for its technology have come under increasing criticism from opponents of the Israel war in Gaza, as well as the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement that has lobbied against companies doing business with Israel. Oracle does have a notable presence in Israel, along with many other tech firms. Mark Ruffalo’s caption referencing Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military. Mark Ruffalo/Instagram THR

articles.title: Emmy Nominee Patrick Ball on His Rollercoaster Journey to ‘The Pitt’ and How His Own Addiction Battle Has Informed His Performance
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All August 21, 2026 7:14pm Patrick Ball Taylor Hill/FilmMagic Patrick Ball , an actor who is quickly becoming one of Hollywood’s top young stars, first burst onto the scene in 2025 with the debut of HBO Max’s emergency room-set drama series The Pitt , on which he plays Dr. Frank Langdon, a senior emergency medicine resident. Langdon works under senior attending physician Dr. “Robby,” who initially regards him as a protégé, but later loses faith in him upon learning that he has been stealing prescription painkillers from the hospital in order to work through a back injury. The show, which marks a reunion of ER star Noah Wyle, writer R. Scott Gemmill and showrunner John Wells, has found a large and loyal audience, garnered massive critical acclaim and last year, for its first season, was awarded five Emmys including best drama series. This year, for its second season, it has landed a field-leading 25 noms, including, in the category of best supporting actor in a drama series, one for Ball, who the TV Academy egregiously overlooked for his work on season one. Over the course of a conversation at the LA offices of The Hollywood Reporter , the 36-year-old reflected on his path to acting and the years-long journey of personal and professional ups and downs that preceded him landing The Pitt ; how his extensive theater background, professional uncertainty on his first major screen project and own battles with addiction (he’s now four years sober) have informed the way he plays Langdon; why, even while shooting season two and the forthcoming third season of The Pitt , he continued to act in theater in L.A. and in New York on Broadway, respectively; plus more. THR

articles.title: Former Child Actress Raquel Lee Alleges Disney Negligent in On-Set Sexual Abuse
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Gary Baum Plus Icon Gary Baum Senior Writer garymbaum Follow Sign Up View All August 21, 2026 8:43pm Raquel Lee Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images In a new court filing, the former child actress Raquel Lee alleges she was repeatedly raped and sexually assaulted by a Disney worker during production of The Poof Point , a 2001 Disney Channel original movie. The suit, which doesn’t name the perpetrator, accuses the studio of negligence. Lee, who was 14 years old at the time, claims that a “middle-aged, male employee who was involved in the filming of the movie” groomed and then assaulted her, first on multiple occasions in his room at a hotel where the cast and crew were staying during production in Salt Lake City and then later on a flight back to Los Angeles. In addition, the alleged assailant “regularly whispered sexually explicit and harassing comments” into her ear while on set and “used hugs to get close to her.” Related Stories TV Darren Criss, Sherry Cola Join Disney's 'Hidden Heroes: A Descendants Story' TV 'Camp Rock 3' Breakout Lumi Pollack on Learning to Play the Cello and the Advice She Got From Demi Lovato The complaint contends that this misconduct was done “in plain view of the cast and crew and could be heard by the sound technicians managing the cast’s microphones” — yet “no one at Disney intervened.” The filing also asserts that the man “regularly made sexually explicit jokes and commentary on the set” around minors, including “sexually explicit comments about” Lee’s body. (In addition, she was allegedly allowed to be separated from her on-set guardian “for the vast majority of each day.”) Lee notes that her professional performance soon noticeably declined and that multiple Disney executives attacked her “changed behavior and trauma response,” accusing her of “being ‘out of control,’ causing the movie to go ‘haywire,’ ‘need[ing] Jesus,’ having ‘a demon inside her’ and engaging in sex acts with a member of the crew at the age of 14.” The litigation adds, “Disney threatened to, and did, cancel” her role in a then-forthcoming production with the studio. Lee is represented by Doug Wigdor, a prominent plaintiffs’ employment and sexual-misconduct lawyer. He has previously represented Cassie Ventura against Sean “Diddy” Combs; Nafissatou Diallo, the hotel housekeeper who accused then-IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn of sexual assault; and multiple women who alleged misconduct by Harvey Weinstein. Disney declined to comment on the litigation. In a statement, Wigdor and his colleague Jane Kim said: “Over the last decade, countless child actors have come forward to bravely share their experiences of abuse by adults in entertainment. As former government prosecutors, our message to the entertainment industry is simple: This conduct is inexcusable, and those involved — directly or indirectly — must be held accountable.” The complaint contends that Lee’s experience was part of a long pattern at the studio: “This is not the first time that Disney has enabled a sexual predator to target and abuse vulnerable victims.” Wigdor’s filing cites a litany of previously reported accusations of predatory misconduct over decades which have been connected to the company. Shortly after The Poof Point , Lee went on to recur as a voiceover artist on the Disney Channel animated sitcom The Proud Family , and recently participated again in its Disney+ revival, The Proud Family: Louder and Prouder . She also worked with the company when she appeared on FX’s Snowfall in 2019. In addition, Lee participated in the hit 2024 docuseries Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV , in which she reflected on her treatment as a Black performer on Nickelodeon’s The Amanda Show . She didn’t levy her The Poof Point claims in the docuseries, which became a cultural phenomenon for its focus on alleged misconduct against child actors. However, after its airing, she noted that Drake Bell’s discussion of experiencing on-set sexual abuse was “retraumatizing” for her. THR

articles.title: Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Wins Best Film in Sarajevo, Ana Urushadze Crowned Best Director
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 2:07am The award winners take to the stage at the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival. Courtesy of Sarajevo Film Festival Sandra Wollner’s Everytime has been awarded the Honorary Heart for best narrative feature film at the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival . As this year’s edition drew to a close on Friday night, filmmakers gathered at the city’s National Theatre where the jury members — including Igor Bezinović, Sara Klimoska, Matthijs Wouter Knol and Athina Rachel Tsangari, led by Emily Watson — unveiled their top picks. A final Honorary Heart of Sarajevo was awarded to Emir Hadžihafizbegović, one of the most prominent actors in Bosnian-Herzegovinian and regional cinema, in recognition of his contribution to film. He joined Watson, Diego Luna, Woody Harrelson and Asghar Farhadi in receiving an Honorary Heart. The festival officially closed with a screening of a restored No Man’s Land by Danis Tanović. Related Stories TV Meghan Markle in Advanced Talks to Join Netflix Show After She and Prince Harry Move Back to the U.K. (Exclusive) TV Edward Bluemel Is Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot in BBC, BritBox First-Look Image for 'Hercule' Austrian filmmaker Sandra Wollner and producers Lixi Frank, Viktoria Stolpe and David Bohun won the best narrative feature film award for Everytime , taking home 16,000 Euros. Led by Birgit Minichmayrhe, the film follows a mother, her young daughter and a teenage boy as they travel to Tenerife in a bid to cope with the tragic death of their eldest daughter and sister. Wollner sat down with THR in Sarajevo to discuss taking the movie on the festival circuit. “The festival being founded during the siege in 1995, I think that’s very powerful,” she said about the Bosnian event. “And you can still feel something of that history here. I felt it yesterday when I had a radio interview. Just from some of the questions, you could get the sense that there might be a different way of approaching trauma or loss here, simply in the way people talked about the film.” The jury said their decision was unanimous. “Moments of cinematic grace float through this mesmerically elastic and transcendental grief-soaked ghost story,” they wrote. The best director prize went to Georgian filmmaker Ana Urushadze for Supporting Role , winning her 10,000 Euros for her next project. It follows Niaz Ninua (played by Dato Bakhtadze), a fading Georgian film star accustomed to playing heroic lead roles. After meeting with a young, female director, who offers him the chance to play a bizarre and deeply unsympathetic character in her debut feature, Niaz leaves the audition unconvinced (and pretty offended). But he soon embarks on something of an odyssey around the city and gradually surrenders to the role. Urushadze said to THR earlier this week : “To me, ultimately, it’s a film about realizing the elusive nature of reality, and taking control of your life.” The judges said they were “enchanted by her irreverent blending of the banal and the oneiric.” Elsewhere, Eva Kostić was awarded best actress for her performance in 17 , winning 2,500 Euros. “A fearless emergence of a young talent. Raw, visceral and deeply instinctive,” the jury said. Best actor, meanwhile, went to Adrian Văncică for You Don’t Belong Here , which comes with the same cash prize as best actress. “For a performance marked by tenacity and understated rigour,” the jury commented. The documentary film jury was headed up by Palestine’s Kamal Aljafari, as well as Austrian Sabine Gebetsroither and film editor Ollie Huddleston, from the U.K. They gave the Heart of Sarajevo to To Hold a Mountain from Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić, who claimed 4,000 Euros. “With astonishingly epic cinematography, this touching portrait of two extraordinary women and a disappearing way of life enchanted us,” said the jury. “Tied together by a traumatic past, their struggle to save the mountain was an unforgettable journey.” The Heart of Sarajevo for best short documentary film was given to Croatia’s Karla Jelić and her project Holy Defiance . She was awarded 2,000 Euros. “This short and extremely powerful film featured a brave act of defiance against resurgent male misogyny,” said the jury. “We salute the film‘s courageous artist who stood alone against reactionary crowds trying once again to confine society and silence women.” The special jury award in this selection went to The Ferry Flows from Zhora Papoian, who also takes home 2,500 Euros. “Without being didactic, this short film showed the power of images to tell stories. We were given time and space to experience the lives of a music teacher and his pupils who are forced to endure grief and loss as part of their daily lives.” Check the full list of winners from the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival below. Honorary Heart of Sarajevo for Narrative Feature Film Everytime , Sandra Wollner Best Director Supporting Role , Ana Urushadze Best Actress Eva Kostić, 17 Best Actor Adrian Văncică, You Don’t Belong Here Documentary Feature Film To Hold a Mountain , Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić Short Documentary Film Holy Defiance , Karla Jelić Special Jury Award The Ferry Flows , Zhora Papoian Narrative Short Film Nobody Said Anything , Tamara Todorović Special Mention Porkatal , Sis Gürdal Student Short Film Unwellness, Réka Pinczés Special Award for Promoting Gender Equality 17 , Kosara Mitić Special Mention Don’t Ask Me If I Killed, Helena Maksyom Special Youth Perspectives Award Skateboarding Is Not for Girls , Dima Duma Katrin Cartlidge Foundation Award Lana Daher THR

articles.title: ‘Harry Potter’ Star Jessie Cave Says It Was ‘Embarrassing’ to Join OnlyFans to Pay the Bills but ‘It Has Saved Me’: Lavender Brown ‘Was a Small Part 20 Years Ago’
articles.full_text: Aug 21, 2026 2:38pm PT ‘Harry Potter’ Star Jessie Cave Says It Was ‘Embarrassing’ to Join OnlyFans to Pay the Bills but ‘It Has Saved Me’: Lavender Brown ‘Was a Small Part 20 Years Ago’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest ‘Harry Potter’ Star Jessie Cave Says It Was ‘Embarrassing’ to Join OnlyFans to Pay the Bills but ‘It Has Saved Me’: Lavender Brown ‘Was a Small Part 20 Years Ago’ 12 hours ago Sandra Bullock Joined Social Media to Fight Scammers ‘Using My Name and Likeness’ to Defraud Fans — Not Just to Promote ‘Practical Magic 2’ 19 hours ago Neutrogena Comments on Hayden Panettiere’s Death Amid Backlash and Says ‘We Made Her Feel Unsupported’; Actor Said the Company Nearly Fired Her for Talking About Postpartum 2 days ago See All ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection Jessie Cave , the actor who portrayed Lavender Brown in three “ Harry Potter ” movies, appeared in a recent interview on the U.K. talk show “This Morning” and spoke openly about her decision to launch an OnlyFans last year to help get her out of debt. Her decision resulted in a “Potter” fan convention barring her from being included. “People just assume I’m rich and I have loads of money and no I don’t,” Cave said, noting her role as Lavender Brown “was a small-ish part and it was 20 years ago.” Popular on Variety Related Stories Noah Kahan Turns His 'Miserable' Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review “So it was embarrassing,” she continued about joining OnlyFans, “because on a certain level, I would have really liked to get a job. But you know what it’s like, you have kids. It costs so much for childcare… [OnlyFans] really has saved me.” Cave referred to herself as a “struggling artist,” noting she mainly does one-woman shows with puppets these days. But her OnlyFans page has afforded her the opportunity to continue with these artistic endeavors: “This is how I’m making a living as an artist which… I want to have less shame about it. I want other people who do weird art like me, I want them to know that there is some way of still making [it].” Cave started an OnlyFans account for her hair in May 2025. She said in an Instagram video at the time that she would be offering subscribers “the best quality hair sounds” and “very sensual stuff.” Cave does not post sexual content to OnlyFans, instead appealing to users with hair fetishes. “My aim? To get the house safe, cover the arsenic/lead wallpaper, build a new roof etc.” Cave explained at the time of her decision. “My aim? To get out of debt. My aim? To empower myself? To prove to those in the past who have misjudged me that I’m not so sweet? To put time into something I never invested in before: self-love.” Cave debuted as Lavender Brown in 2009’s “Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince” and reprised the role in both “Deathly Hallows” movies. While she is best known for her work in the “Harry Potter” movies, Cave has also appeared in films such as “Great Expectations” and on television series like “Black Mirror” and “Industry.” She voiced Lavender Brown in two “Harry Potter” video games. When a “Harry Potter” fan convention barred her from attending a few months later because “OnlyFans is affiliated with porn,” Cave noted the decision was “baffling to me as some actors who do conventions (most actors, actually) have done TV and films in which they’ve done sex scenes and nudity. I’m just playing with my hair!” “I am not upset about the prospect of no more ‘Harry Potter’ conventions,” Cave added. “There’s going to be a new cast now and it’s a different time. Plus, I have done conventions for over 15 years and have enough photos and wizard memorabilia.” Watch Cave’s full interview on “This Morning” in the video below. articles.title: Vertical Media on Track to Generate $150 Billion in 2026 as the Booming Sector Fights Crowded Content Field and High Subscriber Acquisition Costs
articles.full_text: Aug 21, 2026 4:00pm PT Vertical Media on Track to Generate $150 Billion in 2026 as the Booming Sector Fights Crowded Content Field and High Subscriber Acquisition Costs Meta, ByteDance and YouTube projected to generate 94% of vertical revenue outside of China this year By Cynthia Littleton Plus Icon Cynthia Littleton Business Editor @Variety_Cynthia Latest Vertical Media on Track to Generate $150 Billion in 2026 as the Booming Sector Fights Crowded Content Field and High Subscriber Acquisition Costs 10 hours ago LISTEN: Amazon Courts Creators to Build Businesses and Scale the Attention Economy for Brands 13 hours ago LISTEN: How ‘Dateline’ Became a Content Dynamo for NBC News 3 days ago See All AR/COL/Liuyi/Qinfan/Vigloo/ABC TV There’s no doubt that 2026 will go down as a milestone year for the growth in popularity of vertical media content in the U.S. The sector is booming but still incredibly diffuse. That will change as microdramas and other formats proliferate and generate more advertising, subscription and in-app purchase revenue. Those are among the conclusions drawn in a study of the vertical media sector’s growth during the first half of 2026 by Owl & Co., a market research and consulting firm that has zeroed in on microdramas and such as the next big content opportunity for new and traditional outfits. Hernan Lopez, founder and CEO of Owl & Co., is author of “Vertical Economy Report 1H26: Mapping Consumption, Creation, Value Capture Across a $150B Audiovisual Language.” Related Stories Noah Kahan Turns His 'Miserable' Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review For 2026, vertical media is projected to generate $150 billion in revenue in global markets outside of China, where the microdrama biz is well established. That’s projected to be a 42% gain over 2025. Most of that $150 billion is expected to come from advertising revenue ($131 billion) via platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook. The numbers are approaching the volume of revenue generated in the U.S. by subscription streaming platforms. In other words, it’s not insignificant. That’s why Disney unveiled with fanfare a cutting-edge partnership with TikTok to allow authorized use of Disney IP for fan-made content. Popular on Variety “I think it makes sense for every company to lean into this medium which really represents a new native-digital visual language,” Lopez says. “Disney has a brand that’s so unique and it has a global fandom. It makes it obvious why they will be the first ones to do it, but I think the one step that nobody has taken at scale is to produce original verticals.” There’s a scramble amid startup platforms to gain market share and become the brand that is synonymous with the burgeoning medium. It’s increasingly looking like a rerun of the arms race around streaming before the pandemic as many of the top players in vertical apps – ReelShort , DramaBox, PineDrama, MyDrama — spend freely on social media marketing to make a name for themselves. “Some creators and show producers are finding viewership organically. But the apps themselves are spending a significant share of their revenue in customer acquisition,” Lopez says. “It’s a lot like what TikTok was doing in the year 2020 when it was becoming popular. A lot of people were finding TikTok organically, but in addition to that TikTok was promoting itself on ads on Instagram and Snapchat. It’s a similar playbook.” Among the notable stats in the report: ** The U.S. accounts for about 40% of the $150 billion in projected 2026 revenue. ** Meta (Instagram, Facebook), ByteDance (TikTok) and YouTube generate 94% of the $150 billion. ** Meta generates 27% of its total revenue from vertical media. ** YouTube generates 22% of its total revenue from vertical media. ** ByteDance generates 72% of its total revenue from vertical media. The sector is undeniably crowded. Owl & Co. research counts nearly 2,000 apps around the world fielding content and vying for consumer attention. The pace of new series introduction grew 25% in the second quarter of this year but total watch time of new series declined 4%. “Traditional streaming learned years ago about the diminishing marginal returns of launching too many shows,” Lopez writes. Romance stories and drama thrillers are still the dominant genres for short-form serials and recurring series, but that mix is changing. Shows and stars who wouldn’t be out of place on Food Network or HGTV are starting to populate with vertical shows. Programs devoted to business, finance and news accounted for 12% of vertical media views outside of China, per Owl & Co. research. articles.title: Secret Hollywood Group’s AI Plan Focuses on Defining How AI Is Used — While Keeping Humans in Control
articles.full_text: Aug 21, 2026 4:12pm PT Secret Hollywood Group’s AI Plan Focuses on Defining How AI Is Used — While Keeping Humans in Control By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Apple Music to Label AI-Made Tracks Later This Year 2 days ago AI Music Companies Udio and GRAI License Swath of Patents From UMG-Backed Music IP Holdings (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Hook, AI-Powered Music Remixing App, Strikes UMG Deal as It Takes Social-Forward Approach to Fan-Created Remixes (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Getty Images for Disney A group of Hollywood filmmakers, executives and actors has spent the last three years secretly meeting with Silicon Valley executives to try to address a simmering issue in the industry: how to define where AI is useful in the context of a human-controlled creative process. The meetings were first convened in November 2023 by LucasFilm pioneer Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute dean Susan Ruskin. After a meeting last weekend of about 120 participants, the coalition landed on a framework that outlines how AI is already present in the film industry and defines ways humans can maintain control of other use cases — and potentially use AI to produce copyrightable work. Related Stories Noah Kahan Turns His 'Miserable' Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review The group’s framework was first published in the Ankler. Page Six Hollywood reported that attendees included actor and InterPositive co-founder Ben Affleck; A24 partner Scott Belsky; CAA agent Greg Siegel, Paramount+ Originals executive Chris Parnell; “Stutz” producer Diane Becker; 30 Ninjas CEO Jed Weintrob; and director Jon Avnet. Popular on Variety The convening of Hollywood leaders to reshape the conversation around AI comes as the industry grapples with how the transformational technology can be additive to the filmmaking process while recognizing the fear that generative AI has struck into the creative community over everything from how models are trained to the rise of AI-generated deepfakes. The initiative indicates that industry execs and creative professionals are more eager to publicly discuss AI’s place within Hollywood, even if attendees are selectively going public about it. The “ Human Generative Workflows ” document is intended to “stimulate industry discussion and provide a common vocabulary for thinking about authorship in an era of generative AI,” the group said in its first public statement. The group acknowledged that the document wasn’t intended to address some of the more pressing issues surrounding AI, such as how models are trained and the potential impact on jobs. “This conversation is bigger than AI,” the group said about the framework. “It is about bringing the entertainment community together to shape a shared approach to the future of the creative process. The future of entertainment will be shaped not by AI alone, but by the choices we make about how AI is integrated into the creative process.” The framework outlines several issues with how the conversation around AI is framed within the industry, including that the acronym “AI” is “used in the same breath to mean a color grading assist in DaVinci Resolve and a prompted synthetic performance that replaces an actor.” Instead, the group suggests the industry develop a classification system around the different variations of AI in place to aid productions and, in the future, audiences. It also outlines how certain tools within the industry that are built on machine learning are already producing copyrightable work, publishing a list of definitions of industry workflows that are generally assisted by AI such as “upscaling and sharpening” and “markerless mocap.” The distinction comes down to AI-generated assets such as voices and likenesses, which it defines as items that “substitute for human creative work” and “the difference between a set of tools and processes that serve human creative vision and a prompt-based generative tool that replaces it.” Those are not copyrightable, the group says. The group hopes that publishing its framework will provoke a conversation within the film industry — and, too, creatives focused on music, sound and writing — that helps shape the various use cases for AI, including conversations about how artists can consent and be compensated for the use of their likenesses for generative purposes. “The future of entertainment will be shaped not by AI alone, but by the choices we make about how AI is integrated into the creative process,” it writes. articles.title: Emmy Overachiever Jason Bateman on Whether He Considers Himself an Actor or Director First
articles.full_text: Aug 21, 2026 4:45pm PT Emmy Overachiever Jason Bateman on Whether He Considers Himself an Actor or Director First Awards Circuit Podcast: The 'Black Rabbit' star/director and 'DTF St. Louis' star/producer on his multiple nominations and more. On the Awards Circuit Roundtable, we look at the state of the race as Phase 2 voting continues. By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Variety Editor at Large franklinavenue Latest Emmy Overachiever Jason Bateman on Whether He Considers Himself an Actor or Director First 10 hours ago Miss USA, Miss Teen USA Pageants Pulled From The CW Just a Week Before Air 13 hours ago How Did the Emmys’ Documentary Category Get So Star-Studded? 16 hours ago See All JC Olivera/Variety Jason Bateman is this year’s Emmy overachiever, nominated for lead limited series actor and limited series directing on Netflix’s “ Black Rabbit ,” and as both supporting actor and executive producer on another limited series, HBO Max’s “ DTF St. Louis .” So where does the multi-hyphenate’s brain reside more in these days, as an actor or director? “They are in both worlds at the same time, but they kind of always have been,” Bateman tells Variety ‘s Awards Circuit Podcast . “That’s why I was so drawn to having the official job of directing. Acting at an early age became so comfortable for me that I was able to really observe all the incredible work going around me. All the technical work of the camera and sound and lighting and what might be happening with editing later. So I’ve always thought about all of that — what a team it takes.” Related Stories Noah Kahan Turns His 'Miserable' Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review Bateman, of course, has been acting since he was a child — “Little House on the Prairie,” “Silver Spoons,” “It’s Your Move” and even “The Hogan Family” as a teen. But he also started looking at directing as a young actor. Popular on Variety “I’m enormously grateful that I’m still working in this industry in this town,” he says. “I mean, I’ve gained a lot of experience in this business, and one of the things that’s really clear to me is that the best people are not guaranteed employment.” Bateman, of course, saw that firsthand in the lean years that came prior to “Arrested Development,” which set his career on a new, lucrative course that eventually included smashes like Netflix’s “Ozark,” his podcast “SmartLess” with buddies Will Arnett and Sean Hayes, and then most recently the back-to-back success of “Black Rabbit” and “DTF St. Louis.” Bateman talked about all that, as well as his next project — and he took the Awards Circuit Podcast 10 Questions Quiz! — on this edition. Also in this episode, we look at the latest moves in the Emmy race as Phase 2 voting continues — and marvel at the variety special (prerecorded) category, which includes a showdown between Taylor Swift, Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande. Listen below! Is Bateman stunned at the Emmy surplus he’s been given this year with his four nominations? “Obviously you don’t do this work for the money or the accolades, but those things are really sort of exciting and helpful and practical,” he says. “When you do something and it comes together as well as these two projects did, it’s a little bit of magic. There are so many people that go into making these things and making them not fall flat on their face. It’s a miracle that any of these things work because the ball is constantly wanting to drop … I just feel so fortunate.” Bateman also notes that he has the luxury of choosing projects and characters who have such a unique and interesting tone. Both Vince in “Black Rabbit” and Clark in “DTF” are tragic in their own ways. “Vince is just a disaster, kind of a broken, self-destructive guy,” Bateman says. “Clark’s main plot point for him is he wants to cheat on his wife. Yet they are both just heartbreakingly relatable, human and flawed, and they just don’t have the coping skills that most of the viewers have.” Next up, Bateman just directed the film “The Cackling of the Dodos” for Netflix. “Sam Rockwell and Woody Harrelson brought me the script and said, ‘would you would you direct us in this?’ I didn’t even really need to read it, when you get that kind of call from those two guys. It’s a dark, dark comedy about these two guys who run a farm and they find a dead body in the grain bin and try to figure out how to get rid of it — and create a couple of more dead bodies doing it. It’s kind of like an old Coen Brothers-type of film.” For Bateman’s first time in Variety , we found a clip from Nov. 16, 1979, announcing that he had signed with the Dorothy Day Otis/Jack Rose Agency. “I was around 10,” he remembers. “I remember getting an agent for the first time. That was really an interesting process. It was after this educational film, I’d done one of those little films, and then I was like, ‘well, Dad, I should get an agent and maybe do some commercials and try to work my way in.’ So he took pictures of me, and off we went.” 10 QUESTIONS WITH JASON BATEMAN: 1. Childhood nickname: “’Jayco.’ My dad used to call me that.” 2. Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into it now: “I would play arcade games, 10 hours a day, and I think I’d still do that if I had the time. In fact, the first time I made some money, I got my parents to let me buy a Donkey Kong machine, like a real stand-up arcade machine, and we put it in the garage. And I just played it all day, all night.” 3. Go-to karaoke or sing-in-the-shower song: “I’m so horrified with the sound of my own voice singing. I don’t even sing in the shower. Not even alone. I don’t sing. I cringe myself right out of the water!” 4. Give me an alternate title for ‘Black Rabbit’: “One and One Make None.” 5. What’s your secret talent? : “If I properly ball up a piece of chewing gum, I can tilt my head straight back and hover it above my lips by blowing a stream of air.” 6. Favorite ice cream flavor : “I’m a cookies and cream guy.” 7. The one item you couldn’t live without : “Classical music takes me to a place where I think the best part of me lives, and where my best thinking and processing and planning comes from. I just love it for many reasons, and I think it started with my dad getting me into it like he did with movies and television. But then really seeing how classical music is used in film and television, from ‘2001’ or ‘Apocalypse Now’ or ‘Amadeus’ or any of the John Williams films. It’s incredible. I listen to classical music almost all day every day.” 8. What TV show in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of? : “Fawlty Towers.” 9. Fictional character you most admire : “I don’t know. That’s millions and millions of characters. I have to take a pass on that one because there would be many right answers for me.” 10. Your favorite piece of advice : “This sounds a bit earnest and probably a bit cliché, but it really is true, and something that’s so needed for anybody that’s got the kind of complicated thing of fame and having a public job. But in any position of leadership, doing unto others as you would you want them to do to you. When I meet somebody on the street, and I might not be in some great mood, or I’m with the family, or that’s still the one moment that they have. They may have been watching me do stuff for years on television or film, and want to say ‘hi’ and say that they like show X or movie Y. If I were to be short or dismissive of that, that’s louder than anything that they’ve watched. I try to remember that. I’m certainly far from perfect and far from consistent, but I try to be better every day.” Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines, and much more. articles.title: Paramount Slams Mark Ruffalo Merger Attack as ‘Antisemitic,’ Says Company Does Not ‘Tolerate Prejudice of Any Kind’
articles.full_text: Aug 21, 2026 5:01pm PT Paramount Slams Mark Ruffalo Merger Attack as ‘Antisemitic,’ Says Company Does Not ‘Tolerate Prejudice of Any Kind’ By Matt Donnelly Plus Icon Matt Donnelly Chief Correspondent @MattDonnelly Latest Amid ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Leaks, Hollywood’s Battle Against Piracy Enters a Whole New Era 18 hours ago Bob Iger Gets All-Star Send-Off From Robert Downey Jr., Harrison Ford and New CEO Josh D’Amaro at D23 Disney Legends Ceremony 5 days ago Squishmallows Movie in the Works at Amazon MGM (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago See All Getty Images for Tribeca Festiva Paramount has come out swinging against a Friday screed from Mark Ruffalo , in which the award-winning actor accused moguls David and Larry Ellison of “powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world.” A spokesperson for the David Ellison -run enterprise said the company is “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute. Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.” Related Stories Noah Kahan Turns His 'Miserable' Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review Ruffalo took to Instagram with a years-old clip of Paramount board member Safra Catz discussing “really profoundly scary technologies” that Oracle used to assist the Israeli military following the Oct. 7 terror attacks. That 2023 event saw Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups kill 1,195 Israelis and foreign nationals and abduct 251 people. Ruffalo referred to Larry Ellison as a “classic Oligarch,” and warned of the danger of his son’s bid to combine Paramount with Warner Bros. Discovery. Referencing the Catz clip, Ruffalo encouraged his followers to “look how she revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” Popular on Variety Ruffalo was one of the earliest Hollywood figures to decry the proposed Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger. Numerous industry sources have expressed concern over Ruffalo’s conflating the merger with anti-Israel sentiments. Paramount said Ruffalo’s post “brings us to a moment to lower the temperature, not raise it. We’d rather build than further engage in such rhetoric. This simply exposes the true motivation of some who have advocated opposition to this transaction. On the other hand, our commitment to great content is matched by our commitment to acceptance – to every story, every storyteller, and no blacklists, no exceptions, for anyone.” TheWrap first reported Paramount’s statement. articles.title: Paramount and State A.G. to Meet Monday to Discuss Settlement of Antitrust Case
articles.full_text: Aug 21, 2026 5:19pm PT Paramount and State A.G. to Meet Monday to Discuss Settlement of Antitrust Case By Gene Maddaus Plus Icon Gene Maddaus Senior Media Writer @GeneMaddaus Latest Chris Aronson Files $4 Million Age Discrimination Suit Over Ouster at Paramount 12 hours ago Amid ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey’ Leaks, Hollywood’s Battle Against Piracy Enters a Whole New Era 18 hours ago Lawmakers Offer Film Industry a Fix on California Tax Credit Cap 1 day ago See All Getty Images Paramount Skydance representatives are expected to meet on Monday with the California Attorney General’s office to discuss a potential settlement of the states’ antitrust case, according to two sources familiar with the situation. Paramount has been pushing hard for a deal to allow its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery to close. The deal is currently on hold pending a March trial in federal court in Oakland. Related Stories The Beatles Ink Licensing and Merch Deal With Universal Music Ahead of Biopics Attorney General Rob Bonta has said he is open to settlement negotiations, but has also said that Paramount has thus far been unwilling to offer the kind of structural remedies that would be needed to satisfy the states’ concerns. Popular on Variety A Paramount spokesperson declined to comment. Bonta led a 12-state coalition to challenge the merger in July, arguing that it would illegally contract the marketplace for theatrical distribution and basic cable. The merger would consolidate two of Hollywood’s five legacy studios and two of the top three cable programmers. Under federal rules, the two sides will have to at least try to settle the case in front of a magistrate judge at some point. At a hearing this week, Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin asked the parties to identify two potential magistrates who could oversee mediation by next Wednesday. A parade of interested parties has recently come out in favor of a settlement, including the Directors Guild of America, IATSE, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Cinema United, the trade group representing theater chains. “Earlier this week, you heard the attorney general himself say he’d prefer this settle in the boardroom, not the courtroom,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said Friday. “I think there’s some universal sentiment there, if that’s possible. The question is is that possible. And what’s the best deal? That has to be worked through. That’s a process that’s unfolding, I assure you, in real time.” Paramount has pledged various commitments to try to get a deal done, including a promise to make 30 films a year for the next three years, and to keep them exclusively in theaters for at least 45 days. Bonta’s office, however, has argued that such behavioral remedies have proven impossible to enforce in the past. The Writers Guild of America has filed its own lawsuit, which is set to be tried along with the states’ case next March. The WGA is also a party to the stipulation that puts the merger on hold until the trial, and would have be involved the parties are aiming to reach a global resolution. A WGA spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. articles.title: ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher in a High-Concept Comedy Without the Comic Highs
articles.full_text: Aug 21, 2026 6:54pm PT ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher in a High-Concept Comedy Without the Comic Highs The directors of "Bad Moms" satirize the New Age elitism of wellness culture, but they're working in a form that's running out of gas. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher in a High-Concept Comedy Without the Comic Highs 7 hours ago ‘Mutiny’ Review: Jason Statham Dies Hard on a Cargo Ship in a Thriller of Impeccable Bring-the-Pain Timing 3 days ago ‘The End of Tom Six’ Review: The Director of the ‘Human Centipede’ Films Has Multiple Sclerosis and Is Sharing the Horror. This Confessional Doc Is His Witty Self-Defense 5 days ago See All Vince Valitutti Movie genres wax and wane over time in a way that can be borderline imperceptible. The Western did its slow fade through the 1960s, but it took a while to realize that it was heading into the sunset (and then, of course, it came back). On a less exalted level, I watched “ Spa Weekend ” and realized that the genre it’s in — the high-concept comedy with the concept in the title, the movie that puts out a vibe of “Look, I’m crass and dumb and obvious! And that’s why you like me!” — may now be entering its twilight zone. Related Stories Noah Kahan Turns His 'Miserable' Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review Written and directed by Jon Lucas and Scott Moore, who made the brashly clever and likable “Bad Moms” (but were launched by their script for “The Hangover,” and in a way they’re still writing it), “Spa Weekend” is a comedy about four old friends who go on a deluxe spa getaway. The film has its minor-league version of a star cast ( Leslie Mann , Anna Faris , Michelle Buteau , Isla Fisher ), with Fisher cast against type as the Melissa McCarthy character — a foul-mouthed British trainwreck in ridiculously loud clothing who becomes the film’s bull in the aroma-therapy shop. Popular on Variety It’s all very standard, and the idea of putting the satirical screws to the New Age elitism of wellness culture certainly has potential. But watching “Spa Weekend,” you feel how tired and predictable the jokes are (it’s the script that needs a massage). And I’m talking about the “wild” jokes, like when the women take a raucous golf-cart ride through the spa grounds, or when a divorced couple work off their aggression by having a mud fight in a mud bath, or the moment when a session of “goat yoga” devolves — inevitably — into a Who let the goats out? free-for-all. It’s “anarchic” yet weirdly tame and expected. You watch these rote antics and think: Where are Barb and Star when you need them? The four women are cardboard-cutout archetypes, played in amiable lightweight fashion. There’s Jane (Mann), a high-strung attorney and divorced single mother whose birthday weekend this is, and who is such an overscheduled control freak that she can only put a date with a man on her calendar three months in advance; Coco (Michelle Buteau), also divorced with two kids, who’s presented as a walking fount of anger issues (though if you call her on it, she’ll get angry at you for reducing her to the “angry Black woman”); Sophie (Anna Faris), a blonde mouse who’s been the personal assistant to a tyrannical boss for 10 years; and Fisher’s bawdy, antic, disheveled Mel, who the other three can’t stand, but as the movie explains — it becomes a central theme — every female friend group needs one person the others secretly hate. I had mild hopes for “Spa Weekend” when it introduced the Solaris Eden Beach spa, a luxe white-on-white beachfront hotel that turns pampering into a form of exhibitionism. When Jane and her friends arrive at the front desk, they’re offered a choice of Champagne or hibiscus water, and the spa’s general manager is a guru named Shanti (Erika Keynatz) who glows with well-tended superiority. Then, of course, there’s Kai (Adam Demos), the hot Aussie yoga instructor who makes instant eye contact with Jane (“C’mon, Magic Mike,” says Mel, “let’s see your big ding-dong!”). About 45 minutes in, Jane and Kai run into each at the otherwise empty hotel bar, and Jane explains that she can see right through the posh pretense of the spa treatments — the spaced-out music and yoga that’s just “stretching,” the Goopy optics of it all. But it’s as if the movie had already seen through its own joke. By all rights, Isla Fisher’s Mel should be the one making us laugh. I’ve always been a fan of this actor, and she gives a pinpoint performance as a dissolute narcissist who’s like a more unhinged Bridget Jones. But Fisher, in a weird way, gives too grounded a performance. She doesn’t have that spark plug of trashy insanity in her DNA. (We don’t feel her unconscious need to destroy.) Or maybe the lines just aren’t crazy enough. Frankly, I had the same problem with “The Hangover,” a movie I always thought was more prechewed than it pretended to be. And you wish “Spa Weekend” found a way to give Leslie Mann, the film’s straight-arrow center of gravity, a bit more of a spin. “Spa Weekend” is being distributed by Black Bear Pictures — a good company, only this sort of thing used to be the province of major studios, and now it’s being relegated to the indie and streaming market. (See this month’s “Super Troopers 3.”) Nothing wrong with that, of course. But it’s a sign that overly processed bad-behavior comedies like “Spa Weekend” are a form that’s running out of gas. What happens at the spa stays at the spa. But it might as well not, since we’ve seen it before. ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher in a High-Concept Comedy Without the Comic Highs Reviewed at Regal Union Square, New York, Aug. 21, 2026.
