articles.title: ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror
articles.full_text: Aug 17, 2026 12:59am PT ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror Director Joseph Archer and screenwriter-star Cathy Wippell will turn heads with this undeniably stunt-y but eerie novelty set in Victorian London and shot as though with a pinhole camera. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror 1 hour ago ‘Mission’ Review: An All-In George MacKay Performance Anchors a Fevered Mental Illness Portrait 19 hours ago ‘The State of Us’ Review: A Pair of Spirited Performances Lift a Familiar Yorkshire Tearjerker 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Silicon Gothic Found footage may be a fairly stale gimmick in horror these days, but the low-budget British indie “ Snapshot ” finds a way to freshen up the idea — and if that largely amounts to layering another technical gimmick over it, the results are nonetheless striking. Emulating the look of 19th-century pinhole photography, with the entire film presented in a circular 1:1 aspect ratio, this resourceful debut feature from director Joseph Archer and screenwriter-star Cathy Wippell turns the visual restrictions of that device to its advantage: This imagining of the well-trodden Jack the Ripper tale hinges heavily on what can’t be seen, as it follows a group of young Victorian women pursuing their own supernatural theory behind the killings terrorizing London, and the pioneering male filmmaker who takes it upon himself to document their efforts. Related Stories Hollywood Failed Hayden Panettiere Hayden Panettiere, 'Heroes' and 'Scream' Star, Dies at 36 Viewers must swallow a certain degree of contrivance to go along with “Snapshot.” For one thing, it demands we accept that Tamworth (voiced by “All My Friends Hate Me” star Tom Stourton), the heard-but-not-seen inventor behind the camera, could have assumed a near fly-on-the-wall kind of presence in various unseemly locations through east London’s underbelly to have captured these revealingly candid reels. (Complete with leagues-ahead-its-time sound-recording technology, to boot.) Popular on Variety Introductory text informs us that this footage was discovered languishing in the (fictitious) “British Film Archive,” and Archer, also the film’s editor, deftly maintains a jumpy structural sense of reels rather crudely sequenced, with telling gaps between them. As DP, his visual approximation of early-cinema techniques, often wittily distressed, sometimes betrays his contemporary ones; the actors, likewise, slip in and out of period register. Still, if its illusion isn’t entirely complete, “Snapshot” is nonetheless an effectively eerie novelty, sure to attract attention in arthouse horror circles following its competition premiere in Edinburgh. Its next stop will be London’s genre-specific FrightFest later this month, but international festival programmers should take an interest too. The morbidly lilting music-hall staple “Two Lovely Black Eyes” (“Only for telling a man he was wrong,” runs the follow-up lyric) recurs throughout “Snapshot,” becoming the defining musical theme in a story of female exploitation and exasperation in a society not yet rocked by the women’s suffrage movement. Tamworth, evidently a young man, appears sympathetic to the cause, spending much time in female company to chronicle the reality of their lives outside the sphere of patriarchal influence; still, as the film continues, the palpable shadow of the male gaze on proceedings becomes unnervingly hard to shake. His key subjects include Minnie (Wippell, writing herself the juiciest role here), an intrepid, rebellious type who’s also something of a class tourist: Though raised in a well-to-do London family, she prefers to hang out with the sex workers and miscreants of the city’s working-class East End, where her close friend Fanny (Hazel Rogers) practices the oldest profession in the care of maternal madam Evelyn (Nadia Lamin). Of late, women like Fanny have been turning up dead in the area’s backstreets with alarming frequency; a climate of terror is setting in as the Ripper’s body count rises, but there’s still a living to be made. In any case, Minnie and Fanny — along with other women in their circle — have become convinced that the killer is actually a phantom entity, and are determined to hunt the ghost down by patrolling his spooked environs and making spiritual contact with his dead victims — with Tamworth, of course, reliably on hand to make a permanent record of this plainly doomed project. As “Snapshot” becomes a queasily sustained exercise in waiting for the penny to drop, Archer and Wippell keep the story lean and the overt scares sparse, instead cultivating a more subtly pervading mood of disquiet and dread that aims to honor the everyday experience of women in this particular milieu. “Snapshot” does risk feeling more like a very clever exercise than a fully realized narrative: Even with a tight 86-minute running time, the drama begins to spin its wheels a bit in the second half, while the characters have limited room to grow in this confined formal setup. But the payoff is mordantly effective, and the film’s fine sense of gallows humor gives it some welcome tonal breadth. It promises bigger, even more ambitious things from Archer, Wippell and their production outfit Silicon Gothic, and stakes out a commitment to horror filmmaking that doesn’t merely chase Hollywood trends, instead using both the resources and the cultural baggage on their doorstep. ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, July 30, 2026. In Edinburgh Film Festival (Competition), FrightFest. Running time: 86 MIN. Production: (U.K.) A Silicon Gothic production in association with Fieber.Film, Serge Cedrick, TrainTripper Films. (World sales: Alief, Paris.) Producers: Joseph Archer, Cathy Wippell, Mario Stefan, Suresh Cedrick Pereira, Chippy Babu. Executive producers: Mickey Andro, Chippy Babu, Michael Osowski, Suresh Cedrick Pereira, Tushar Rakheja, Mario Stefan, Megan Teo, Barry Vonk. Crew: Director, camera, editor: Joseph Archer. Screenplay: Cathy Wippell. With: Tom Stourton, Cathy Wippell, Hazel Rogers, Lydia Helen, Nadia Lamin, Rosie-Bella Johnson. articles.title: ‘Heartstopper’ Star Rhea Norwood, ‘Enola Holmes’ Actor Susan Wokoma, ‘Dear England’ Writer James Graham Join U.K. National Youth Theatre’s 70th Anniversary Show (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 17, 2026 1:00am PT ‘Heartstopper’ Star Rhea Norwood, ‘Enola Holmes’ Actor Susan Wokoma, ‘Dear England’ Writer James Graham Join U.K. National Youth Theatre’s 70th Anniversary Show (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Deluxe Media and Tohokushinsha Film Corporation Set Strategic Asia-Pacific Localization Partnership (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘Heartstopper’ Star Rhea Norwood, ‘Enola Holmes’ Actor Susan Wokoma, ‘Dear England’ Writer James Graham Join U.K. National Youth Theatre’s 70th Anniversary Show (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Korea Box Office: Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Outpaces ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Again in Strong Second Weekend 2 hours ago See All National Youth Theatre The U.K.’s National Youth Theatre has announced a further wave of star names for “Letters to My Younger Future Self,” the one-night performance marking the organization’s 70th anniversary. The show, supported by Netflix, is set for Sept. 20 at the Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall in London. The new names joining the lineup include chart-topper Sophie Ellis-Bextor, BAFTA Breakthrough Brit Susan Wokoma (“Enola Holmes”), leading dramatist James Graham (“Dear England”), Daniel Ings (“The Gentleman”), Calam Lynch (“Rings of Power”), Fay Ripley (“Cold Feet”), Rhea Norwood (“Heartstopper”) and Megan Bolton (TikTok comedian). Additional letters will be penned by NYT patron Chiwetel Ejiofor, Joanna Lumley, Joan Collins, Richard E. Grant and Matt Lucas. Related Stories Hollywood Failed Hayden Panettiere Hayden Panettiere, 'Heroes' and 'Scream' Star, Dies at 36 They join the previously announced lineup of BAFTA winner Adeel Akhtar (“Four Lions”), India Amarteifio (“Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story”), Fehinti Balogun (“Down Cemetery Road”), Jessica Henwick (“Game of Thrones”), Rob Rinder (“Judge Rinder”), Takunda Muzondiwa (2026 Roundhouse Poetry Slam winner) and Jack Thorne (“Adolescence”). Further appearances and letters are set to be announced. Popular on Variety The evening is directed by National Youth Theatre CEO and artistic director Paul Roseby alongside director Josie Daxter, with dramaturgy from Krishna Istha and Sophie Ellerby. Will Duke handles video design, Prema Mehta lighting design, Nicola T. Chang sound design and Matthew Wells movement direction. The show will be powered on stage, behind the scenes and on screen by young talent nurtured through Netflix and National Youth Theatre’s “Ignite Your Creativity” program. NYT patron Sophie Ellis-Bextor said: “I’m proud to be a Patron of the National Youth Theatre, which gave me a great confidence boost as a young person and continues to do the same for thousands of young performers around the country.” Wokoma added: “NYT shaped everything for me… I learned how to be a good company member and it’s absolutely one of my strengths as an actor and writer. It’s the way you learn and grow and surprise yourself.” Ings said: “A lot of the people I’m closest to today are friends I made at NYT, and it shaped the way I approach acting and being part of a company. That being said, I have a lot to say to my younger self, so I can’t wait to be back with the NYT this September for a night to remember.” Lynch added: “I’m looking forward to returning to my NYT roots for a special evening celebrating seventy years of youth theatre.” Bolton said: “NYT is where I started my performing journey and is a company that means a lot to me. I’m looking forward to joining some amazing talent on stage for an evening to remember.” Netflix has backed National Youth Theatre since 2023 through a partnership that has generated more than 4,000 free places aimed at steering young people toward behind-the-scenes creative careers. The charity points to its alumni roster as evidence that a majority of the U.K.’s top screen talent got their start in theater. That roster includes Daniel Craig, Helen Mirren, Adeel Akhtar, Andrea Riseborough, Matt Smith, Regé-Jean Page and Susan Wokoma, along with dramatists Jack Thorne, James Graham, Miriam Battye, Lennie James and Sarah Solemani, comedians Tom Allen and Joel Dommett, and musicians Ed Sheeran and Sophie Ellis-Bextor. Tickets for “Letters to My Younger Future Self” are on sale now, with proceeds benefiting the national charity in its 70th anniversary year. National Youth Theatre named Netflix as headline sponsor of the event, with additional backing from Arts Council England and Eon Productions. articles.title: Deluxe Media and Tohokushinsha Film Corporation Set Strategic Asia-Pacific Localization Partnership (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 17, 2026 1:00am PT Deluxe Media and Tohokushinsha Film Corporation Set Strategic Asia-Pacific Localization Partnership (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Deluxe Media and Tohokushinsha Film Corporation Set Strategic Asia-Pacific Localization Partnership (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago ‘Heartstopper’ Star Rhea Norwood, ‘Enola Holmes’ Actor Susan Wokoma, ‘Dear England’ Writer James Graham Join U.K. National Youth Theatre’s 70th Anniversary Show (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Korea Box Office: Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Outpaces ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Again in Strong Second Weekend 3 hours ago See All Deluxe/Tohokushinsha Film Corporation Deluxe Media Inc. and Tokyo-based Tohokushinsha Film Corporation have formed a strategic partnership to expand localization services across the Asia-Pacific region. The non-exclusive deal pairs Deluxe’s ties to top studios and streamers, its scale and its tech-driven localization workflows with Tohokushinsha’s creative and in-market strengths built up over decades in Japan. Both companies said the aim is to add localization capacity as demand for high-quality localized content keeps rising across APAC and globally. Related Stories 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Hits $2 Billion Worldwide in Three Weeks Korea Box Office: Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Outpaces 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Again in Strong Second Weekend Deluxe has also opened a Japan office inside Tohokushinsha’s Tokyo headquarters, a move meant to tighten coordination between the two companies’ project teams. The companies said the setup has sped up response times and added flexibility as they work to keep pace with rising regional demand for subtitling, dubbing and localization work. Popular on Variety “Partnering with TFC strengthens our ability to deliver exceptional localization services across one of the world’s most dynamic entertainment markets,” said Cyril Drabinsky, CEO of Deluxe. “By combining Deluxe’s global capabilities with TFC’s deep expertise and trusted presence in Japan, we’re creating greater value for our clients and helping premium content reach audiences everywhere. We look forward to continuing to build on the strong foundation we’ve established together.” Kosaka said the collaboration unites two companies with parallel commitments to quality and client service, adding, “As demand for premium localized content continues to grow, we’re proud to partner with Deluxe, whose global reach and relationships with the world’s leading studios and streaming platforms complement our decades of experience in the Japanese market. Together, we’re creating new opportunities to deliver exceptional dubbing, subtitling and localization services for clients in Japan and around the world. We are pleased with the progress we’ve made together and look forward to expanding our collaboration in the years ahead.” Deluxe traces its roots to 1915, when it started out as a film processing lab. The company has since grown into one of the largest full-service media firms in the industry, handling localization, distribution and post-production work for studios, streamers and content creators around the world. Platinum Equity owns Deluxe. Tohokushinsha dates back to 1961 and has long been a leader in Japanese localization work. The company has since branched out into production, broadcasting and distribution, linking international content with audiences in Japan. Its shares trade on the Tokyo Stock Exchange’s Standard Market, as well as the Nagoya Stock Exchange’s Main Market. Warner Bros. articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi Netflix Assembles YA Stars Past, Present & Future For End Of Summer Bash Event To Reassert Presence In The Genre ‘Finding Her Edge’ Season 2 To Get Back On The Ice For Start Of Production Later This Month Netflix Acquires Digital YA Series ‘Sunshine Girls’; Sets December Premiere Window View All January 27, 2026 1:00pm L-R: Jason Segel, Lukita Maxwell and Luke Tennie in 'Shrinking' Season 3 Apple TV Apple TV has renewed Shrinking for a Season 4. The news comes a day ahead of the launch of Season 3 with an hourlong first episode . The beloved comedy series stars Emmy nominees Jason Segel and Harrison Ford. Core cast members also include Christa Miller, Emmy nominee Jessica Williams, Luke Tennie, Emmy nominee Michael Urie, Lukita Maxwell and Ted McGinley. Season 3 contains 11 episodes, which will roll out every Wednesday through April 8. Related Stories News Everything We Know About ‘Shrinking’ Season 3 So Far Cancellations and Renewals 2026 TV Series Renewals Photo Gallery The third season of the show centered around Segel’s grieving therapist, Jimmy, will focus on the theme of moving forward, not just for him but for his colleagues Paul Rhoades (Ford), Gaby (Willaims) and their whole friend group of neighbors, patients and more. articles.title: Jason Segel Says ‘Shrinking’ Season 4 Will Move Past Acute Grief: “Like A Rom-Com To Me To Try Again At 45 Years Old” – Contenders TV Nominees Studio
articles.full_text: They’re already shooting Season 4 , but the Shrinking cast — co-creator/co-writer Jason Segel , Harrison Ford , Jessica Williams and Michael Urie — took a break to chat about their Emmy-nominated third season at Deadline’s Contenders Television: The Nominees Studio. Segel, who stars as Jimmy and serves as executive producer and writer alongside Bill Lawrence and Brett Goldstein, teased a little about the upcoming season of the Apple TV comedy series, after Season 3 scored 10 Emmy nominations including for Outstanding Comedy Series. Related Stories News Why ‘Shrinking’ Closed Longstanding Plot Doors As It Prepares To Open New Ones After a Time-Jump – Contenders TV News Emmy Nominations 2026: The Complete List “We knew that we wanted to get out of the acute stage of grief as a show because it will run out of steam eventually,” Segel said. “So we had a lot of talks about what another cycle could look like. What was interesting to me is what does it look like when you then decide, ‘OK, I’m ready to take it for a spin now. I’ve reached the end of the acute stage. I’m going to walk out this front door and try to have a good day.’ Sounds great, but it turns out it’s its own set of clumsiness and hilarity, and it almost feels like a bit of a rom-com to me, to try again at 45 years old. I think there is a lot of fun in there.”

articles.title: Myki Meeks On Life-Changing Experience Winning ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race’ & How The Team Raises The Bar Every Year – Contenders TV Nominees Studio
articles.full_text: After 18 seasons on the air, RuPaul’s Drag Race has received a total of 88 Emmy nominations with 29 wins. To celebrate its most recent slew of Emmy nominations , executive producer Natalia James , co-executive producer John Polly , production designer Jen Chu , choreographer Jamal Sims and Season 18 winner Myki Meeks joined Deadline’s Contenders Television: The Nominees Studio to discuss how the show consistently hits the mark each year with critics and award voters alike. articles.title: ‘Lanterns’ Creators On That OMG First Episode Ending – Crew Call Podcast
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Lanterns’ Creators On That OMG First Episode Ending – Crew Call Podcast Johnny Depp In Talks For ‘Pirates 6’, Says Jerry Bruckheimer At D23; ‘Top Gun’ Producer Wants To Keep Paramount In Hollywood ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ $70M Is Second-Best 3rd Weekend Ever; ‘Odyssey’ Sails Past Half Billion, Dino Pics $20M+ Apiece – Box Office Update View All August 16, 2026 7:00pm L-R: Damon Lindelof, Chris Mundy and Tom King PMC Photo / Getty Images Warning : This podcast and write-up has spoilers about the ending of tonight’s first episode of HBO/DC’s Lanterns We can’t even say it in a blunt, straight sentence. But, first episode in, something crazy happened to Kyle Chandler’s O.G. Green Lantern, Hal Jordan, in a time jump. It’s an outcome that sets up for an interesting timeline for the rest of the season. And we haven’t even seen him fully train the Green Lantern’s back-up guardian for Earth, Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart. In addition, Lanterns hasn’t taken us to space out, nor has it rolled out Sinestro or Nathan Fillion’s Guy Gardner. Related Stories Podcast 'DTF St. Louis' Creator Steve Conrad On Tapping Into The Exotica & Underbelly Of The Midwest - Crew Call Podcast News 'Lanterns' Release Schedule: When Do New Episodes Come Out? On tonight’s special episode of Crew Call , Lanterns co-creators and EPs Chris Mundy , Tom King , and Damon Lindelof unpack that shocker ending for Jordan, and how and why the trio teamed up to revive Green Lantern for the new DC under James Gunn and Peter Safran. Watch on Deadline What’s interesting is this: We’re given a hint about Jordan’s ultimate fate at the onset of tonight’s episode. That’s when he appears as a digital carbon copy (or “back-up”) to Stewart following the latter’s survival from a car-crash. That was a major tip-off as to how tonight’s episode would end. Why did Mundy, King and Lindelof leave a breadcrumb? Listen below. L-R: Kelly McDonald, Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in ‘Lanterns’ HBO Max Jordan might have his doubts about whether Stewart has the grit to wear the ring of a Green Lantern, but from the looks of it, he did quite well after having the jewelry tossed at him by the former. It was then that Jordan jumped out of the car, as it careened with Stewart off a cliff. The new recruit powered the ring to provide a cushion from the crash. But, it’s clear as Jordan proved to local sheriff Kerry (Kelly Macdonald): There are aliens in Rushville, Nebraska. Kerry learned this the hard way after allowing Jordan to question what appeared to be a local yokel over the mysterious shooting at a Rushville high school football game. The older Green Lantern taunted the alien so much, that the creature detonated itself, blowing a hole into the side of the jail. Jordan and Stewart also got to meet Kerry’s powerful, rancher kingpin father-in-law, William Macon (Garrett Dillahunt). He takes a liking to at least Jordan. However –oops– Stewart slept with Macon’s wife! We’ll soon see whether Macon is a villain behind the scenes or an ally. The theory out there is that Macon is a future foe, harboring a big secret on his ranch. For the time being, he’s under an N.D.A. and can’t disclose to the Green Lantern corp what’s up his sleeve. Wow, an N.D.A., standing in the way of a potential villain’s plans. How often do you see that in a superhero story? Green Lantern has long been prized by fanboy screenwriters, but a hard needle to thread. Mundy, King and Lindelof share with us their theories on why Green Lantern is hard to crack, in addition to its appeal. There was a 2011 movie, which on paper looked great with Casino Royale director Martin Campbell and a pre- Deadpool Ryan Reynolds in the title role . But at a $200M cost before P&A, Green Lantern was a red light at the box office, dimming with a $237.2M global gross. Greg Berlanti co-wrote that movie, and he tried to revive the property for Warner Bros TV before Green Lantern glowed into Lanterns . With Mundy involved, the series became akin to True Detective crossed with Green Lantern, grounding what is often a labyrinth storyline of galactic proportions. articles.title: ‘Lanterns’ Star Kyle Chandler Weighs In On Premiere Twist That Sets In Motion “The Whole Mystery” Of HBO Series
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Katie Campione Katie Campione Senior TV & Labor Reporter @katie_campione More Stories By Katherine ‘Lanterns’ Star Kyle Chandler Weighs In On Premiere Twist That Sets In Motion “The Whole Mystery” Of HBO Series ‘Frozen 3’ First Look Teases Wedding Bells & An Icy Villain From A Land “More Wild And Dangerous” Than Ever Before – D23 Ahsoka’ Season 2 Trailer: ‘Star Wars’ Series From Lucasfilm & Disney+ Returns After Nearly Three Years – D23 View All August 16, 2026 7:15pm 'Lanterns' HBO SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from the premiere of HBO ‘s Lanterns . All is not what it seems in HBO’s Lanterns. The series premiered Sunday night, introducing audiences to Kyle Chandler as the legendary Lantern Hal Jordan and his trainee John Stewart (played by Aaron Pierre). Whatever plans Hal has for John’s training regimen are quickly interrupted by murder in Rushville, Nebraska, that Hal suspects has something to do with aliens. Much of the first episode sets up the mystery that the Green Lantern and his protege are aiming to solve before ending with a twist. The final moments flash forward from 2016 (when Hal is training John) to 2026. Hal Jordan is dead — and John is ostensibly not the Green Lantern. The pair largely haven’t spoken in a decade, and Rushville’s sheriff has only summoned John after finding Hal’s body at the football stadium, where their intergalactic murder investigation began all those years ago. Related Stories Podcast 'Lanterns' Creators On That OMG First Episode Ending - Crew Call Podcast Commentary Emmy Nominees Head To Final Campaign Stops; Why Showbiz Docs Rule With Voters - Notes On The Season This, Chandler explains, is what “opens up the whole mystery of the show.” Watch on Deadline “The whole search is to find out what happened to him,” he told Deadline. “I like the fact that the show is non-linear and they’ve layered it like that.” The reveal introduces audiences to the fact that there is not one murder mystery being solved throughout this series, there are two , and the events in 2016 clearly have some sort of influence on what’s to come. Chandler likened the experience of telling a non-linear story to “three-dimensional chess” because of the layers involved in playing the characters’ emotional truth at any given moment in the series. “Once you get all your pages taped on the wall and you know where all your scenes are, then you can take this page in the script and this page in the script, and figure out how to play with the material to reveal things differently, or to lay Easter eggs as the actor,” he said. “So, maybe later on, if not anyone else, I remember I did that. You can have fun doing things, but it’s complicated.” Lanterns is from co-creators Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King. articles.title: Hayden Panettiere Dies: “Heroes,’ ‘Nashville’ & ‘Scream’ Star Was 36
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom Hayden Panettiere Dies: “Heroes,’ ‘Nashville’ & ‘Scream’ Star Was 36 Harrison Ford, Robert Downey Jr. & Ellen Pompeo Pay Tribute To Bob Iger As He Becomes A Disney Legend Watch Kevin Costner’s “Field Of Dreams” MLB Game Intro View All August 16, 2026 8:27pm Hayden Panettiere Storm Santos Hayden Panettiere , who is best known for playing the superpowered cheerleader on NBC’s Heroes , has died at the age of 36. Her rep confirmed the news to Deadline. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen,” her father, Skip Panettiere, said in a statement to ABC. He asked for privacy “as our family takes time to process this unimaginable loss.” Related Stories Obituaries Hayden Panettiere: Her Life & Career In Photos Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries The actress died in South Carolina, according to a source. Details are scant about her passing, but there is an ongoing investigation into the matter. Panettiere had been open about her struggles with depression and addiction. The actress told people she was given “happy pills” at the age of 15. She got Heroes at 16, and graduated to drinking and occasionally taking opioids. “My saving grace is that I couldn’t be messy while on set and working,” she said . “But things kept getting out of control [off set]. And as I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn’t live without.” The birth of her daughter Kaya in 2014 brought postpartum depression, which the actress was open about. She began drinking again and and her relationship with Kaya’s father, former world heavyweight champion Wladimir Klitschko, ended. “He didn’t want to be around me,” she said. “I didn’t want to be around me. But with the opiates and alcohol I was doing anything to make me feel happy for a moment. Then I’d feel worse than I did before. I was in a cycle of self-destruction.” In 2018, still battling addiction, Panettiere sent Kaya to Ukraine to live with her father full time. “It was the hardest thing I ever had to do,” she says. “But I wanted to be a good mom to her — and sometimes that means letting them go.” Panettiere was a child star who appeared in commercials and had a four-year run as Sarah Roberts on One Life to Live (1994 to 1997), and then on The Guiding Light as Lizzie Spaulding. She made her big screen debut at the age of 9 in A Bug’s Life . The same year she also appeared in The Object of My Affection . In 2000, she played the daughter of a coach in the Denzel Washington starrer Remember the Titans. In 2004, Panettiere landed her first starring roles a the daughter of actor Bill Pullman’s character in Tiger Cruise on The Disney Channel. Then, in 2006, came Heroes . Panettiere played high school cheerleader Claire Bennet in the NBC drama about superheroes juggling normal life and saving the world. The show was originally supposed to involve new characters each season, but the popularity of the show and audience investment in the character played by Panettiere and Milo Ventimiglia was such that the original actors remained through all four seasons of its run. DEADLINE RELATED VIDEO: She soon played a cheerleader again, this time on the big screen in Chris Columbus’ 2009 film I Love You Beth Cooper . While the film underperformed for Fox, it soon became a mainstay on basic-cable movie stations. Panettiere appeared as Kirby Reed in three Scream films: Scream 4 (2011), cameo in its sequel Scream (2022) and Scream VI (2023). Reed was the best friend of Jill Roberts, franchise protagonist Sidney Prescott’s younger cousin. Reed’s status as the so-called “final girl” alive at the end of Scream 4 raised her profile to more of a main character, especially with fans. She moved back to TV in 2012 for Nashville . Panettiere played rising country music star Juliette Barnes opposite Connie Britton as a Nashville legend named Rayna Jaymes. Much of the show’s drama — and a good portion of ABC’s marketingl campaign — centered on the rivalry between their two characters. Nashville ran for six seasons, first on ABC and then CMT. In 2023, the actress’ brother Jensen died of at age 28 due to and enlarged heart “coupled with aortic valve complications.” Earlier this year, in her memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning , Panettiere wrote that her brother was smoking crack and snorting heroin before he died. ‘Nashville’ & ‘Heroes’ Star Hayden Panettiere Dies At 36; Career In Photos Depp In Talks For ‘Pirates 6,’ Bruckheimer Says; Disney Poised For Huge 2028: Analysis 2nd Fastest To $2B Global; $70M Third Frame; Dino Movies At $20M+ In U.S. ‘Call Her Daddy’ Host Alex Cooper In Talks With CAA After UTA Exit Under Cloud Read More About: 9 Comments

articles.title: ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: “This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist” – Edinburgh Film Festival
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: “This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist” – Edinburgh Film Festival ‘Borges And Me’ Review: Marc Turtletaub’s Hallucinatory ’70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful – Edinburgh Film Festival Ewan McGregor: The Actor Opens Up About His Career, His Return To Scotland & Taking A Chance With Obi-Wan: “Deciding To Do ‘Star Wars’ Was Hard” – Edinburgh Film Festival View All August 16, 2026 11:20pm ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ EIFF On the face of it, Finlay Pretsell’s first feature, Time Trial (2017), seemed like any other underdog sports movie, chronicling the last hurrah of disgraced Scottish cyclist David Millar in his last year as a professional rider at the Tour De France. Others might have taken the easy option and milked this against-all-odds story for dramatic tension, but Pretsell chose instead to focus on the complex mass of confidence and insecurity that lay behind Millar’s public image — the question it asks is not whether Millar will defy the odds and win, but can he survive a loss? His new film Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon is just as insightful, a portrait of the Scottish artist behind such works as 24 Hour Psycho — Hitchcock’s film slowed down to one frame per half a second — and Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait , in which 17 cameras tracked the course of a football match by focusing on a single player. As the title suggests, Gordon was not a passive subject, actively fighting his director for authorship of the story. The result is a fascinating deconstruction of the documentary process, with Pretsell both charmed and exasperated by his mercurial and temperamental subject. Related Stories Festivals 'Borges And Me' Review: Marc Turtletaub's Hallucinatory '70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful - Edinburgh Film Festival Festivals Ewan McGregor: The Actor Opens Up About His Career, His Return To Scotland & Taking A Chance With Obi-Wan: "Deciding To Do 'Star Wars' Was Hard" - Edinburgh Film Festival DEADLINE: Did you know Douglas Gordon’s work beforehand? Watch on Deadline FINLAY PRETSELL: Yes. He was the biggest inspiration to set me on the journey to make films, to be honest. I saw Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait while I was attempting to make a cycling film and I wanted it to be something else. I wanted it to be experiential . I saw Zidane and it blew me away in its ability to take me onto the pitch. Then I met him. I was kind of blown away by his generosity. DEADLINE: When did you first meet him? PRETSELL: It was 20 years ago, here at the Edinburgh Film Festival , funnily enough. And he just stood and talked to me and he was so warm and generous and interested and sort of empowered me to do what I wanted to do. Not pretentious, not standoffish, not too busy. I think that’s what I really liked about him. I saw this amazing character. He was so comical, there was something behind the eyes, behind this very Glaswegian accent. There was something about him that made me think, “Oh, this isn’t what I expected.” Artists are generally sort of quiet and introverted, but there was some sort of… not danger about him, exactly, but there was something going on that was exciting and intriguing. I didn’t think about making a film about him then, but we stayed in touch by email. And then during COVID, I said, “Look, are you up for doing something together?” I heard nothing back. I thought, “OK, whatever, fine.” And then out of the blue, I got a call from Berlin. A Scottish accent. I didn’t know who it was. It was Douglas. “So, what are we going to do?” he said. “Film? Fiction? Drama? Series? Episodic?” From then on, we just started talking, and it took me probably about a year to finally get into his studio, during which time I would record our conversations that we were having. It became this kind of confessional thing, because I’d get him at all times of the day: First thing in the morning, or in the afternoon, or late at night, I was recording our conversations. I never really thought I’d ever use them. But in the end, we used them quite a lot. and it became quite critical to the arc of the film. DEADLINE: How do you start a project like this? Do you just start filming and see what happens? PRETSELL: Sort of. I’m quite slow, in a way, at coming up with an idea. I think I saw various scenes in my head, but I have to be in the room with someone to really understand things and start to work it all out. I can’t just make something up and say, “Right, this is what I want to do.” But in my head I thought, “This is an experience of a successful working artist, and I want to capture this somehow.” I want to be a fly in the wall. DEADLINE: Were you looking for moments in the life of an artist then? PRETSELL : Yeah. The thing with Douglas is that he let us into something deeply personal. But he had to do it when he was ready to let us in, and it was really difficult to pin him down. I just had to let go [of the reins], and he would sort of deliver a performance of what he thought I would want to know about him, which was just amazing. Thematically, it runs all the way through the film. He’s in charge. Initially, I would always try and control everything, and I would get quite frustrated — as you see in the film — and he would get frustrated with me. But I realized that there was no other way, and I think it was that relinquishing of control that was essential to make the project work and not get too concerned with my own ego getting burnt all the time. DEADLINE: When did you realize he wasn’t going to give anything away? Because people might go to this film thinking, “Why did he make 24 Hour Psycho ? Why did he make Zidane ?” What would you say to those people if they think that’s what they’re going to get? PRETSELL: I would tell them, this is the mind that created them. And him explaining it would make it no clearer to anyone. Watching the film will explain it in a non-didactic way, I suppose. This is the mind of a conceptual artist. Too much context, I think, kills many documentaries. People feel like they’re forced to contextualize absolutely everything in docs, and I’m like, why are we not allowed just to be a bit freer with these narratives? It’s not about being smart or holding something back, I just want to create an experience. As soon as you’re giving facts and dates, it starts to get in the way of the experience, or the feeling of what it is that he does. As he says in the film, ambiguity is what it’s all about. Not that the film itself should be ambiguous, necessarily, but you ask yourself, “Is he acting? Is he telling the truth? Are we seeing the real Douglas Gordon now?” Who cares! We’re telling a story, and he’s part of that story. He’s a performer. DEADLINE: So, it becomes another artwork to hang next to the others? PRETSELL: Yeah, exactly. It sort of does. But what I can say is that everything he did for us was authentic. It’s from him, and a;; these beautiful moments he would just produce out of nowhere. It wasn’t like we’d say, “Maybe we should talk about your mum now. Maybe we should talk about…” It would just come out. I’d often email him some points before we talked, and if we managed to do get to of these points, great. But if not, it didn’t matter. Something better would happen. DEADLINE: Is there ever a chance he could have just walked away and destroyed the project? PRETSELL : Oh, of course. Totally. I was thinking that all along, because I could imagine him doing just that. He doesn’t need me. He doesn’t need a film about him. It was in the back of my mind the whole time. But I never give up in these situations. I’m like, “No, no, no. We are going to make this film.” So, yeah, of course, he could have absolutely walked away at any point. It’d be much easier for him not having us around, to have me not calling him up all the time, but he likes that discussion, that discourse. DEADLINE: What did you learn about conceptual art? PRETSELL: Oh God, I don’t know. Nothing. [Laughs.] I think what I learned is that everything is grist to the mill. All these discussions we would have around his kitchen table, he would write them on the walls all over his studio. That made me realize that everything could be turned into an artwork, in a way. He’s got an amazing mind. articles.title: Kenneth Branagh On Moving From Shakespeare To Action-Comedy In ‘Mayday’: “I Thought Zach Galifianakis Should Play The Part, But I Was Very Pleased They Asked Me” – Edinburgh Film Festival
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: “This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist” – Edinburgh Film Festival ‘Borges And Me’ Review: Marc Turtletaub’s Hallucinatory ’70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful – Edinburgh Film Festival Ewan McGregor: The Actor Opens Up About His Career, His Return To Scotland & Taking A Chance With Obi-Wan: “Deciding To Do ‘Star Wars’ Was Hard” – Edinburgh Film Festival View All August 17, 2026 12:12am Kenneth Branagh and Ryan Reynolds in 'Mayday' courtesy of Apple Actor-director Kenneth Branagh arrived in Edinburgh to accept the festival’s inaugural Outstanding Contribution to Cinema award from festival director Paul Ridd and immediately joked that he would break it up into little pieces. “Actually, I wouldn’t,” he told the audience, “but if I did, I would give to you , and I’m not just being sappy. Certainly, the reason why I’m standing here is that because over the last number of years, so many of you have been kind enough to support the films that we do and that are celebrated here at the festival. It just wouldn’t be possible to be working in this industry without appreciative audiences who take a risk and who spend their cash and invest their time.” Related Stories Festivals 'Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon' Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: "This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist" - Edinburgh Film Festival Festivals 'Borges And Me' Review: Marc Turtletaub's Hallucinatory '70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful - Edinburgh Film Festival Speaking to The Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, Branagh discussed his 40-year career in movies both as an actor and director, having screened his 1989 debut Henry V . The event began, however, with an entertaining sample of his upcoming Apple film Mayday , an ‘80s-set action film in which he plays a disillusioned KGB agent who teams up with a US Navy pilot ( Ryan Reynolds ) who is stranded behind enemy lines. Watch on Deadline Branagh was full of praise for writer-directors, Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley. “You may know their work from Game Night and Dungeons & Dragons ,” he said, “both films of deceptive ease. Really entertaining, popular movies that are very cannily done. They had planned all the action and the style sequences, so the invitation was for me to step up and enact their imagination. They’re both excellent directors, but I find it terrific to be directed by two directors. They can gang up on you in a really good way, in a helpful way. “I read the script in one sitting,” he recalled. “I was in an airport, during a long delay in coming back home. And I remember thinking, ‘This knows exactly what it’s meant to be. It’s grasp of the period and its sheer desire to entertain — but with a lot of very skillful touches — is great. Why the hell are they asking me to be in?’ I thought Zach Galifianakis should play the part actually, but I was very pleased they asked me.” Since the part he’s playing is Russian, Bradshaw asked if he would consider playing Vladimir Putin. “It depends on the writing,” said Branagh. “But it also depends on whether you feel that somehow, you can serve [the role] appropriately. But there’s no question that such characters, for all the reasons we’re all too familiar with, are riveting. I guess it’s pretty important to analyze, investigate and understand how and why, in as much as we can draw inferences from what little we know of the inner lives and inner machinations of such regimes, how these people operate. He’s a figure that dominates our experience in many ways, along with a number of other key figures. So just like Shakespeare wrote about all those people in control of the power in our lives, he’s a creature that fascinates us, and from whom we might learn something in the investigation.” Branagh went on to say that his next project was a little more traditional, given his theatrical background, being a documentary about the history of British theater in the 20th century. “It’s directed by a young British actor, Freddie Fox ,” he said. “You may know him from numerous pieces of work and movies, but most recently Slow Horses . He has incredible access to a number of significant people across that period. He particularly focuses on what made the impact of the theater, socially, and the change that it spoke about — whether it was to do with LGBTQ rights or the political situation in Northern Ireland, et cetera — but it also contains a really keen interest in performance.” ‘Nashville’ & ‘Heroes’ Star Hayden Panettiere Dies At 36; Career In Photos Depp In Talks For ‘Pirates 6,’ Bruckheimer Says; Disney Poised For Huge 2028: Analysis 2nd Fastest To $2B Global; $70M Third Frame; Dino Movies At $20M+ In U.S. ‘Call Her Daddy’ Host Alex Cooper In Talks With CAA After UTA Exit Under Cloud Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Hollywood Flashback: When Dudley Moore Intoxicated Audiences in ‘Arthur’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All August 15, 2026 12:00pm Dudley Moore became best known for the title role in 'Arthur,' which landed Oscars for supporting actor John Gielgud and for the original song “Arthur’s Theme (Best That You Can Do).” Warner Brothers/courtesy Everett Collection A toast is in order for Arthur , which became a comedy classic despite a quiet release 45 years ago. After penning Carl Reiner’s 1978 comedy The One and Only starring Henry Winkler, Steve Gordon was hired to direct his own Arthur script for Orion . Gordon initially considered George Segal and John Belushi for the title role before casting Dudley Moore off the success of 10 , in which the actor starred opposite Bo Derek. Arthur centers on alcoholic playboy Arthur Bach, who will be cut off from his family fortune unless he marries a woman he doesn’t love, which becomes complicated when he falls for working-class Linda, played by Liza Minnelli . At the time, Moore praised the script for its barrage of jokes: “Ten laughs a page, instead of one laugh every 10 pages.” Related Stories Hollywood Flashback Helloooo, Emmy: Art Carney's Enduring 'Honeymooners' Triumph Hollywood Flashback 40 Years Ago, Rob Reiner Turned Stephen King's Most Personal Story Into a Surprise Hit Actress Anne DeSalvo, who played sex worker Gloria, tells The Hollywood Reporter that Moore, a classically trained pianist, would warmly greet her on set. “Dudley would be playing the piano, and he’d say, ‘Good morning, Anne,’ ” she recalls. “He was such a gentleman.” The lead character was written as American, but Moore convinced Gordon to let him keep his British accent: “Steve kept phoning me up and saying, ‘Are you sure you can’t do an American accent?’ I told him if I tried, it would be the most distorted performance.” Arthur hit theaters on July 17, 1981, with THR ‘s review extolling the “hilarious comedy” and Moore’s “impeccable timing.” The film got off to a slow box office start amid marketing challenges, but word of mouth drew crowds for weeks to come, as Arthur became the year’s fourth-highest-grossing title. The film earned four Oscar nominations, winning for best supporting actor for John Gielgud as butler Hobson. It also won an Academy Award for Christopher Cross’ main theme song, “Best That You Can Do” — co-written by Burt Bacharach and Carole Bayer Sager — which hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Gordon died suddenly of a heart attack a year later at age 44, making Arthur his only feature. Moore and Minnelli returned for a 1988 sequel, while a 2011 remake starred Russell Brand , Jennifer Garner, Greta Gerwig and Helen Mirren, but neither matched the success of the original, which was named one of AFI’s top 100 comedies. Moore, who died in 2002 at age 66 after battling progressive supranuclear palsy, once called Arthur his favorite role: “I love the character.” This story appeared in the Aug. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: The TikTok Comment That Let Megan Gallagher Know She Nailed the Representation of Motherhood in ‘All Her Fault’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Brande Victorian Plus Icon Brande Victorian Deputy Awards Editor View All August 15, 2026 12:30pm Sarah Snook and Jake Lacy in All Her Fault Sarah Enticknap/PEACOCK Megan Gallagher is something of an adaptation whisperer. The writer and executive producer whose credits include the BBC miniseries Wolf , based on the Jack Caffery novels by Mo Hayder, and the upcoming ITV drama The Blame , adapted from Charlotte Langley’s novel, delivered Peacock’s most watched original series to date — 46 million hours viewed in its first three weeks — with All Her Fault . The adaptation of Andrea Mara’s best-selling novel stars Sarah Snook as Marissa, a mother in distress when her son, Milo (Duke McCloud), goes missing and secrets about everyone in her inner circle — particularly her husband, Peter (Jake Lacy) — begin to unfold, raising doubt about their culpability. But more than a thriller, the Emmy-nominated limited series created a dialogue about parenthood — specifically the unspoken feeling of being a single mother, even in a partnered relationship — which Gallagher was all too eager to explore. Related Stories TV 'Paradise' Executive Producer Explains Why Julianne Nicholson's Character Had to Go Down with the Bunker in Season 2 TV 'Heated Rivalry,' 'Hacks' Top GALECA Dorian TV Awards Winners List Sarah Snook initially said there was no way she could do this series, and then you told her you could shoot in Australia and she said yes. What was it about her and this role that wouldn’t let you take no for an answer? For the majority of the series, Marissa is in DEFCON 5 trauma. A mother’s worst nightmare: child missing, at any moment you could get the call that he’s dead; it doesn’t get any worse than that. Because of that, we knew that there was going to be a lot of crying. And you need such an incredible actress for a role like that because if you don’t, you can lose a character in the crying. The crying can become the dominant thing, and the acting is the crying as opposed to being able to convey a personality underneath all of that, being able to find the nuance of who this character is outside of the crying. The way that we cry, the way that we emote, the way that we break down, it’s not universal. So I wanted an actress who could handle all that, not just somebody who would be a good crier but somebody who’s really sophisticated, and she so thoroughly and ridiculously fit that bill. How did you pull off moving the setting of the book from Dublin to Chicago and shooting in Australia? So I’m American, but I live in Norway. My producers are in London. The broadcaster’s in L.A. We shot it in Melbourne, and it’s set in Chicago, where I’ve never been. So it’s a testament to how everybody’s global. Andrea’s books — and I’m working on another [adaptation] of hers now — on one end, they’re really interesting because who doesn’t like looking at Ireland, but the stories themselves are, for the most part, quite universal and can translate anywhere. So there was nothing culturally about the story that she told that couldn’t easily be translated to America. In terms of setting it in Chicago, once we knew we were doing it in America, what mattered to us is that the show felt accessible and relatable to all Americans. That’s why we didn’t want New York or L.A. or Miami. Those cities have such distinct personalities, whereas Chicago was very Middle America and more universally understandable. How did we pull it off though? A hell of a lot of postproduction. In the book, the investigator on Milo’s case is a woman. How did Michael Peña end up as Detective Alcaras in the series? The detective is a very small character in the book named McConville. So that character — Andrea wouldn’t mind me saying this — that’s entirely me. It felt like in a show that was quite critical, obviously, of men, that having some positive male energy in there was not just the right thing to do in terms of ticking boxes, but the fair thing to do. I have a son who’s quite disabled, and my husband’s an incredible father and really runs the show. I wanted to touch upon that from a very personal place. And it just felt like in a show that’s so critical of men and of men not being involved on the home front, why not show a man who is — despite the fact that he’s got one of the more complicated home fronts you could possibly have. Alcaras still takes his son to school. He still knows the names of the other kids. He still knows the teachers. He still packs his son’s lunch. He still does pickups. That all came from my heart and soul. The big conversation that was had on social media about the series was the representation of the realities of parenting, particularly motherhood. Is there any aspect of that response that surprised you? I knew that the theme would resonate with women. I’m the neurotic, worried writer. I think, “Oh, it’s going to be terrible, it’s never going to come together, it’s not going to work.” That’s me. But I was quietly confident about that theme because every woman I know in my age bracket who is working and raising kids is just breaking down in their car crying, and they don’t understand how it’s supposed to all get done. And we’ve seen little bits and pieces of it on TV, but we haven’t really seen it front and center. I knew this isn’t just me and my friends. This is everyone. So why the fuck isn’t it on television? So I knew it would resonate. I did not know it would resonate as much as it did. I don’t know if I could say I’m surprised. I’m just really pleased. And every little, tiny breadcrumb-y feminist thing that I put in there — even the most subtle stuff — is all over TikTok. It was dissected endlessly. The nicest response that I saw was a comment on TikTok that said, “These are two of the worst husbands I’ve ever seen on television and neither one of them was having an affair.” We’ve seen affairs a hundred million times, and that’s not always the most hurtful thing you could do. The series’ ending is satisfying on so many levels, but I’m curious, were there any alternate endings you considered that were particularly intriguing? No. The way that it plays out in the series is unique to the series. The sequence of events, like [Milo’s abductor Carrie, played by Sophia Lillis] being at the house — Carrie never shows up at the house in the book or any of that kind of stuff. However, the broad strokes of Peter switching the babies early on, which is why Carrie did what she did, and Marissa killing Peter is 100 percent in the book. And I completely give credit to Andrea Mara. So many thrillers start out great and then the ending is just kind of [blah], whereas this was a whopper of an ending. So no one considered anything else ever, because you don’t mess with something [that good]. It’s like the opening. The opening of the series is the opening of the book. And no one ever considered anything else because there is no better way to open. There is no better way to close. You also have Such a Nice Girl coming, which is another adaptation from Andrea Mara. Anything you can foreshadow about this new project? Such a Nice Girl is a really fun read and it’s a great examination of female friendship that crosses two generations. There are two characters who are late 40s, early 50s. And the story is about a crime that appears to have taken place between their two daughters who are also best friends. It’s twisty-turny. It takes place over just a day, so it’s really, really tight. But just like with her other stories, there’s something to say about female friendship and the power of it that’s just really, really satisfying. We’re diving into it right now and it’s really fun. This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. To receive the magazine,

articles.title: ‘The Beast in Me’ Showrunner Knows That the Violent Murder Scene Was a “Potential Tune-Out Point” For Some Viewers
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Beatrice Verhoeven Plus Icon Beatrice Verhoeven Awards Editor bverhoeven Follow Sign Up View All August 15, 2026 1:00pm Matthew Rhys as Nile Jarvis Chris Saunders/Netflix The Beast in Me showrunner Howard Gordon knows there was one scene in the Netflix limited series that was divisive because of its brutality. “There were people for whom that was a potential tune-out point. Maybe some others tuned in extra because of it. It’s hard to tell,” Gordon, producer of 24 and Homeland , tells THR . The scene in question is — spoiler alert — the flashback scene in which Nile Jarvis’ (Matthew Rhys) wife, Madison (Leila George), is violently killed. The moment answers the question the entire show sets up, and the question Claire Danes’ character, Aggie, who is grappling with the death of her son, tries to answer while writing a book about her mysterious neighbor: Did he or didn’t he kill his wife? Related Stories TV The TikTok Comment That Let Megan Gallagher Know She Nailed the Representation of Motherhood in 'All Her Fault' TV 'Paradise' Executive Producer Explains Why Julianne Nicholson's Character Had to Go Down with the Bunker in Season 2 Gordon breaks down with THR why The Beast in Me was a hard premise to tackle and why Rhys was the right guy to play Nile. I know Gabe Rotter wrote this six or seven years ago, and it took a while to gain momentum. Why do you think it was such a difficult premise to get moving? A couple things. I think the secret of the pilot and Gabe’s creation is a character who is a writer [Danes], who is stuck really in this existential kind of “stuckness” because of this terrible loss. Those things were very evident in the premise. But when she has a killer move in next door, or someone she suspects to be that, and writes this book … writing a book about somebody is a pretty static idea, so we had to find the dramatics of what happens. What does that cat-and-mouse actually look like? Nile in the earlier version was kind of exiled to the suburbs but was painting. These two solitary characters who don’t have a lot of people around them, that’s not a very dramatic premise. It’s a very challenging premise. So we gave Nile [the real estate development] Jarvis Yards. He has still been exiled, but he still has a very important hand in a very big, controversial development. And who is his father? And Aggie’s relationship had to be explored. There were a lot of balls in the air, but what was evident to us was this essential loss, this essential grief, which is the most unimaginable thing any of us can go through and that universal fact of loss and how it can bend us. But there were too many multiple traumas and trauma swappings that wound up obscuring the issues. So most of it was about clearing the brush and finding the story. Before the final reveal, the audience is constantly left wondering whether Nile did it or didn’t. How did you keep it in the gray zone? The journey of whether he is or isn’t [a killer] … keeping that possibility open [was important], but ultimately we have to also look at the audience’s awareness of: If he wasn’t, where would the story go? We planted certain flags at various points. Part of the other problem was that there were these backstories of Aggie’s own loss, of Nile’s previous marriage and that unsolved mystery. So there’s a lot of backstory, which, you don’t want to be reading headlines for an entire eight episodes. So you have to bring the backstory into the present and keep it alive. When you ask what the storytelling challenge was, the idea of a guy who you meet, and at the end of the pilot, you’ve now whispered your darkest secret to him [that Aggie wished her son’s killer was dead], and then that darkest secret becomes enacted makes very little sense. I mean, what was he hoping to achieve here by doing that? Only when refracted through the prism of a sociopath can you answer that question. So when you’re looking for rational cause and effect within the parameters of a healthy human being with a conscience, you’re not going to find very many answers there. You have to embrace the sociopathy in that way. As for how we did it: As a showrunner, you really take the temperature of the people who are readers and your fellow writers and your actors. How do you keep people leaning forward and wanting to watch the next episode? What did you see in Matthew for this incredibly complex, terrifying role? We had high expectations, but he blew them away. I will say that the character of Nile Jarvis was the hardest to figure out and decode. The language of a sociopath is very easy to have a mustached, twirly guy speaking and pontificating and vaguely threatening tropes, but to really give him a kind of humanity, vulnerability. … I think Matthew’s secret was not just to make him charming, but to make him, by turns, dangerous and vulnerable. So he took the music that we gave him and just made it better. He’s a charming guy, so you bring that kind of charm to bear on a character as ruthless and damaged as Nile. And look, this is an improbable love affair. What was also interesting was to have a love affair and to take sex out of the equation really made it great, made it so much fun, and these are two people who are uncomfortably alike who find each other and actually connect in a way. But then with that love comes the inevitable betrayal that he feels once Aggie, his new friend, turns out to be after him. The eventual murder scene is very violent. Where do you draw the line in how graphic you want to go with scenes like this? I tended to be the grandpa in the production. I have to bring [executive producer] Antonio Campos into this equation. Antonio obviously was the captain of the ship on the set, but he really was an active producer as well, so there is a sort of rough democracy. Being the showrunner, I got to cast the winning vote often, but I do hear it when I’m outvoted. In instances like that, where I felt it was, “Whoa,” where I was a little squeamish, you have to just embrace that this is a really violent moment, and this is a very broken, evil, awful person. And you may as well go all in — in for a dime, in for a dollar. A lot of it is seasoned to taste, and I think there were people for whom that was a potential tune-out point. Maybe some people tuned in extra because of it. It’s hard to tell. At the end of the day, you have to be the sort of lightning-rod litmus test for your audience. That really felt like it was consistent with the tone and the texture. This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. To receive the magazine,

articles.title: CBS News Chief Correspondent Matt Gutman Accused of Harassment in Wrongful-Termination Suit by Former ABC News Producer
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All August 15, 2026 2:46pm Matt Gutman Lorenzo Bevilaqua/ABC/Getty Images CBS News correspondent Matt Gutman has been accused of workplace harassment in a wrongful-termination lawsuit filed by a former ABC News colleague, who alleges he made inappropriate comments while they worked together. Samira Said, a field producer who worked for ABC News from May 2021 until March 2025, filed the lawsuit Friday in Los Angeles Superior Court against ABC News and its parent company, The Walt Disney Co. Gutman is also named as a defendant. Said alleges that Gutman created a hostile work environment through two incidents while they were colleagues at ABC News. Related Stories TV CBS News Pushes Into Live Events as 'Sunday Morning' Teams With 92nd Street Y (Exclusive) Business David Ellison Breaks Silence on Antitrust Lawsuit: It's Not About Market Share, It's About CNN Gutman joined CBS News on Jan. 5, as chief correspondent, the first major on-air hire under CBS News editor in chief Bari Weiss. He previously served as ABC News’ chief national correspondent, where he worked in various roles for nearly two decades. According to the lawsuit, Said was placed on a “male-only team.” During one assignment, the suit alleges, “While the team waited in a public queue during the assignment, Gutman initiated a discussion rating a female correspondent’s appearance and reducing her professional standing to a numerical score based on her physical attributes. The male crew joined in, continuing to assess the woman’s body and looks in Said’s presence. The men attempted to draw Said into the conversation by soliciting her views. Said declined and stated the conversation was inappropriate.” In another alleged incident, Said and Gutman disagreed about whether the team should leave a work site while covering a press event for a movie release. “In front of multiple coworkers, Gutman responded by making a sexualized insinuation that Said must have an after-hours date in the city and that this is why she did not want to relocate,” the lawsuit states. “The remark, made audibly to others, demeaned Said and reduced her professional judgment to a sexualized stereotype.” The lawsuit’s claims against ABC and Disney extend beyond Gutman’s alleged conduct. Said alleges that the companies later mishandled her requests for medical accommodations following an assignment covering the 2022 mass shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas. According to the lawsuit, Said was assigned to interview child survivors who witnessed the killings of their classmates. Following the assignment, she “experienced severe psychological symptoms” and “was still experiencing symptoms from COVID-19,” the suit states. From August 2022 through January 2023, Said was granted medical leave, during which her “psychiatrist continued to certify the medical necessity of her leave on a recurring basis,” according to the lawsuit. By early 2023, Said’s psychiatrist had cleared her to return to work “subject to reasonable accommodations designed to enable her to perform the essential functions of the position while protecting against re-exposure to trauma triggers.” Said alleges that ABC denied her accommodation requests. She also claims that ABC News’ Los Angeles bureau chief David Herndon “made it clear that unless she returned without restrictions and with full-week availability, she would not be permitted to resume her role.” “Following her medical leave and accommodation requests, Plaintiff was subjected to materially adverse treatment than she had experienced at any time prior to engaging in protected activity,” the lawsuit states. Said alleges that she was subsequently assigned to weekend desk shifts. In January 2025, while covering the Los Angeles wildfires and other hazardous weather-related events, Said alleges that she was injured on the job when heavy equipment struck her foot, resulting in a bone contusion. According to the lawsuit, she reported the injury to her supervisors and was evaluated by a Disney physician, who determined that she did not need to take leave. ABC News terminated Said on March 5, 2025, according to the lawsuit. She is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, as well as attorneys’ fees. CBS News had no comment. The Hollywood Reporter also reached out to representatives for ABC News and Gutman but did not hear back by the time of publication. THR

articles.title: Selena Gomez’s Attorney Fires Back at Wondermind Lawsuit: “Completely Meritless”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson , McKinley Franklin August 15, 2026 3:49pm Selena Gomez at the 2026 Golden Globes. Christopher Polk/2026GG/Penske Media via Getty Images Selena Gomez ‘s legal team is speaking out after the Only Murders in the Building star was accused of fraud by investors in Wondermind, a company she co-founded alongside her mother Mandy Teefey and their former business partner Daniella Pierson. Responding to the claims, Gomez’s litigator, Mathew S. Rosengart, shared a statement with People , which reads, “The allegations that Selena Gomez engaged in any way whatsoever in any purported ‘fraud’ or other wrongdoing are completely meritless, both factually and legally. We will vigorously defend these false allegations and indeed are filing a motion to dismiss the baseless claims against her.” Related Stories Music The Playlist: Seventeen's Vernon on His Hyperpop Roots, K-pop's Evolution and What Inspired 'V8' News Courtney Love Reveals Doctors Told Her She "Was Going to Die" in 2019: "My Body Just Exploded" Filed on Thursday, Wondermind SRS 44 LLC and Bespoke Wondermind SPV LLC sued Gomez, Teefey and Pierson for falsely representing their mental health startup’s leadership and partnerships. Wondermind, a startup focused on mental fitness practices and tools, was co-founded by the trio in November 2021, and they allegedly told investors that the brand would feature an app and be boosted by major advertising deals, celebrity photo shoots and cover stories. The suit alleges that Gomez was touted as a key part of marketing for the brand and that Pierson was pitched to investors as a “$200 million executive” with a “full slate of revenue-generating initiatives.” “The partnerships did not exist. In a statement shared with USA Today on Thursday, a representative for Pierson said she “welcomes the opportunity to present concrete documentation and financial records that establish the facts,” denying the allegations and asserting that she is an investor. “To be clear, she has never used investor funds for personal expenses. articles.title: Disney and Epic Games Launch Game That Connects Star Wars Theme Park Ride to New Fortnite Adventure
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All August 15, 2026 4:30pm Millennium Falcon Smuggler's Gambit Disney/Epic Games The Walt Disney Co. and Epic Games are debuting an unprecedented new effort that will connect one of Disney’s real-life theme park rides with a bespoke adventure in Fortnite . The company’s on Saturday unveiled Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run | Fortnite , which will enable visitors to the Smuggler’s Run attraction at Disney’s theme parks in Orlando and Anaheim to accept a special mission while in the queue for the ride, and if they succeed, they will get a unique Forsworn Trooper Outfit in a newly-created Fortnite adventure called Smugglers Gambit set in that same universe. Related Stories Movies 'Frozen 3' "Royal Wedding" Between Anna and Kristoff Is Crashed by New Villain in First-Look Movies 'Zootopia 3' in the Works at Disney “ Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run | Fortnite marks the first time this attraction has reached beyond its physical walls into a connected game world — a story that starts in a queue in Orlando or Anaheim can now continue on a screen almost anywhere,” said Sean Shoptaw, executive vp of Disney Games and Digital Entertainment. “ Smugglers Gambit, built in-house by an incredibly talented team, is an immersive, high-quality game, and together these experiences reflect our ambition to connect stories and worlds across formats into one converged entertainment ecosystem.” Millennium Falcon: Smuggler’s Run is one of two flagship rides within the Galaxy’s Edge Star Wars lands at Disneyland and Walt Disney World, with visitors working together to pilot Han Salo’s famous spacecraft. The cockpit technology in the ride was actually created using Epic’s Unreal Engine, which allows for many assets from the ride to appear in Smugglers Gambit . “Building on Epic’s technology, Disney’s Imagineers are shaping the future of interactive entertainment, where an experience goes from the physical world into Fortnite,” said Adam Sussman, president of Epic Games. “Whether you’re at a Disney Park or playing Fortnite with your friends, fans have new ways to keep their Star Wars adventures going. This is only the beginning of what’s possible when world-class storytellers bring their creativity into Fortnite.” Disney, of course, is an investor in Epic Games, and the two companies have been at work building a new world that will connect to Fortnite with all of the Disney’s beloved characters. Until now, however, that collaboration has taken the form of special seasons and minigames associated with Fortnite, featuring characters from Star Wars, Marvel, The Simpsons , or other IP. This new collaboration, however, extends to the real world for the first time, bringing some video game magic to Disney’s parks, and some of that theme park magic to the video game. THR
