articles.title: California Bill to Cap Concert Resale Ticket Prices Dies After Lobbying Frenzy
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All August 13, 2026 4:18pm A view of the California State Capitol on August 19, 2025 in Sacramento, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images A California bill intended to limit how much tickets are allowed to be re-sold for in the state has failed, as AB 1720 failed to make it out of the Senate appropriations committee on Thursday. AB 1720 was first introduced by state assembly member Matt Haney back in February. The bill as originally published would’ve capped concert ticket resale prices at no more than 10 percent higher than a ticket’s original price. Since its introduction, the bill was reduced with an amendment limiting the law to smaller 3,000-capacity or lower venues, removing a majority of the shows that usually draw much of the activity on secondary ticketing sites. 1720 had garnered support from groups like the National Independent Venue Association, Music Artist Coalition, National Independent Talent Organization and live music giant Live Nation, who argued the bill would help rein in ticket scalpers, who’d be unable to list tickets at extreme markups. The bill faced significant resistance from ticket resale platforms, with StubHub spending a record-high $3.4 million in lobbying expenses in California this year fighting the bill, including $2.6 million in this most recent quarter. In a statement on the move, Haney said that he is “going to keep working with the coalition of fans, artists, and venues who recognize the urgency of this issue and continue pushing for solutions that put tickets back in the hands of the people they were intended for.” “This isn’t a fringe idea, and it isn’t partisan,” Haney said. “From Kid Rock to Noah Kahan , artists across genres have called for solutions to runaway ticket resale practices. Independent venues have spoken out. Fans have demanded change. Several states and countries have already adopted resale caps because they recognize the urgency of this issue. AB 1720 would have helped remove the incentives that fuel predatory ticket resale while still allowing someone who can’t attend a show to resell their ticket and recover their costs.” A rep for StubHub didn’t respond to request for comment on the bill’s failure on Thursday. Previously, the company told THR that we believe that more choice, flexibility, and access put fans first and help everyone get into the events they love.” While California’s price cap bill has failed, similar bills have passed in other parts of the country including Maine, Vermont and Washington, D.C., while Massachusetts governor Maura Healey placed a price cap bill into the state’s supplemental spending bill last month. THR

articles.title: NY Film Festival Sets Currents Lineup Led by ‘Bardi’ World Premiere
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All August 13, 2026 4:39pm 'Bardi' Courtesy of Film at Lincoln Center/NYFF64 The New York Film Festival has announced the lineup for its Currents section, featuring films that expand the possibilities of the medium, including boundaries of narrative and form. The slate of 15 feature films and 28 short films has as its centerpiece the world premiere of Bardi , from filmmaker and photographer Tala Hadid, for which she immersed herself in the world of horse riders in Morocco. Other notable Currents selections include feminist meditation At Night , from experimental filmmaker Beatrice Gibson; Sebastian Brameshuber’s London , about a driver and ride sharers traveling along the Westautobahn; Bruno Dumont’s observational yet fanciful Red Rocks , about kids on the French Riviera; John Torres’ neo-noir The Remotes ; and Luise Donschen’s Tomorrow a Long Time Ago , a supernatural story about unemployment and social estrangement amid German reunification in 1990. Related Stories Movies Tom McCarthy's 'A Statement,' Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut,' Jordan Firstman's 'Club Kid' Set for NY Film Fest Movies NY Film Festival Reveals 2026 Main Slate With Cannes Winners 'Minotaur,' 'Fatherland' and 'All of a Sudden' The section also includes Jacqueline Lentzou’s expansive coming-of-age story A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra ; Ana Vaz’s surreal Hanabi , set in contemporary Japan; Carlos Reygadas’ Heil Jupiter! featuring a dreamlike look at authoritarian surveillance and transgression; Tiffany Sia’s serene but sonically complex landscape film Overt Listening , tackling the Cold War legacy of China and Taiwan. And there are more intimate, personal stories including Éric Baudelaire’s improvisatory For the Moon , a world premiere collaboration with kids at the National Institute for Blind Youth in Paris; Ted Fendt’s Foreign Travel following four friends over a year in Berlin as they engage with Anna Maria Ortese’s novels; Dan Sallitt’s neurotic comedy What Can’t Be Mentioned , catching up with characters from his The Unspeakable Act . And, as both a Currents and Revivals selection, NYFF will world premiere a new restoration of Fred Camper’s Suicide Note , a diary-like work shot in New York in the 1970s and meant to be slightly different at each screening. And, as a blend of both an epic and small-scale film, Currents will screen Mariano Llinás’ 330-minute biographical Life of Jorge Luis Borges . Among the noteworthy filmmakers represented in the shorts lineup is Laura Poitras , who collaborated with Rachel Lauren Mueller on They’re Here , a look at battles between ICE agents and anonymous Minneapolis residents using dashcam footage, crowdsourced data and POV cinema. “The Currents lineup pushes against the conventions of cinematic form, putting into relief the standardization that dominates the film landscape,” New York Film Festival artistic director Dennis Lim said in a statement. “This year’s selection is especially thrilling in its scope and diversity, encompassing multiple modes of production and possibilities for film language and visions that range from the dynamically intimate to the genuinely — sometimes literally — cosmic.” The 2026 NY Film Festival is set to run from Sept. 25-Oct. 12. THR

articles.title: Tyler Duckworth, ‘The Challenge’ Winner, Dies at 44
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All August 13, 2026 4:46pm Tyler Duckworth Kevin Winter/Getty Images Tyler Duckworth, the two-time winner of MTV’s The Challenge and former Real World: Key West star, has died. He was 44. His mother, Toni, announced his death on Facebook Thursday. “My son, Tyler, passed away earlier this week. Cause of death has yet to be determined,” she wrote, adding that she would share a follow-up post when a cause of death was made available. The Grand Forks Police Department told People that officers were sent to his residence on Tuesday after a neighbor reported water coming through the ceiling from his apartment. Duckworth was found dead in his bathroom, with police telling the outlet an investigation is pending “there. doesn’t appear to be any signs of foul play or suspicious death.” Related Stories TV Christy Knowings, 'All That' Star, Dies at 46 Movies Bill Jersey, Two-Time Oscar-Nominated Documentarian, Dies at 99 Duckworth joined the MTV family as a castmember on The Real World: Key West in 2006. From there, he appeared on six seasons of The Challenge . His first stint was on The Duel (2006-07), and he also competed on The Gauntlet III (2008); Cutthroat (2010); Rivals (2011); and the second and third seasons of the All Stars spinoff across 2021 and 2022. He won his first season of the show on Cutthroat , alongside his teammates Brad Fiorenza, Dunbar Merrill and Tori Fiorenza. Duckworth also won Rivals with his teammate Johnny Devenanzio; Evelyn Smith and Paula Meronek also won that installment. In early August, Duckworth shared an Instagram post after attending a Challenge Mania event alongside a few Challenge alumni. “So proud to represent my hometown of Minneapolis along with these other challenge legends. The fans are what keep us coming out! Hearing your stories of courage, inspiration & joy that you’ve got being a fan of the franchise is humbling each and every time. Also, pretty sure we nailed the cast photo for the lost season of The Real World : Minneapolis!! Thank you Minneapolis,” he wrote. Fellow Challenge contestant and Big Brother player Paulie Calafiore, who appeared in Duckworth’s August post, penned a tribute on Instagram , resharing photos from the fan event. “Life is crazy. RIP Mighty Duckworth! You were so vibrant 2 weeks ago, it’s so wild to imagine your vibrant energy no longer here,” he wrote. “Sending prayers and love to your family and friends. The Challenge fam lost a legend.” THR

articles.title: The War Over Warner Bros. Is Splintering Hollywood’s Labor World
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All August 13, 2026 5:40pm California Attorney general Rob Bonta speaks during a news conference at Gemperle Orchard on April 16, 2025 in Ceres, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images When the antitrust trial over the planned $111 billion merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery was scheduled for March 2027 , the delay was viewed as a major blow to studio CEO David Ellison and his team. It turns out the leaders of the Directors Guild of America and IATSE unions think the prolonged timeline is a disaster for them, too. In a letter sent to California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Ellison on Wednesday, union heads projected the lengthy timetable would harm workers and called for a settlement or, at the very least, an expedited trial. This pro-settlement approach put them at odds with their compatriots at the Writers Guild of America, which has not only supported the attorneys’ general suit but has launched its own lawsuit to block the merger, presenting another hurdle to a quick resolution. SAG-AFTRA is seemingly splitting the difference by supporting the state regulators’ suit and opposing the deal unless “enforceable safeguards” are put in place, theoretically through a settlement. The Teamsters previously called for the Department of Justice to block the deal unless specific conditions were met and, in a statement , motion picture division head Lindsay Dougherty called on Paramount Skydance to “stop playing games and show us more of your commitment to the workforce.” Why the divided front in Hollywood’s solidarity-obsessed labor world? To understand the split, it’s helpful to look at the exposure that each of the unions have to production fluctuations, as well as the roles they typically play in the high drama of entertainment labor relations. The triple whammy of the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2023 writers’ and actors’ strikes and the ensuing pullback in content spending from major companies hit all Hollywood workers hard. But combine that with additional outsourcing of production from California, not to mention the U.S. all together, and union members dependent on freelance production work in their areas have had little reason for hope the last few years. Work has begun to rebound, but not nearly fast enough for many. IATSE, which represents an array of crew members including gaffers, grips, camera assistants and costume designers, has reported that hours worked by members in 2025 were down nearly 36 percent from 2022. While the Directors Guild certainly counts in-demand helmers as members (its president: Christopher Nolan himself), it also represents plenty of rank and file crew workers, such as unit production managers, assistant directors, associate directors and stage managers. The union has seen a 40 percent decrease in employment since 2022, a union source tells THR . According to DGA and IATSE leaders, they’ve already seen a retreat in jobs as a result of the uncertainty swirling around the future of Warner Bros. Discovery. And it’s spooked them. “We cannot overemphasize how damaging the current timeline for the trial … is to an already struggling industry,” Russell Hollander and Matthew Loeb wrote in their letter to Ellison and Bonta. Contrast their position with that of the Writers Guild of America, whose members don’t depend on the short-term fluctuations of physical production happening in their areas. The WGA is also vulnerable to studios trimming their slates and buying fewer ideas and scripts, and saw a significant downturn in jobs following their 2023 strike. Still, their labor can’t be easily outsourced and the greater threat to them, perhaps, is in the long term: the reduction of five major studios, or major buyers of scripts and employers of writers, to four. “ The Merger would eliminate competition for buying film and television writing, resulting in suppressed compensation, worse deal terms, and reduced programming volume and diversity,” the Guild argued in its lawsuit to block the deal. It added that the transaction “threatens the economic and creative health of the American entertainment industry.” Then there’s the matter of union personality and track record. Make no mistake, the writers like to shake things up. The WGA did it in 2019 with their war against talent agencies and again in 2023 with their battle against streaming-era economics. Time and time again, the WGA has demonstrated a high tolerance for risk, most recently through their decision to go into negotiations with studios and streamers while much of their own staff was on strike, and an interest in remaking the entertainment industry on a grand scale. They’ve faced the wrath of studio heads before and always claim, at the very least, that they’ve come out on top. Who’s afraid of David Ellison? The DGA hasn’t historically shown that same appetite. The union prides itself on its pragmatism, careful research and selectivity in its battles with management (which typically take place outside the public eye). Its leaders believe power lies in diplomacy, not war — and appear to be suggesting that more uncertainty and another production downturn, however short, could present an existential risk to their members’ professions. This time, it appears IATSE leaders are in the same camp as the DGA. The crew union has been no stranger in recent years to talking tough when they feel they can gain an edge. But with crew members so battered by the production downturn in recent years, the prospect of more short-term pain appears to be anathema to Loeb. SAG-AFTRA and the Teamsters also seem open to a settlement with binding promises on production, though they haven’t yet gone so far as to plead with state attorneys general to devise one. The actors’ union, a mix of superstars and unknown performers, has supported the antitrust suit but called for “enforceable safeguards against reduced production by the studios with guarantees of increases in the percentage of productions made in the USA.” In her statement to THR, Teamsters leader Dougherty says her union has yet to see any data illustrating how the merger would be good for the industry and its workers. And she faulted Ellison for claiming the merger would benefit workers while also threatening to leave L.A. if his suit isn’t settled by Oct. 1. ”Touting worker prosperity, without commitments, while simultaneously threatening their livelihood in the press as a bargaining chip begs the question — what is in this deal for American film and television workers?” she asked. “Fast-tracking corporate greed often leads to the creative and skilled workforce losing.” Both Teamsters and SAG-AFTRA members rely heavily on localized production, but both unions have also proven that they’re open to a fight in recent years. That’s not to say any of the unions are jazzed about the merger. “We have been consistent in our view that mergers, such as this one, historically offer few benefits to workers,” the DGA and IATSE leaders conceded in their letters. Some labor groups are simply arguing their members may not have the stamina required to fight it. THR

articles.title: ‘American Horror Story’ Season 13: Everything We Know
articles.full_text: Skip to main content (L-R) Emma Roberts, Frances Conroy, Gabourey Sidibe, Sarah Paulson, Leslie Grossman, Avantika Vandanapu and Alex Consani are seen filming 'American Horror Story' in SoHo on July 9, 2026 in New York City. TheStewartofNY/GC Images Logo text Get ready horror fans, because a new season of American Horror Story is approaching, and it brings back some of the series’ most beloved characters — and the actors who play them. Created by Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk, AHS first debuted in 2011 with Murder House and has since taken viewers through season two’s Asylum, season three’s Coven, season four’s Freak Show, season five’s Hotel, season six’s Roanoke, season seven’s Cult, season eight’s Apocalypse, season nine’s 1984, season 10’s Double Feature, season 11’s NYC and season 12’s Delicate . Now, the anthology series is nearly back for season 13, with franchise favorites including Jessica Lange, Evan Peters, Sarah Paulson, Emma Roberts and more stepping back into the Emmy-winning series, which has become a staple of the Murphy-verse The season is executive produced by Murphy, Falchuk, Ned Martel, Charlie Carver, Eric Kovtun, Nissa Diederich, Scott Robertson, Tanase Popa, Crystle Roberson Dorsey, Jennifer Salt and Tim Minear. It’s produced by 20th Television. Below, The Hollywood Reporter breaks down everything there is to know about AHS: 13 — from its new and returning castmembers to what Murphy has teased about the franchise’s future and the first official footage. When Will Season 13 Be Released? Logo text After AHS: 13 was originally indicated to premiere around Halloween 2026, FX set its official release date for Sept. 24 at 9 p.m. ET / 6 p.m. PT on FX and Hulu. The season will include 13 half-hour episodes, with premiere week and week two each featuring three episodes. Following that, two episodes will be released each Thursday leading up to the 13th and final episode on Oct. 29. What Is Season 13 About? Logo text According to FX, here is the official logline: “An unrivaled 13th installment that will do justice to everyone’s most feared number. Bringing together an all-star cast, many of whom are reprising fan favorite roles, American Horror Story: 13 continues to build on the anthology’s decades-long legacy that has been streamed more than 700 million hours across the globe and spawned a legion of dedicated fans. American Horror Story has redefined the genre with various installments featuring a creepy murder house, a coven of witches, a traveling freak show, a haunted hotel and the apocalypse itself. Which iconic horrors will return to haunt the hallowed halls of 13 and what new terrors await? Light your candles, draw your pentagrams and prepare for a supreme surprise.” Murphy recently told THR , “This season is a thank you to the fans for continuing to watch.” He also teased to be on the lookout for certain nods to past seasons. “We also had a lot of the original costumes still in storage that we got to use,” Murphy said. “So there are little Easter eggs threaded around in the set decoration where fans can be like, ‘Wait, wasn’t that in season two?’ It was.” Who Is Returning for Season 13? Image Credit: Getty Images (4) Logo text A plethora of franchise veterans are returning for AHS: 13. Find out who and which seasons they’ve previously been in below. Sarah Paulson : Murder House, Asylum, Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke, Cult, Apocalypse and Double Feature Jessica Lange: Murder House, Asylum, Coven, Freak Show and Apocalypse Evan Peters: Murder House, Asylum, Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke, Cult, Apocalypse and Double Feature Angela Bassett: Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke and Apocalypse Kathy Bates: Coven, Freak Show, Hotel, Roanoke, Apocalypse and Double Feature Emma Roberts: Coven, Freak Show, Cult, Apocalypse, 1984 and Delicate Billie Lourd: Cult, Apocalypse, 1984 and Double Feature Gabourey Sidibe: Coven, Freak Show, Hotel and Apocalypse Leslie Grossman: Cult, Apocalypse, 1984 and Double Feature John Carroll Lynch: Freak Show, Hotel, Cult, Apocalypse and 1984 Mat Fraser: Freak Show Mena Suvari: Murder House , Apocalypse Zach Villa: 1984 Seth Gabel: Hotel And Who Are They Playing? Image Credit: Prashant Gupta/FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection; Ray Mickshaw/FX/Courtesy Everett Collection; Michele K. Short/FX Networks/Courtesy Everett Collection (2) Logo text Over the past few months, Murphy has posted first looks of actors returning in character on his Instagram. This has included Jessica Lange as Constance Langdon ( Murder House ), Sarah Paulson as Cordelia Goode, aka The Supreme, ( Coven ) and Emma Roberts as Madison Montgomery ( Coven ). Speaking with Entertainment Tonight at The Shards premiere in July, Murphy further revealed more details on the seasons’ characters brings together elements from previous seasons. “Everybody thinks it’s a Coven season and it’s not. It’s all the seasons,” he said. “Sarah Paulson is playing six or seven roles. Jessica Lange is playing all four of her iconic characters. Evan Peters is playing five characters… It is like the Avengers. They all come together to defeat the ultimate evil.” Perhaps the biggest surprise for fans was Lange’s return. The actress has repeatedly said to press over the years that she would not return to the show after leaving in 2015. However, Murphy was able to convince her. He recently told THR , “It all started with Jessica [Lange] because Jessica, after we did the first four seasons, wanted to go off and do different things, which I understood completely. But I reached out to her thinking she would say no, and if she had said no, I probably wouldn’t have done it. She told me a story about how she was doing Broadway last season and she would go out after the show, and there were all of these young people who were there because they all watched her work on American Horror Story . And she was very moved by that. I said, ‘Well, that’s funny, because my idea is for you to do all four of your favorite characters.’ And she said, ‘Sign me up. I’d love to do it.’ I was so grateful.” “Before I started writing it, I had all of them — Emma [Roberts] and Evan [Peters] and Kathy Bates; Angela Bassett and Gabourey Sidibe and Leslie Grossman,” he said, in addition to Paulson. While promoting Murphy’s other series, The Beauty in January, Peters told THR that he was “shocked” Lange agreed to return: “Ryan knows how to have those dinners. He will get you in a second. I was definitely shocked, but thrilled, honestly.” ( See more details on character’s in the trailer section. ) Who Are the New Cast Members in ‘AHS:13’? Image Credit: Getty Images (4) Logo text First-time AHS actors include Paul Anthony Kelly, Alex Consani, Avantika, Madelaine Petsch, John Waters and Joey Pollari. Kelly most recently worked with Murphy on Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. & Carolyn Bessette , where he played JFK Jr. The 37-year-old actor appears with blonde hair in AHS: 13 , as far as his character, Vogue reported that he is “the linchpin of the season.” What Happened to Ariana Grande’s Role? Image Credit: Monica Schipper/Getty Images Logo text On Halloween 2025, Murphy announced on this Instagram that Ariana Grande was set to join a slew of American Horror Story veterans for season 13. However, in July, THR confirmed that the Grammy winner had dropped out of AHS: 13 due to a scheduling conflict with her Eternal Sunshine tour. Murphy recently spoke with THR about Grande’s exit, saying, “I love Ariana Grande. We’re great friends. I had an idea and I came to her and she, very immediately, said, ‘I’m not sure because I think I’m going on tour.’ I don’t think the tour had been announced, and she had obviously just finished the Wicked movie. So when it came time to do that episode, I called her up and she was like, ‘I don’t know how I’m going to juggle the tour with this.’ And I said, ‘OK, if you can’t, we can push to another season.’ She said, ‘Great.'” “You have to be respectful,” he continued. “Who is busier than Ariana Grande? No one. She had told me at the time, ‘I have this album that’s dropping.’ It was really, truly a scheduling conflict. … Ariana is a big fan of horror. She’s obviously done homages of that in her work; she did Scream Queens for me and loved the experience, and people love her in that show. So I will always work with her. I love her, and I support her. It was a very big swing, but I might bring that back for another season, per Ariana’s availability.” Has There Been a Trailer? Image Credit: FX Logo text A teaser trailer released Thursday , showing the franchise’s most beloved stars and characters back on screen — in addition to some of its most infamous villains. Twisty the Clown (John Carroll Lynch) from Freak Show opens the teaser, which then pans to the inside of what appeared to be a hotel, seemingly nodding to Hotel. Peters appears as Kai Anderson ( Cult ), Lange as Constance Langdon ( Murder House ), Angela Bassett as Marie Laveau and Emma Roberts as Madison Montgomery — both from Coven. Rubber Man ( Murder House ), the sinister figure known to wear a skintight black latex BDSM suit, who Peters played in the first season, also appears. Kelly is seen in a bathtub with a snake, hinting that he could be a villain, while the trailer ends with Paulson as Cordelia Goode looking at herself in the mirror — which breaks. (

articles.title: Jenna Ortega’s Sister Reacts to Public Discourse Over ‘Wednesday’ Star’s Appearance
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 13, 2026 7:23pm Jenna Ortega Monica Schipper/Getty Images Amid the recent online commentary surrounding Jenna Ortega ‘s health and body, her younger sister is coming to her defense. On Wednesday, a fan of the Emmy-nominated actress took to Instagram to tell people to “mind their own business and leave @jennaortega alone, especially after her recent interview has created so many questions and assumptions about her health.” The fan’s comments were in response to the wave of discourse on social media about Ortega’s appearance in a recent Esquire video interview, with many fans pointing out her noticeably thinner physique in the footage, comparing it to past videos and photos of the actress. Related Stories Movies Jenna Ortega on Why She'd Go "All Day" Without Eating or Drinking on Set in Early Career Movies Jenna Ortega, Rose Byrne to Star in New Movie from 'If I Had Legs' Director Mary Bronstein “She doesn’t owe anyone an explanation her life is her life, and her body belongs to her,” the fan, named Amrita Singh, continued in their lengthy post . “She has every right to make whatever decisions she feels are best for herself without being judged, discriminated against, or subjected to unnecessary speculation. We don’t know what she may be going through, and we shouldn’t assume anything based on appearances or a few comments from an interview. Sometimes the most respectful thing we can do is simply give someone privacy, support them, and let them be.” “Please, For God’s sake, she is a human being first, before she is a celebrity in the public eye, and I think that’s what people tend to forget. She deserves privacy, peace, and the freedom to live her life without constantly being questioned or analyzed. Stop concerning yourselves with her personal life and asking intrusive, unnecessary, and random questions just leave Jenna alone and allow her to live her life on her own terms,” they added. Ortega’s sister, Aliyah Ortega, commented on the post, “!!!,” seemingly emphasizing that she agrees with the fan’s perspective. Her sister didn’t appear to add any additional remarks. The Wednesday star isn’t the only celebrity to be battling online commentary about their body recently, as Ariana Grande has also been at the center of the conversation , especially after the release of her “Petal” music video. Earlier this month, it was revealed that Grande would be “taking a step back from visibility after she completes the Eternal Sunshine Tour” and “taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.” The singer later clarified that the announcement “was not a reactive or impulsive thing. It was something that I have decided. A plan that I had quietly made a long time ago.” Ortega is currently busy filming Wednesday season three for Netflix and will next be heading out on the press tour for the dystopian sci-fi adaptation Klara and the Sun , which hits theaters on Oct. 23. THR

articles.title: Alexa Nikolas Wins Key Ruling In Defamation Case Against Bryan Freedman Over Smear Claims
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All August 13, 2026 7:43pm Attorney Bryan Freedman has represented many controversial Hollywood figures. CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP/Getty Images Logo text Months after a resolution to the sprawling legal battle over the filming of It Ends With Us , Hollywood power lawyer Bryan Freedman is still dealing with fallout from the case. Zoey 101 alum Alexa Nikolas won a key ruling on Wednesday in a defamation lawsuit against Freedman, with a court finding that she’s established a probability of prevailing on defamation claims accusing him and those in his orbit of marshaling a smear campaign against her. Nikolas, founder of advocacy organization Eat Predators, has a long and contentious history with Freedman, who had represented her ex-husband Michael Milosh when she sued the musician for sexual abuse. She had organized protests outside of his offices in 2022 after discovering that he had also been accused of sexual assault in a case that resulted in a no-fault settlement in 1991. Around the time of these protests, a smear site that aimed to undermine her activism — including through assertions that her current husband was a predator — popped up about her. Nikolas didn’t connect Freedman to the site until Lively sued It Ends With Us director Justin Baldoni and his production company Wayfarer. The thrust of Lively’s lawsuit focused on alleged sexual harassment on the set of the film, but it also accused Baldoni and his public relations team — led by top crisis publicist Melissa Nathan and digital fixer Jed Wallace — of spawning a smear machine that threatened her reputation. This led to sister lawsuits, including one from publicist Stephanie Jones, who claimed that Nathan and Wallace have long engaged in creating smear sites targeting women. That gave Nikolas the ammunition to file a lawsuit, which points to alleged data identifying Freedman as involved in the generation of some of the sites. In Wednesday’s ruling, Los Angeles Superior Court judge Michael Whitaker rebuffed Freedman’s bid to dismiss the case. He concluded that Nikolas has produced enough evidence to potentially prove the alleged campaign was defamatory. Among the findings: Nikolas sufficiently demonstrated a probability of proving the allegedly defamatory statements were untrue. This includes a claim on a second smear site about her that she partnered with former California senator Joe Dunn to push others into making false accusations of sexual assault. Whitaker also pointed to court records across multiple cases in which several plaintiffs describe a “similar modus operandi and common website traffic optimization tactics.” Freedman had argued that Nikolas can’t prove the assertions advanced in the sites were false and that some were simply statements of opinion, which can’t give rise to a defamation claim. On this front, the court said that the allegations in the site “all imply provably false assertions of fact” that Nikolas is “either a criminal who has committed criminal acts, or she is not.” Multiple smear sites identified in the case between Jones and Baldoni appear to have evidence of common authorship, including Alexanikolas.net, which claimed she extorted multiple ex-boyfriends by threatening them with manufacturing sexual abuse claims, among other things. In Jones’ case, a cybersecurity expert submitted an expert report indicating that those who created the site about Nikolas may have also created ones about Amanda Ghost, who’s engaged in a defamation battle against Rebel Wilson. “There is a tangled web of connections between these sites and numerous others in addition to that authored about plaintiff,” Whitaker wrote, noting a “conspiracy to smear various individuals” who had adversarial connections to Freedman’s clients. That not only suggests a motive, the court found, but also indicates that the lawyer may have been “involved in directing or otherwise effectuating all of those alleged smear campaigns.” Earlier this year, Wilson’s crisis public relations team — comprised of Nathan and Wallace — was heard discussing plans to create anonymous sites that accused Ghost of sex trafficking as part of an alleged smear campaign solicited by the actress against The Deb producer. In a recording obtained by The Hollywood Reporter, Wallace instructed Nathan to assert without evidence that Ghost is a “madame” whose work involves procuring young women for wealthy and powerful men. “We can’t just do, like, oh, she’s a bitch, she sucks,” Wallace says in the recording. “It’s, like, it’s got to be really, really heavy and connected to something that heavy.” At one point in the conversation, Wallace referenced the involvement of Freedman, Wilson’s then-counsel in the case. Freedman and Nathan didn’t respond to requests for comment, though they’ve previously denied involvement in the creation of the smear sites. THR

articles.title: Busan Film Festival to Honor Its Founder Kim Dong-ho with Korean Cinema Award
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All August 13, 2026 10:30pm Kim Dong-ho in 'Walking in the Movies' Courtesy of the Cannes Film Festival For this year’s Korean Cinema Award, the Busan International Film Festival will be honoring one of its own — the event’s founding OG, in fact. Kim Dong-ho, who established BIFF in 1996 and ran the event for its first 14 years, will receive the prize at the festival’s opening ceremony on Oct. 6. The award goes annually to figures who have advanced Korean cinema’s standing in the world — and few, perhaps, are as worthy as the founder of the festival himself. When BIFF launched in 1996, Korean films were still routinely submitted to government censors for pre-screening before public exhibition. Kim refused to put the festival’s program through that process, a stand that established BIFF’s independence, won the trust of filmmakers across the region and helped turn a first-year event in a Korean port city into the leading cinema showcase in Asia . The festival became the meeting ground and incubator for the Korean directors who would sweep the world in the early and mid-2000s, contributing significantly to the broader Korean cultural wave that continues today. Related Stories Movies China's $300M Sleeper Hit 'Dear You' Unveils U.S. Trailer Ahead of September Release TV Gerhard Zeiler to Receive 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award Kim brought a rare but essential combination of skills to BIFF’s early days — a bureaucrat’s background but a cinephile’s instincts. He spent roughly three decades at what is now South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, rising to vice minister. He also served as president of the state film body now known as the Korean Film Council, as well as founding president of the Seoul Arts Center. After stepping down as festival director in 2010, he stayed in the field as dean of Dankook University’s Graduate School of Cinematic Content, chairman of the Presidential Committee for Cultural Enrichment and, later, chairman of BIFF. He has sat on festival juries at Cannes — where he presided over the Un Certain Regard section — Rotterdam and Fukuoka. At age 85, Kim, quite improbably, began work on his first feature. His full-length directorial debut, the documentary Mr. Kim Goes to the Cinema , premiered as a special screening at BIFF’s 30th edition last year and opened in Korean theaters in February, when he was 88. Shot as the pandemic emptied theaters worldwide, the film follows him around the globe in conversation with filmmaker friends, including Bong Joon Ho, Park Chan-wook, Lee Chang-dong, Hirokazu Kore-eda, Tang Wei, Luc Besson and the Dardenne brothers about what purpose cinema now serves. He had previously directed a 2013 short, Jury , and was himself the subject of Walking in the Movies , a 2024 documentary that played Cannes Classics. “I feel deeply moved and humbled to be recognized by the very festival I helped establish and served for over 15 years,” Kim said in a statement released Thursday. The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs Oct. 6-15. Kim will be honored at an opening ceremony that also hands Michelle Yeoh the Asian Filmmaker of the Year award and Ann Hui the Chanel-backed Camellia Award, with Pachinko star Kim Minha hosting. “Even today, I attend more than ten film festivals each year to promote Korean cinema,” Kim added, “and I hope to continue this journey for as long as I can.” THR

articles.title: ‘The Ones With the Tempered Flowers’ Will Document a Woman Studying “Her Body’s Relationship to Self and Society” in Tanzania
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 13, 2026 11:59pm 'The Ones With the Tempered Flowers' Courtesy of Locarno Open Doors Tanzania-born director Neema Ngelime is working on her feature documentary debut. And the essayistic project has a title with poetic vibes: The Ones With the Tempered Flowers . It was among the works-in-progress presented at the 2026 edition of Open Doors , the Locarno Film Festival ‘s co-production platform and talent development program for filmmakers from equity-seeking communities and regions where artistic expression is at risk. The Tanzania-Kenya co-production is being produced by Ivy Kiru. The filmmaker has so far made shorts, namely A Country In A Corner , Hooyo, Why Here and An Ode to A Time I Loved Bread . At the end of the Locarno Open Doors program, her new project won the Sørfond Award and the ARTEKino International Award . Related Stories Movies China's $300M Sleeper Hit 'Dear You' Unveils U.S. Trailer Ahead of September Release TV Gerhard Zeiler to Receive 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award THR has compiled highlights about the movie and insight from Ngelime about The Ones With the Tempered Flowers and the themes it explores. Synopsis For Neema, being a woman has always meant a script: school, marriage, babies. When a doctor tells filmmaker Neema that having children might be hard, she doesn’t expect it to confuse her. Those expectations wound her. Raised in a multi-religious home, her identity was forged by questions of what is haram and what would please Jesus. All Neema cared about was which hell she’d end up in. To her, the older women in her family are a mystery beyond work and family. Their lives feel prophetic to her own. She and her sister try to rewrite their scripts through tarot. Her father taught her that anything is possible. Now he reminds her of her fate. She stages performances with her family, reenacting fragments of their lives. They believe these are fictions. But they’re memories, repurposed, hidden truths surfacing through play. This is the story of a woman studying her body’s relationship to self, society, and the political weight placed on women’s bodies in Tanzania, challenging duty masked as love. Director’s note Growing up felt like watching the women I loved fade into mysteries. Now, with fibroids, a condition society pins on “unused” womanhood, I fear becoming a mystery too, lost to the weight of expectations. The women in my life shaped me deeply, yet I knew little about who they were before becoming mothers or wives. This erasure fills me with grief. Through this film, I channel that grief, exploring how families shape dreams, identity and autonomy. I look inward and center myself and my family to reflect on my past and imagine my future. The film relies on metaphor to reflect the absurdity of how womanhood is confined. It captures the reality of existing in a patriarchal world, where women are bound by timed beauty and defined by their choice to give birth. While rooted in the experiences of young African women, it speaks to a universal audience, inviting viewers to reflect on their own relationships with identity, self-expression and societal constructs. What was the inspiration for you, personal or otherwise, to want to make this film? The film itself starts from a personal point of view, from my confronting and going through an existential crisis because of my diagnosis. When I got my diagnosis, I was angry that I found out so late in life that this could happen, and angry at how it could happen. I was also angry at how little interest there is in understanding women’s bodies. Out of that, the film became about someone wanting to find answers. So in a way, this was my way of creating a space for people going through what I’m going through, a space to talk. But mostly, it was a way to have these conversations with the people close to us, i.e. our families. Making my small inquiries with the people I love, that is the inspiration. Can you share some thoughts on how universal the themes of the film are, and why people outside your home should see it? The universal themes are womanhood and its place in 21st-century society, identity, and curiosity as an act of care across generations. Do you know what the next step or focus for you and any collaborators on the film will be after Open Doors? We’re going back home with so much clarity, thanks to the guidance we’ve received. I’m going to continue my treatment, and the project will also participate in the Durban FilmMart in October, and the Sørfond pitching event in November THR

articles.title: Sarajevo Film Festival Boss Jovan Marjanović on Owning Its Powerful Origin Story: “We Connect This Legacy of War… and Build Bridges”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 14, 2026 2:00am Jovan Marjanović Sarajevo Film Festival Jovan Marjanović is aware just how special the Sarajevo Film Festival is. He would know, having worked for the Bosnian festival since he was just 19. Marjanović is 46 now, and comes into his fifth edition as the event’s sole director with buckets of confidence in what this fest has to offer European cinema. Sarajevo is a film festival born out of war — its first edition, in 1995, took place while the city was still under siege — and that sense of resistance, of using film to empower communities, still sits at the heart of the festival today. Related Stories Movies China's $300M Sleeper Hit 'Dear You' Unveils U.S. Trailer Ahead of September Release TV Gerhard Zeiler to Receive 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award British actress Emily Watson has been tapped to head up the Sarajevo Film Festival jury this year, with the event running Aug. 14-21, alongside director of the European Film Academy Matthijs Wouter Knol, Yorgos Lanthimos’ producer Athina Rachel Tsangari, filmmaker Igor Bezinović and actress Sara Klimoska. Watson will also receive the prestigious Honorary Heart of Sarajevo, also being presented to Asghar Farhadi , Diego Luna and Woody Harrelson at this installment. “Because it is an award tied to the city, it doesn’t have to be specifically about Sarajevo, but [about] representing similar values or understanding the world of cinema,” Marjanović tells The Hollywood Reporter about how the team selects their Honorary Heart recipients ahead of the 32nd edition. The fest continues to spotlight a wealth of regional talent, including competition features from Zvonimir Jurić ( Small Things ), Urša Menart ( Everything That’s Wrong With You ), Kosara Mitić ( 17 ) and Dina Duma ( Skateboarding Is Not For Girls ). They’re still balancing that with a glitzier, Hollywood-skewed lineup that includes Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland with Sandra Hüller (set to open the festival ), as well as Luna’s Ashes and Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Cannes-premiering Minotaur . And, of course, the festival’s rich, cultural history will be honored with the closing-night film, a screening of the Oscar-winning, newly restored No Man’s Land , with Harrelson’s 1997 feature Welcome to Sarajevo also set to screen. Below, Marjanović teases what’s to come from the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival. He talks about the success of the Open Air Premiere Programs, why the CineLink industry lineup helps to underline the importance of Sarajevo’s place on the festival circuit, and the fascinating origin story that still looms large over everyone passionate about this festival: “[We] realized [the power of] communicating through culture and communicating through cinema with the outside world, because Sarajevo was so closed and besieged. That understanding is, I think, what makes this festival really important.” Jovan, how long have you been in charge? Well, I’ve been with the festival for a very long time. Since I was 19, and I’m 46 now. ( Laughs .) So that’s been pretty much all my life. But I’ve been in charge for the past four years. This will be my fifth edition at the helm alone — there were another two editions before that as a co-director. It’s safe to say you care a lot about this film festival. Oh, absolutely! And I’m not alone. A lot of the team has been with the festival for a long time. But at the same time, we always have young people coming up through the ranks and taking over, and it’s been like that since the very beginning. It was always a close group of friends around the festival. We’re not an institutional body or government-owned body. We’re, let’s say, a non-profit based on an association of citizens. That’s the legal framework. So it’s really up to us, you know? We are our own, and it’s really important to have a group of people who care for what they do and have been nurturing it since day one. [The Sarajevo Film Festival] really came from a difficult place. This festival came [during] war and siege and a complete lack of… everything — what Sarajevo went through in the ’90s. When I say everything, I mean food and electricity. It’s a really specific origin story for a festival, but then [we] realized [the power of] communicating through culture and communicating through cinema with the outside world, because Sarajevo was so closed and besieged. That understanding is, I think, what makes this festival really important. Danis Tanović’s ‘No Man’s Land’ Everett Collection How does the festival continue to honor the history of Sarajevo, the Bosnian War, through its programming? I like to think that it’s in the DNA of the festival first and foremost. Somehow, you see things through that prism and understand the world through that prism and try to take important lessons. On the other side, this year there are two films that are coming back after a couple of decades [away from] the festival. We are closing with No Man’s Land . It’s been 25 years since we showed it last time, and it’s a Bosnian film that won the best international Oscar. But it really was a film that changed a lot of things [for] cinema in Bosnia, and put [the country] on the international stage. That’s the closing film of the festival with [director] Danis Tanović and the team in attendance, so I think it’s going to be very emotional. There’s also Woody Harrelson, who is receiving the Honorary Heart of Sarajevo, and we wanted to show the film that he shot here. So we’re honoring him not just with the Heart, but with the screening of Michael Winterbottom’s Welcome to Sarajevo , a film actually shot back in 1996, just a year after the siege was lifted. Both films [ Welcome to Sarajevo and No Man’s Land ] are actually not present that much on streaming. They’re hard to find, for various reasons… Canal+ in France has restored No Man’s Land fully, so it’s an opportunity to screen the brand new, digital 4K restoration of that film. Welcome to Sarajevo , sadly, did not go through that restoration, but we’re going to screen it in 35mm, which has its own magic to it. Other than that, the festival has programs that are human rights-focused and focused on dealing with the past. The spirit of the festival is really in cooperation. Especially regional cooperation. It connects this legacy of war and division. I think the role of the festival was to build bridges between filmmakers. Is that how you would describe the ethos of a festival like Sarajevo? These mid-tier festivals can have a really important cultural impact, especially in European cinema. What kind of conversations do you want to prompt? It’s a festival that really has a reason to exist. But that’s not enough on its own. There needs to be a clear concept of the festival, and our concept has pretty quickly evolved around filmmakers from our region. We wanted to be geographically focused because of this turbulent history and because of the need to be a bridge between very specific territories [in] the Balkans. It’s a myriad of smaller countries with a lot of smaller languages, with a lot of history, but it’s a powerful mix in the end, and I think the festival serves as a common place for filmmakers and cinemas from many of these countries. We’re also a big festival for the city and for the country, where people want to see the best of cinema from elsewhere — arthouse cinema, conversational pieces, and you want to see them as soon as possible. This is a showcase of the best films to come out this year up until now… And there’s no other festival in the world that shows more films from this part of the world than Sarajevo. You won’t see that many films from this part of the world in Berlin or in Cannes or in Venice. Then they have their home here in a way. We are a premier festival for films coming from this part of the world, and then there’s the whole industry side of things that’s also organized around [that], creating an ecosystem based around cinema from this region. How do you balance those projects with the industry lineup? Some big stars come to Sarajevo, but it’s also a great networking opportunity. True. And that’s one of the key things. It has grown organically, the CineLink Industry Days [program]. We started it some 25 years ago, so the festival and the industry section grew together in a way. The festival was always more audience-oriented. But then, when we introduced the competition sections, which are focused on regional cinema, suddenly those gained industry attention as well. So I think there is the question is of, as you said, balance — finding the equilibrium between the two. And I think once you have built an ecosystem that functions, then [one] feeds into the other. A lot of the execs who come here, they maybe have had films at the festival before, [or] they will have them in the future, and a lot of the projects that are at script stage will end up participating in CineLink to [try] fundraise and promote them. Some of them will go on and premiere elsewhere. Others will premiere with us. It’s a lot of meticulous work. Those CineLink sessions are really wide-ranging… The talks are great. Some speakers I’m really looking forward to hearing. Over the years, there’ve been so many different initiatives that then sprang out of these talks, which is another amazing thing. [They have been] directed either at gender equality or completely business[-focused]. It’s important to be a meeting point, and Sarajevo is really a meeting point. People feel that they can meet each other here. It’s kind of buzzing — the city is not too big, it’s not too small either. So there’s enough space. But at the same time, you can feel the festival everywhere in the city. This atmosphere, I think, adds to people being more open to exploring different futures. So the talks are inspirational in my view. You have a really broad mix of Honorary Heart recipients this year. I’m curious to know how exactly you decide who to honor, and why it’s important to have some high-profile Hollywood names in the list. Well, just looking at the list, there is a thread. The award is called the Heart of Sarajevo, and it really has to do with the city and embracing these people. Emily Watson has been coming to the festival for the past 25 years [or so]. Breaking the Waves was the film that won the second Sarajevo Film Festival before we had the regional focus. She won our hearts back then with that film. And then she kept coming back. She was here, pregnant with her daughter, and now she’s coming with her as a 20-something-year-old! So it’s pretty emotional to welcome her back, and she’s gonna head our jury and dive into the selection of films from this part of the world. She’s going to work fantastically with her fellow jurors. Asghar Farhadi was head of the jury in Sarajevo a few years ago, and when you discuss films with someone like him, you build a connection and an understanding of how we see cinema, what he sees, what we like. That’s another strong bond. I’m saying this in addition to their careers, which are all exceptional. Diego Luna… The people from Mexican and Spanish cinema, from Gael García Bernal to Alfonso Cuarón. Alfonso was actually here for the first Sarajevo Film Festival ever, back in 1995. In the middle of the war, he came to show A Little Princess to the children of Sarajevo. And Y tu mamá también is maybe one of the films that defined the generation of the early 2000s, both for cinema-goers and people making films. Alfonso [is] the leader of that generation, with Diego and Gael… And I already told you about Woody Harrelson. He shot a film here back in 1996 and hasn’t been back since. It’s amazing to welcome him back. So it’s important that these recipients have a special connection to Sarajevo? Well, it just so happens [that way]. That’s not what we award. It really is about the respect for their work in cinema first and foremost. Because it is an award tied to the city, it doesn’t have to be specifically about Sarajevo, but [about] representing similar values or understanding the world of cinema. So we need to be close, maybe without ever meeting each other, but through work and worldviews and world values. That’s the key. I know you can’t show any favoritism, but are there any projects you’re particularly excited about this year, maybe out of competition? Yes. Last year, we opened a new section called Open Air Premieres. This has really grown quickly. We have it at a very prominent venue, a thousand-seater outdoor [theater] with a view of the beautiful Sarajevo City Hall. These films are [typically] something that was missing from the overall mix [or] more popular films from the region [such as No Good Men , Ashes , Minotaur ]. Stuff that’s more audience-driven, that can communicate to a bigger crowd. We [also] gave [the Open Air Premiere selection] a new award this year, the Audience Award, that comes with about 20,000 euros in marketing through Cineplexx, so that’s really exciting. I hope the addition of more popular choices for audiences can complete this regional selection. In our summer screen section, we have a lot of the best films of the year from Berlin, from Cannes, from last year’s Venice Film Festival. In both the Midnight Screenings and Kinoscope, there are a lot of new voices in cinema, a lot of genre-bending stuff. So I’m sure that a lot of the audience will drop in for that. We are opening with Fatherland from Paweł Pawlikowski and I think it’s going to be a great opening. It’s exactly the film that fits the profile of the festival. And No Man’s Land , as I said. There are great films in between that I’m really looking forward to: the Berlinale opener No Good Men , the Afghani film. I think it will resonate with the Bosnian audience very much. Palestine 36 from Annemarie Jacir, also something the audience will want and need to see. Then there’s Minotaur from Andrey Zvyagintsev, which carries a lot of weight in terms of what the story is, the corruption it depicts. I’m really looking forward to the entire Open Air program this year. It’s 3,500 seats and a huge screen and a really special place to see films. The 2026 Sarajevo Film Festival runs Aug. 14-21. THR

articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers Leads Delighted Fans Around the Rink at a Rollerskating Listening Party for ‘Lost Weekend’
articles.full_text: Aug 13, 2026 9:28pm PT Phoebe Bridgers Leads Delighted Fans Around the Rink at a Rollerskating Listening Party for ‘Lost Weekend’ The beaming singer relished in taking slow songs out for a spin, as she made a surprise appearance at the YouTube-sponsored event, also doing a Q&A about an album she hasn't otherwise discussed publicly. By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Phoebe Bridgers Leads Delighted Fans Around the Rink at a Rollerskating Listening Party for ‘Lost Weekend’ 5 hours ago Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’ 1 day ago The Band Perry’s Family Feud Lights Up: Neil Perry Says He Was ‘Terminated’ From Sibling Trio, as Kimberly Perry’s Husband Stepped In to Make It a Marital Duo 2 days ago See All @linusandhiscamera Phoebe Bridgers tends to stand out in a crowd, and not just because of her celebrity or natural star quality, but because of the hair; other women around L.A. may go for the platinum blonde look, but not quite that platinum. So it was fairly easy to pick her out for the entirety of the 10 minutes or so she spent skating with her fans Tuesday night at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California. But she was easy to spot, in this instance, from head to toe, as she was the only skater on the floor in brightly strobing light-up skates… an equipment option that the Moonlight was not able to offer any of the couple hundred fans who joined her. At this very action-packed listening party for her. The beaming Bridgers had earned the right to wear skates that special; this was not her first rodeo, clearly, when it came to making dozens of laps around a rink and outpacing a crowd. Related Stories ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery As one fan commented on Reddit after the YouTube-sponsored event: “She was skating right with everyone, and if you could match her speed then you could say hello, but she is FAST so it may have been a bit difficult.” Popular on Variety Of all the albums that could be previewed with an evening out at an old-school roller rink, “Lost Weekend,” the singer’s long-awaited third solo album, would not jump out as the most obvious candidate… even if Bridgers is hell on wheels, as it turns out. The 16-track record has as many hushed passages as you’d expect from a Bridgers album, and it does not sound at all designed to inspire extended bouts of cardiovascular activity. And Bridgers did use the word “weird” in characterizing the juxtaposition when she spoke about her reasons for hosting the event there in a brief Q&A she did with fans at the event after the skating wound down. Yet, for her, it was an aspiration being realized. “I’ve had this idea forever” she said to the crowd of about 200 sitting on the rink’s floor. “I always thought it would be cool to do like a Grouper Moonlight night… You always kind of skate to ABBA or something. I thought it would be interesting to listen to sad and slow songs and skate.” Phoebe Bridgers skates at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera She’s had the same impulse at amusement parks, she pointed out. “I always thought about that at Six Flags,” she said saying that, while waiting in line for rides, she’d wished she could take the typical revved-up theme-park soundtrack and “catapult it somewhere” and replace it with music that was “30 bpm or something.” To her mind, slowcore and Tatsu might be the perfect fit. Anyway, Bridgers’ promotional campaign for “Lost Weekend” has been unusual enough that a rollerskating listening party almost — almost — doesn’t stand out as that unusual. ,The singer-songwriter first began teasing “Lost Weekend” a few months ago with a series of pop-up gigs in small towns and middle American cities, places like Roswell, New Mexico, before the album was announced or even widely known to be in production. WIth the moment of release finally at hand, her team booked planetariums across the country and even in Europe for Spotify-sponsored listening parties where fans could experience the album for the first time this week with trippy visuals, if sore necks — a way of getting “Lost” in space, sort of. (And no phones allowed, as with virtually every pre-release event for the record.) Another fairy unusual element of the promo campaign: no interviews. She hasn’t done a single one for “Lost Weekend,” so the roughly six minutes she spent answering fan questions at the Moonlight Rollerway may have constituted as much talking about the record as she plans to do, at least right away. Bridgers didn’t exactly talk anyone’s ear off in her quick, friendly response to the fan queries, but the answers still offered glimpses of insight as to where she’s coming from with this album and its attendant cycle of events and touring. One of the first hands that went up from the crowd was to ask whether she’d been inspired by any other artistic media while making the record. “Well, there’s a movie called ‘Lost Weekend’ that’s about alcoholics’ kind of fugue state,” she said, referencing the harrowing 1945 Billy Wilder drama that some of her younger fans might not know. “That probably goes well (with the album), unfortunately.” She hesitated while trying to think of another example, then did come up with a musical reference point. “Do you guys know ‘The Lemon of Pink’ by the Books?” (Not everyone did — the Books are not exactly a household name — but some murmured their assent for the 2003 album, which has a strong following as a seminal indie-oughts cult record.) Phoebe Bridgers does a Q&A with fans at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera Someone else wondered: Why the small-town pop-up tour? And what was her takeaway from what seemed like it might be an experiment? “I just wanted everything with this album to feel like it’s happening in real life,” she explained. “Like, I didn’t live through a time where I didn’t find out about something on the internet. Even cool pop-up shows and stuff, it was all kind of phone-based. So I just liked the idea of plastering a small town (with flyers)… It was so fun.” Her answer to the second part of the question: “The biggest takeaway was like, yeah, the internet’s not real. It’s all a fake,” she said, to laughter. Another question: How did she decide it was time to come back? — the unspoken assumption being that six years between albums counts as a lot, even if there was a monumental Boygenius album and tour in between that came to feel like a very viable separate career. “I mean, I didn’t love all parts of being away,” she said, with a chuckle, noting that while she knew she needed to pull away for a bit, it wasn’t necessarily a plan to wait this long. “I kept booking studio time and then putting it off… and booking studio time and putting it off, and putting it off… I really wanted to be making something,” she allowed, but the album was not yet ready to take shape. “So I just started going in and then taking six months off and then going (back). So this album took forever. Which is great!,” she added, harboring no regrets about leaving anyone in suspense. After those and a few other questions, it was time for her to sign the big stack of posters commemorating the event. Prior to the Q&A, meanwhile, Bridgers premiered a rough cut of the second video for the album, for the song “I Can’t Wait,” which she said was nearly done, except for some drone footage that was shot during this very event that will be folded in. Phoebe Bridgers signs posters for fans at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera There was a no-phones policy, but there were also no NDAs, so fans freely shared their experiences on Reddit and other forums after the event… including their impressions about Phoebe Bridgers being as good at skating as at music. “I ate shit 3 times out there and got a sore ass today,” wrote one fan. “It was even more embarrassing because she was shredding around the rink.” Others spoke of approaching Bo Burnham or Bridgers’ mother, Jamie Bridgers, for off-rink convos. But when it came to meeting the star attraction, some found her intimidating, despite her best efforts to be a fairly unassuming skatergrl. Some agonized afterward about not having found the right words when they made it to the front of the signing line. One spoke of becoming tongue-tied, but “I was towards the end of the line and it had been almost 2 hours at that point. She probably did appreciate our efficiency lol!!” Another wrote, “I just said ‘Yo this album fucking rips,’ and she laughed and said thanks.” One person who admitted being unable to do anything but blurt out their name said that as they left the signing table, Bridgers politely called out, “It was nice to meet you.” Phoebe Bridgers skates at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera What will she do for an encore? That’s obvious: do sold-out two- and three-nighters at the nation’s biggest arenas, like the three-night stand she has upcoming at the Intuit Dome Oct. 30-31 and Nov. 1. Between now and then, there is much parsing of the 16-track album’s rich content to be done, with millions of words of formal and informal think-pieces to come. (Read Variety ‘s own take on the album here .) While fans who didn’t make it to the Moonlight Rollerway may have a lingering case of FOMO, it may still be possible to replicate the feel that Bridgers was going for, as she’s longed to marry slow sounds with frenetic action. You could go to Magic Mountain and do X2 while listening to “Lost Weekend” on earbuds; we can now be certain the author would approve. articles.title: COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 14, 2026 12:00am PT COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund 2 hours ago Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation 3 hours ago COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago See All COL Group COL Group has launched COL AI Studios, a new entertainment vertical designed to help platforms, studios and brands develop, test and scale content beyond traditional licensing deals. The studio builds on a distribution network that now counts over 5,000 live-action titles, up from a base of just over 1,000 when the network first launched, with content sourced from the United States, Europe, Southeast Asia and China. COL AI Studios adds a development layer that can move proven IP and original concepts into animation, short-form and long-form series, advertising, branded entertainment and live action. Related Stories 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ The launch comes as generative production tools make content creation faster and more accessible, a shift that has also driven a surge in programming built mainly for speed and volume. COL AI Studios is positioning itself differently, pairing established creative teams, commercially tested IP and audience data with what it calls responsible AI, aiming for stronger storytelling and franchise longevity rather than sheer output. Popular on Variety The company frames AI as one production method among several rather than a finished product, arguing it can help creators and partners test ideas and gauge audience response before greenlighting bigger-budget productions. COL Group’s library of more than 5,000 titles sits at the center of the model, built in part on thousands of commercially proven microdrama titles and backed by a roster exceeding 500 creative and production personnel – among them writers, directors, producers, editors and artists – based in Los Angeles, China and Southeast Asia. The company’s existing studio operations have already delivered more than 300 AI productions. For partners, the new studio widens the path for IP development, running from licensing and localization through animation, AI-powered production, branded entertainment and potentially premium live action. COL AI Studios is also pushing into branded AI entertainment, working with commercial partners to tap into the company’s creative and production network. Some early projects have already scaled into franchises. “Love Missions Across the Galaxy” has grown into a three-season franchise with localized versions in more than 10 languages, reaching number one in five overseas language markets. Several other AI-native titles are moving toward live-action development. Timothy Oh, general manager of COL Group International, said, “AI is ultimately another way of delivering a story. It can help creators and platforms understand how a concept performs before making the larger commitment required for live action. But greater access to these tools does not automatically lead to better entertainment, so storytelling, creative direction and responsible use of the technology still have to come first.” The company says protecting original IP and respecting creators remain central to how it applies the technology, positioning AI as a tool to strengthen development rather than replace the people driving it. Ray Tong, CEO of COL Group, said, “In China, AI-powered content is increasingly becoming part of mainstream storytelling, and we have had the opportunity to learn from that evolution first-hand. We now want to bring that experience to international platforms and brands, while recognizing that different markets will have different levels of receptiveness.” Meta AI Can Now Use Your Instagram Photos Without Consent. articles.title: Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation
articles.full_text: Aug 14, 2026 12:16am PT Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Nigel Farage Documentary ‘Where Does the Money Come From?’ Set at U.K. Broadcaster 5 as Parliamentary Standards Watchdog Reopens Finance Probe 38 minutes ago Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund 2 hours ago Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation 3 hours ago See All Yash Raj Films Bollywood star Rani Mukerji has been awarded an Honorary Doctor of Letters by Australia’s La Trobe University for three decades of work in Indian cinema and her contributions off screen, the university said. She is the second Indian film figure to receive the distinction, after superstar Shah Rukh Khan’s honor in 2019. “Receiving this honorary doctorate from La Trobe University is one of the most humbling moments of my life,” Mukerji said. “For someone who has always believed that films can change hearts before they change minds, this recognition means more than I can possibly express.” Related Stories ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery Khan’s doctorate marked his charitable work and standing in Indian film, and came with a Ph.D. scholarship set up in his name at the university. Mukerji’s own citation draws on similar ground: her screen career and the causes she has backed alongside it. Popular on Variety Mukerji said her film choices have always come down to what moved her personally first – stories that needed telling, that could inspire and empower. Every artist, she said, carries a responsibility beyond performance. “We quietly become ambassadors of our culture,” she said. On the impact of her work, she said, “If my films have helped even one person understand India and its women a little better… If they have encouraged dialogue… If they have created empathy… Then I feel I have fulfilled a responsibility far greater than simply being an actor.” Mukerji was separately honored with a special citation for acting excellence by the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (IFFM), which cited her three decades of memorable roles and the international reach of her work. This year’s IFFM, running Aug. 13-23, gathers Indian filmmakers and films from around the country as part of its wider program. Her filmography includes “Black,” “Hum Tum,” “Yuva,” “Bunty Aur Babli,” “No One Killed Jessica,” “Hichki,” the “Mardaani” franchise and “Mrs. Chatterjee vs Norway.” On the IFFM honor, Mukerji said, “When I entered the Indian film industry as a young girl, I never imagined that one day my films and the characters that I have been fortunate enough to play, would take me across oceans and that people in a beautiful country like Australia would embrace me with so much warmth. Entertaining people across the world with my cinema is the greatest gift this profession has given me. Australia has always welcomed me & Indian cinema with open arms. It has become a place where cultures meet through storytelling, where films remind us that emotions don’t need passports and where love, laughter and hope speak a language we all understand.” Mukerji said that the real story of a performance begins only once it reaches an audience, not when it’s shot in front of a camera. “To know that for three decades my films, my characters and my voice have traveled so far from home and still found a place in your lives is incredibly humbling,” she said. “I’ve been fortunate to play women who laughed loudly, loved deeply, fought fearlessly and never stopped believing in themselves. In many ways, every character has changed me a little. They’ve made me a better actor, but more importantly, they’ve made me a better human being.” Meta Suspends AI Image Feature After Days of Backlash Meta AI Can Now Use Your Instagram Photos Without Consent. articles.title: Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund
articles.full_text: Aug 14, 2026 12:38am PT Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund 2 hours ago Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation 3 hours ago COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago See All Asian Cinema Fund The Busan International Film Festival ‘s Asian Cinema Fund (ACF) has selected three international co-productions for its 2026 Co-Production Support Fund, backing films from directors Fukada Koji , Jakrawal Nilthamrong and Boo Junfeng with a combined KRW140 million ($100,000) in production funding. The three projects – “Grateful,” “Rhizome” and “Trinity” – were chosen from 15 submissions following a two-round process of materials review and interviews, the ACF said. The lineup marks a threefold jump from last year’s single recipient, and together the films span 13 countries, including Korea, across majority and minority production roles. Related Stories 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ Fukada Koji directs “Grateful,” a Korea-Japan co-production in which Korea holds majority status and Japan participates as the minority partner. Song Dae-chan and Kameda Yuko produce. The project received KRW60 million ($42,900), the largest of the three grants, with the strength of the Korean production team’s track record cited as a deciding factor in its selection. Popular on Variety Jakrawal Nilthamrong directs “Rhizome,” produced with Thailand carrying majority status while Korea, France, Laos and Singapore hold minority roles. Chatchai Chaiyon, Samavee Pummuang, Kim Hyejin, Yohann Cornu, Mattie Do and Panuksmi Hardjowirogo produce. The film centers on the wartime history shared across Asia and received KRW40 million ($28,600). Boo Junfeng directs “Trinity,” led by Taiwan, France and Singapore as majority partners, joined by eight minority partner countries: Poland, Greece, Germany, Japan, Brazil, Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines. Raymond Phathanavirangoon, Aileen Li, Sophie Erbs, Huang Junxiang, Boo Junfeng, Danny Yong, Takafumi Yuki, Mariusz Włodarski, Marta Gmosińska, Giorgos Karnavas, Danae Spathara, Jonas Katzenstein, Maximilian Leo, Eric Shih, Samuel Sagan, Mayra Faour Auad, Gabrielle Auad, Ilda Santiago, Yulia Evina Bhara, Oh Jungwan, Anita Tung, Bradley Liew, Bianca Balbuena and Stefano Centini produce. The film turns on a theme rooted in religion. The film also received KRW40 million ($28,600). Established in 2025, the Co-Production Support Fund was created to spur cross-border productions involving Korea. It supports long-form narrative features and animated theatrical releases structured as formal co-production pacts with Korea, requiring projects to have financed 60% or more of net production costs. Total funding rose to KRW140 million ($100,000) this year from KRW65 million ($46,400) in 2025, while the minimum guaranteed recipient count grew from one project to at least two. ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim said, “It is encouraging to see support for co-productions expanding since the launch of the Co-Production Support Fund last year, including the resumption of the Korean Film Council’s international co-production support program. The three projects have already made substantial progress in co-production and financing through collaboration with numerous international partners,” adding, “Now that these projects are close to bearing fruit, I hope this support – modest though it may be – will help put the final piece of the puzzle in place and bring each film to successful completion.” The ACF also runs a Script Development Fund, Post-Production Fund and Asian Network of Documentary (AND) Fund, connecting supported projects to distribution and industry access through BIFF and the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) programs. The 2026 ACFM runs Oct. 10-13 at Exhibition Center 2, BEXCO in Busan, alongside the 31st Busan International Film Festival, running Oct. 6-15.
