articles.title: StubHub Is Spending Millions Trying to Stop a Bill That Would Cap Concert Ticket Resale Prices
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All August 12, 2026 4:57pm A Stubhub banner hangs at the New York Stock Exchange as the company prepares to ring the opening bell on September 17, 2025 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images StubHub ’s lobbying expenses have reached an all-time high in California, as the ticket resale platform has spent millions of dollars over the past few months looking to stop a bill that seeks to place limits on how much concert tickets are allowed to sell for on resale services in the Golden State. The company reported nearly $2.6 million in lobbying expenses in California from April to June, per filings reviewed by The Hollywood Reporter. According to the Capitol Morning Report, that makes StubHub the second-largest lobbying spender in the state for the quarter, behind only Pacific Gas & Electric and ahead of the likes of Chevron, Verizon, AT&T and OpenAI, among others. It’s the most StubHub has ever spent on lobbying in any quarter in California, per publicly available documents. Overall, StubHub has spent $3.4 million this calendar year. The company’s record spending follows AB 1720, a bill from state assembly member Matt Haney introduced in February that, if passed, would limit concert ticket resale prices to no more than 10 percent higher than a ticket’s original price. Since its introduction, the bill already has been abated with an amendment limiting the law only to smaller 3,000-capacity venues or lower, removing most of the major amphitheater, arena and stadium dates that usually draw much of the activity on secondary ticketing sites. When asked for comment, StubHub said the platform “exists to give fans access to live events on their own terms through a secure, verified marketplace — including fans who couldn’t get tickets during the original on-sale, or who want the option of grabbing a great deal as prices shift closer to the event.” “We believe that more choice, flexibility, and access put fans first and help everyone get into the events they love,” StubHub said. AB 1720 received support from groups representing artists and indie venues including the National Independent Venue Association, the Future of Music Coalition and the Music Artist Coalition. It’s also drawn support from live music giant Live Nation Entertainment, owner of the eponymous concert promoter and the oft-bemoaned Ticketmaster, the primary ticketing provider for most of the major concert venues in the U.S. Proponents for price caps argue adding a hard limit on secondary ticketing would be a major step in ending ticket scalping, as brokers would no longer be allowed to list tickets at extreme markups, and thus their profit motive would be taken away. Price cap bills have begun picking up steam over the past several years, particularly as long-held fan outrage over concert ticket prices has grown louder in the 2020s. California isn’t the only state that’s considered price caps this year. Maine, Vermont and Washington, D.C . all passed price cap laws in recent months, and Massachusetts governor Maura Healey announced in July that she was placing a price cap law for review in the state’s supplemental spending bill. Noah Kahan was one of dozens of New England acts who voiced his support for the Massachusetts bill, and he appeared over video during Healey’s press conference announcing the law. He also helped get a price cap bill passed in his home state of Vermont. “The artist community and fans greatly benefit from limiting ticket scalping,” Kahan said last month. “I love my fans and I want to protect them however I can. Artists alone could not tackle the market manipulation of secondary resellers.” During a press conference on Tuesday, Haney, the state assemblymember who introduced AB 1720, said that “right now, fans are getting ripped off.” “Today, professional scalpers have turned it into a massive multi-billion-dollar business,” Haney said. “They buy up tickets as soon as they go on sale, not because they want to go to the show, but because they know you want to go to the show. Then they charge you two, three, four, sometimes five times’ what they paid for. Then regular fans are left with a choice: pay hundreds of dollars more to go, or don’t go at all.” Price caps overall, though, have received significant pushback from ticket brokers and resale platforms like StubHub, SeatGeek and Vivid Seats. (SeatGeek and Vivid Seats both reported significantly smaller lobbying expenses, as SeatGeek has spent about $40,000 this year, while Vivid Seats reported $500). Financially, caps represent a potential hurdle for their revenue streams, as their business models are built on collecting fees attached to ticket sales, and those fee amounts depend on a ticket’s sales price. Both StubHub and Vivid Seats mention price caps in their risk factors to their businesses in their most recent 10-K reports. Stephen Parker, the executive director of the National Independent Venue Association, a supporter of 1720, called StubHub’s lobbying spending on the bill an act of “desperation.” “They are staring into a future that does not allow them to make millions across the entire sector by price gouging consumers across the country,” Parker says. “California is one of the biggest concert markets in the country. If California goes in terms of consumer protections around ticketing, we think the rest of the nation will soon follow.” Parker also turned attention toward StubHub CEO Eric Baker, who’d drawn backlash last month over revelations that he also runs Andro Capital, a hedge fund that funds ticket brokers who sell tickets on the platform. House Democrats announced a probe into StubHub in July, and both Baker and the company were hit with a class action suit over claims of fraudulent misrepresentation and violation of state consumer protection statutes. (In a statement on the matter, a StubHub rep said that Baker’s affiliation with the fund was listed publicly, and that “This relationship with Andro Capital makes up only a small fraction of StubHub’s total revenue.”) “Their CEO is not just a platform operator, he’s also funding scalpers,” Parker says. “They have a lot to lose.” Much of StubHub’s lobbying expenses this quarter has gone to the Ticket Policy Forum, a coalition that represents StubHub and other resale platforms including SeatGeek, Vivid Seats and TickPick. StubHub paid Ticket Policy Forum over $1 million this quarter, and the organization’s work has included mail ads calling for voters to tell their representatives to vote no 1720, describing the bill as a Live Nation-Ticketmaster initiative to exact more control over the market. In an email, Ticket Policy Forum executive director Brian Berry further stated that the bill only further empowers Ticketmaster because it places caps only on resale and doesn’t address rising ticket prices on the primary side as well. “Exempting Ticketmaster from price controls will not result in lower ticket prices since the illegal monopoly often secretly holds back ticket inventory to create artificial scarcity to support higher prices, and uses dynamic and platinum pricing to arbitrarily raise ticket prices while tickets are on sale,” Berry said. “Capping only resale does nothing to address this source of rising ticket prices. AB 1720 would let the Live Nation-Ticketmaster monopoly keep raising costs unchecked while jeopardizing the benefits fans stand to gain as remedies are decided in the ongoing Live Nation-Ticketmaster antitrust case. Legislation that fosters open, fair and safe competition, improves transparency and fights fraud and deception is more effective and should be made a priority.” As Berry says, scalpers on the secondary market aren’t the only problem in the concert business. Prices continue to grow higher on the primary side as well, and dynamic pricing and higher fees are two of concertgoers’ most frequent complaints about purchasing tickets. Fans have hated Ticketmaster for years, and back in April, Live Nation lost its antitrust lawsuit , with a jury determining the company operates as a monopoly. Live Nation-Ticketmaster’s support has led to skepticism toward the bill — the company has reported about $91,000 in lobbying in 2026 in California — though 1720 has also drawn support from groups that have been particularly vocal in advocating for a Live Nation breakup, such as NIVA and the Future of Music Coalition. Kevin Erickson, the Future of Music Coalition’s executive director, calls framing price caps as a Ticketmaster-friendly measure “dishonest,” adding that a better ecosystem requires reform on both the primary and secondary marketplaces, and that they aren’t mutually exclusive. “The behaviors [secondary platforms] have been engaging in and the practices that have become core to their business model are indefensible,” Erickson says. “The point isn’t to get rid of the secondary market but to create a system that aligns with the needs of fans, ticket buyers as well as artists and presenters. What we’re advocating for is the ability for artists to charge less than what the market could theoretically bear, and they can’t control that when scalpers use that dynamic to profit. Why accept this impoverished version of the music business where it’s just a cash grab above everything else? When we accept that level of cynicism, we’ve lost a whole lot of what makes live music special.” THR

articles.title: California Pressured By Two Hollywood Unions to Settle Paramount-Warner Bros. Lawsuit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All August 12, 2026 5:36pm California attorney general Rob Bonta. Eric Lee/Getty Images Logo text Two top Hollywood unions are calling for California attorney general Rob Bonta and Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison to reach a settlement on their pending antitrust case because, they argue, industry workers are being harmed by the delayed timeline. The leaders of the Directors Guild of America and IATSE made the request on Thursday in a letter that claimed their members are already seeing productions being put on hold or canceled as the two companies prepare for a March 2027 antitrust trial . Against a backdrop of already scant work, particularly in the L.A. area, DGA national executive director Russell Hollander and IATSE international president Matthew Loeb argued that the consequences of additional uncertainty would be borne by the rank and file. “We write to raise concerns about the potential for a prolonged timetable for the litigation… and express to you the importance that you engage directly with each other to negotiate a resolution that ameliorates the anti-competitive aspects of the proposed merger,” their letter stated. “Should such an agreement prove impossible, we would ask that both parties seek to move the start of the trial to an earlier date, as continued delay and uncertainty around the future of WBD only harms our members.” The leaders of the unions, which together represent roughly 200,000 workers in the entertainment business, conceded that in the past mergers have offered “few benefits” to workers. Still, “While we continue to have significant concerns about the proposed merger, we believe many of these concerns can be addressed through the imposition of enforceable conditions in a binding agreement,” the letter stated. Suggested conditions include keeping Paramount and Warner Bros. operating as entirely separate film and television studios and remaining sellers in the marketplace. Hollander and Loeb also suggest that the combined company could commit to producing projects in the U.S. “at no less than the average percentage produced in the United States during the past five years” and to keeping Paramount based in Los Angeles, among other suggested provisions. The letter puts the two unions at odds with their colleagues at the Writers Guild of America, a labor group that has been vociferously opposed to the $111 billion mega-merger and sued to block the deal itself . The performers’ union SAG-AFTRA has also opposed the deal unless “enforceable safeguards” are put in place. The Teamsters union previously called for the Department of Justice to block the deal (which it did not do) unless worker protections are instituted. The objective with their approach, said the two unions’ leaders, was to mitigate harm to their members. “Our goal, with respect to the proposed merger, has always been to achieve an outcome that ensures a vibrant, competitive marketplace for the production, distribution, and licensing of film and television programming that serves the interests of consumers and filmmakers alike,” the labor leaders stated. “We believe that these conditions, if secured through a binding agreement, will largely serve this purpose.” Read the full letter below. articles.title: ‘End of Oak Street’ Box Office Aims to Take Bite Out of ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All August 12, 2026 5:41pm Ewan McGregor (left) and Anne Hathaway in 'The End of Oak Street.' Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures Logo text It’s dinosaur mayhem at the box office as two newcomers about the prehistoric beasts — The End of Oak Street and PAW Patrol : The Dino Movie — set out to challenge the behemoth that is Spider-Man : Brand New Da y. Warner Bros. releases director David Robert Mitchell’s The End of Oak Street in 3,400 North American theaters on Friday, with the studio projecting an opening weekend in the range of $18 million to $23 million. Warner Bros. expects to add between $20 million to $25 million internationally for the sci-fi survival movie that hails from Bad Robot and carries an $80 million production budget. Related Stories Movies A Movie Theater Didn't Get Sent 'Spider-Man' Posters, So an Employee Drew His Own Movies X-Men: All the Actors Lobbying to Play Marvel's Mutants Anne Hathaway continues her busy 2026 , leading the cast that also includes Ewan McGregor , Maisy Stella and Christian Convery. Mitchell, known for the 2014 horror hit It Follows , helmed the movie from his own script about a family in the early 1980s as they realize that their suburban neighborhood has been transported to an area with prehistoric predators. The End of Oak Street holds an 82 percent approval rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney called the movie “mindlessly entertaining in a big-dumb-fun kind of way.” At the Oak Street premiere, Hathaway expressed to THR her gratitude “that audiences want to go see original things, and this movie is really original.” PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie Paramount Pictures /Courtesy Everett Collection For those seeking a more family-friendly dino adventure, Paramount Pictures releases PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie in more than 3,500 locations in North America. For the third feature installment in producer Spin Master Entertainment’s animated franchise, the studio projects a domestic opening ranging in the mid-to-high teens after having already surpassed $27 million in 30 international markets. Dino Movie has a $39.5 million production budget. Carter Young, Mckenna Grace , Terry Crews, Jennifer Hudson and Snoop Dogg are among the voice stars for director Cal Brunker’s film that sees our Paw Patrol canine heroes end up in a world containing dinosaurs. The previous sequel, 2023’s PAW Patrol: The Mighty Movie , opened to $22.7 million domestically in late September. Its $205 million global run improved upon the $144 worldwide total for 2021’s original PAW Patrol: The Movie , which adapted the series that first launched on Nick Jr. in 2013. The release of a PAW Patrol movie can be counted on to increase interest in all iterations of the brand, including merchandise and streaming for the shows. PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie has earned an 85 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, with THR critic Frank Scheck writing that, “while the material is thoroughly juvenile, the films impart valuable messages to their impressionable viewers.” Meanwhile, Spider-Man: Brand New Day will continue flying high with its third straight weekend at the top of the box office chart. Sony Pictures expects filmmaker Destin Daniel Cretton’s smash hit to bring its domestic total to $700 million in the next day or so as the film looks to soon surpass the global sum of $1.9 billion that previous franchise title Spider-Man: No Way Home collected after opening in December 2021. Starring Tom Holland , Zendaya and Sadie Sink , Brand New Day has notched no shortage of records in its historic run. Thanks to hits like Brand New Day , The Odyssey , Toy Story 5 and others, the summer box office surpassed the $4 billion mark this week, representing just the second time that the prime moviegoing season has achieved this since the COVID pandemic. (The first time was 2023, aka the summer of Barbenheimer.) This means that the all-time summer mark of $4.755 billion from 2013 could still remain within reach. Other new theatrical options this weekend include thriller The Rivals of Amziah King , starring Matthew McConaughey , and the Kristen Stewart -led stoner comedy The Wrong Girls . THR

articles.title: ‘The Matrix’ Director Lilly Wachowski Says Hollywood Won’t Finance New Film With Trans Cast
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 12, 2026 8:25pm Lilly Wachowski Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival Lilly Wachowski , who co-directed The Matrix franchise, is opening up about the struggle to get financing for her new film that features a “wall-to-wall trans cast.” During a recent interview on KCRW’s The Business podcast , the filmmaker acknowledged that it’s unfortunately “not the greatest time in the industry to be trying to make these kinds of things because all of these opportunities are dwindling for folks with those kinds of stories to tell,” specifically those with “underrepresented voices and marginalized points of view.” Related Stories TV Lilly Wachowski's Anarchists United Sets Writers Discovery Fellows Amid Shifting Hollywood Landscape: "Making Television Looks Very Different" Movies Lilly Wachowski Shares Advice to Her Pre-Transition Self at 'Bound' Reunion Screening: "Start Taking That Estrogen" Wachowski used her next project, The Hunted , as an example, saying it’s been a challenge because when she showed the script around Hollywood, nobody wanted to finance the dystopian political thriller that’s budgeted at roughly $10 million. “People like it, but they really don’t want to make it because it’s [got a] wall-to-wall trans cast,” she said of the film. “I have to get creative and figure out different ways that I can get this in front of people.” Wachowski added that the script, which she co-wrote with her partner, Mickey Ray Mahoney, “was extremely important for me to write.” She continued, “It was a response to what is happening in the world for trans people, and it gave me a hugely cathartic receptacle to dump all of my anger and rage and frustration into.” Despite her funding obstacles, Wachowski said she’s pivoted to other ways to get this story in front of people “that maybe isn’t a $10 million movie,” such as holding a live table read at Los Angeles’ Dynasty Typewriter theater earlier this month. “I’m just going to go out and I’m going to grab that trans joy with all of my friends. And we’re going to hopefully experience this together.” Wachowski said of The Hunted table read. “It’s not the thing that I had imagined it was going to be, but the end result is the same.” In addition to Wachowski and Mahoney, The Hunted is being produced by Lawrence Mattis and Sarah Marie Flores at Anarchists United and Natasha Lyonne at Ariadne Collective. Wachowski is best known for helming 1999’s The Matrix , 2003’s The Matrix Reloaded and 2003’s The Matrix Revolutions alongside her sister, Lana Wachowski. She’s also directed 1996’s Bound , 2005’s Speed Racer , 2012’s Cloud Atlas and 2015’s Jupiter Ascending , as well as co-created the TV series Sense8 . THR

articles.title: Asia Argento Discusses Playing “a Racist,” Locarno Honor and Exec-Producing a Gia Carangi Doc
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 13, 2026 1:30am Asia Argento Courtesy of Fabrizio Cestari Italian actress, filmmaker and musician Asia Argento is about to take the big outdoor stage in Locarno in the Italian-speaking part of Switzerland. The 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival will celebrate the creative with its Life Achievement Award on Thursday evening in the city’s Piazza Grande in front of around 8,000 people. While in Locarno, Argento is also presenting Jorge Thielen Armand’s Death Has No Master ( La Muerte No Tiene Dueño ), which premiered in this year’s Cannes Directors’ Fortnight. “Since making her onscreen debut as a child in Lamberto Bava’s cult sequel Demons 2 (1986) and starring in Palombella rossa (1989) by Nanni Moretti, Asia Argento , one of the most distinctive European performers of her generation, has built a singular body of work that encompasses passionately beloved genre films, auteur cinema, and intimate self-portraiture,” Locarno said when it unveiled the honor. And Giona A. Nazzaro , Locarno’s artistic director, lauded her as “an artist who has always managed to reimagine what it means to make films, constantly challenging herself and taking personal risks.” Related Stories Movies Zurich Film Fest Galas Set for Award Contenders 'I Play Rocky,' 'Possible Love,' 'Josephine' News Analysis The Emmys Rules Are Excluding Tons of Great International TV Argento spoke to THR about the honor, her role in Death Has No Master and the documentary about late U.S. supermodel Gia Carangi that she has boarded as an executive producer. Congratulations on the special Locarno honor. How does it feel to get this recognition? It feels incredible. I truly didn’t expect it. Actually, lately I was thinking, my God, I’ve never been invited to Locarno, and I never had a movie at Locarno. I was self-deprecating as usual, thinking they must hate me and everyone is against me. And then this came totally out of the blue, and I was moved to tears. In the last few years, I had a big shift of energy, and I guess life has a way of teaching you to be humble sometimes when you don’t want to learn. So I see this as a sign of the universe that I’m going in the right direction. With my work, I was in the past [sometimes] criticized for it being a little bit extreme and pushing the boundaries of what was accepted from a woman, as an actress, as a filmmaker. What I was trying to achieve created this gut unease, and now this is a way of the universe telling me that I did the right thing at the right time. When you pass through a door, you always receive a lot of blows to your head, so that other people can walk through it a little bit more easily. Now I see that everything is making sense. Okay, I wasn’t wrong to always be who I was, to be honest about who I was, even though I’m somebody who’s far from being perfect. It was a big shine of love. You are presenting Jorge Thielen Armand’s postcolonial thriller Death Has No Master ( La Muerte No Tiene Dueño ), in which you star, at Locarno. Why did you want to work on that film with its themes of colonialism and trauma? What about it spoke to you? I always find characters that are nonlinear, that are a bit tormented and that have a vast history and things to face from the past fascinating. I like complex characters with a lot of suffering. I find it a lot easier and more interesting to do that than, say, a comedy, which I’ve done in my life, and I’m not very talented at that. It’s really not my genre. So when I find something really dark, really obscure and weird with depth, then I dive into that. I just read the script, and I also loved the idea of the adventure of going to Venezuela and this challenge of also acting in yet another language, Spanish, since I’ve done French and English. It was also a huge challenge physically and mentally. At this point in my life, I prefer the challenges that keep me curious and keep me alert. Asia Argento in ‘Death Has No Master.’ Cannes Film Festival How was the production of the film? It was very tough to shoot. I didn’t immediately understand from the script that it would turn into a psychological thriller, almost paranormal in a way. I thought it was a colonial drama about family history and all that, but it’s a lot more than that. And when I saw the movie, I was so immersed in the experience. Jorge is such a great director. I love his movies, and I think that with this one, he found yet another register to his art. So just working there with him fueled my fire and my love. Speaking about colonialism: How do you get into a role like this? Did you ever travel and experience the weight of colonialism? Or how do you find the access point as an actress to something that is so painful for so many people? It was pretty hard, because we developed the script and the character a lot while we rehearsed for a month before the shoot in the locations with all the non-actors there. As we were preparing, I realized, “My God, my character is a racist; she’s really not somebody that I would like to meet.” To play that, you have to really understand and love to prepare for that. I was in Venezuela. There were a lot of stories about the richer people that went away amid all the political problems, and the people working for them, the descendants of the slaves. I hate to even use the word [“slave”], but they took over houses where they worked if somebody was gone for over 10 years. I think people have the right to occupy the house and live there. So this is what the movie is about, and so I spoke at length with both sides – people who went away, whose house was squatted, so to speak, and they had this colonial anger; and the people who squatted, who lived there. It’s very political, and I felt for both sides. So it was important for me to understand both sides. There are always two sides. You recently signed on as executive producer on Rosita Larocca’s directorial debut feature documentary Gia – The Shadow of Beauty , about Gia Carangi (1960–1986). The U.S.-Italy co-production approaches her “not as a pop-cultural icon but as a young woman navigating desire, abandonment and visibility in 1980s New York.” Can you tell me a little bit about what brought you to this project and why you wanted to do that? I was always fascinated by Gia Carangi and her arc in this show business world. She was somebody who was a very smart girl who was not fully inside the system. She was very broken and then had her battles with addiction. And there is also the fact that she was lesbian at a time when that was a huge taboo. So, there are many fascinating [themes and issues] to explore. THR

articles.title: Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 8:30pm PT Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Drishyam’ Producer Panorama Studios Invests in Indian Vertical Streaming Platform Rocket Reels (EXCLUSIVE) 39 minutes ago BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub 3 hours ago See All Collective Studios A new original series exploring the life of Indian freedom fighter Bhagat Singh is in development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse . The project is being made in association with Hathiramani Commercial Ventures and co-produced with investor and entrepreneur Manish Hathiramani, who marks his producing debut with the show. The series is designed to move past the familiar episodes of Singh’s story and instead examine the man beneath the myth – his childhood, intellectual development and the social and political forces that shaped his convictions in early 20th-century India. Rather than revisiting the widely known chapters of Singh’s life, the show will track how his ideas evolved across the different stages of his journey, culminating in the revolutionary figure whose legacy continues to endure. Related Stories Errol Spence, Jr. vs. Tim Tszyu Livestream: Here's Where to Watch the Middleweight Pay-Per-View Match Online 'The Traitors' India Sets August Season 2 Bow on Prime Video (EXCLUSIVE) Sudeep Lahiri, head of channels and distribution at Collective Media Network, said: “There are some figures in our history whose stories we think we know completely. Bhagat Singh is one of them. But behind the icon was a young man whose ideas, influences and experiences shaped the person he would become. That is the story we are interested in exploring. Having Manish come on board as a co-producer makes this collaboration particularly exciting, because we share a strong belief in finding new perspectives within stories that have already been told many times and bringing them to audiences with scale and ambition.” Popular on Variety “Bhagat Singh is a figure whose life has always fascinated me, but what interests me most is the person before the legend,” Hathiramani added. “We know the revolutionary, the freedom fighter and the icon; this series gives us an opportunity to understand the many facets of Bhagat Singh’s life and the journey that shaped him. I am delighted to be producing this project with Historyverse and to bring a fresh perspective on his life and legacy to audiences.” Title, cast and additional details are to be confirmed. Singh has been the subject of at least five Indian features, among them “Shaheed” (1965), “Shaheed-E-Azam” (2002), “23rd March 1931: Shaheed” (2002), “The Legend of Bhagat Singh” (2002) and “Rang De Basanti” (2006). The Bhagat Singh project joins a Historyverse slate that already encompasses titles drawn from Indian mythology and history, including projects centered on Shivaji and Swami Samarth. articles.title: Andreas Dresen, Doris Dörrie Films to World Premiere  at Zurich Film Festival
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 9:00pm PT Andreas Dresen, Doris Dörrie Films to World Premiere at Zurich Film Festival By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Andreas Dresen, Doris Dörrie Films to World Premiere at Zurich Film Festival 6 hours ago 1-2 Special Takes U.S. Rights to Michal Marczak’s Sundance Documentary ‘Closure’ (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago Oscar Nominee Barkhad Abdi, Jim Deddes Lead Teddy Cherim’s ‘Maalstroom’; First-Look Image Released (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All "Love, After All" (Courtesy of Andres Dresen, Kordes und Kordes Film, Pandora) The world premieres of two major German films, Andreas Dresen ’s “Love, After All” and Doris Dörrie ’s “How Can I Help?,” are among 11 titles to feature in the Gala Premieres section of Zurich Film Festival . The selection also includes Oscar contenders “I Play Rocky” and “Josephine,” and Switzerland’s most anticipated film, “111 – Echoes From Halifax.” Christian Jungen, CEO of the festival, said the section is “dedicated to auteur cinema for a broader audience.” Related Stories 'The Legend of Kitchen Soldier,' 'Yumi's Cells' Lead Prime Video India's Slate of 100-Plus New CJ ENM Titles 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe “We are particularly delighted that two major figures of German auteur cinema, Andreas Dresen and Doris Dörrie, have entrusted us with the world premieres of their new films,” Jungen said. “Their films are grounded in everyday life and, with a little wink, reflect on the state of our society.” Popular on Variety He added, “We present films that will play an important role later in the award season, such as ‘I Play Rocky.’” The film tells the story behind the making of the cult classic starring Sylvester Stallone, which won the Academy Award for best picture in 1977. Jungen explained that, from a Swiss perspective, “111 – Echoes From Halifax” deserves special mention. “From multiple perspectives, the film sheds light on a major event that shook our nation: the crash of a Swissair aircraft near Halifax,” he said. The full program of the 22nd Zurich Film Festival, which runs Sept. 24 to Oct. 4, will be revealed on Sept. 9. I PLAY ROCKY European Premiere Biography U.S., 2026 Director: Peter Farrelly Cast: Anthony Ippolito, Matt Dillon, Stephan James, AnnaSophia Robb, PJ Byrne, Toby Kebbell, Tracy Letts, Jay Duplass Unknown actor Sylvester Stallone is writing a screenplay titled “Rocky” that a studio is desperate to acquire. But Stallone refuses to sell the rights – unless he gets to play the lead himself. Despite numerous setbacks and rejections, he remains determined to make his dream a reality: playing Rocky Balboa. The result is the ultimate underdog story behind the legendary underdog film. JOSEPHINE Drama U.S., 2026 Director: Beth de Araújo Cast: Channing Tatum, Gemma Chan, Mason Lily Reeves When 8-year-old Josephine witnesses a violent crime, her world is out of joint. She is trying to find a way to regain a sense of security. While her emphatic mother (Gemma Chan) wants to help her process what happened, her father (Channing Tatum) believes in preparing Josephine for the harsher realities of life but increasingly finds himself overwhelmed by the situation. With the suspense of a thriller, director Beth de Araújo tells a deeply empathetic family drama about fear and the limits of parental care. Channing Tatum gives one of his strongest performances in this year’s great Sundance Film Festival sensation. WICKER Comedy U.S., 2025 Director: Alex Huston Fischer, Eleanor Wilson Cast: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Peter Dinklage, Elizabeth Debicki, Marli Siu, Nabhaan Rizwan An audacious comedic fable about sex, marriage and the absurdities of social convention, “Wicker” tells the wholly original love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Colman) who commissions a husband to be made by the local basketmaker (Dinklage). When her wicker husband (Skarsgård) proves more spectacular than she ever imagined, his soulful spirit and unique prowess awaken something inside her, setting off a wave of jealousy, fascination and upheaval that threatens the very fabric of village life. 111 – ECHOES FROM HALIFAX International Premiere Drama Switzerland, Canada, 2026 Director: Mauro Mueller Cast: Ursina Lardi, Kris Holden-Ried, Djebril Zonga, Fathia Youssouf, Natalie Brown On Sept. 2, 1998, the crash of Swissair Flight 111 off Halifax changes the lives of many people forever: relatives struggle for certainty about their loved ones, helpers try to offer comfort, and the residents of the Canadian coast are confronted with the traces of tragedy. As time passes and questions remain unanswered, the film shows how grief connects, relationships change, and new perspectives emerge. Mauro Mueller’s film is a quiet, poignant drama about loss, memory and the power of human closeness. COMPANY Mystery Canada, U.S., UAE, 2026 Director: Casey Affleck Cast: Nick Nolte, Ben Mendelsohn, Adelaide Clemens, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, Caylee Cowan On a winter night in 1975, a mysterious woman named Evelyn arrives uninvited at a holiday gathering and tells the story of Tom, an aging hermit who rescues a stranded actress during a Colorado blizzard in 1953. To pass the night, the actress recounts an older tale of a farming couple who take in a troubled young drifter as a series of grisly murders spreads fear across the frontier. As the stories intertwine across generations, “Company” becomes a meditation on grief, vengeance, forgiveness and the quiet acts of compassion that can heal even the deepest wounds. POSSIBLE LOVE Drama South Korea, 2026 Director: Lee Chang-dong Cast: Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-jeong “Possible Love” follows the intertwined relationship of two married couples facing different paths and hidden desires. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) lives quietly with her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu) and their young son Cheol until a funeral brings them into the orbit of Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a documentary filmmaker chronicling laid-off workers, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung) – a couple whose affluent lifestyle stands in sharp contrast to their own. When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed, she grows close to Ye-ji, and finds herself uneasily drawn to the unreadable Sang-woo. As their worlds collide, fractures begin to appear in their daily existence. Marking his first release in eight years, highly acclaimed director Lee Chang-dong (“Burning,” “Poetry,” “Secret Sunshine”) brings his signature nuance to “Possible Love,” capturing shifting emotions, conflicts, and contrasting outlooks that shape these relationships. LOVE, AFTER ALL World Premiere Tragicomedy Germany, 2026 Director: Andreas Dresen Cast: Dagmar Manzel, Joachim Król Lore (Dagmar Manzel) and Harry (Joachim Król) have been married for nearly 40 years and there is rarely a moment of silence between them. Old stories, missed chances and the uncertainties of retirement fuel heated discussions. Lore is afraid of growing old and bitter in the garden alongside Harry while he longs for stability and peace. There is only one thing they agree on: Their daughter Gloria has little luck in love. Now, she wants to get married for the third time – this time to a wealthy man who is almost the same age as Harry. A warm-hearted love story inspired by real life, drawing the audience in with its authentic characters and lots of humor. IT WILL HAPPEN TONIGHT Romance Italy, France, Spain, 2026 Director: Nanni Moretti Cast: Louis Garrel, Jasmine Trinca, Hippolyte Girardot, Angela Finocchiaro, Melina Åkerman Kvie, Elena Lietti, Andrea Lattanzi, Antonio De Matteo, Nanni Moretti I’ll wait for you, for as long as you want me to. But will it ever happen? BURGUNDY Documentary France, 2026 Director: Michael Dweck, Gregory Kershaw Cast: Enzo Ferraroli, Céleste Kalis, Eric Goettelmann, Patrick Maniere, Guillaume Baroin, Bertrand Devillard Burgundy is one of the world’s most famous wine regions. Through the eyes of novices in hospitality and viticulture, the film offers a fascinating glimpse into its unique wine culture, where time-honored traditions live on in rituals centered on luxury and indulgence. Blending documentary and fictional elements, directors Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw pay homage to the remarkable and charming people whose zest for life shapes and preserves this unique region and its centuries-old culture. HOW CAN I HELP? World Premiere Drama/Comedy Germany, 2026 Director: Doris Dörrie Cast: Angela Winkler, Laura Tonke, Josef Ellers, Via Jikeli, Eugene Boateng, Zoë Baier Mrs. Winkler has a fall and becomes a nursing case. Her daughter, overwhelmed by her needs, hires a care robot. After some initial resistance, Mrs. Winkler grows quite fond of him. He takes perfect care of her and keeps her entertained – except that he is also supposed to kill her in case her condition deteriorates further… THE HAMMER World Premiere Documentary France, U.S., 2026 Director: Simon Wallon Cast: Simon de Pury, Jeff Koons, Marina Abramović, Chloe Wise, Lou Zhenggang A documentary portrait of famed auctioneer Simon de Pury, whose career saw him leading auction houses such as Sotheby’s and Phillips, being the curator of major world collections, an artist, even a DJ, and always being an unavoidable personality “the Mick Jagger of auctions” takes us behind the curtain of the extravagant art market. Art fairs, collectors’ homes, artists’ studios, galas… The film is a welcoming and entertaining dive amongst the 1% and explores the complicated relationship between artists and commerce. Ultimately, it questions what it means to be an artist today. It was shot between New York, Tokyo, London, Cannes, Miami and Monaco. articles.title: Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 9:27pm PT Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’ By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’ 6 hours ago The Band Perry’s Family Feud Lights Up: Neil Perry Says He Was ‘Terminated’ From Sibling Trio, as Kimberly Perry’s Husband Stepped In to Make It a Marital Duo 16 hours ago Kennedy Center Ordered to Pay $250,000 to Jazz Musician It Unsuccessfully Sued for Backing Out of Concert After Trump Rebranding 2 days ago See All Universal Archive/Universal Imag Most Deep Purple fans had long since given up any hope of seeing the band ever share a stage with founding guitarist Ritchie Blackmore again, due to a well-know, decades-long estrangement. But that’s exactly what took place near the end of the group’s show Wednesday night at Jones Beach in New York, as hatchets were buried and Blackmore rejoined his old mates for a rendition of the group’s most famous song, “Smoke on the Water.” “It’s gonna be interesting,” Blackmore said in a podcast appearance the night before the show, in which the 81-year-old guitar legend leaked news of his imminent appearance. “i have not played rock music in 25 years.” Related Stories Errol Spence, Jr. vs. Tim Tszyu Livestream: Here's Where to Watch the Middleweight Pay-Per-View Match Online 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe At the conclusion of “Smoke in the Water” Wednesday, singer Ian Gillan showered praise on his ex-bandmate before he left the stage. “A couple of days ago I got a message from a local lad… saying ‘I only live around the corner, do you mind if I come and jam with you?’ It was an absolute pleasure to have back on stage the founding member, the great legend,”the immortal Ritchie Blackmore. Thanks, Ritchie. i have to say, it was a great pleasure. I’ll see you in the bar.” Popular on Variety Probably few in the audience were taken by complete surprise by Blackmore’s cameo, since the previous night, the guitarist had spilled some of the beans in a livestream conversation with his wife, singer Candice Night, the evening before the Jones Beach gig. Blackmore said on Tuesday’s live podcast that he was revealing the secret in advance because he wanted fans who had waited for this moment for decades to at least have a shot at making it to New York in time for Wednesday’s show. Blackmore, who co-founded Deep Purple in 1968, had a fallout with other members in 1993 that resulted in him leaving the lineup in 1993 for the second and last time. The fallout was bad enough that Blackmore did not show up at the band’s Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction in 2016, after being told that the currently touring lineup — which still includes three original or near-original members in Gillan, drummer Ian Paice and bassist Roger Glover — would not reunite with him under any circumstances, even for a short, one-off performance at the ceremony. So hell seemed to have frozen over when Gillan recently sent a message gingerly asking if he could come up on stage for one number at a tour date… and the band proved surprisingly agreeable to that notion, after so much water under the bridge. “it is a secret and i don’t want anybody to know, but I’m probably going to go up and do an encore with the band, Deep Purple,” Blackmore blurted about eight minutes into the livestream with his wife, singer Candice Night. “But you can’t tell anybody, and I know this will be kept a secret. won’t it?” he joked, even as the web lit up with the news quickly being spread among hard rock buffs. Blackmore explained the genesis of this unexpected reunion: “I sent my AI pigeon to Ian Gillan in Portugal, where he lives at the moment, and I said, ‘How would you feel if I got up just for an encore on one of the songs. Don’t want to intrude.’ And I said, ‘No pressure, just kind of old times’ sake.’ You know, I’m 81 now. So (Gillan) seemed to li0e the idea, put it to the band, got a thumbs up, and it looks like we might be doing that.” The guitarist admitted he was hardly in practice for a performance with Deep Purple, given the drift in his musical focus since 1993, as he moved on to gentler brand of folk-rock with Blackmore’s Night, the band fronted by his wife. “I changed my strings on my Strat, which i haven’t done in over 25 years,” he revealed. “It’s kind of frightening. I haven’t played rock in 25 years. I’ve been playing acoustic guitar for 25 years. And at first i was very uncomfortable playing (acoustic guitar), but i got used to it, and now I’m more used to playing the acoustic, more so than the electric.” He said he needed some medical assistance in being able to withstand “Smoke on the Water.” “I did have my injection in my lumbar area yesterday,” he explained on the podcast, of needing a steroid shot. “it’s a special injection i have that enables me to stand in one spot, because if I’m playing a Strat, i have a hard time… I have four herniated discs, if anybody wants them. And I had my injection yesterday of a steroid which helps me get through standing on stage. But I have kind of a stool there, just in case I start toppling over or something.” Of his reasons for giving fans 24 hours’ notice, he said he “wanted to warn the people living in Romania, so they could fly over… Not really. I just thought it might be an idea to let a few people know because I think a lot of people would like to see that.” what a moment in time… pic.twitter.com/tTOq2RUXP6 — Candice Night (@TruCandiceNight) August 13, 2026 His announcement of sitting in with the group concluded with the thoughts: “I hope people enjoy it.” And: “it will be good to see the old guys again.” well, this warms my heart… pic.twitter.com/2nArOmSihz — Candice Night (@TruCandiceNight) August 13, 2026 Fans from afar turned to the web to look for footage of the show. Perrin Wolfson and Jimmy Kay of the Metal Voice podcast livestreame through the latter part of Deep Purple’s set, waiting for confirmation that it had gone down, and putting up photos and video that were shared with them from inside the show. “History has been made,” Wolfson and Kay crowed as they first got word “Smoke in the Water” was in progress with Blackmore aboard. “I feel like we just walked on the moon.” Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review Loading comments... articles.title: ‘Far From the Trees’ Director Meritxell Colell on Turning Exile and Endangered Languages Into a ‘Body of Memory’
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 10:22pm PT ‘Far From the Trees’ Director Meritxell Colell on Turning Exile and Endangered Languages Into a ‘Body of Memory’ By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest Edinburgh Industry Program Features Ewan McGregor, Kenneth Branagh and Bruce Dern and an Inaugural U.K. Film Conference 3 weeks ago ‘Cowboy’ Director Nathan Grubbs on Betting the Farm to Make His Louisiana Western 4 weeks ago Canary Islands’ Documentary Voices Look Outward as Sector Gains Range 2 months ago See All In “Far From the Trees,” (“Lejos de los árboles”) Meritxell Colell asks viewers to listen before they try to understand. Premiering in Locarno’s international competition, the Spain-Italy-Peru production from Allegra Films follows Adela, a 50-year-old Mexican sound artist who travels from the Peruvian jungle to the Andes recording endangered languages. Accompanied by a guide and translator, she is continuing the work of her grandfather, a Catalan Republican exiled in Mexico. But news of her grandmother’s possible death fractures the journey, drawing Adela into childhood memories, family silences and fantastical visions. Related Stories Inside Netflix and Prime Video’s Fight to Reshape France’s Streaming Rules: 'It's an Unsustainable Equation' 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe For the director, the film began with an absence. Popular on Variety “‘Lejos de los árboles’ came into being in 2020 following the death of a very close family member. At the time, I knew only that I wanted to address the inability to say goodbye—the inability to view a dead body and the emotions that entails—and to link this to sound,” Colell told Variety. She initially searched for displaced or migrant sound artists and encountered Angélica Castelló, a Mexico-born, Vienna-based composer whose grandfather had also gone into exile. “The film emerged from her story and those initial impulses; years later, I realized it also connected deeply with my own life – specifically, with the legacy of silence passed down by my grandparents,” Colell explained. Rather than reconstructing her own family history directly, she created Adela: a fictional figure whose identity is formed by migration, artistic vocation and the simple fact of being often elsewhere. “I was determined to center the film on the complexity of hybrid identities shaped by exile and migration –identities where the status of ‘foreigner’ becomes the self – and on the burden of that inheritance,” she said. The geographical distance was crucial. Adela follows her grandfather’s footsteps while transforming his political and anthropological work into art, weaving a sound map from languages at risk of disappearing. The connection between Indigenous languages in Peru and Catalan exile was not part of the earliest drafts, but became the idea that brought the film into focus. “Once the idea of vulnerable languages came up, everything fell into place,” said Colell. “It became clear that her work was carrying on her grandfather’s legacy, adding a new dimension to his figure.” The grandfather became an activist-anthropologist dedicated to recovering native languages in Mexico, a calling linked to his flight from a Catalonia where Franco’s regime suppressed languages other than Castillian Spanish. “In a way, the film is an ode to the beauty of languages, to their collective value, and to multilingualism as a viable social reality,” Colell says. “Language is a form of thought, a way of seeing and inhabiting the world. We don’t necessarily have to understand every form; we simply need to listen to them, however we can.” That principle shapes the film itself. We hear the birds, wind, voices, music, the whirr of a grandmother’s sewing machine and a thud against a trunk of a tree. “Sound is essential in cinema – not only on narrative and contextual levels but also on perceptual and emotional ones,” observed Colell. “That is why I was so eager to make a film featuring a sound artist as the protagonist.” The film’s Super 16mm passages, which inhabit memories, visions and reveries, were shot without synchronized sound. The voices of Adela’s grandparents and Paula were recorded separately, leaving Castelló free to build what Colell calls “a sonic tapestry woven from a multitude of sounds.” Castelló’s presence reshaped the film over years of residencies, meetings and debate. The director was determined, however, that Adela would firmly be fictional rather than becoming a portrait of the performer. “It was a way to lighten the role, turn it into a game, and distance it from reality,” she said. “It was crucial for me to portray a person in her fifties who had left her home country to pursue her passion– music – and to depict a type of woman rarely seen on screen.” “As time went on, my initial intuition upon meeting her was confirmed: She was the film.” Producer Mayca Sanz L-Higueras began assembling the project in 2021, initially seeking a European structure that could connect with Latin America through Ibermedia. Italy’s Exit Media joined first; Peru’s Animalita Cine later came on board, while RTVE helped complete the financing. “In Peru, the biggest challenge has been finding someone willing to commit to filming with a fiction crew – albeit a very small one – in a country completely unprepared for such a project, and with a story that required the commitment of non-professional actors whom the director had sought out, selected and worked with over time, following location scouting trips spanning three years,” said Sanz. The shoot unfolded in five blocks over more than a year, beginning in February 2024 and ending with Teresita Sánchez’s scenes in July 2025. Colell also became a mother during production. “At times, I worried that shooting in such fragmented stages might result in something of a Frankenstein’s monster; I’m used to filming in chronological order,” she says. “The surprise came when we started editing and saw that everything actually fit together perfectly.” For Allegra Films, Locarno’s selection validates a leap into a more ambitious international model. For Colell, it offers a setting suited to a film that resists tidy explanations. “I love open cinema– films that engage the viewer and connect them to their own lived experience. Cinema that pierces you and settles deep in your gut, beneath your skin, in your chest,” she says. She hopes younger viewers will leave the screening wanting to investigate the history of exile, or to ask their own relatives what was never said. “The film speaks to the need to listen, the importance of passing things on, and how we people act as both transmitters and receivers of memory,” said Colell. “And, in a sense, the film itself is a body of memory.” The collaboration between director and lead allows “Far From the Trees” to examine the cost of building a life elsewhere. Adela’s strained relationship with those tasked with caring for her grandmother, raises questions about who stays, who leaves and who inherits responsibility. “Distance is inherently complicated, yet it can also be liberating,” said Colell. “I wanted to explore this issue without judgment: to discuss the consequences of living far from family, how that shapes one’s identity, and how it affects those who take on caregiving duties.” She recalls Castelló telling her: “I am a permanent foreigner. My home – my refuge – is sound. Music.” “That statement encapsulates the film’s central quest,” Colell concludes. “I would love for the film itself to become that home, that refuge.” Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review Loading comments... articles.title: Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 13, 2026 12:21am PT Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub 3 hours ago Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago See All Busan ACFM The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) has selected Japan as the 2026 Focus Country for its Producer Hub, a co-production networking platform tied to the Busan International Film Festival . Japan will send 10 producers to Busan in October for project pitching, speed meetings and case-study sessions. Now in its third year, Producer Hub gives producers pursuing international co-productions a forum to trade information and build relationships. The initiative singles out one focus country annually, using the selection to showcase that market’s production landscape, incentive programs and slate of in-development projects. Related Stories American Film Market Expands With Launch of AFM House, Site of Its Innovation Hub 'The Traitors' India Sets August Season 2 Bow on Prime Video (EXCLUSIVE) This year’s Japanese delegation will pitch active co-production projects, detail how the country’s production system operates and look for new partners across the region, according to ACFM. Popular on Variety ACFM launched Producer Hub in 2024 as a dedicated space for producers to compare notes on financing, investment and local support schemes across different territories. Korea held the inaugural focus country slot in 2024, co-hosted by the Korean Film Council. Canada took the spot in 2025 alongside Telefilm Canada, an edition that drew 154 producers representing 25 countries. That exchange takes on added significance following an audiovisual co-production treaty Canada and the Korea signed in 2026, which organizers expect will deepen ties between the two countries. Producer Hub’s partner network has meanwhile grown from eight organizations in seven countries at launch to 13 organizations across 10 countries today. Producer Hub 2026 runs four days, from Oct. 10 to 13 – one day longer than the 2025 edition. The Japanese delegation will pitch in-development projects and detail the country’s production environment, while separate case-study sessions will examine past co-productions between Japan and other countries. Speed meetings and networking sessions round out the schedule. Organizers added the extra day to give participants more room to build on early conversations. Follow-up sessions are being arranged specifically with the Japanese producers so that discussions started during speed meetings can continue, moving past introductions into details on projects, production conditions and potential collaboration, according to ACFM. ACFM Director Ellen Y.D. Kim said, “Japan today is Asia’s most dynamic co-production partner. Building on its longstanding strength in independent and arthouse cinema, international collaboration is expanding on all fronts to encompass commercial films and series, backed by bold policies centered on grants and incentives,” adding, “Together with Japan, this year’s focus country, Producer Hub aims to serve as a platform offering producers across Asia tangible opportunities for collaboration.” Producer Hub plans to keep expanding its roster of partner organizations beyond the current 13 across 10 countries. Producers interested in international co-production can apply via the ACFM website, with the application window open through Aug. 31. ACFM runs in Busan each October alongside BIFF. The market’s 20th edition in 2025 was its largest yet, with registration reaching 1,222 companies and 3,024 professionals across 55 countries and total on-site attendance hitting 30,006. Its Sales Market logged 8,438 business meetings, with a transaction value estimated at $71.1 million. The 2026 Asian Contents & Film Market runs Oct. 10–13 at BEXCO’s Exhibition Center 2 in Busan, alongside the 31st Busan International Film Festival, set for Oct. 6–15. Japan was also the country of honor at this year’s Cannes Film Market. Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review Loading comments... articles.title: ‘The Wrong Girls’ Review: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Are a Good Time in Dylan Meyer’s Shaggy Stoner Comedy
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 13, 2026 12:47am PT ‘The Wrong Girls’ Review: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Are a Good Time in Dylan Meyer’s Shaggy Stoner Comedy Following two burnout friends on an absurd LA quest, the writer-director's debut feature aims for late-night cult status and might well get it. By Katie Walsh Plus Icon Katie Walsh Latest See All Courtesy of Neon Debut writer-director Dylan Meyer practically achieves liftoff with her absurdist stoner comedy “ The Wrong Girls ,” starring Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat . If Method Man and Red Man once posited “How High” with their 2001 comedy, Meyer counters with a pair of pals who achieve psychic powers through experimental psychedelics. And while Dave Chappelle was “Half Baked” in 1998, put a fork in Frankie (Stewart) and Molly (Shawkat), because they’re fully done. The burnout duo, who live in an LA apartment dubbed Casa de Chill Zone, put Cheech and Chong to shame with their reefer madness. Related Stories 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe AI-Generated Turkish Series 'Castle Walls' Launches on Prime Video in What Is Being Touted as a Worldwide Streaming First – Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) Meyer blends together almost a few too many familiar strains for the plot of “The Wrong Girls,” which takes a minute to gain coherence before almost immediately losing it again. In this crazy California yarn, Frankie and Molly have to come up with rent money by the next day, as in F. Gary Gray’s 1995 LA stoner classic “Friday” (as well as last year’s “One of Them Days”), a quest that sends them on an odyssey fit for “Harold and Kumar Go to White Castle.” Meanwhile, a mistaken identity twist has a mercenary nicknamed Not Metal Head Dave (LaKeith Stanfield) and a team of Danish scientists and security contractors hot on their heels. Squid brains, talking cats and telepathy, oh my! Popular on Variety It may be loosey-goosey, but Meyer’s film is far from a bad trip. The ensemble cast is especially charming, and the good humor oozing out of the entire project means it’s hard to avoid a contact high. Stewart and Shawkat have a fun and amiable vibe together, even if their characters aren’t immediately in focus. Frankie is a Stanford engineering student who failed out of college and now works as a “Kwik Things” delivery driver. Codependent bestie Molly is a weed-inspired aspiring chef whose utterly reasonable boyfriend Josh (Zack Fox) would really love for her to get her life together and move in with him. Frankie, on the other hand, discovers that her latest beau Mike Z. (Morgan Krantz) has replaced her with a straitlaced doppelgänger upgrade, Frances (Stewart in glasses). At a Mannequin Pussy show, she confronts the pair, then runs into the aforementioned Not Metal Head Dave, who passes her a secretive briefcase, thinking that Frankie is high-level researcher Frances. Which is how Frankie and Molly find themselves in possession of some seriously heady psychedelics derived from deep sea squid testes. They make themselves unwitting test subjects for the stuff before trying to sell the drugs at a Stanford alumni event hosted by Martin (Tony Hale), and suddenly find themselves highly valuable assets for the drug researchers, including Dr. Olsen (Kate McKinnon), when it’s discovered they’ve gained telepathic powers during their trip. McKinnon is a comedic MVP as always, and Stanfield proves himself again to be a Swiss Army knife as a performer, ably fitting into any genre, role or ensemble cast, and demonstrating both comic chemistry with McKinnon and sexual chemistry with Stewart (one-sided on her part). Seth Rogen and Kumail Nanjiani voice Frankie and Molly’s cats to great effect. A Geena Davis cameo reminds us of another great film about female friendship, “Thelma & Louise,” though this one has a happier ending. Cinematographer Todd Banhazl achieves the ‘90s retro druggie look with a brightly saturated palette, hazy filtered light, Dutch angles and wide lenses, while rocker-turned-composer Ty Segall lays down some nasty psych-surf rock guitar licks on the score — though some of the twangy flourishes get a touch repetitive. “The Wrong Girls” feels heavy on inside humor, much of it LA-centric — jokes about freeways, anyone? But Meyer is generous enough to want to bring the audience in on it, and she does make tangible her references. Those not in SoCal might not quite get the depths of the bit about Frankie and Molly mourning a restaurant called “Souper Starz Buffet” (R.I.P. Souplantation), but Meyer makes their tearful goodbye, and final feast, palpably emotional and fun to watch. It all feels like a cult hit in a good way: the kind of movie you’d watch over and over on Comedy Central or on DVD because it’s just so silly, a little rough around the edges, but highly specific. It seems like that’s exactly what Meyer was going for too, so if that’s your thing, light it up and pass that Dutch. ‘The Wrong Girls’ Review: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Are a Good Time in Dylan Meyer’s Shaggy Stoner Comedy Reviewed at Wilshire Screening Room, Los Angeles, Aug. 11, 2026. articles.title: BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 13, 2026 1:55am PT BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub 3 hours ago Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago See All Getty Images BTS member V told fans in a Wednesday livestream that he is being treated for hearing loss affecting his right ear, which he said now functions at roughly a third of the level in his left. He said he initially did not take the issue seriously, calling it “a matter of mental strength,” but is now taking medication and attending regular hospital appointments to manage it, according to BBC News . Related Stories Inside Netflix and Prime Video’s Fight to Reshape France’s Streaming Rules: 'It's an Unsustainable Equation' Sony Pictures Sets Viral X-Inspired Short-Form Thriller ‘Los Hilos del Miedo’ at Prime Video Spain (EXCLUSIVE) The disclosure landed midway through the band’s Arirang World Tour, which launched in South Korea in April and reunited all seven members for the first time in years following their individual stints in the military. Wednesday’s livestream came after the group wrapped tour dates in Baltimore, Maryland; upcoming stops include Los Angeles, Buenos Aires, Bangkok, Sydney and Hong Kong. Popular on Variety V, whose real name is Kim Tae-hyung, said his hearing problems worsened during his military service, which he began in 2023 before being discharged in June 2025. South Korea requires nearly all able-bodied men to complete 18 months of service, a rule that applied to all seven BTS members, who began enlisting in 2022 at the height of the group’s global popularity. Jungkook, V’s fellow BTS member, also joined the livestream, describing a shin injury he has been managing throughout the tour. He said he is close to developing a stress fracture and will need to carefully manage the injury in order to keep performing. In July, BTS sent shockwaves through the music industry when they said they would not submit its music for consideration at the 69th Grammy Awards, after the Recording Academy unveiled a new Best Asian Pop Music Performance category. In response, Grammy CEO Harvey Mason jr. said , “The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 13, 2026 2:30am PT ‘Drishyam’ Producer Panorama Studios Invests in Indian Vertical Streaming Platform Rocket Reels (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Drishyam’ Producer Panorama Studios Invests in Indian Vertical Streaming Platform Rocket Reels (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub 3 hours ago See All Panorama Studios India’s Panorama Studios , the producer behind the Bollywood “ Drishyam ” franchise, has invested in Indian original stories vertical platform Rocket Reels , fueling the platform’s next phase of growth and global expansion. Panorama Studios is chaired by veteran film producer Kumar Mangat Pathak and led by filmmaker and managing director Abhishek Pathak. The studio has built a slate that includes “Omkara,” “Special 26,” “Pyaar Ka Punchnama,” “Raid,” “Shaitaan” and the “Drishyam” franchise, earning more than 50 awards. Abhishek Pathak directed “Drishyam 2” and is directing and producing “Drishyam 3,” due in theaters Oct. 2. Related Stories Spain's World Cup Triumph Gets Prime Video Series Prime Video Launches Games With Luna App Integration; 'Tomb Raider,' James Bond Titles Won't Be in the Mix Panorama Studios’ backing is expected to deepen Rocket Reels’ slate of programming, bolster its tech infrastructure and speed up output of new original series. The deal comes as vertical storytelling gains traction as one of digital entertainment’s fastest-growing formats. Popular on Variety Founded by Kranti Shanbhag, Rocket Reels was among the first movers in India’s vertical streaming category, building a catalog that ranges across thrillers, romance, crime, mystery, sci-fi, horror and comedy. The platform is built for viewers on mobile devices, packaging its stories into brief, emotionally charged episodes. The platform offers stories in six Indian languages: Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Bengali and Gujarati. It has also expanded beyond India and is now available in 10 countries, including the U.S., the U.K., Canada, Australia, the U.A.E., Singapore, Malaysia, Bangladesh, Nepal and South Africa. Kumar Mangat Pathak, chair of Panorama Studios, said, “At Panorama Studios, we have always believed that compelling stories will find an audience, regardless of the format. Rocket Reels has built a strong platform that understands the evolving viewing habits of today’s digital-first consumers while staying rooted in quality storytelling.” Abhishek Pathak, managing director of Panorama Studios, said viewing habits are shifting quickly and that vertical storytelling is becoming a major format for viewers who consume content primarily on their phones. “Rocket Reels has built an innovative platform backed by compelling storytelling and a clear vision for the future. We are excited to partner with them as they redefine short-form entertainment and expand their reach across India and global markets,” he said. Kranti Shanbhag, founder of Rocket Reels, said the company set out from the start to tell engaging stories in a format built around how people actually live and consume media today. “Panorama Studios’ investment is a strong validation of that vision,” he said. “Their belief in our journey gives us the confidence and resources to create even more original, high-quality stories while expanding our reach across India and international markets.” Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review Loading comments... articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 13, 2026 2:30am PT ‘Stranger Things’ Star Noah Schnapp to Make Stage Debut in London (EXCLUSIVE) Running at Riverside Studios, 'Affluenza' is set amid the ultra-wealthy of the Hamptons and will explore power and privilege By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest U.K.’s Largest Harry Potter Store Opening in London Ahead of HBO Series Launch 1 day ago ‘The Office’ U.K. Star Lucy Davis Reveals ‘Incurable’ Cancer Diagnosis: It’s ‘Too Late for Chemo’ and ‘I’m Not Scared of Whatever Comes Next’ 2 days ago Jessica Reynolds and Charlotte Rampling to Star in Opera Drama ‘Maya Butterfly’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Evelyn Freja From the Upside Down of Hawkins to the boards of London. Noah Schnapp , best known as Will Byers in “ Stranger Things ,” is set to make his world stage debut in the British capital. The actor, who became a household name thanks to the Netflix phenomenon, is adding theater to his resume as the star of “Affluenza” at Riverside Studios as part of its Mainstage Season 26/27. Related Stories Spain's World Cup Triumph Gets Prime Video Series 'The Traitors' India Season 2 Unveils Trailer With Karan Johar and 21-Celebrity Cast (EXCLUSIVE) Written and directed by Mainstage Season artistic director Andy Sandberg and running Sep. 26 to Nov. 21, “Affluenza” is set against the ultra-wealthy social haven of the Hamptons, and is described as raising “thought-provoking questions about moral accountability, family legacy, and the American justice system.” Popular on Variety In the play, when a teen’s drunken car ride ends in devastation, the verdict comes down to one question – is it possible to be too affluent to know the difference between right and wrong? Inspired by true events surrounding a shocking legal defence, “Affluenza” explores the “ripple effects of power and privilege.” “I am so excited to make my stage debut in London with ‘Affluenza,'” said Schnapp. “I started talking with Andy Sandberg a few months ago about finding the right opportunity to work together, and it’s thrilling to now be bringing this play to life in London. I wanted to be very intentional about what I took on next, and as I spend more time with this excellent script, I feel so connected to the characters. Without giving away too much, I get to play two very different roles, and it’s a story that’s really going to leave audiences talking and thinking.” “Affluenza” opens Riverside’s Mainstage Season 26/27, which comprises five new plays, largely set in contemporary America and exploring globally relevant themes. “I am incredibly excited to be launching this play and this season in just a few weeks — and now with Noah Schnapp at the helm,” said Sandberg, a Tony-winning producer who also serves as Mainstage Season artistic director. “Noah is a brilliant young actor who has captivated audiences on screen, and now London audiences will have the opportunity to see him in his stage debut. I’m honoured that Noah has connected with the script, and I think it speaks volumes that he has chosen an original play for his stage debut.” Following “Affluenza” the season will continue with “Sacrilegious,” by Tom Schulman, the Oscar-winning writer of “Dead Poets Society” and “Honey, I Shrunk the Kids,” and “Expecting,” by Scott Elmegreen and Drew Fornarola. Both are being are directed by Sandberg, who also serves as artistic director for the Hermitage in the U.S. Further productions and casting will be announced soon.
