articles.title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Boss Explains Finale’s Big Book Change
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Josh Wigler Plus Icon Josh Wigler Contributor roundhoward Follow Sign Up View All August 9, 2026 7:15pm Emma D'Arcy and Matt Smith as Rhaenyra and Daemon Targaryen. HBO Logo text [This story contains major spoilers from the season three finale of House of the Dragon .] Whenever a Targaryen is born, the gods flip a coin, and the world waits to see if the child will achieve greatness, or succumb to madness. Where has the coin landed when it comes to House of the Dragon hero Rhaenyra Targaryen? As of the season three finale, the results are in — and they are decidedly mixed, pending one’s viewpoint. Certainly, there are major Daenerys vibes throughout the HOTD finale, including turning to violence against her own constituents in her quest for power. Beyond ordering the immediate execution of a faith leader turned political rival, Rhaenyra’s rampage was bloodless, and yet, bone-chilling. In a moment that deviates wildly from George R.R. Martin’s source material, the queen stands before the masses of King’s Landing and reveals the Song of Ice and Fire prophecy: the White Walkers coming, and only Rhaenyra can stop them, as the prophesied Prince Who Was Promised. Related Stories TV 'House of the Dragon' Star Fabien Frankel Finally Gets His Flowers TV Streaming Ratings: 'The Bear' Slips in Final Season Premiere, 'I Will Find You' and 'Love Island' Soar Martin’s book Fire and Blood , which HOTD takes its cues from, never mentions the Ice and Fire prophecy. Likewise, there’s no mention of Rhaenyra making such a public declaration. Given what she says, one would think the history books would reverberate with details about the Dragon Queen and her stark warning (or her stark madness, as some might have seen it). In a press conference about the shape of season three and specifically its finale, executive producer and showrunner Ryan Condal revealed his answer to that very question: “Targaryens say crazy shit all the time.” He’s joking — mostly. “It’s not in the book and it’s not in the history, but there is a bunch of talk about how Rhaenyra became very despotic, and became a tyrant at the end, and was very unpopular with the people,” says Condal. “So much of [the Targaryens’] existence is their self-aggrandizement. For the stonemasons standing there in the crowd just looking up at this [speech], it could just sound like somebody trying to make something of themselves.” Condal continues, saying he and the show’s writing staff were seeking “a real seismic change, a sea change in Rhaenyra’s relationship to her people.” Pronouncing herself as the savior of her people, just moments after killing the people’s religious leaders, is meant to not only feel like a real change between the queen and her realm, but also between the queen and us, the audience. “Power turns out to be incredibly fragile, and that, seats of power — their sort of apparent stability, can also turn out to be illusory,” says Emma D’Arcy, the actor charged with bringing Rhaenyra to life. “It’s a conversation which remains very pertinent. How do you manage the ego? How do you manage the human ego in the political sphere? That feels like a pressing question.” What comes next, now that Rhaenyra has revealed her destiny to the world? The answers lurk in the Fire and Blood book, though it’s anyone’s guess to see if and how the show might change course from the source material. Whatever happens now, Condal promises that season four — which will be the final season of HOTD — will be bigger than anything that’s come before. “It’s a great privilege to be able to tell a story, and to be able to control and write the ending, and to control when and where that happens,” he says. “This is not a given in making television, certainly. So, we’re very excited to get back in, and we have new characters, and new dragons and new locations all to come, that I think are gonna make it a very worthy final season.” *** House of the Dragon season three is now streaming on HBO Max; read THR ‘s finale coverage. articles.title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Shares the Bright Side of That Tragic Finale Twist
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Josh Wigler Plus Icon Josh Wigler Contributor roundhoward Follow Sign Up View All August 9, 2026 7:20pm Phia Saban as Queen Helaena Targaryen with Olivia Cooke as Alicent Hightower. HBO Logo text [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the House of the Dragon season three finale.] “Do not trust the queen. Aegon has returned. His dragon lives. Your unborn child is a hostage, a prize by which she can hold power over her enemies. She will never release you.” These end up being among the final words Queen Helaena Targaryen ever hears. In the House of the Dragon season three finale, a newly ousted Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) issues her stark warning to the recently imprisoned Helaena (Phia Saban), who internalizes that information and weaponizes it: first, by way of speaking ugly truths about Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy) right to her face, and then, finally, by way of an open Red Keep window. Just as King Tommen once plummeted from that very same location in Game of Thrones , so too now has Helaena fallen. The season ends with Rhaenyra coming upon Helaena’s vacant quarters, while Team Green’s queen herself lies on the ground below, impaled on spikes. Related Stories TV 'House of the Dragon' Boss Explains Finale's Big Book Change TV 'House of the Dragon' Star Fabien Frankel Finally Gets His Flowers It’s a haunting image, perhaps appropriately so, given Helaena as a character who knows a thing or two about nightmares and dreams. It’s also a hinge upon which much of the rest of House of the Dragon will turn, according to the folks behind the scenes. In a press event held ahead of the season finale, D’Arcy spoke about Helaena’s death and what it means for the show’s future: “Helaena is sort of the moral heart of the show, I think. She’s maybe the only character who has a proximity to power, but remains kind of uncontaminated. And so, I think her death sort of condemns Rhaenyra to the path she’s chosen. I think there’s sort of no way back after that.” If there’s a way back, it exists somewhere far beyond the fallen Helaena. Below, Phia Saban chats with The Hollywood Reporter about building out the dream-seeing queen’s final chapter. *** How much did you know about Helaena’s fate in advance? When I got the job, I spent a lot of time Googling and searching the Wikis, so I’ve always known this was coming. Plus, there are so many fans out there in the world, and I know so many people who knew and would make a point to tell me about what was going to happen to me. When it’s a show this big with a character fate this crucial, is it pretty much impossible to avoid that kind of spoiler on your end? Totally. It was never an option not to know. I’m just happy I made it three seasons! You’ve had a lot of time to think about her death, then. What are some of your first thoughts when you think about the character, now that her arc ends in this way? Objectively, it’s very sad. The story is sad. I love Helaena. I feel for Helaena. I try to find hope, by thinking she felt as though she had been killed already in many ways, but… it’s very sad. But for me? Kind of a bucket list thing: I got to die on TV! ( Laughs .) I got to do the thing where you keep your eyes open… everyone wants to do that! How was that experience? The prosthetics were amazing. It made me want to do a thing where I’m entirely in prosthetics. It was so genius, getting to work on that. You really work with the most talented people on House of the Dragon . I could go through every department right now and tell you all about them, but the people I had never really worked with much before were the prosthetics people, and it was amazing. I sat there while they created my neck, which had this incredible spike, and they painted it on me in a way that was so lifelike. It was so fun. What went into crafting the force-feeding scene? It involved a few weeks of what we’d call “gruel meetings.” I would try all these different slops, and they would say, “Choose the one you want to get force-fed.” The one we picked, it was a dal, low spice level. It was okay! Before that goes down, literally, you have one final scene with Emma. What do you remember about it? I really loved it, because it came from a conversation I had with executive producers [Ryan Condal and Sara Hess] about it. I felt a lot of ownership over Helaena and have loved building that character. And I felt it was important to get across some of the things that I had always had as Helaena mantras in my mind in that moment. And I felt like that was the justice for Helaena. So we spoke a lot about Joan of Arc, and this idea that there’s more to life than not being dead. I found it really delicious that Helaena could be like, “There are things in the world that you’ll never know how beautiful they are, and they’re not even beautiful.” And that’s truly what she wants to get back to: having a relationship with the world and not being kept and silenced and used. That links up with the scene in the courtyard, when Helaena looks out at all the birds in cages being taken away. Is there a shot of her holding something in her hand? If there isn’t, what might be some context is that when we shot that scene, I was holding a dead caterpillar. To me, that moment became more about her relationship with nature, mourning her freedom and how strongly she feels for her creatures — and exactly as you say, how it strikes her that to see something that won’t live and fly again. I think to me, that’s what that was about, but they might’ve done some clever editing and just not got me holding it. What was your last day on set like? I saw Fabien talk about this, and I wonder how much it’s clever scheduling from the team, but the last thing I shot was my death shot. I was on a soundstage surrounded by spikes feeling pretty proud of myself in my prosthetics, trying to keep my eyes open with the whole team. And then Ryan came out and he said some nice things and lots of lovely people were there. And yeah, it was really amazing. It’s very hard in the moment to take in the finality of it. This is something I’ve been working on, and a character I’ve been caring for, for five years now. But there is joy in this. There’s pride and there’s excitement. It will probably hit me once I see the full episode and it’s out there, or perhaps when they all get back to work without me. *** House of the Dragon season three is now streaming on HBO Max; read THR ‘s finale coverage. THR

articles.title: Tedde Moore, Ralphie’s Teacher in ‘A Christmas Story,’ Dies at 79
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All August 9, 2026 9:08pm Tedde Moore Reg Innell/Toronto Star via Getty Images Tedde Moore, the actress who is best known as playing young Ralphie Parker’s teacher in A Christmas Story , has died. She was 79. Moore died Wednesday in Huntsville, Ontario, according to a post on her Facebook page. A cause of death was not given. “On Wednesday August 5th under sunny skies overlooking Fairy Lake, Tedde passed away surrounded by family physically and spiritually in her beloved Huntsville Muskoka,” the post reads. “Her bravery in this choice was almost overwhelming, beyond beautiful and also difficult. Forever the teacher, she had a quote for every occasion and a special way of touching the lives and hearts of everyone she met. Her magic and love will be remembered by all she took under her generous and welcoming wings.” Related Stories TV Ben Jones, Cooter Davenport on 'The Dukes of Hazzard,' Dies at 84 Movies James Gray Told His Wife He Would Get an Award at Locarno. She Reminded Him to Take Out the Trash Moore played Miss Shields in the 1983 Christmas classic opposite Peter Billingsley. She memorably gives Ralphie a bad grade on his paper about wanting the Red Ryder BB gun for Christmas and also has to deal with Flick (Scott Schwartz)’s getting his tongue stuck on a ice-cold flagpole. Moore was nominated for a Genie Award, presented by the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television, for best performance by a supporting actress. She reprised her role for 1994’s My Summer Story , which, like A Christmas Story, was based on Jean Shepherd’s semi-autobiographical stories. Her other TV appearances include spots on Friday the 13th: The Series, RoboCop: Prime Directives, Odyssey 5 and This Is Wonderland. Moore played Mrs. Claus in the 2011 TV movie Mistletoe Over Manhattan and portrayed Nanny Shaw in the miniseries The Kennedys that year. According to IMDb.com, her final credit was the 2017 TV movie Magical Christmas Ornaments. Born on April 11, 1947, Moore was the daughter of Darwina Faessler Moore and actor Mavor Moore, best known for playing the title role in a Canadian radio drama adaptation of Nero Wolfe in 1982. Her grandmother was Canadian theater pioneer Dora Mavor Moore. She attended the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London, graduating in 1967 with the Principal’s Medal of Honor. After that, she starred opposite Christopher Walken in the Stratford Festival production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. In 2009, she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Moore had two children with Canadian film and television director Donald Shebib, who directed many documentaries, including 1970’s Goin’ Down the Road and 1973’s Between Friends . Their children are daughter Suzanna, a child actor (A re You Afraid of the Dark? ) turned teacher, and Noah, a child actor ( Goosebumps ) turned Grammy-winning music producer, also known as “40,” who is a frequent collaborator of Drake’s. 40, who produced the Drake hits “Hold On, We’re Going Home,” “One Dance,” “God’s Plan,” “Toosie Slide” and “Take Care,” was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2007, two years before his mother. Moore has another daughter, Zoë, from a previous relationship with actor Patrick Christopher Carter, and she raised a foster daughter, Chaunce Drury. THR

articles.title: Aubrey Plaza and Christopher Abbott Are Parents to a Baby Daughter
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All August 9, 2026 9:13pm Aubrey Plaza and Christopher Abbott at the 2026 Tony Awards. Adela Loconte/Variety via Getty Images Aubrey Plaza and Christopher Abbott have become first-time parents. The couple reportedly welcomed a baby daughter in late July, according to reports. TMZ posted photos of the actress carrying a baby in New York after seeing Death of a Salesman on Sunday, which marked Abbott’s last performance. Abbott played Biff Loman in the Broadway revival of Arthur Miller’s classic play opposite Nathan Lane and Laurie Metcalf; he earned his first Tony Award nomination for the role, and they attended the ceremony as a couple (see photo above). Plaza, meanwhile, earned an Emmy nom for best supporting actress in a drama series for her role in The White Lotus in 2023. She also was the co-creator of Prime Videos animated series Kevin . Her other credits include Agatha All Along and Parks and Recreation. News first surfaced in April that Plaza was pregnant with her first child. The couple have worked together previously, in the 2020 movie Black Bear as well as in the off-Broadway play Danny and the Deep Blue Sea . She was previously married to writer-director Jeff Baena ( Life After Beth ), who died by suicide in January 2025. THR

articles.title: China Box Office: ‘Spider-Man’ Holds No. 1 as ‘The Odyssey’ Storms Previews
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All August 9, 2026 11:24pm Tom Holland in 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Spider-Man: Brand New Day held its grip atop China ‘s box office for a second weekend, pulling in $28.9 million (RMB 196.6 million) over the Aug. 7-9 frame for a local total of $185.4 million (RMB 1.26 billion) in 12 days. The Sony tentpole launched in China with a massive $121.3 million five-day haul, of which $19 million came from Imax, a record for the format in the market. The film is now days away from surpassing the $199 million earned by 2019’s Spider-Man: Far From Home , the last U.S. superhero release to clear $100 million in China. Related Stories Movies 'Spring Story,' 'The Surubí,' 'Yazz' Among Locarno Pro Winners Movies 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Scores $145M for Third-Best Second Weekend Ever But it was Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , which doesn’t officially open in Chinese theaters until Friday, that arguably delivered the weekend’s most surprising number. Playing Saturday and Sunday only, and exclusively on Imax and CINITY screens, Universal’s adaptation of the Greek classic took $6.9 million (RMB 46.8 million) in previews — enough for fifth place and roughly 7 percent of the entire weekend’s business from a tiny sliver of the nation’s screens. Earlier four-city previews on Aug. 1-2 drew a 95.2 percent occupancy rate, which local media reports, citing Dengta, described as an all-time high for the market. The 177-minute epic, the first feature shot entirely on Imax film cameras, has scored 8.3 on review site Douban, the summer’s highest rating for a live-action release. The Matt Damon-starring epic crossed $1 billion worldwide last week, and China now appears poised to boost its global sales significantly. Pearl Studio’s All Wishes Come True held to second in its fourth weekend with $20.4 million (RMB 138.8 million). The animated comic fantasy from director Mu Zhengyang, which reimagines the classic folk tale of the Eight Immortals, has now earned $210.6 million (RMB 1.43 billion), China’s biggest peformance by an animated feature this year. Third place came from previews for another yet-to-open tentpole. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East collected $15 million (RMB 101.8 million) across two days of previews ahead of its Tuesday release. Directed by Wen Muye ( Dying to Survive ) and produced by Ning Hao’s Dirty Monkeys Studio, the Imax-shot war comedy stars Shen Teng, one of China’s most bankable comic actors, as a Chinese cook who travels to the Middle East to work off his debts, opens a restaurant with a local partner — and then finds himself trapped when a military conflict erupts. To Your Island opened in fourth with $7.9 million (RMB 53.6 million). The animated fantasy romance — adapted from a web novel and directed by Zhou Haoran — is the first film produced in-house by Enlight Animation, the specialty arm of Ne Zha 2 backer Enlight Pictures. Absent from the top five for the first time since its July 11 release was Stephen Chow’s Kung Fu Soccer , which stood at around $318.5 million after the weekend and remains the summer’s biggest title. Nationwide grosses totaled $97.3 million for the weekend, down about a quarter from the previous frame. China’s 2026 box office now stands at $3.57 billion, off 31.8 percent from the same point last year — a comparison distorted by Ne Zha 2 , which alone took more than $2 billion in the market in the first half of 2025. The gap has narrowed steadily since March, when the market trailed by nearly 56 percent. The Odyssey opens wide on Friday, in a test of whether Chinese moviegoers’ renewed appetite for Hollywood extends beyond the friendly neighborhood spider. THR

articles.title: ‘Tear Gas’ Is a Fiction Film Shot Inside Georgia Anti-Government Protests. And It Is “an Act of Resistance”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 10, 2026 12:01am 'Tear Gas' Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Elene, 16, and her war-scarred family are drawn into a mass protest in Tbilisi that transforms the streets of the capital of Georgia into a battleground for freedom. But it also forces them to confront the conflicts that are already threatening to tear them apart. Does this read like a synopsis for a fiction or a documentary film to you? Well, whatever answer you give, you are kind of right. Because this is not just any film. It is Tear Gas from Georgian writer-director Uta Beria ( Negative Numbers ). And it is a fiction film shot inside real demonstrations. Related Stories Movies James Gray Told His Wife He Would Get an Award at Locarno. She Reminded Him to Take Out the Trash Movies 'Spring Story,' 'The Surubí,' 'Yazz' Among Locarno Pro Winners The movie will world premiere on Aug. 12 in the Filmmakers of the Present competition program of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival . At the International Film Festival Rotterdam’s IFFR Pro industry section, the project last year won two awards: the inaugural HBF Empowerment Award, worth €10,000 ($11,000), with the jury highlighting its urgent themes of freedom of expression and political tension, and the Outward Gaze Award, another €10,000 honor, from the PJLF Arts Fund. Produced by Nino Chichua, Anna Khazaradze and Beria, and co-produced by Guillaume Dreyfus, Delphine Schmit, Daniel Tenné and Junus Baker, Tear Gas features a cast including Taisia Eradze, Mzia Arabuli, Gaga Shishinashvili, Kato Kalatozishvili and Boris Andronikashvili. The cinematographer is Goga Devdariani, while the editor is Nodar Nozadze. The title has a deeper meaning. “Tear gas is a weapon created to disperse us, tear us apart, make us cry, and restrict our breathing,” highlights Beria. “But in reality, when you inhale it and panic takes over, you instinctively begin fighting for what is most precious to you.” ‘Tear Gas’ film still, courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Tear gas is regularly used by police in Tbilisi to break up anti-government demonstrations that have taken place without interruption for more than 600 days. The reason is that protesters fear that the Republic of Georgia will continue following an authoritarian path similar to Russia’s, crushing their hopes and dreams of being another Western-style democracy that is a member of NATO and the EU. One of the symbols of their fear and anger is the so-called Foreign Agents Law, often simply called “the Russia law” as it is seen as similar to one that Russian President Vladimir Putin had rubber-stamped to allow crackdowns on civil society. Ahead of the film’s world premiere at Locarno, the filmmaker talked to THR about the genesis of Tear Gas , shooting inside actual anti-government demonstrations, which have now gone on for more than 600 days without interruption, and why the creative team feels the need to stand up for freedom of expression, no matter what the consequences may be. Tear Gas took five years to make. “I wanted to make it faster, but it was not possible,” Beria tells THR . “The situation in Georgia is so difficult and tough, both when it comes to getting funding and because of stricter rules by the Georgian Film Center not to give money to people who don’t think the same way they do – that even starts feeling like censorship. My colleagues think that maybe my film is one of the last independent projects because the situation is very tough now.” In fact, Beria shares that there is institutional pressure back home. The film got a contract with the Georgian National Film Center (GNFC) in December 2022, he says. “We delivered the first-stage accounting and audit on time, but the second stage of financing was never paid by the GNFC – we asked three times over 18 months and were never given a reason. Despite their efforts to hinder the production, we managed to complete the film. We cut the budget, raised the remaining funds ourselves and finished the film.” ‘Tear Gas’ behind the scenes of the shoot, courtesy of Giorgi Kolbaia Courtesy of Giorgi Kolbaia After the GNFC became aware that the film was set to premiere at Locarno, “we received a threatening letter from them,” Beria tells THR . “They are not consenting to a public screening, and they refer to a financial sanction of 10 percent of the contract value.” But the Locarno world premiere is on. “Our agreement with all filmmakers submitting work to the festival requires them to confirm that they hold the relevant rights to their film; this agreement was signed by the producer(s) of Tear Gas ,” says Olly Osborne, the Locarno Film Festival’s chief communications officer, in a statement shared with THR . “Any dispute regarding financing or contractual obligations between the production and the Georgian National Film Center is a matter between those two parties. The world premiere of Tear Gas will take place as planned on 12, 13, and 14 August in Locarno.” So, the Tear Gas team did get their film finished, but says it is now facing financial pressures. And shooting amid real-life demonstrations in the capital also proved a huge challenge. “It was unpredictable,” Beria explains. “You go to shoot with a script for the actors. Usually, you have a plan. But in the demonstrations, we had a plan A, plan B, plan C, plan D. And there were days where we needed to think as the demonstration was going on to follow the flow.” Asking the filmmaker if he felt a sense of danger is a rhetorical question. “Of course, it was very dangerous, and especially when the police were dispersing people with the use of tear gas, which happened almost every day,” Beria tells THR . “Sometimes they did not announce that they would start using tear gas. We were making sure that when this brutality was starting, the actors were in a safe place. But I, the camera crew, and my DOP would stay and continue shooting.” ‘Tear Gas’ behind the scenes of the shoot, courtesy of Nino Chichua Courtesy of Nino Chichua How do you communicate amid the chaos of street protests? “Communication is very difficult in big demonstrations,” Beria shares. “We didn’t want to use walkie-talkies, because the authorities argue that the demonstrations are not spontaneous but are organized, and they have arrested people as organizers. So, we thought if the police see us with walkie-talkies, they will not ask us if we are making a film but assume we are organizers of the protests.” Mobile phones then? Not really. “Phones were sometimes not working. I don’t know if it was because a lot of people using them overloaded the network or if the police were shutting it down,” the filmmaker says. “So my assistant director came up with a smart idea. We had short and long flags, and we were using these flags to see each other in the sea of people. People who watch the film will notice that we are shooting with a long lens at a great distance, and between the actors and us, there are thousands of people.” That also affected his guidance for the cast walking around the demonstrations. “I told the actors that they should stay in their role, and they really did so for hours, in the state of the character,” Beria explains. “I told them that sometimes maybe they wouldn’t know when they were in the frame. So, this incredible magic was happening where we would lose the actors, and then we would find them again, and then lose them again. It was so pure, so authentic, so natural. We really fell in love with that.” Does Beria not fear repercussions for making Tear Gas ? “For me, this film was an act of resistance,” he tells THR . “Some of my friends and colleagues are in prison. I can’t free them. But I could put all of myself into this film.” Asked if he thinks he will end up in prison as well, Beria says: “I don’t know. Let’s see. They don’t need a reason to put you into prison anymore in Georgia. There are so many good and innocent people in prison. I don’t know what to expect. They do what they want. I don’t know. I’m not going to hide so I don’t go to prison.” ‘Tear Gas’ behind the scenes of the shoot, courtesy of Juda Khatia Psuturi Courtesy of Juda Khatia Psuturi The creative also emphasizes: “Every member of the crew showed remarkable bravery, and I couldn’t be more grateful for their commitment under such extraordinary circumstances.” The filmmaker hopes that the film will make more people around the world aware of the situation in Georgia. And Tear Gas seems like a powerful title to attract attention. “I love the process when you are thinking about a title,” Beria tells THR . “There were different titles before I had this idea for Tear Gas . Tear gas is a strange weapon. It’s created to disperse us, to tear us apart. But in reality, when you inhale it and the panic takes over, you start to instinctively fight for the things that are precious to us and fight to not lose each other.” Concludes Beria: “This is the main thing that I want to say with this title. In reality, tear gas forces us to fight for each other and brings us together.” THR

articles.title: Marco Perego, in the Presence of Wife Zoe Saldaña, Tells Locarno Pro: Don’t Produce Indie Film for the Money
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 10, 2026 1:30am Marco Perego Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival/Ti-Press “If you decide to be a producer in the independent world, don’t do it for the money.” Producer Marco Perego didn’t mince words during a Locarno Pro keynote appearance. If money is all you care about, “go [work for] a bank.” The Italian native, conceptual artist and movie lover made his feature directorial debut in 2023 with The Absence of Eden , starring his wife, Oscar winner Zoe Saldaña . Perego then launched the production company Leaf Entertainment with Michael Cerenzie. Its goal: back the best global auteurs to help them get their projects made. Related Stories Movies 'Tear Gas' Is a Fiction Film Shot Inside Georgia Anti-Government Protests. And It Is "an Act of Resistance" Movies China Box Office: 'Spider-Man' Holds No. 1 as 'The Odyssey' Storms Previews At Cannes this year, Perego had three competition films: Cristian Mungiu ’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord , Andrey Zvyagintsev ’s Minotaur , and James Gray ’s Paper Tiger . On Sunday night, he appeared at the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival on stage with Gray, who was honored with the Swiss festival’s Career Leopard ahead of a huge Paper Tiger outdoor screening. Just hours before that, he shared his take on the role of a producer at industry strand Locarno Pro in a session that was well-attended despite the busy weekend. Among the people in the audience was Saldaña. “Independent film is for people who take risk,” Perego emphasized. “It’s about respecting the vision, and the vision is not yours. … Just let [directors] do what they want.” You want to support them, and you may every now and then help with suggestions, but in general, step back and let the creatives do the magic, he said. Emphasizing the significance and importance of ensuring and maintaining artistic integrity, the producer highlighted: “We need to be sure that we really protect the filmmaker.” Money may talk, but Perego didn’t talk about money details beyond sharing: “I invest quite a lot.” He signaled that he has no strict rules for the size of investments. “I’m a disruptor. I’m a radical,” Perego also told the Locarno crowd, adding that he wasn’t afraid of slipping up. “I’m going to fail. I’m going to fail so many times, but I promise, I will stand up.” THR

articles.title: Beatles Films Producer Pippa Harris, ‘The Zone of Interest’s James Wilson to Headline London Film Festival Industry Forum
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 10, 2026 3:00am Pippa Harris, James Wilson Courtesy of Getty Two of the U.K.’s most successful producers will have individual Spotlight Conversations at the 70th BFI London Film Festival ‘s Industry Forum this October. Neal Street Productions co-founder Pippa Harris ( The Beatles , Hamnet , 1917 ) and indie producer James Wilson ( The Zone of Interest , The Voice of Hind Rajab ) are set to discuss their careers, current projects and navigating the international film and TV market in a rapidly changing landscape. The LFF Industry Forum welcomes industry delegates from all over the world for a program of “thought-provoking conversations with some of the most exciting practitioners working in the screen industries and networking events with professionals from all over the world.” The full lineup will be announced in mid-September. Related Stories Movies Marco Perego, in the Presence of Wife Zoe Saldaña, Tells Locarno Pro: Don't Produce Indie Film for the Money Movies 'Tear Gas' Is a Fiction Film Shot Inside Georgia Anti-Government Protests. And It Is "an Act of Resistance" Harris will take a deep dive into her work on the hugely ambitious and much-anticipated quartet The Beatles films, directed by her Neal Street co-founder Sam Mendes, and discuss the challenges of development, production and her relationship with talent across her career. A prolific British film producer, her credits include the Oscar, Golden Golden Globe and BAFTA-winning Hamnet and 1917 , Oscar and BAFTA-nominated Revolutionary Road , as well as Jarhead and The Magic Faraway Tree , Call the Midwife , Penny Dreadful and more. Wilson is one of the U.K.’s most successful independent producers. He has worked for three decades in the business — for Fox Searchlight Pictures and Film4 before heading up his own company in the 2000s — and will speak during his Spotlight Conversation about the bold creative collaborations that have shaped his career so far. He has worked on the Oscar and BAFTA-winning The Zone of Interest and Under the Skin from Jonathan Glazer, as well as Lynne Ramsay’s You Were Never Really Here , Kaouther Ben Hania’s The Voice of Hind Rajab and Aneil Karaia’s Hamlet . “This year our industry programme puts a spotlight on producers and the vital role they play in shepherding artistic visions from their earliest stages through to the screen,” said Kristy Matheson, BFI London Film Festival Director. “I’m delighted that industry colleagues will have the opportunity to hear from Pippa Harris and James Wilson — two esteemed producers whose unique creative careers have given us some of the most memorable and critically acclaimed films of recent years.” Attendance of international industry professional delegates to the LFF has doubled over the last five years. The 70th BFI London Film Festival, running Oct. 7-18, is set to open with Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman’s Elsinore , and close with Jesse Eisenberg’s musical-comedy The Debut . THR

articles.title: Can FIFA Boss Infantino Survive?
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All August 10, 2026 3:20am FIFA President Gianni Infantino Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty Images FIFA president Gianni Infantino appears to have snatched defeat from the jaws of victory. A month after the final of 2026 World Cup, which earned FIFA a record $15 billion in revenues, Infantino is fighting to keep his job. His controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup to a group of private investors led by Joshua Kushner, the brother of President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, sparked a global backlash that shows no signs of abetting. The past week, soccer legends, sports authorities and even world leaders have called for Infantino to resign. Related Stories Movies Beatles Films Producer Pippa Harris, 'The Zone of Interest's James Wilson to Headline London Film Festival Industry Forum Movies Marco Perego, in the Presence of Wife Zoe Saldaña, Tells Locarno Pro: Don't Produce Indie Film for the Money “Infantino must go,” wrote Portuguese soccer legend Luis Figo in an op-ed for the Daily Mail . “The Infantino era is over,” added Javier Tebas, president of Italy’s La Liga, an interview with French newspaper Le Monde . “It should be fatal,” said Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, on Infantino’s misstep with the sell-off plans. “Certainly I don’t have confidence in Mr. Infantino.” The pile on has continued despite Infantino dropping his plan, officially ditching the proposal on July 31. The deal would have seen FIFA, a 96-year-old nonprofit, spin off its commercial interests into a new division, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). Kushner’s private equity group Thrive Capital would then buy a 21 percent stake in FFE for $4.2 billion. FIFA had argued the arrangement would raise billions to fund global sports development. European soccer body UEFA called it an attempt to sell “the soul” of soccer and threatened to boycott future FIFA tournaments if the deal went through. The Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF, which represents national organizations in North America, Central America and the Caribbean. also rejected the proposal. FIFA quickly backed down. UEFA has not. Last week it said its boycott is still in place. The group reiterated its position that it has “lost confidence in Gianni Infantino’s presidency.” UEFA’s boycott will be tested at FIFA’s Under-20 Women’s World Cup, which kicks off in Poland Sept. 5. On Friday, Norwegian soccer association directly called for Infantino to resign. “The trust is now gone for us,” Norwegian Football Federation president, Lise Klaveness, told T he Guardian . “There is no way back for Infantino.” Adding to the pile on was a report on Friday that a female employee alleged to have been in a relationship with Infantino when he was general secretary at UEFA, received a six-figure “departure payment.” UEFA confirmed the payment but FIFA said the allegations of inappropriate conduct by Infantino are “categorically untrue” and “defamatory,” adding that “no employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino’s behavior because there never was an incident where he was involved.” FIFA on Saturday fired back at Infantino’s critics, accusing them of trying, “through allegation, insinuation or misinformation” to undermine “FIFA’s established democratic processes” by trying to oust Infantino before presidential elections next March. UEFA is reportedly seeking support from other soccer confederations to call an emergency FIFA Congress to trigger a vote of no confidence in the president. UEFA, with 55 members, easily meets the threshold of 43 votes to call an emergency meeting. To topple Infantino, however, would require a majority of FIFA members, or 106 of the 211 national associations. The Confederation of African Football and South American confederation CONMEBOL have both publicly announced their backing for Infantino. Last week, Mexico broke with North American confederation CONCACAF to support FIFA’s beleaguered president. The pressure is mounting on Gianni Infantino, but there is still time on the clock for him to turn this defeat back into a win. THR

articles.title: ‘Letters From the Silenced Country,’ Documentary About Oppression in Belarus, Boarded by Filmotor Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 9, 2026 11:50pm PT ‘Letters From the Silenced Country,’ Documentary About Oppression in Belarus, Boarded by Filmotor Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest ‘Letters From the Silenced Country,’ Documentary About Oppression in Belarus, Boarded by Filmotor Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Béla Tarr’s Legacy to Be Celebrated at Sarajevo Film Festival 3 days ago Be For Films Acquires Ione Hernández Sáenz’s ‘Sisters’ Ahead of Toronto Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago See All Courtesy of DocEdu Foundation Filmotor has picked up world sales rights for “Letters From the Silenced Country” by Belarusian writer-director Andrei Kutsila , which has its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival . The partly animated documentary, screening in the Venice Open – Out of Competition section, is a portrait of contemporary Belarus told through stories of individuals who have endured imprisonment, repression and exile – voices silenced by an autocratic regime. Related Stories Locarno Sufi Trance Doc 'As Light as Air' Director Umair Bilal on Surrendering to a Pakistani Shrine Town: 'I Became Part of Its Rhythm' Germany’s Patra Spanou Film Boards Rodrigo Plá’s ‘The Newcomers’ After World Premiere at Locarno’s Kids Screenings (EXCLUSIVE) Following Belarus’ peaceful protests in 2020, the regime’s violent crackdown left many dead, injured, imprisoned or forced into exile. The war in Ukraine triggered anti-war resistance and even harsher repression, making public dissent nearly impossible. Against this backdrop, letters became one of the few remaining connections between political prisoners and the outside world. Popular on Variety The film “transforms private stories into a cinematic space of dignity, intimacy and reflection, revealing the human cost of resistance and exploring themes of sacrifice, solidarity, and survival in a country where dissenting voices have been silenced,” according to a statement. Here’s the synopsis: When the streets are quiet and people are afraid to even discuss politics in Belarus, letters can give us an insight into the feelings of pain, despair, love and hope. Each story reveals a different facet of repression. A father lives in hiding, evading surveillance to avoid arrest and separation from his daughter. A former criminal investigator breaks with the system, flees Belarus, and, in exile in Poland, faces repeated interrogations and an increasing sense of isolation and powerlessness. Kasia, a young student imprisoned for her participation in protests, turns to drawing as a means of survival – preserving her identity and expressing what cannot be spoken openly. Fifty-year-old Vitold’s story unfolds through photographs sent by a friend from home: carefully chosen fragments of a life beyond prison walls that offer moments of freedom while revealing both what is visible and what remains hidden. Kutsila is a Belarusian documentary filmmaker based in Poland. His documentaries have been screened and awarded at major international festivals, including IDFA, DOK Leipzig, Hot Docs and the Krakow Film Festival. His documentary “Summa” (2018) won the IDFA Award for Best Mid-Length Documentary, followed by the Silver Hobby-Horse for Best Documentary in the National Competition at the Krakow Film Festival in 2019. “When Flowers Are Not Silent” (2021) received the Best Feature Documentary Award at the Warsaw Film Festival. Forced to leave Belarus after the 2020 protests, Kutsila settled in Poland, where he continued his artistic development through an internship at the Łódź Film School. Over the past five years, his work has focused primarily on documenting the experiences of Belarusians living under repression and in exile. Michaela Čajková, founder and sales and festivals executive at Filmotor, said, “Using an innovative blend of animation, archive and personal correspondence, Kutsila crafts an essential, unforgettable portrait of human dignity against autocratic repression.” Producer Mirosław Dembiński, president at DocEdu Foundation, said, “Twenty years ago, I directed the film ‘Lesson of Belarusian,’ which chronicled the repression of the Lukashenko regime: street brutality by the police, mass arrests and long sentences. Since then, it’s been the same: the same batons, the same prisons, the same Lukashenko. Since 2020, it’s been even worse, because the scale of repression has become more widespread. Andrei Kutsila took on the challenge of making a documentary about political prisoners in Belarus. It’s also an artistic challenge: how to make a film about someone who can’t be filmed. I think he’s found a way.” “Letters From the Silenced Country” is produced by DocEdu Foundation in Poland in co-production with Moonmakers in Lithuania, and Inselfilm Produktion in Germany. It was supported by the Polish Film Institute, the Lithuanian Film Center and Connected Foundation, and was co-produced by TVP, EC1 – Lodz City of Culture and ZDF, in collaboration with ARTE and Deutsche Welle. articles.title: ‘Primo Viaggio,’ Presented Last Year at Locarno’s Alliance 4 Development, Has Wrapped and Heading for Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 9, 2026 11:50pm PT ‘Primo Viaggio,’ Presented Last Year at Locarno’s Alliance 4 Development, Has Wrapped and Heading for Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) Produced by Nanni Moretti's Rome-based Sacher Film and Andrea Marcelli's Halley Production in Paris, the film, seen as a Locarno success story after shooting in Italy, Spain and France By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest Latin Quarter Distribution Acquires World Rights to José Dell’Acqua Uruguayan Crime Thriller ‘Maltrato Animal’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘Primo Viaggio,’ Presented Last Year at Locarno’s Alliance 4 Development, Has Wrapped and Heading for Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Florian Hoffmann’s U.N. Compound Drama ‘Yazz’ Takes Main Alliance 4 Development Prizes at Locarno Pro Awards 17 hours ago See All From left: Casey Kauffman, Andrea Marcelli, Benedetta Barroero and Alessandro Cassigoli during the shooting of 'Primo Viaggio' in Marseille Courtesy of Andrea Marcelli Less than one year after the producers met at the Locarno Film Festival ‘s Alliance 4 Development co-development platform, “Primo Viaggio,” produced by Italy’s Sacher Film and France’s Halley Production , has wrapped after shooting on location in Naples, Málaga and Marseille between June and July of this year. Written and directed by Alessandro Cassigoli and Casey Kauffman, behind award-winning pics “Californie” and “Vittoria,” “Primo Viaggio” is now bound for the Venice Film Festival’s Gap-Financing Market, where the producers aim to connect with potential sales agents, festival programmers and investors. Related Stories ‘Letters From the Silenced Country,’ Documentary About Oppression in Belarus, Boarded by Filmotor Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar Launch Excel Origins, Initiative to Discover Filmmakers Under 30, as India's Excel Entertainment Marks 25th Anniversary (EXCLUSIVE) Mario Di Frenna stars as Carlo in ‘Primo Viaggio.’ Courtesy of Sacher Film “Primo Viaggio” (which translates to “First Trip”) follows Carlo, a 20-year-old from Naples who, in an effort to improve his bleak existence, agrees to transport narcotics from Málaga, Spain, back to Italy. It’s the first time he has stepped out of his neighborhood and his insular world, however, and the people he meets while in Spain awaken something within him, leading to a detour that alters the course of his life. Popular on Variety The project initially came together last year when Andrea Marcelli of Paris-based Halley Production met Sacher Film’s Benedetta Barroero, who is producing alongside Nanni Moretti , at Locarno during the Alliance 4 Development co-development platform for film projects from Austria, France, Germany and Switzerland. “We hit it off immediately, and given the film’s story, a co-production with France felt natural and organic,” Marcelli told Variety . “A relationship grew from there that deepened over time into a genuine collaboration, with the directors as well. I’m a French producer but Italian by origin, so exchanges between us are quick and fluid, and also keeping Italian cinema and Italian stories alive matters a great deal to me.” The project, he added, is “very much in the great tradition of the Franco-Italian co-productions of the past.” In making the film, Cassigoli and Kauffman sought to retain the realism that characterized “Californie” and “Vittoria,” which won Venice’s best Italian film prize in 2024. It was those elements that drew Marcelli to the project: “It’s precisely the directors’ method, the way they move between reality and fiction, and their attentive, deeply human gaze on the fate of this young character whose life changes radically through a change of environment. Whether it’s a new place or a chance encounter, this film is about the kind of experience that alters our inner chemistry and allows us to imagine ourselves differently. A universal theme.” Cassigoli and Kauffman’s embrace of realism really distinguishes the film, he added, noting that the lead cast, Mario Di Frenna, Sarah-Louna Darnon and Lucky Salvadori, are all non-professional actors. “Their cinema starts from reality and feeds off it,” Marcelli pointed out. “Mario Di Frenna, the protagonist, who was cast through a long street-casting process, is a young man who could have lived Carlo’s story exactly, his alter ego in the fiction.” The story of Carlo’s first journey abroad also offers an interesting cross-border dimension, he added. “The film traces a Mediterranean arc, and we were struck by how much the three cities, Naples, Málaga, Marseille, resemble one another: similar young people, similar problems, but also a shared rhythm and atmosphere.” Halley Production’s other recent credits include Manuel Gómez Pereira’s 2025 Goya-winning Spanish hit “ The Dinner ” (“La cena”), on which it also served as co-producer. articles.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Highest Grossing Hollywood Film in India
articles.full_text: Aug 10, 2026 12:36am PT ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Highest Grossing Hollywood Film in India By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Sadhguru, Graphic India Team on Animated Epic ‘Shiva: The Adiyogi’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Highest Grossing Hollywood Film in India 2 hours ago Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar Launch Excel Origins, Initiative to Discover Filmmakers Under 30, as India’s Excel Entertainment Marks 25th Anniversary (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Sony’s “ Spider-Man: Brand New Day ” has become the highest-grossing Hollywood film in India, dethroning “Avatar: The Way of Water.” A $10.6 million weekend boosted the “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” India total to $52.8 million, according to Sony. “Avatar: The Way of Water” had a lifetime gross of $50.8 million. The result was expected after “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” delivered a historic theatrical debut in India, dethroning “Avengers: Endgame” to claim the biggest opening frame for a non-Indian film in the country’s box office history. Related Stories 'Donkey Princess' Review: A Princess Escapes the Kingdom, but Not the Patriarchy, in an Inventive, Shape-Shifting Fairytale ‘Abbott Elementary’ Stars Sheryl Lee Ralph and Janelle James on the Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: ‘We’ve Lost Too Many People’ The superhero tentpole generated a gross collection of INR72.44 crore ($7.6 million) on its first day, surpassing the previous Hollywood launch benchmark set by “Avengers: Endgame”. The opening frame saw nearly 1 million moviegoers flocking to cinemas on its opening Thursday alone. Popular on Variety Across India’s largest cinema chain, PVR Inox, the film grossed over INR135 crore GBOC ($14.1 million) during its opening weekend, welcoming nearly 3 million moviegoers at an average occupancy of 60%. Nationwide, the film’s four-day extended opening weekend produced a gross collection of $35.4 million, according to Sony, across 17,250 screens. Gautam Dutta, CEO, revenue and operations, PVR Inox Limited, had said about the film’s historic opening weekend: “The response to ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ has been truly outstanding and reflects the enduring appeal of global event cinema on the big screen. What has been particularly encouraging is not just the scale of the opening weekend, but the breadth of audience participation across markets. We have seen exceptional demand from metros as well as Tier II and Tier III cities, with advance bookings, healthy walk-ins and repeat viewership contributing to sustained momentum throughout the weekend.” Metropolitan centers recorded unprecedented demand, with Bengaluru leading all cities by contributing 23% of tracked top-city grosses, followed by Hyderabad at 17%, Mumbai at 15%, and Delhi at 14%. Linguistic versatility and broad penetration across India’s regional circuits drove the record gross numbers, with strong demand spanning major metropolitan centers as well as Tier II and Tier III cities. The original English-language version led theatrical collections with a 55% occupancy rate across nearly 8,000 shows. The Hindi-language dubbed edition generated an extraordinary 95% occupancy across some 7,000 shows, demonstrating the character’s reach into regional markets. Southern regional language dubs in Telugu and Tamil added further momentum across key circuits. The film crossed 6 million ticket sales on ticketing portal BookMyShow on its opening weekend. “The film has struck a chord with audiences nationwide, with English leading the charge, closely followed by Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, while markets such as Hyderabad, Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Bengaluru and Chennai continue to drive exceptional demand. The film is doing superbly in all non-2D formats including 3D, 4DX, Dolby and Epiq formats,” said Ashish Saksena, COO – cinemas, BookMyShow. “What’s particularly exciting is that ‘Brand New Day’ has now surpassed the lifetime ticket sales of several landmark titles including ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home,’ ‘Avengers: Infinity War,’ ‘Spider-Man: Far From Home’ and ‘Spider-Man: Homecoming’ on BookMyShow,” Saksena added. “This is a clear reflection of the growing appetite for tentpole cinematic experiences and the unparalleled excitement that beloved franchises continue to generate. The response has been extraordinary, reiterating that when it comes to event films and large-screen spectacle, audiences continue to choose the magic of the theatrical experience.” Webtoon Productions, Espotlight Forge First-Look Pact for Spanish-Language Wattpad Adaptations (EXCLUSIVE) World Cup Final Ratings Skyrocket Across Europe, Despite England and France Losses What’s Coming to Netflix in August 2026 Netflix Comedy Series ‘I Suck at Girls’ Casts Anna Konkle, Taegen Burns and More Anne Sweeney Resigns From Netflix Board ‘The Inbetweeners’ Reunion Movie in the Works at Netflix With Original Lead Cast to Return Loading comments... articles.title: Sadhguru, Graphic India Team on Animated Epic ‘Shiva: The Adiyogi’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 10, 2026 1:00am PT Sadhguru, Graphic India Team on Animated Epic ‘Shiva: The Adiyogi’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Sadhguru, Graphic India Team on Animated Epic ‘Shiva: The Adiyogi’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Highest Grossing Hollywood Film in India 2 hours ago Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar Launch Excel Origins, Initiative to Discover Filmmakers Under 30, as India’s Excel Entertainment Marks 25th Anniversary (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Graphic India Indian yogi and mystic Sadhguru is teaming with Graphic India on “ Shiva: The Adiyogi ,” an animated feature retelling the origin story of Hindu God Shiva as the first yogi. Sadhguru and Sharad Devarajan share story credit on the film. Graphic India is the studio behind India’s animated mythology franchise “The Legend of Hanuman.” Devarajan, who co-created that series and co-founded Graphic India, is producing, co-writing and co-creating “Shiva: The Adiyogi.” Related Stories David Ellison Is Promising Theater Owners Contractual Guarantees for Paramount-Warner Bros. 30-Film Annual Slate. But What if Moviegoers Don't Care? Kiran Abbavaram's Mythological Action-Fantasy for India's Zee Studios Reveals Title as 'Indraputra' (EXCLUSIVE) The film spans from before creation to the peaks of Kailash, taking in the rage of Veerabhadra, a being formed from grief, and the devotion of two women whose bond keeps Shiva connected to existence. It builds to a scene at Kanti Sarovar in which Shiva imparts 112 methods for transcending physical existence to seven seekers. Popular on Variety “In the yogic culture, Shiva is not seen as a God. For us, Shiva is the Adiyogi – the first yogi, and the Adiguru – the first guru. For the first time in the history of humanity, Shiva the Adiyogi introduced the idea that the simple laws of nature are not permanent restrictions. If one is willing to strive, one can go beyond all limitations and attain to liberation. Breaking the laws of physical nature is spiritual process. In this sense, we are outlaws, and Shiva is the ultimate outlaw,” said Sadhguru. “This is the story of how wisdom itself was born, and why it was shared with humanity,” added Devarajan. “As a storyteller, there is no greater canvas, a cosmic love story, a tale of devastating loss, and action on a scale no epic has ever attempted. Armies of gods fall before a warrior born of pure grief. A blind conqueror storms the gates of heaven. A third eye opens and burns desire itself out of existence. And through all the fury and spectacle runs the most tender story imaginable, of the two women whose love was fierce enough to reach an infinite being, and the final gift he gave humanity because of them. To craft this story alongside Sadhguru, the defining voice of the Adiyogi in our time, is the greatest creative honor I could imagine.” Sadhguru is also a bestselling author whose videos stream in 35 languages on social media. He founded the Isha Foundation , a nonprofit human-service organization, more than three decades ago; it is now supported by over 19 million volunteers worldwide. Devarajan’s credits also include the “Baahubali” animated series, comprising “Baahubali: The Lost Legends” and “Baahubali: Crown of Blood,” and the co-creation of Pavitr Prabhakar, the Indian Spider-Man character for Marvel who appeared in the Oscar-nominated “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse.” “Shiva: The Adiyogi” is targeting a worldwide theatrical release. Jeevan J. Kang and Subrah S. Iyar serve as executive producers and Navin Miranda and Nayana Bijli as co-producers. articles.title: ‘Brave New Love’ Review: Infidelity Isn’t the End in an Unusual, Open-Minded Marital Drama
articles.full_text: Aug 10, 2026 1:02am PT ‘Brave New Love’ Review: Infidelity Isn’t the End in an Unusual, Open-Minded Marital Drama Kathrine Thorborg Johansen and Anders Danielsen Lie gives fine performances in the second fiction feature from Swedish-Danish director Maria Bäck, in which a woman's long-term extramarital affair puts her life in perspective. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Donkey Princess’ Review: A Princess Escapes the Kingdom, but Not the Patriarchy, in an Inventive, Shape-Shifting Fairytale 1 day ago ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine 2 days ago ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Snowglobe “I would never fall in love if I was in a good relationship.” So says one participant in the women’s church group where Copenhagen-based wife and mother Kate (Kathrine Thorborg Johansen) confesses that she’s been having a three-year affair with another man, and doesn’t much regret it. It’s a line that sounds like sturdy, suitably Christian advice, but is it true? Kate’s husband Orla (Simon Sears) is attentive, attractive and empathetic; so is Andreas ( Anders Danielsen Lie ), the smart, offbeat archaeologist she’s smitten with at first sight. Alternately droll and emotionally acute, Maria Bäck’s “ Brave New Love ” never presents this romantic triangle as a problem with one solution; it’s considerably less judgmental than the church ladies as it gives its protagonist space to figure out if she really loves two people at once, or just loves nobody — herself included — quite enough. Related Stories Alessandra Sanguinetti on Her Dreamy, Grounded Directorial Debut ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’ Olivia Wilde Says She’s Become ‘So Much More Romantic’ Because of ‘The Invite’: ‘It Melted the Cynic Out of Me’ Premiering in the main competition at Locarno, this is an emotionally intelligent, gently wry character drama of a distinctly Scandi stripe, occupying a comparable arthouse lane to Dag Johan Haugerud’s Oslo Trilogy and recent works by Joachim Trier, albeit with a distinctly feminine point of view behind the camera. It’s not just Danielsen Lie’s reliably interesting presence that brings to mind “The Worst Person in the World” at points, as Bäck’s script (on which Trier collaborator Eskil Vogt was a consultant) ponders similar feelings of middle-class millennial female unrest in a character who simply opted for marriage and family earlier in life. Relatable and discussable, Bäck’s second narrative feature likely reps an easier sell to international distributors than her first, the darkly heightened psychodrama “Psychosis in Stockholm.” Popular on Variety It’s on a camping trip with her family that Kate first locks eyes with Andreas — they’re both stark naked, having just swum in the same forest lake, but that’s rendered almost incidental by the telling intensity of their shared gaze. When he walks off, Kate scribbles down her number and leaves it under his towel. But then “Brave New Love” takes the first of several swerves: Instead of charting its protagonist’s first steps into infidelity, it skips breezily through snapshots from the ensuing years-long affair. Andreas becomes almost as entrenched a partner in her life as her husband, though she manages to keep the relationships strictly separate — a rationalized arrangement in her mind, though that collapses when Andreas calmly announces that he’s moving to Greece for a job. It’s only with the affair on ice that disorder creeps into Kate’s life, while Orla and their teenage daughter Athena (an excellent Noemi Carbone Mannov) begin to sense something amiss. Editor Julius Krebs Damsbo artfully toggles between present and past, gradually filling in the sensual specifics of the affair — which aren’t entirely as you’d expect — while tracking Kate’s spiraling sense of mourning for whatever it was they had. Without it, her comfortable marriage to Orla seems that much more confined, the increasingly separate islands they seem to be on underlined by DP Maria Von Hausswolff in one tense bedtime argument scene, with the couple’s faces visible only in their respective bathroom-vanity mirrors. Kate seeks solidarity in the aforementioned church group, despite not being much of a believer herself; she doesn’t quite find it, but the candor enabled by all-female company is its own kind of liberation. Thorborg Johansen’s subtly nervy performance articulates Kate’s antsy anxieties and erratic moods without making her too much of a scatty romantic heroine. She’s believable while not straining too hard for our sympathy, which winds up fairly evenly divided between all the principals anyway — with a slight advantage to Sears’ beautifully modulated turn as Orla, battling his own emotional and bodily securities while trying to hold down the fort. Handed the most script’s least knowable character, Andersen Lie nonetheless sharply gestures to a life outside his relations with Kate, something she herself hasn’t much considered. In its efforts to be fair to all these characters — via a key, spirit-lightening change of scene — “Brave New Love’s” final act winds up a little fuzzy, though that’s a preferable flaw to tunnel vision: Bäck’s film prefers untidy personal drama to a tidy moral verdict. ‘Brave New Love’ Review: Infidelity Isn’t the End in an Unusual, Open-Minded Marital Drama Reviewed at Locarno Film Festival (International Competition), Aug. 9, 2026. Running time: 106 MIN. Production: (Denmark-Sweden-Greece) A Snowglobe presentation in co-production with Garagefilm, Studiobauhaus, Film Stockholm, Kalabalik. (World sales: Reinvent Yellow Sales, Copenhagen.) Producer: Anna-Maria Kantarius. Executive producers: Mikkel Jersin, Katrin Pors, Eva Jakobsen. Co-producers: Mimmi Spång, Konstantinos Vassilaros, Anne-Marie Söhrman Fermelin, Maria Bäck. Crew: Director, screenplay: Maria Bäck. Camera: Maria Von Hausswolff. Editor: Julius Krebs Damsbo. Music: Jenny Hval. With: Kathrine Thorborg Johansen, Anders Danielsen Lie, Simon Sears, Noemi Carbone Mannov, Angeliki Papoulia. articles.title: Alessandra Sanguinetti on Her Dreamy, Grounded Directorial Debut ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’
articles.full_text: Aug 10, 2026 1:45am PT Alessandra Sanguinetti on Her Dreamy, Grounded Directorial Debut ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’ By Alex Petrescu , Manahil Tahira 'The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer' Courtesy of Alessandra Sanguinetti In the Argentine Pampas, cousins Guillermina and Belinda cannot wait to grow up. When they are not swimming in the river and dancing through the long, breezy afternoons, they re-enact funeral ceremonies and feign surgery on dead animals. This quotidian desire to accelerate the inevitable passing of time animates photographer Alessandra Sanguinetti ’s debut feature, “The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer.” Presented in world premiere in Filmmakers of the Present at the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival , the film was produced by distinguished director-producer Julia Solomonoff (“Nobody’s Watching”), with financing from Mubi and Impact Partners. Related Stories Andrew Lloyd Webber Is 'Gutted' on 'Cats: The Jellicle Ball' Closing Night: Producing on Broadway Is 'Unsustainable' 'House of the Dragon' Star James Norton on the Irony of Ormund's [SPOILER], His 'Oddly Intimate' Dynamic With Roddy the Ruin and Why His Love for Daeron Needed to Feel 'Real' Sanguinetti’s gaze follows Guille and Belinda while they grow up, fall in love, raise children and slowly drift toward separate lives over two and a half decades. The seemingly home-footage structure forms a familiar and intimate setting, in which the grainy footage narrates the life passing between the moments Sanguinetti captured as part of her extensive, decades-long photography of close cousins Guille and Belinda. Popular on Variety “We’re just like extended family now,” says the director about her relationship with the duo, spanning over 25 years. “It was really organic. I did not want to make a project about two women growing up. I just knew them and wanted to be with them.” Static framing and pixelated vignettes of tranquil farmland in Sanguinetti’s work trace back to formal similarities to “ Dry Leaf ,” directed by Alexandre Koberidze, another Locarno title, screened in 2025. The Argentinian prairie is adorned with imaginary houses, castles and theatres as the young girls construct spontaneous, invisible cities, stories and games in which Koberidze’s likewise unseen characters could live. Lively farm animals populate the backgrounds against which Guille and Belinda confidently perform their silly and earnest singing and dancing. Although the result bears some resemblance, the two directors employ the graininess for different aesthetic reasons. In Sanguinetti’s practice, the video camera appeared as a natural prop that watched and filmed Belinda and Guille’s performances while the director captured with her photographic camera “what happens slowly in the moment.” Comparing photography to video, she says about her relationship with the first, “I’m always more in control and looking for something. With video, I could let life flow in front of me and then later think about what to retrieve or not.” These snapshots of life, then overlooked as common moments, might be actually foundational to one’s trajectory, as “we don’t realize that we’re defining ourselves in that moment. You can only see that when you’re at a certain distance, when you’re knowing and loving them, but you’re not being their mother.” This in turn enabled Sanguinetti to observe “patterns in the girls’ lives — what kept repeating or changing, what things they had escaped from, and what they achieved through sheer will.” Sanguinetti’s tender film detours through the motions of time and eventually brings fleshiness to her presence. “In the beginning, I didn’t want to be a part of it. I thought my voice would ruin it. As the time went by, I realized that I was there and I just had to accept it.” If women constitute the film’s heart, animals form its pulse. Neither pets nor crude products of an economy, Sanguinetti deftly places cattle, dogs and cats alongside people and land. Essential to the farmland Pampas, the girls’ grandmother repeatedly confesses to the director about the joy of taking care of chickens and their innate beauty or the bovines’ way of behaving as a tightly knit community. This sentiment is personal for Sanguinetti: “I’ve always considered animals equal to humans,” adding on their importance to the rural ecosystem: “I always felt that the animals in that space were ignored. But these people are here because of the animals in that area, because there is no agriculture.” ‘This Summer Will Be Different’ Netflix Series Adds 6 to Cast as Production Begins Veteran Reality Exec Mike Darnell Seals Overall Deal at Netflix, Where He’ll Also Provide Guidance on the Streamer’s Unscripted Slate Netflix Paid $587 Million for Ben Affleck’s AI Startup InterPositive Chloe Fineman Among Four Cast in ‘Myron Bolitar’ Series at Netflix Morgan Spector to Play Robert Langdon in Netflix Series From Carlton Cuse, Dan Brown ‘Operation Safed Sagar’: Inside Netflix’s High-Altitude Bet on the Untold Story of the India-Pakistan Kargil War Loading comments... articles.full_text: Aug 10, 2026 2:08am PT Latin Quarter Distribution Acquires World Rights to José Dell’Acqua Uruguayan Crime Thriller ‘Maltrato Animal’ (EXCLUSIVE) Presented at Locarno's First Look focus, the film follows a desperate veterinarian forced into criminal activity to survive during Uruguay's 2002 economic crisis By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest Latin Quarter Distribution Acquires World Rights to José Dell’Acqua Uruguayan Crime Thriller ‘Maltrato Animal’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Florian Hoffmann’s U.N. Compound Drama ‘Yazz’ Takes Main Alliance 4 Development Prizes at Locarno Pro Awards 17 hours ago Atlanta-Based Liaison Pictures Joins France’s Because the Night Productions on Locarno Match Me! Title ‘Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All 'Maltrato Animal' Courtesy of Latin Quarter Distribution Latin Quarter Distribution has acquired world sales rights to José Dell’Acqua’s Uruguayan crime thriller “Maltrato Animal” (“Animal Budget”). The deal was closed after a screening of “Maltrato Animal” at Locarno’s First Look, a pix-in-post competition focused on rough-cut screenings of emerging and established talent from a territory around the world, this year Uruguay . Presented in Locarno by the Agencia del Cine y el Audiovisual del Uruguay (ACAU), which is still building Uruguay’s film-TV ecosysytem, the film, currently in the editing stage, is set against the backdrop of Uruguay’s 2002 economic crisis and explores a generation shaped by that pivotal moment in the country’s history. Related Stories Andrew Lloyd Webber Is 'Gutted' on 'Cats: The Jellicle Ball' Closing Night: Producing on Broadway Is 'Unsustainable' Ariana Grande Debuts at No. 1 on Album Chart With 'Petal,' Earning Her Best First-Week Numbers in Seven Years Bankrupted by the financial crisis, a Montevideo veterinarian is pushed to desperate straits and doesn’t have enough money to eat. In order to survive, he enters a clandestine network of illegal breeding operations and pharmaceutical peddling. In this downward spiral, an unexpected encounter potentially opens a new chapter in his life. Popular on Variety Produced by Dell’Acqua and German Ormaechea, the film was shot over a four-year period — one week each year — with the support of numerous Uruguayan technicians and rental companies. The project brought together many first-time department heads, including cinematographer Germán Couto and costume designer Victoria Zavaleta, as well as an entirely Uruguayan cast, according to Dell’Aqua. Developed over eight years, the film blends fiction and reality to portray a deeply personal and collective memory. “‘Maltrato Animal’ was born from the need to revisit the generation that grew up during Uruguay’s 2002 economic crisis,” Dell’Acqua said. “Over eight years, I wrote, directed, and produced the film, seeking to blur the boundaries between fiction and reality. It is also a celebration of the talent of a new generation of Uruguayan filmmakers, many of whom took on leading creative roles in their first feature film.” “After such a long and personal journey with ‘Maltrato Animal,’ I’m very happy to begin this next stage with Latin Quarter Distribution,” Dell’Aqua told Variety . “Their bold approach and distinctive curation feel deeply aligned with the spirit of the film. I believe they understand the kind of cinema we are trying to make and, most importantly, have the commitment and passion to bring it to audiences beyond Uruguay.” Juan G. Castro, founder and managing director of The Hague-based Latin Quarter Distribution, added: “We’re excited to add ‘Maltrato Animal’ to the Latin Quarter slate. We’re always searching for new gems and distinctive voices in Latin American arthouse cinema, and José Dell’Acqua’s first feature immediately stood out to us. Discovering the film through ACAU’s presentation of Uruguayan cinema at Locarno makes this acquisition particularly meaningful, and we’re proud to support a film that showcases the talent and originality emerging from Uruguay today.” Post-production on “Maltrato Animal” is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.
