articles.title: Obama Blames Larry David For 2014 Tan Suit Debacle In ‘Life, Larry & the Pursuit of Unhappiness’ Finale
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Obama Blames Larry David For 2014 Tan Suit Debacle In ‘Life, Larry & the Pursuit of Unhappiness’ Finale Matthew McConaughey Performs “Quill” In Scene From ‘The Rivals of Amziah King’ — Watch Jane Schoenbrun On Deconstructing The “Toxic Soup” Of The Slasher Genre In ‘Teenage Sex & Death at Camp Miasma’: “It’s There In The DNA” View All August 8, 2026 8:08pm Larry David and President Barack Obama in 'Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness' John Johnson/HBO As Larry David ‘s comedic trip through U.S. history comes to an end, he took credit for one of the nation’s more recent presidential scandals. On Friday’s season finale of the HBO sketch comedy miniseries Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness , President Barack Obama made a surprise appearance as himself in a sketch set in 2014, as David advised him to wear the now-infamous, outrage-inducing tan suit during his live press conference on military response to ISIS. Following some banter on how the POTUS avoids stains, David accidentally spills juice on Obama’s suit jacket when he leaves the room. When the 44th president returns, the comedian recommends he wear the tan suit that Obama planned on taking it to Turin for NATO Summit, for “a daytime event, it’s outdoors, a little more casual.” Related Stories News “Curb In Costume”: How President Obama Persuaded Larry David To Return To TV With HBO’s ‘Life, Larry And The Pursuit Of Unhappiness’ News Larry David Jabs Anti-Vaccine Activism Of Cheryl Hines’ Husband In Latest ‘Life, Larry And The Pursuit Of Unhappiness’ “First of all, it’s a gorgeous suit,” David declared. “And this is casual Friday!” Watch on Deadline “It is a great suit,” admitted Obama, as David told him, “Oh boy, oh boy. I think this is the move. … Old lips won’t let you down. You’ll thank me!” As Obama models the look, David gives him his signature, “Pretty good! Pretty, pretty, pretty, pretty, pretty good.” “You sure about this?” asks Obama, as David assures him, “Never been more sure about anything in my life. People are going to be talking about this for a long, long time.” Obama’s cameo in the finale comes as David marks the United States Semiquencentennial with the seven-part sketch comedy limited series, which recounts major events in U.S. history through the comedian’s signature observational humor. David’s longtime Curb Your Enthusiasm partner Jeff Schaffer, who serves as an executive producer on Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness , previously told Deadline that Obama, who produced under his Higher Ground banner, reached out to his buddy David to ask if he’d be interested in making the show to celebrate the country’s 250th birthday. “When you’re doing a show about American history, you want to do it warts and right now we have this orange saggy wart that we wish would go away,” said Schaffer. “But the nice thing about having President Obama produce this and be a part of it is that this country’s had a lot of fuck ups, we’ve seemed to have learned very little, but we’re still moving forward sometimes, and then we move back a little bit, but we always move forward again. While Larry’s pointing out a lot of the steps back, the President is telling us we can still step forward.” ‘Brand New Day’ Eyes Third-Best U.S. 2nd Weekend With $135M-$140M+ Andrew Lloyd Webber “Gutted” By ‘Jellicle’ Closing Tonight Justice Smith & Charlie Gillespie Join ‘Heated Rivalry’ As Harris & Troy; S2 Set For Spring Epic Tops $1B Global; Poised To Become Nolan’s Top-Grossing Pic Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Kirill Sokolov, Director of ‘They Will Kill You,’ Tackling Sci-Fi Action Movie ‘Blur’ for Netflix (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Borys Kit Plus Icon Borys Kit Senior Film Writer View All August 7, 2026 1:49pm Kirill Sokolov Sami Heiskanen Logo text Netflix has tapped Kirill Sokolov , the helmer behind horror action movie They Will Kill You , to direct the original sci-fi thriller Blur . Shawn Levy and Dan Levine will produce via 21 Laps. Netflis is keeping the logline a hop, skip and a jump from prying eyes but it is known to be a mother-daughter story involving teleportation. The project is based on a previous script by Christy Hall and Dan Casey. Sokolov will co-write the new draft with Ellen Shanman. Bryan Oh is overseeing for 21 Laps. Sokolov is the Russian filmmaker who broke out with Why Don’t You Just Die , his 2019 dark crime action comedy that was infused with early Tarantino influences. After writing and directing another Russian dark action comedy, No Looking Back , he journeyed to the U.S. in the early 2020s, he landed in Hollywood as he tried to land representation and work. He made his English-language debut earlier this year with They Will Kill You , an action-horror-comedy released by Warner Bros. in March. Set in a Manhattan luxury building whose Satan-worshipping tenants engage in ritualistic killings, the movie starred Zazie Beetz. THR praised the movie for its gonzo style . Sokolov is repped by CAA, Harvest Hill Entertainment, Kaplan Perrone, and Yorn, Levine, THR

articles.title: Virginie Efira’s Love for Cinema and Locarno Has No Limits — Even If Her Mic Does
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 7, 2026 2:02pm Virginie Efira at Locarno 2026 on her way to receiving the Leopard Club Award Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival/Ti-Press Belgian-born actress Virginie Efira ( All of a Sudden , Parallel Tales , Benedetta , Paris Memories ) took the stage in the central Piazza Grande square at the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival on Friday evening to receive this year’s Leopard Club Award . “It is truly a joy, a privilege and an immense honor for me to be here with you to receive this award,” she said in French in front of a huge crowd in the Italian-speaking part of Switzerland, before adding: “I sincerely apologize for only speaking French. Do most people understand?” The crowd’s answer was a loud “yes.” Related Stories Movies 'I Is Another' Review: Claes Bang Plays Himmler's Masseur in Weighty Meditation on a WWII Footnote Lifestyle As Tom Holland and Zendaya Rule the Box Office, We Look at Their Reported Wedding Bash at the Decadent Beaverbrook Hotel She continued with praise for the Locarno festival. “I also want to say, and I feel this very strongly when I see you all here in this square, … that Locarno is perhaps the festival with the greatest faith in the audience,” Efira offered. “The idea [is] that we, as viewers — and I share this belief, like you — are all hungry for films that resonate with us, that move us, that innovate, that offer us something greater, and that we are not finite entities with predictable desires, that we want to be surprised. And Locarno truly has that trust in the audience, and that warms my heart.” She continued: “The Locarno Film Festival is truly avant-garde. It discovers artists, it looks at a cinema that is being invented, and that is extremely important.” Efira also got emotional, sharing: “I think it’s the first time I’ve received an award like this. I’ve received awards before, at Cannes, for example, but not a recognition like this for several films and for a career. It touches me deeply.” But the star emphasized that film is about more than one actor. “I share this award with the public who love films, and I also share it with directors, who are true creators,” Efira told the Locarno crowd. “Because for an actor, this award is a very heavy burden. An actor on their own isn’t much. It’s truly a collective profession. And to achieve something that might have some merit, you need a vision.” Virginie Efira Efira then namechecked various directors she has collaborated with, such as Ryusuke Hamaguchi, Justine Triet, Rebecca Zlotowski and Valérie Donzelli. “On your own, you’re not much,” Efira concluded. “And without the audience, you’re nothing at all. So, thank you for your curiosity.” While at the Swiss festival, Efira will present Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden ( Soudain ), for which she won the Palme for best actress at Cannes and for which she learned to act partly in Japanese. With that film and Asghar Farhadi’s Parallel Tales , Efira pulled double duty in this year’s Cannes competition, winning the best actress honor together with her All of a Sudden co-star Tao Okamoto. When she mentioned that people in the square can see that film in Locarno on Saturday, her microphone cut out for a few seconds, but the star quickly decided to simply continue talking without amplification, just more loudly. When the mic started working again seconds later, she said to laughs: “Oh, it works, great!” Locarno artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro had introduced the star, also in French, full of pride. “It is an incredible honor to welcome Virginie Efira, an incomparable artist,” he said, also praising her for “always remaining true to herself.” And he concluded: “Virginie Efira embodies the modernity of cinema.” After Efira received her honor, it was time for the world premiere of I Is Another ( Ich Ist ein Anderer ), written and directed by Felix Randau and starring Claes Bang ( The Square , Bad Sisters , Home ) and Valerie Pachner ( The Stories , Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore , Four Minus Three ), which tells the story of Nazi Heinrich Himmler ‘s former massage therapist. The creative team briefly discussed their film and shared their excitement about being on stage in front of a crowded square full of film lovers. Shared Bang: “I must say: This looks much better than in photos. People, you are amazing! Thank you for coming!” The crowd erupted into applause and cheers before the star added: “This is so pretty and beautiful and wonderful.” THR

articles.title: A Man Is Trapped Inside a Netflix Billboard Above Sunset Boulevard
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All August 7, 2026 2:09pm Living billboard for The Last House from Netflix on Sunset Boulevard, Aug. 6 Logo text Call it Netflix and still . A man is seemingly trapped inside a Netflix billboard above Sunset Boulevard. The potential traffic-stopping (or perhaps even accident-causing) sight is a marketing stunt for the streamer’s new thriller The Last House . The unidentified actor entered the installation — which is crafted to look like the front window of a house — on Thursday and will leave on Saturday, Aug. 8. From Netflix: “He’ll attempt to maintain a sense of normalcy over extended periods of time while ‘stuck’ in his elevated, enclosed set 30 feet above the ground at Selma Avenue and Sunset Blvd — communicating with commuters and passersby below via whiteboard as an eerie nod to the family’s own isolation in the film.” Related Stories TV 'My Life with the Walter Boys' Love Triangle Resolved: Showrunner, Cast Weigh in on Long Awaited Pairing, "Brutal" Outcome and What's Next Movies 'The Last House' Review: Greta Lee and Wagner Moura in a Claustrophobic Netflix Thriller Most Effective While the Threat Remains Unknown A video, below, shows the man looking like he’s eating cereal and rather confused and miserable. In case you’re wondering, yes, it’s the same actor the entire time, not multiple actors working in shifts. Living billboard for The Last House from Netflix on Sunset Boulevard. The Last House stars Greta Lee and Wagner Moura, is directed by Louis Leterrier ( Fast X ), and is about a family of four who are “suddenly sealed inside their home with no way out, and must work together to survive against both their dwindling resources and the mysterious, looming threat that is keeping them trapped.” The film could probably use a bit of buzz — the project only has a 36 percent positive critics’ score on Rotten Tomatoes (though only it has 22 reviews so far, so that percentage will likely change). The Hollywood Reporter’ s critic enjoyed the film, however, writing, that “despite its sci-fi and horror elements, [ The Last House ] is as much a psychological chamber drama and survival thriller about four people using their wits and dwindling resources to stay alive, even as their close-knit ties start fraying.” There's a guy in there 👀 pic.twitter.com/L79Q7pisNP — Netflix (@netflix) August 6, 2026 The Last House drops on Netflix on Friday. THR

articles.title: Spencer Pratt Joins the Chat on the Federal Film and Television Tax Incentive
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All August 7, 2026 3:17pm Spencer Pratt at the 2025 American Music Awards held at the Fontainebleau Las Vegas on May 26, 2025, in Las Vegas, Nevada. Getty Images The federal film and television tax credit has a new lobbyist, it seems. Reality TV star and former L.A. mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt on Friday posted on social media that he had recently met President Donald Trump to advocate for the tax incentive. This legislative effort has been stop-and-start for well over a year. “Working with the President on a 25% FEDERAL film tax credit to bring back Hollywood,” the former The Hills star said, sharing images of himself and the president speaking at the Trump National Golf Course Los Angeles. After making a few accusations about California’s film commissioner and Attorney General Rob Bonta, he added, “The adults in the room are actually trying to repatriate the most quintessential American industry. I’m committed to saving Hollywood, and I’m very grateful for the President’s remarkable generosity and focus on this issue.” Related Stories TV The Man Behind David Lynch, Kathryn Bigelow and 'Beverly Hills, 90210' Gets His Moment at Locarno TV John Oliver Says Taco Bell Has the Moral High Ground Over Trump Administration Amid "Explosive Diarrhea" Parasite Crisis The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to the White House for comment. A representative for Pratt declined to comment further. A large coalition of industry advocates and organizations, from the Motion Picture Association to industry unions to President Trump’s “special ambassador” to Hollywood Jon Voight, has long been championing the idea of a stackable incentive for films and TV series produced in the U.S. Several sources in this cohort reached on Friday said they didn’t believe Pratt was working in coalition with the larger group. “Although we haven’t had conversations with Spencer or his people, we appreciate the support of anyone who has the President’s ear that can help push this initiative forward,” said SP Media Group president Scott Karol, who is part of Voight’s team advocating for the credit. “At the end of the day, what matters is getting a meaningful federal incentive, and bringing good paying jobs back to America.” The idea has bipartisan support, as THR previously wrote , with Rep. Laura Friedman of California and Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia emerging as key backers of the potential legislation in the House. Sen. Adam Schiff has long been a proponent in the Senate. It’s unclear, however, whether Pratt is advocating for the same kind of credit as they are. After becoming an outspoken critic of politicians’ responses to the 2025 Palisades Fire, Pratt ran for L.A. mayor earlier in the year on a populist platform, gaining the support of President Trump along the way. After his defeat, Pratt has emerged as a vocal detractor of a lawsuit from 12 state attorneys general aiming to block the $111 billion Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. He has claimed that California Gov. Gavin Newsom and attorney general Bonta are attempting to “cripple two of the greatest film studios of all time over politics.” (Newsom has not weighed in on the suit publicly yet, though a Wall Street Journal report in early August suggested he was concerned about the impact on state employment if the merger were blocked.) Now, it appears, the TV personality has turned his attention to legislative efforts to boost the entertainment industry. Said Pratt in his social media post, “He [Trump] is very passionate about revitalizing the entertainment industry and we will not let Canada, or the U.K. or Budapest steal our lunch anymore.” Pratt’s advocacy for a federal tax credit arrives after Paramount Skydance head David Ellison made headlines for traveling to Washington to lobby Republicans on the idea. Can the involvement of Pratt, a registered Republican, and other conservatives finally enthuse the president on the long-gestating idea? Only time will tell. In the meantime, below Pratt’s post on Instagram, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt posted two raising hands emojis. Aug. 7, 6:16 p.m. Updated with Scott Karol statement. THR

articles.title: Keen Ruffalo Never Intended to Get Into the Family Business
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Keen Ruffalo stars in the new Prime Video series ‘Sterling Point.’ Photography by Evan Mulling Keen Ruffalo never planned to get into acting. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, the now-25-year-old was in school for fashion design. Understandably, he wanted to find his own path instead of jumping into acting like his father Mark Ruffalo. But the pandemic changed his plans. He found himself not knowing what he’d do next with his life. “I was depressed as most people were during COVID and needed to figure out what to do,” Ruffalo tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom. He realized that acting had brought his father joy, so he decided to explore why. Instead of looking for roles, Ruffalo opted to study the craft first. He instantly fell in love. “I went to so many goddamn conservatories,” he says. Related Stories TV How Ella Rubin Went From Being a Briefcase-Wielding 11-Year-Old to the Star of 'Sterling Point' TV Inside 'Sterling Point': Why Megan Park's YA Series Trades Tired Tropes for a Refreshing Dose of Realism But Ruffalo was waiting for one specific OK. “Finally, my dad saw a play that I did, and he was like, ‘You might be ready now,’” he recalls. “He gave me the A-OK to go out into the world.” Getting out into the world was clearly the right move, as the actor’s releasing two projects in Prime Video’s Sterling Point and the Green Day comedy Nimrods . In Sterling Point , he plays Connor, the twin of the show’s main character Annie, played by Ella Rubin. Given his father’s long career, one would assume that Ruffalo basically grew up around it. But he found his childhood to be quite removed from Hollywood, both in the figurative and literal sense, having grown up on a farm in upstate New York. He didn’t even realize that what his dad did for work was different from his neighbor’s dad, a dairy farmer, until he was a bit older. “It wasn’t until someone came up to me and was like, ‘Hey, can you have your dad sign this Hulk Funko Pop for me?’ [that I realized],” he says. “I was like, ‘No, you’re horribly mean to me.’” “I really didn’t understand the gravity of it all until a little bit later in life, and even then I was kept pretty far away from it all,” he says. However, working with the Sterling Point cast allowed the actor to collaborate with a host of other young people also newer to the industry. “It’s such a cool thing to be doing with them because we’re all at this weird point [in our careers],” he says. “Being able to work with such talented creators and artists at that point in their career where we’re all still getting the hang of it a little bit is something that’s really special and not very common.” In a conversation with THR , the the actor digs into Sterling Point , the best advice he’s received, his favorite non-acting activities and why he doesn’t want to get behind the camera (for now). You said you initially weren’t planning to get into acting. Is it more rewarding to figure it out on your own that you want to be there? Definitely. My parents were never ones to make us do anything or, especially, impose any of their own ideas for what our career paths might be, which I appreciated a lot. Maybe [they were] a little bit more enthusiastic about playing soccer, but they were kind of like, “Yeah, do whatever.” Sunrise Coigney, Mark Ruffalo and Keen Ruffalo at the 2015 Toronto Film Festival. Harold Feng/Getty Images for LiveNationStudios What’s the best piece of advice you’ve received? It doesn’t have to be from your dad. God, I don’t know. I feel like it’s a hard one because so many different people say so much. A lot of time people ask me for advice, which I’m like, “Dude, I’ve been here just as long as you have. I don’t know what you want.” I think the thing that always kept me going is hearing about … and this is actually from my dad, so sorry. I’m not breaking the mold here, apparently. You’ve got a good source for information. I get it. Yeah, resident expert, but he was always talking about how he had to do so many auditions before he even got into a room, where they even gave him a chance. Keeping that in mind and not beating myself up over not getting something that I was really excited for, or knowing that eventually something will come around, [and] you just really need to keep up until you get there and don’t drive yourself crazy. I think that’s a really hard part about it. Is there anything in the world you feel you can’t live without? Probably my bed. I love a pillow. I think I couldn’t go without that one pillow. Music is another one that’s super important because that’s always shifting just throughout life. What do you listen to these days? I’ve listened to a lot of Midwest emo punk recently. I feel like that’s a little bit of an embarrassing one to admit. There’s one song that I really liked recently, I’ll tell you because honestly, I think that they deserve more eyes on them. It’s “Will They Blame Me If You Go Disappearing?” by Hail the Sun. It is so good. That is the best emo title song as well. It’s always a full sentence. It is a full sentence question mark at the end. Correct grammar. It’s a really cool song that I’ve been jamming out to a lot recently. I love it. But definitely wouldn’t show it to many people. I’ll go to a photo shoot or something and they’ll ask me if there’s a song I want to put on. I say no whatever they want. Keen Ruffalo at the Dior Cruise 2027 show. Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for Christian Dior Are you still interested in fashion? Fashion’s something that I’ve kind of been around for a long time. My mom used to be a model, so she’s always been outspoken about fashion. It was jewelry-making that I actually was really into. I used to hammer, fire, the whole thing. That’s my medium in that, but I’m definitely still interested. It’s just a cool thing seeing how it’s always changing. I don’t know. I went to my first fashion show. How was that? That was a trip. It was really cool. It was the Dior show. I was just enjoying the show, and I looked around and everyone had their phone out. I thought, “Oh, wait, I should be doing this too.” I’ve never experienced anything like that. Being invited to an event was surprising. I don’t know. I’m like, why do they want me there? I’m just a farm boy. How old were you when you started making jewelry? That’s quite an intensive hobby to just pick up. I’ve always been a bit of a hands-on person. I didn’t do great in school — I’m ADHD, dyslexic — [and] always had a hard time there, but I liked making stuff. I think the first time I ever did anything like that was maybe at a summer camp. They told us we were going to make leaves out of sheet metal. I really enjoyed that, and then kept going back to this person that ran that little class and doing more stuff with them. [I’ve] probably been doing metal working since, God, maybe I was like eight or seven. Then I started building boats for a while there. I’m also an ADHD kid, and every few weeks I wanted a new hobby. It seems like you actually stuck with yours. I’ve given up on plenty of hobbies. But I’ve built a few canoes. They were usable? Yeah, I sold them. Wow. You’ve lived a lot of lives. I’ve done a bunch of different things. I think they all kind of fall into the creative sphere of it all. I wish I was good at music. I wish I could play a guitar or something. That’d be cool. Keen Ruffalo as Connor in Sterling Point. Courtesy of Prime Is there anything that people would be surprised to know about you? I feel like building boats is a pretty random one. I don’t know my months. That’s another one that I find weird. In what way? What do you mean? I know next month’s August because I keep being told that, and the show’s coming out next month. I don’t know what the next month after that is though. I don’t know what happened there, but something got lost in translation. The worst time management. I can also relate to time management, but at least you have a device with a calendar at your fingertips. At this point, I’m doing it out of the spite. I’m like, “It gets cold at one point and then it warms back up. That’s all.” That is very funny. Yeah, you are definitely the first person to tell me that. Maybe an elementary school kid won’t know their months, but 25 years old, doesn’t know his months. It’s pretty out there. How are you feeling with the release of Sterling Point and Nimrods and people seeing them? It’s definitely anxiety-inducing, I’d say. It’s hard because I’ve grown up seeing that a little bit. When I got older, I’d be able to go to premieres and stuff and see that. Both of my things are coming out within 10 days of each other. I’m getting my money’s worth out of my PR team right now, which I’m sure they appreciate. I’m excited and anxious. I hope that people can get what they need from these projects and that they enjoy it. So much of this job is balancing making the thing and going out there and telling people to see it. It sounds like you saw it at least a bit from a distance growing up. Have you figured out the balance? I feel like [my dad’s] a bad example for that. He’s a very polarizing person. ( Laughs .) I’d definitely say a lot of our cast is like, “We need to do what? I don’t have TikTok.” Do I almost just not make a TikTok at this point out of standing on business with that one? I already have a panic attack every time I open up Instagram. I’m like, “Oh God, do I have to post today?” We’ll see. It’s definitely a part of it, and at the end of the day, you get opportunities through doing press. I’m amazed that you guys, for example, reached out and wanted to have this meeting. I’m just very honored and feel lucky to be here. Keen Ruffalo attends the premiere for Sterling Point . Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Prime Video You’re coming to terms with that still then, I guess? Yeah. I’m like, “The other guy should be here not me.” Imposter syndrome. That’s pretty common for people in their 20s. I imagine it’s maybe a bit more when you are doing something that your father is quite famous for? Yes. There’s definitely been a lot of trying to navigate and cope around that. Obviously, I’m very proud of him and love my parents. I’m just trying to not disappoint them in the long term and stand on my own at the end of the day. What kind of roles are you into? Any audition that comes across, I usually do because I just enjoy it. But I love period pieces. I love dramas. I went to drama school, so give me something sad and depressing. I’ll eat that up. I guess also indie projects. I think it’s really important to do as many smaller productions as possible, especially just in this day and age where a lot of creatives aren’t getting that opportunity because they’re smaller. Any way I can use my platform to get something that I think needs the voice to get made, that’s kind of the end goal of all of this. I want to take European jobs from European actors. Put me in a medieval project. I’ll learn the accent. But I think movies are where my head’s at. Doing shows is great, but after doing a long show like this, I want to meet these different people. I want to be able to give a voice to many different people, not just Connor. Do you have any interest in the filmmaking part of it? Oh, boy. I think that there are a lot more people who deserve that more than me, who’ve put a lot more time into learning how to do that. Maybe someday I’d love to. I have a production company, and my entire thing is if I’m going to make a project, I’m going to do it with two known people and everyone else is unknown. People come and watch, and then people stay for the new faces. I’d want to do that, first of all. Then, maybe, who knows in future but definitely not right now. THR

articles.title: Jake T. Austin Says He Wasn’t Invited to Partake in ‘Wizards of Waverly Place’ Revival: “Disappointed”

Danny Feld / © Disney Channel / Courtesy: Everett Collection Original Wizards of Waverly Place star Jake T. articles.title: Dwayne Johnson Addresses ‘Moana’ Mixed Reviews After Film Underperformed at Box Office
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All August 7, 2026 7:38pm Dwayne Johnson in Disney's live-action 'Moana.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Dwayne Johnson is speaking out on Disney ‘s live-action Moana not exactly being a hit with critics. Johnson, who voiced Maui in the original 2016 animated film Moana and its 2024 follow-up, recently spoke to People magazine about how the movie’s early reviews started positively before the reception shifted. “Our first two reviews came out. I’ll never forget it… They were amazing. I was like, wow,” the actor recalled, before adding that then “it went another way — as sometimes happens. That’s just the way it goes because we’re in this business.” Related Stories General News Former Walt Disney Imagineering President Bob Weis Signs With WME for Representation Movies Disney Admits 'The Mandalorian and Grogu' Disappointed at Box Office The Hollywood Reporter’s chief film critic, David Rooney, did, however, give the film a favorable review, calling it “one of Disney’s better live-action remakes.” He added, “The new Moana is a captivating family entertainment that deserves to find an audience.” The live-action Moana, released in theaters last month, earned a 31 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, while its audience score was significantly higher at 88 percent. The Smashing Machine star added that he and his wife, Lauren Hashian, had many conversations about the response. “The challenge was, OK, let’s remember, though, what’s going to be beyond this opening weekend. Let’s remember what’s happening right now and the noise that’s happening right now,” he said. “If you love it, great. If you don’t, no problem,” the Jumanji actor said. But what meant the most to him was that “the culture really stood up,” as Johnson is of Samoan heritage. “Because of me and our kids who can now look at the big screen and go, ‘That’s us for the first time on a big screen. That’s us up there. How cool is that?’,” he said. Catherine Laga’aia starred in the title role , taking over from Auliʻi Cravalho, who voiced the character in the animated films. Johnson reprised his role as Maui in the live-action adaptation. The film, though, didn’t make waves at the box office, grossing $264 million worldwide against a reported $250 million production budget . THR

articles.title: Filmmaker Elham Ehsas Wants You to Know Afghanistan Sent a Man to Space in 1988
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 7, 2026 10:00pm 'Forgotten Spaceman' Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. In 1988, Afghanistan sent its first cosmonaut into space. Yes, really. Abdul Ahad Momand went where no Afghan had gone before — or has gone since — making Pashto the fourth language ever spoken beyond Earth. So why does barely anyone remember his name, his journey, or the hope it sparked among fellow Afghans at the time? Part of the answer may lie in timing: just as the spaceflight took place, Afghanistan was on the brink of civil war, a conflict that would soon force millions of its people into exile. As a new film argues, the country’s story has been shaped by conflict, exile and diaspora ever since, with science, culture and ideas pushed to the margins. Related Stories Movies Virginie Efira's Love for Cinema and Locarno Has No Limits -- Even If Her Mic Does Movies 'I Is Another' Review: Claes Bang Plays Himmler's Masseur in Weighty Meditation on a WWII Footnote Elham Ehsas ( There Will Come Soft Rains , Yellow , Our Kind of Love ), a London-based Afghan filmmaker and actor, is working to change that narrative and spotlight a piece of history too often left out of it. His short film Forgotten Spaceman — which blends documentary and essay elements while uncovering a surprising link between Afghanistan’s space history and his own family’s past — will world premiere on Aug. 9 in the Pardi di Domani – Concorso Internazionale program of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival . Ehsas wrote, directed and edited Forgotten Spaceman , which is executive produced by Catherine Tschaepe and Jack Thomas-O’Brien of Ken Loach’s Sixteen Films, which backed the film. World sales and festivals are being handled by María Vera of Kino Rebelde. Beyond the story of Afghanistan’s spaceman and Ehsas’ own family history, the short also examines “shadows of colonialism and the memory of a fractured and silenced nation,” per its synopsis. Ehsas spoke with THR about his surprise at discovering Momand’s story, how Forgotten Spaceman came together, and what he hopes audiences take away from it. Can you share a little bit about the journey behind Forgotten Spaceman ? I feel this film was almost a coming of age for me in terms of getting to know my own past and my country’s past. I was researching a short fiction film that I was trying to make around space. And then I came across Abdul Ahad Momand, and I was like, “Who is this guy? How is it possible that we have an Afghan cosmonaut who went to space?” He put Afghanistan on the map in 1988. When he called his mom, Pashto became the fourth language ever spoken in space. It’s Russian, English, Mandarin and Pashto. And it just blew my mind. So I went to my parents and spoke to my mom and dad, and I was like: “How did you guys not tell me about him?” And it’s interesting because I’ve spoken to a lot of my cousins and family members my age and asked, “Do you guys know we have a spaceman?” And they were all [reacting the same way]: “What? Come again?” So, almost at every turn, this was a teaching opportunity for my own cousins and friends as well. It was such a discovery. And I also learned a lot. Through this experience of listening, I learned about making a documentary because it’s my first documentary. I learned to just relinquish control and go where this story is taking me. Sometimes, letting go is one of the best things you can do. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. The film starts out as a story about the Afghan spaceman, but then it also connects to your family story, and then you zoom out to show us a universal story. Did you know from the start that Forgotten Spaceman would also touch on these bigger themes? This whole film was a complete accident. I was trying to make this fiction film about space and then found Momand. And then I realized that he’s a refugee out in Europe somewhere, so then my idea was that I’d make a documentary about me looking for him. I put in about four, five months of work, shooting different footage around London. When I found out that he’s in Stuttgart in Germany, I thought I’ll go to Germany and speak to him. And then several months into this whole process, my dad gave me a picture. “Oh yeah, I have this photo of Momand.” That completely blew the whole thing open for me. It was insane. I can’t believe we have this photo, and I can’t believe that this photo speaks so much of my own family and of my own relationship with Momand and space, but also all of us and our relationship to home, to our country, to Afghanistan. Do you want to talk more about the photo and what it shows, or is that too much of a spoiler? And what did you do? I pivoted because I felt something was happening here. I am being guided by this film, and this film wants to be something else. Because I come from a narrative background, I’m used to scripting, casting, shooting, crafting, and engineering this whole narrative. But here is a true story that kept evolving, and it kept changing, and I felt the best thing here was to surrender to what’s happening. Maybe the story isn’t about me looking for Momand. Maybe the story is about this photo. And what if I can build something around this one photograph? No spoilers, but for people who see it, they’ll realize why this picture is so important, and that gave me the architecture for the rest of the film. Parts of the film felt a bit like a detective movie to me. And it also felt like a journey of discovery where another layer is uncovered. We see some family footage but also official, I assume, TV footage from Afghanistan about the space trip. Where did you find all this footage? It’s so interesting that you speak about the detective element. I almost felt like a detective trying to find this footage, these different pieces of archive. It’s really hard to find pre-Soviet era archive footage around Afghanistan, especially around such a niche as the space program. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy pf Foreigner Ltd. I reached out to a bunch of official, independent archive houses, [Russian Space Agency] Roscosmos, as well as the Afghanistan archive in Kabul. Because my dad is a journalist, he still has his network in Afghanistan. So I was speaking to a bunch of really interesting people, and through that, we found all of this beautiful footage. But I wanted the texture of the footage to not just be about his flight, but also about the rest of Afghanistan, about the history of his country. So that meant I had to dig deeper into the Soviet invasion from ‘79 to ‘89. At one point, I licensed about six hours of random footage that I didn’t know what it was. I just knew it was coming from Afghanistan and from that part of history. An archive house said, “Look, the deal is we’ll give you this for an affordable price, but we don’t know what’s in it, so you have to just take a blind shot.” So I had all of this footage, and it really helped me get the whole thing together. So, yes, the whole thing is a discovery. You have big-name executive producers on the film, such as Ken Loach’s Sixteen Films… I’m incredibly lucky for this project to attract such incredible collaborators, including someone like Ken Loach and Sixteen Films. They are renowned for telling stories that aren’t often told, telling human stories from different times and from different social and historical backgrounds. One of the executive producers is Sixteen’s Jack Thomas-O’Brien, who worked on this amazing film On Falling [by Laura Carreira]. So I have had a bunch of collaborators that I was sending the film to and getting their thoughts. The story started in my bedroom, and it just started getting bigger and bigger with all of these collaborators. It’s all about the magic of the moment [of the Afghan space trip], but also space and what it tells us about home and ourselves. I’m very lucky for the film to have resonated with incredible collaborators who have come on board and championed us and supported us. It’s just an incredible privilege and honor. You mentioned how Forgotten Spaceman goes into what space tells us about Afghanistan and, actually, also the exile experience. Can you talk about that a little bit? When I started this film, I thought I was making a film about this really super cool guy called Momand, who was an Afghan spaceman. But as the film was evolving in front of my eyes, I realized that there’s this family connection, so it’s also about me and my family. But then you keep going, and you keep discovering, digging deeper and deeper, excavating. And then I realized that actually this film isn’t just about Momand, me and my family. It’s about all of us and all of those people who have left home and moved. It’s about migration, it’s about refugeeship, it’s about the loss of home and the things we leave behind. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ director Elham Ehsas Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Here is Momand, an astronaut who went up to space, took the Quran with him and spoke Pashto up there. And then he came plummeting back down, went into exile, lived in Germany and became an accountant. So, it’s also about what a country loses when its children go into exile. That also speaks to memory, history and this divide between the East and the West. The East has these incredible stories, this incredible history, but this fragile memory, while the West has a short memory. As an Afghan filmmaker, I thought it was almost my duty to bring this story to life. I need more people to learn about Momand, and I need more people to know that he was Afghan. We’re not just bullets and blood and violence. We’re more than that. The West has chosen to only show Afghanistan in a specific light, which speaks to a bias. My colleagues from the diaspora and I feel it’s our duty to tell these stories in different ways. The film mentions that Afghans’ and Afghanistan’s stories usually get told through violence, conflict and war… Yes, for most of my lifetime, Afghanistan has been defined in the world’s imagination by conflict, headlines of war, statistics of death. But that’s not the country that my parents grew up in, or my grandparents. And it’s not the whole story of the place. Afghanistan is a country of poets and scientists and filmmakers and history and art and music, as I’ve shown in the film as well. And it’s a country that sent a man into space in 1988. When you start pulling on that thread, you find the whole landscape of achievement and imagination that has been buried and the tragedy of the lost potential of those people who had no choice but to move. Is that also why Forgotten Spaceman features Afghan music? I was faced with this incredible, epic tale of this man, and then through that tale, I zoom out and talk about our country and migration and refugees. But how do I tell that story, especially in a short documentary, in the most succinct way? I love music, especially Afghan music. I grew up on it, especially old folk songs. So, I thought, what if I engineer the film like a music album? What if it’s built around three different songs for the three different acts of the story? And that’s where the inspiration for that came. I went down this deep rabbit hole of old Afghan music that I grew up listening to, but also discovering new songs and remembering which songs my mum or dad used to listen to when I was a kid. I found these three beautiful, beautiful songs, and the fourth one in the credits by an incredible artist called Zarsanga. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. Does the film’s original title Hershewe Fazanawerd mean exactly the same as the English title – Forgotten Spaceman ? It literally translates to the man who went to space, or the spaceman. But Afghanistan has two national languages: Pashto and Dari. I was mindful that my previous films had dialogue in Dari, and I never included Pashto, which is actually my mother tongue, and it’s the language that Momand spoke in space. So, I decided to do the voiceover in Pashto, almost as an ode to my mother tongue and to Momand. I heard that you are working on your first feature as a writer and director? Yes, it’s a feature film called Our Kind of Love, and it’s based on my first-ever short film. We’ve been working hard on developing it with the BFI, and we’re just coming out of the script stage. Making films is so hard, and telling stories is so hard. I think there is value in putting a lot of time into trying to get it right, especially when you want to speak about a specific theme. Our Kind of Love ultimately is about the East and the West meeting. The short film was about an Afghan woman who was on a first date with an Afghan man who was born here [in the U.K.], and she was born in Kabul. It’s about how, if you put the East and the West together in a room, they interact. I’m a first-generation refugee. I came from Afghanistan to this country, and so I juggle two identities, and I juggle two cultures and countries. That’s what really always informs my work. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. What’s next for Forgotten Spaceman ? We’re really excited that the film will premiere at the Locarno Film Festival , and then it is going to Toronto. I’ll be so curious being there for the first screening at Locarno to look at the audience and their reactions. It will be such a privilege for me to see them experience it. The film is how the legacy of Momand survives, and the legacy of these refugees who have done great things. Do you ever think that Forgotten Spaceman could be expanded into a feature-length film? Well, it’s such an epic story, and it’s such a beautiful story that speaks to so much. So, I’d be very curious to see and discover how it would look as a feature film. Is there anything else you’d like to highlight or mention? I want to also speak about my collaborators, the people I worked with on this film, and especially the music. My co-producer is Lorraine Bhattachary, and our composer CJ Mirra. Our sound designers are Rob Szeliga and John Cohen, who did such an incredible job because a lot of the film lives and dies in the sound. A lot of these experiences are so sonic, especially in space, and we wanted it to be something grand and beautiful. They all smashed it, and that’s what this film, and film in general, is about — collaboration. THR

articles.title: ‘Asphalt Guerrilla’ Blends Fact, Fiction, AI and a Story About Filmmaking to Hold Up a Mirror to Our Time
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 7, 2026 11:00pm 'Asphalt Guerrilla' Courtesy of Bando à Parte Real history, fiction and AI blend together for a look at a former radical far-left underground armed organization in Portugal in the new film from auteur Edgar Pêra ( Telepathic Letters , Manual of Evasion LX94 ), Asphalt Guerrilla ( Guerrilha no Asfalto ). The movie marks the Portuguese writer-director’s return to the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland, where it will world premiere in the Out of Competition program during its 79 th edition on Monday, Aug. 10. The militant group that the film revisits is the FP-25, short for Forças Populares 25 de Abril, or Popular Forces 25th of April, which was active between 1980 and 1987. It carried out dozens of bombings, shootings and bank robberies. The film is based on the eponymous book by Manuel Ricardo de Sousa, a member who ended up being lynched by a mob in the aftermath of a bank robbery. Related Stories Movies Denis Côté on Making 'Nobody's Violence,' His Assisted-Death Drama, While Fighting for His Own Life Music William Orbit, Grammy-Winning Producer for Madonna, Blur and Britney Spears, Dies at 69 But there is also a meta level to the movie. “It’s also about trying to make a film that ought to be shot in a guerrilla mode, with no compromises with the system,” notes the Locarno website. A synopsis teases the mind-bending quality of the movie by describing it as “a fictional film rooted in reality about a utopian time in Portuguese democracy.” And it continues: “Set in the early ’80s, it begins with a quiet student who becomes involved in a radical organization and ends up being shot and lynched by the mob in the aftermath of a bank robbery. Throughout the film, we witness the sometimes comical, sometimes tragic problems of these ‘asphalt guerrillas’ fighting against the system; at the same time, the director of the film quits the organization in order to fight to make films in a guerrilla mode.” ‘Asphalt Guerrilla,’ courtesy of Bando à Parte Pêra wrote the screenplay with Rodrigo Areias, and the voices of Pêra and Albano Jerónimo feature in Asphalt Guerrilla . Jorge Quintela is the cinematographer, while João Mora is the editor. The cast features Miguel Moreira, Maria Leite, Ivo Arroja, Jerónimo, Bernardo Santo Tirso and Luke Eberl. Pêra talked to THR about Asphalt Guerrilla , what inspired it and what it says about his latest take on the use of AI in filmmaking. “There are many films in this film,” Pêra highlights. “The very beginning was this book, which I read in the ’90s and basically shows a very amateurish group of guerrilla men or terrorists, depending on your point of view, but it gradually transforms into a film about my own guerrilla [film] scene, mainly because my friend and producer Rodrigo Areias made me do it.” Indeed, Pêra started making an underground name for himself in the mid-1980s with his avant-garde style as a “neuro-punk” filmmaker associated with DIY counterculture and the Portuguese music scene. “I would never pitch a film about me, including an autobiography, but I really understood that Rodrigo proposed it,” he tells THR . “I told him that I wanted the film to be about the future, not about the past, not about the ’80s and the problems we had back then in Portugal, but about this society and the state of cinema.” If you are watching the film and can’t quite tell which parts are real and which ones are fictional, Pêra won’t mind. “This fusion, or blur, of fiction and reality is something that I like, but it’s also something that I must fight against,” he explains. “So the film is also a mirror of what’s happening, where you sometimes don’t really know what’s real.” ‘Asphalt Guerrilla,’ courtesy of Bando à Parte Does he really feel like a film guerilla? “Actually, when I was in my 30s, there was this producer who called me the Sniper,” Pêra tells THR . “I think he said that with respect. I think I have that respect from other filmmakers of my country because I never tried to do anything that was not myself.” As the filmmaker did in his 2024 Locarno film Telepathic Letters ( Cartas Telepáticas ), Asphalt Guerrilla uses AI images. “I always try to leave some clues for what is AI-made,” he highlights. “But there are moments where, to show the danger of AI, you have to behave like a dangerous AI, which is why this film has moments [referencing] what worries me most, news becoming fabricated. And actually, the worst part is that AI also gets the most fun part of creating, such as [people] asking AI to write prompts.” Concludes Pêra: “So I try to fight all of that and create my own prompts and create my own algorithm. If you leave things to the YouTube algorithm, you know what you get.” Added the auteur: “You have to make at least a playlist so that you’re not invaded by this ultra commercial thing. That’s my fight inside of AI to create some images that are original in the way that they are recombinations of things that already exist. That’s what every artist does.” How does that fit into Pêra’s early neuro-punk days? “I was always interested in the effects of cinema on the minds of people and how the mind works,” he tells THR . “Neuro-punk was meant to say that we have to fight things with ideas, not with violence. So, cameras are weapons. Make films, not violence.” ‘Asphalt Guerrilla,’ courtesy of Bando à Parte The auteur didn’t necessarily know how timely his film would feel in a time full of wars, a rise in political and other radicalism and, of course, AI when he first started conceiving it. “I think it’s not a coincidence. It’s a synchronicity,” he offers. “But even when we think times are okay, we have lots of things that worry us. Now, we are in the worst of times, as they say. But even in the best of times, there’s still exploitation, people dying and all that. So yes, I think it’s a timely moment to go to the roots of the problems and not only focus on radicalism. I think radicalism is a symptom; it’s not the problem.” He sees the underlying issue this way: “Radicalism is a symptom of the decay of our system. I’m not an expert, but I feel that it’s not the radicalist we have to fight because that means [we are] becoming another radical. So that’s a trap. Instead, let’s talk about what makes our planet worse.” Pêra is working on another movie, which will keep speaking out about worries he has. It’s called The Spiral of Fear, and it’s about “big tech and what media says about the masters and all that.” THR

articles.title: No, Brian Eno Is Not Behind the Film Soundtrack for ‘At Night.’ Experimental Musician Elvin Brandhi Is.
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 8, 2026 2:40am 'At Night' In At Night , British filmmaker and artist Beatrice Gibson’s first feature-length film, the nightly sights and sounds of Paris interweave with the stories and conversations of six women – from hopes, dreams and sexual desires to worries about the future. Rhythm and mood are key elements that make the experimental and “autofictional” movie, which world-premieres on Saturday, Aug. 8, in the Filmmakers of the Present competition program of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival , a special kind of cinematic ride. Just ask Locarno’s artistic director, Giona A. Nazzaro. In a chat with THR , he described the movie as “this nocturnal, ambient film where you can almost hear music that makes you think of Brian Eno . If At Night were a record, it could be music for lonely people at night.” Related Stories Movies 'Asphalt Guerrilla' Blends Fact, Fiction, AI and a Story About Filmmaking to Hold Up a Mirror to Our Time Movies Filmmaker Elham Ehsas Wants You to Know Afghanistan Sent a Man to Space in 1988 Written and directed by Gibson, At Night features cinematography by her long-time collaborator Ben Rivers and editing by Liyo Gong. But the music doesn’t come courtesy of Brian Eno. No, it is the creation of Elvin Brandhi. If you don’t follow experimental music, here are some basics to know about her. Elvin Brandhi is the pseudonym of Freya Edmondes, an improvising voice and sound artist who was born in Wales, but has become a citizen of the world. Her music features unusual beats created from field recordings, her own voice, tape, vinyl and instruments. She is also part of all sorts of music collaborations, including father/daughter “noise-improv berserkers” Yeah You, Pollution Opera with Nadah El Shazly, the duo Avril Spleen with Joseph Jadam, the band PFL with Peter Kutin and Lukas König, and the project Bahk with Daniel Blumberg. At Night , which features an array of Gibson’s non-professional actor friends and influences as they discuss and explore such topics as sexuality, money, motherhood and mental health, is the musical artist’s first-ever feature film soundtrack. And it seems fitting that she collaborated with Gibson on this film that press notes call “a love letter to friendships, relationships, and the quiet yet poignant stories women share together but rarely to an audience.” Brandhi took time out of her busy schedule to talk to THR about the creation of the soundtrack for At Night , her other music work and whether we may be able to hear more from her on future cinematic journeys. The artist confirms that the work on At Night marks a new step for her. “It’s the first time I’ve done a soundtrack for a feature film,” she tells THR . “I did a couple of short films with friends, and I make my own music video-type thing. So I consider myself more of an audiovisual artist. I think in both realms, but this was obviously very different. I’ve worked with Daniel Blumberg a little bit, hanging out with him a lot in the process of The Brutalist and then the Anne Lee film, [ The Testament of Ann Lee ]. I was doing quite a lot of vocal stuff, also with [avant-garde improvisational vocalists] Phil Minton and Maggie Nicols. And Daniel has been creating this nice bridge between the experimental scene in London and Hollywood cinema.” ‘At Night,’ courtesy of Night Films Courtesy of Night Films Ltd. So, this must be a good time for Brandhi to get her first feature film soundtrack under her belt, you may wonder. “It was probably helpful for me to get involved in the experience of how to make a soundtrack,” she confirms, but notes that it required a different focus from her usual work. “It was quite a unique experience, and I had to adjust a little bit how I think about composing. A lot of my music is quite in your face and trying to be as present as possible. But with a soundtrack, you have to almost make it sneak in from the sides, or be somehow invisible, coming out of the background.” Given that Brandhi works a lot with field recordings, how did the Paris setting of At Night play to her passions? “What was really nice about this film was that the metro is such a big center of the narrative, and that’s already quite a noisy place,” she tells THR . “It has a lot of the kind of frequencies and ambient noise and things that I might feel like field recording and be inspired by anyway. So it was this perfect entry point for coming into that film world.” Gibson and Brandhi have all sorts of connections but made their acquaintance by coincidence. “I met Beatrice for the first time at [the experimental music festival] Borealis [in Bergen, Norway], but only very briefly,” the music artist recalls. “We were in the same taxi going somewhere, and I was playing, and she was screening something. I think she knew of my music, and then a common friend, Leonardo Ruvolo, from Alcamo in Sicily, put us in contact because I also did his residency, and she’s living in Palermo [in Sicily] now, so there were various coincidences.” And the women quickly got along. “When we started working together, we became very good friends immediately,” Brandhi shares. “And working on At Night was a very intimate and special process.” But what was this process like, and how early did Brandhi start crafting music for the film? “Beatrice wanted to have as much sound as possible before even starting to shoot. So I did get sent a first draft of the script, but that did get changed as the film went through different shifts,” she recalls. “We spent a week going through ideas before any shoot. I sent her some drafts of things that might work. And she had one reference of a song that she really liked, which was actually from a collaboration I have that is called Insin [with Palestinian producer/MC Bashar Suleiman]. The track is called ‘Kidney Spears,’ which is a little bit more dreamy. I’m also singing in that. So I tried to send her other things within that kind of dynamic.” When Gibson started shooting in Paris, Brandhi also came to the French capital. “I was taking some recordings when they were going into the metro,” the musician tells THR . “And there was originally even a scene of me performing in Paris in the film.” ‘At Night,’ courtesy of Night Films Courtesy of Night Films Ltd. All in all, the soundtrack came together in an ongoing collaboration. “There were some core themes that we developed, and then little bits that needed a very specific kind of mood or dynamic,” she says. The collaboration also included editor Liyo Gong. “She is really amazing,” says Brandhi. “She’s also a DJ, so she has a very strong sense of the musicality in film and in how she edits.” Crystabel Riley also contributed, drum sounds, to the soundtrack. “I asked her if she would contribute some drumming that I could weave into different parts of it,” Brandhi recalls. “She was actually involved in the film, doing some of the makeup, because she’s a makeup artist as well as a musician.” Fans of the artist’s work may get to hear more from her in feature movies in the future. “I definitely would like to,” Brandhi tells THR . “I would be really up for it; it was really interesting entering the story and composing from a different perspective.” She adds: “I saw her playing live for the first time last year, and I was just so blown away because she’s such an incredible performer, and her stage energy is so engaging. There’s this warmth and tension as well. It feels very urgent. I was just watching her and felt the state of mind of the women in the film echoing in her performance.” Concludes Brandhi: “It was really special for me and Bea that she was part of it.” The creative mentions that she has also worked with video herself, and being involved with At Night inspired her to return to more of it. “In the lockdown, I did a lot more filming and editing stuff, so I feel that this soundtrack world is also a nice potential way to get back into the editing of my own film material,” she shares. Not that Brandhi doesn’t have all sorts of music stuff in the works. Including an album with Berlin-based Kenyan musician KMRU under their name A|||oy, which will be released on KMRU’s label offnot. “He is associated a bit more with ambient music. But we have so much in common and are both fans of each other’s music, even though it might seem like we have quite contrasting dynamics,” she tells THR . “There’s a strong similarity in the way we work with field recordings and sounds, textures and spaces.” Concludes Brandhi: “We’ve been collaborating for three years now, and we have an album coming out that we made between a couple of residencies, one at [Swedish electroacoustic music and sound art center] EMS in Stockholm, and then one in [Max Richter and his partner Yulia Mahr’s] Richter Mahr studio in Oxfordshire. We just listened to the test pressing, and it was really exciting. We’re both singing, and it’s completely different from both of our works.” THR

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo Debuts ‘Pretty Sad’ Songs at Sweltering Brooklyn Surprise Show: Concert Review
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 2:28pm PT Olivia Rodrigo Debuts ‘Pretty Sad’ Songs at Sweltering Brooklyn Surprise Show: Concert Review By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Olivia Rodrigo Debuts ‘Pretty Sad’ Songs at Sweltering Brooklyn Surprise Show: Concert Review 11 hours ago Peter Katsis, Veteran Manager for Backstreet Boys, Korn, Jane’s Addiction and More, Dies at 69 1 day ago Music Industry Moves: Alicia Keys Signs With CAA in All Areas; SONA’s Emerging Songwriter Award Nominations Now Open 2 days ago See All (Photo by Xavi Torrent/Getty Images) The announcement dropped on a pulverizingly humid Thursday afternoon in New York City: just a few hours later, an Olivia Rodrigo surprise gig would take place at Brooklyn’s intimate, 1,100-capacity venue Warsaw. The expected mad dash for tickets — only available at the venue’s box office — ensued, with fans lining up in heat that was technically 91 degrees but with a “real feel” of 105. But of course, the venue was packed long before the 8 p.m. showtime, even though it was just as hot inside. Related Stories Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Rodrigo, clad in a red flowered schoolgirl dress and black go-go boots, dove in at the deep end, starting the set ambitiously with the album’s first single, “Drop Dead” — a challenging song to sing, with its upper-register chorus that offers few opportunities to take a breath — but she pulled it off with ease. “We’re going to be playing a lot of songs from my new album for this first time,” she said, and promptly obliged with three more tracks from “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” concluding with the Wet Leg-esque “My Way.” Popular on Variety Her five-piece band was razor-sharp — they’ve played a number of concerts this year, from the Primavera Festival in Spain and “Saturday Night Live” to a surprise cameo with the Smashing Pumpkins at Lollapalooza last weekend — but apart from an “Austin City Limits” taping last weekend, this was indeed the first time most of the eight new songs have been performed for a concert audience. Olivia Rodrigo performs “Expectations” at an intimate one-night-only show in Brooklyn pic.twitter.com/HQk0jOlimU — Variety (@Variety) August 7, 2026 After the opening blast, Rodrigo then sat at the keyboard for a brace of ballads from her previous albums, including “Drivers License,” before rolling out four more new songs — including the fan favorites “Maggots for Brains” and “The Cure,” the latter of which she said is “probably” her favorite song from the album, as well as an emotional debut performance of “Less Than” — before finishing off the set with “Good 4 U” and “Déjà Vu.” Throughout the set, she was her usual effervescent self, bouncing, spinning, holding out her arms, pumping her fists and leading the audience in several singalongs — and not a word about her latest altercation with the president . The “Pretty Sad” songs were note-perfect, but new material always takes a few gigs to break in and it’s likely they’ll be looser as time goes on. Likewise, a few older songs will probably be added to the setlist before they begin touring in earnest, beginning with Rodrigo’s own Daisy Chain Fields festival in Southern California at the end of this month, and the months-long “Unraveled” tour, which launches on Sept. 25. articles.title: Judy Collins on Doing a Farewell Tour While ‘Having a Lot More Steam in My Engine’: At 87, ‘I’m the Betty White of the Folk Movement’
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 3:42pm PT Judy Collins on Doing a Farewell Tour While ‘Having a Lot More Steam in My Engine’: At 87, ‘I’m the Betty White of the Folk Movement’ Collins performs Friday night at the Ford in Hollywood as part of her "Sweet Judy Blue Eyes' tour, co-joined by Bruce Cockburn. By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Judy Collins on Doing a Farewell Tour While ‘Having a Lot More Steam in My Engine’: At 87, ‘I’m the Betty White of the Folk Movement’ 10 hours ago Phoebe Bridgers Will Unveil ‘Lost Weekend’ Album in Planetariums in More Than 30 Cities 2 days ago Sienna Spiro on Writing Candidly as a Young Woman, While Being Frank About Adoring Sinatra and Twiggy: ‘Being 20 Is Just Tricky, Period’ 3 days ago See All Courtesy Image How sweet — or suite — it still is. Judy Collins is doing a valedictory lap or two around the country on what is billed as a farewell tour, even though, at 87, she’s showing little in the way of weariness about maintaining a full concert schedule or lack of prowess in pulling these shows off. “It’s time” is the fullest explanation she’ll give about why it might be time to think about slowing down her schedule. In the meantime, there is a long way to go on her “Sweet Judy Blue Eyes Farewell Tour 2026-2027,” named for the song pal Stephen Stills wrote to celebrate her almost six decades go.
