Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale If she thought she’d looked at clouds from multiple angles when she had a top 10 hit with the Joni Mitchell-penned “Both Sides, Now” in 1968, imagine how many more cloud sightings she’s had in her career since then. She changes her sets nightly, but ticketholders for the tour are likely to get a sampling of her most well-known covers — like Stephen Sondheim’s “Send in the Clowns,” Leonard Cohen’s “Suzanne” and the hymn “Amazing Grace” — as well as her self-penned material, as highlighted in her most recent studio release, 2022’s “Spellbound.” Whichever songs she picks, fans won’t likely regret a chance to see her for what may or may not be a local last time. In L.A., she headlines the Ford on Friday night, joined by a fellow monster of folk-rock, Bruce Cockburn. (Openers on some of the other tour dates include such big-name acolytes as Richard Thompson, Amanda Shires, Rosanne Cash and Mary Chapin Carpenter.) Popular on Variety Variety caught up with Collins via Zoom from her New York home as she prepared to fly out for the tour’s west coast swing. Your official farewell tour kicked off July 4, but looking back, you already had had a really busy year. It looks like you’ve done over 35 shows so far in this calendar year, and you’re just getting started. Yeah, we usually do 100 a year, so that’s good. You haven’t yet put an end date on your farewell tour. Does it really feel like this is farewell, or is there some ambiguity as far as how long you might keep going? No, it is a farewell tour. You know, I’ve been doing this for 67 years. I don’t know if anybody took note of that. But I think I’ve done a farewell tour later than most people do. I don’t know anybody to compare it with. But I think a lot of bands and a lot of organizations and groups have done farewell tours, and I think it was appropriate for me to do mine now. And why so? As you said, you’re doing it further along in years than a lot of people who have officially done a last tour. But you have also frequently talked about how you actually enjoy touring. Oh, I do. I love it. But I have a lot of other things in my life that I have to deal with, which is writing a couple of new books, and I have a commitment with a Broadway (producer) with a stage show that I’ve written all the music for. So there are other things, of course, that have to be dealt with. And, it’s time. It feels like you are… I don’t want to say wholly unique, but somewhat unique among performers, in loving being on the road so much. We talk to so many performers who say, “I love the two hours on stage. It’s the other 22 that I can’t deal with.” Yet you’ve said you enjoy the part of touring that other people hate, which is transit of getting from one place to another. I love touring. I love it. And this has something to do with first experiencing being on the road with your father? When I was a little girl, my father was a great entertainer, and it was through him I found my reason to have a career and be doing what I wanna do. He had a a radio career for 30 years, and he also toured at the end of the war. I first was on the road with him when I was a little girl. I was 3, and he was touring with National School Assemblies, and we were up in Butte, Montana when I had my first time on stage. He said, “You want to sing for these nice people?” And I sang “I’ll Be Home for Christmas.” It’s the one I knew. It was April. He said, “Do you want to sing for the people?” And, “do you want to ride in the car?” I said, “I want to do both.” And I love traveling. I love living in New York, but I also get to travel all over. The other day we were with the High Kings, and we were in Duluth, and we had a big show at this huge, wonderful place in the woods [the Big Top Chautauqua]. I was there with Don McLean years ago, and he called me up because he saw that I was gonna be there, and he was reminding me of our show at that wonderful venue. And we were driving in the most beautiful area in Wisconsin, near Lake Superior. I get to see all these places. And I get to ride in planes; I don’t mind planes at all — I love planes. But also we get to drive, and I get to see every tree that’s ever been considered to plant somewhere. I love it. Do I know what they all are? No, because I’m not a botanist. But I love everything that grows. You know, Saturday night I got home, and I raced around and watered all my plants. So your father was a role model for being in show business? I do a lot of things that he did. I tell a lot of jokes. I want to make people laugh. I grew up on the wonderful entertainers who always told jokes. You know, we were babies of that culture. And also, you know, I’m the Betty White of the folk movement. Like Betty White, just in terms of endurance and still being around and enjoying it? Sure. I mean, she certainly kicked off pretty late. And I have a lot more steam… a lot more juice in my engine, I’ll tell you that. Judy Collins Shervin Lainez You’re not bidding farewell because your voice is gone. Everyone still loves to hear you sing. Sometimes we have to wonder if a lot of it is just genetics — that Tony Bennett can sing well into his 90s, and you are doing great well into your 80s, but other people start having voice problems when they hit 70 or even 60. Yeah. Well, the voice is a very tricky thing, and it’s a superb instrument if you can keep it with you. If you can’t… I’ve had my issues with my voice, and I had incredible, unbelievable fortune. First of all, I was given a gift from two people in New York. One was the great teacher who taught me how to sing. By good fortune, I found Max Martley, who was an incredibly gifted teacher, and he taught a lot of people and taught me for 32 years, and I learned what to do. But also, I was an alcoholic. I am an alcoholic but I was drinking for about 20 years. And when I hit 1977, I suddenly couldn’t sing anymore, and I canceled many shows. But then I was lucky because the doctor I was seeing, an ENT doctor named Donald Wiseman, was a genius. And there was no cure for what I had. I had a what’s called hemangioma. People who drink for years get these on their faces, and I was a heavy drinker, but I didn’t get mine on my face — I got it on my vocal cord. It would have stopped me completely forever, and there was no cure at the moment. So Don Wiseman kept at it. He kept saying, “You’re not gonna be singing anyway, so let’s try this.” And it was a process that he did on the vocal cord, and it was removed. I don’t know how miracles happen — I mean, I’m not supposed to be in charge of those — but I got one. And from then on, I went straight back to a clean vocal cord that has been working perfectly ever since. And of course, I know what to do. I mean, I know from Max that I have to remember clarity and phrasing — two things that are my watch words. And so it’s not a mystery really, but it is in terms of technique, because I know exactly what to do, and I also have this clean vocal cord to work with. So I think that what I was given was a gift from the higher power, from whatever, and of course, I immediately… Well, within the next few months, I also stopped drinking, and I’ve been sober for 48 years, which doesn’t hurt. So you got a second chance at life, or your career, in the ’70s… Well, I got another life because I not only stopped drinking, but also, about four days before I went into treatment, I met the man that I was to be living with and married to [Louis Nelson]. We were together for 46 years, and I lost him. Well, I didn’t “lose” him. He died at the end of 2024. So I have gone through this widowhood and the difficulties that come with it. It’s painful, it’s heartbreaking, it’s everything you could think of. But on the other hand, I had all those years. He was an amazing man. He did not have to live in your shadow, with such prominent accomplishments. Among other things, he designed the [mural for the] Korean War Veterans Memorial on the Mall in Washington, D.C., and that’s been very much a part of our lives, too. All of the wonderful people that he was working with, and our trips to D.C., and our engagement with the generals, and all the Koreans, and the people who made it such an extraordinary gift not just to the Koreans, but to us, the Americans. So he was splendid and brilliant and wonderful and all of those things. And I lucked out, that I got to spend all those years with him. For an old hippie like me, I think it’s pretty good luck. Quite a confluence of events, between meeting him and getting your voice repaired… And getting sober. It happened all at the same time, which I think is extraordinary. And I know people that have lost their voices in similar situations to mine. So it is the luck of the draw — I love that old song. The title of this tour is “Sweet Judy Blue Eyes,” a la the Crosby, Stills and Nash song inspired by you, but spelled without the “suite” pun. I think I faintly recall that you might have been mildly embarrassed by Stephen Stills’ song when it came out. But you embraced it enough to make it a tour title this time around. Oh, I wasn’t embarrassed. I mean, that was the greatest compliment he could have given me, and we have been friends ever since. We’ve been friends for close to 60 years, and we still talk, and we still get together. We did a fabulous tour in 2017 and ’18, where we did 115 shows in a year and a half. We just had a ball. We were on the stage for two hours a night together. Each of us had one song that we sang (solo), but everything else was together. He is one of the great guitarists of all time, and playing in that environment with him was such a privilege. I don’t know that he’ll go out again. I don’t know. I see him from time to time. I saw him a couple weeks ago in L.A., and we had a wonderful morning together with his wonderful wife, Kristen, and we always have a lot to say to each other. He came out in March of last year, after Lewis had died, and was on a show that I did at the Town Hall here with a lot of other artists who sang songs either that I’d recorded or that I’d written. And at the end, he came on. We did “Helplessly Hoping,” and then he said, “She married the right guy.” Because he and Lewis were good friends. You change your setlist around a lot, from night to night. But people are generally likely to hear at least one song from your last album, “Spellbound,” which was the first album where you wrote every song on it. So it’s a lot of repertoire to draw upon. Yeah. I like to keep it fresh, for me, but also for the audience, to reach into songs that I haven’t done for a while. And I have a lot. You know, I didn’t start writing songs until I met Leonard Cohen in 1966. And of course, I recorded “Suzanne” immediately. Then he said to me, “I don’t know why you’re not writing your own songs.” So I started. I wrote a song called “Since You Asked,” and I’ve been writing ever since. A couple years ago I came out with a poetry book called “Sometimes It’s Heaven.” And the reason was that my husband had dared me to write every day, in 2017. I had said, “Well, now it’s a new year. I’ll start a new notebook…” And he said, “Why don’t you write 365 songs or pieces of songs, and then you’ll have a whole book of poetry,” which I did. It came out a year and a half ago. And I harvested all of “Spellbound” from all of that writing. I should have called it “365 Days,” but I didn’t. You must imagine Leonard Cohen would have been proud? Oh, yes. Oh, he would be so happy. You know, he was sort of like having an angel on your side. We were friends for a long time. He used to call me and read me verses of “Hallelujah” — he wrote about 40 — and he would say, “Do you like it?” And I said, “Well, it’s not me that is gonna have to like it. You’re gonna have to like it.” He finally narrowed it down, but it wasn’t easy. Is there any song you’re most proud of adding to our musical vocabulary? Well, I’ve written a lot of songs that people seem to like to sing. I just found out that one of the young rock and rollers in the ’80s recorded “My Father.” I went to the doctor this morning, and my doctor’s nurse is a fiend about collecting and listening to rock bands, and she found this rock band —. I don’t remember the name — who recorded “My Father” in the ’80s, and I was so happy to hear about that. [The version of “My Father” referred to was likely This Mortal Coil’s.] Sometimes you’ve done Dylan’s “Masters of War” in concert, although not lately. which You’ve said you’re a big fan of Heather Cox Richardson and people like that. Do you feel political at this moment in time? Oh, gosh. I don’t know what to do about it all the time, but I do. And yeah, Heather Cox Richardson is my favorite. I met her with Lewis, my husband, and they just went nuts. We went out to a big event with my brother Mike, who died five days after Lewis did. My brother had had a terrible, cancer of the mouth for five years. It’s a horrible disease. But we happened to have met Heather Cox Richardson in Illinois somewhere, and it was a good meeting and such a good time that we had with her. So, yeah, I think she’s wonderful. I told her, “I’m trying to be a Lincoln Republican” — trying to follow her, course. You know, I think we all do what we can. I have something in my hip pocket, though, that I do almost every night. I have had two dozen roses in a vase under the piano for decades now. They never go anywhere; they just sit there. And starting this past Jan. 1, I was in England, there they were, the flowers. So when we finished singing “Amazing Grace,” I took the flowers out of the vase, and I started singing “Where Have All the Flowers Gone?” and I distributed the flowers to the audience. It has continued to be a very wonderful moment. And it is my political statement of the night, and it works wonders. Going back to this being a farewell tour, you mentioned at some point that there may be some kind of “encore” shows after the tour ends… Well, I don’t know about that. I just know that I’m on a farewell tour, and I like being here. And billing it as such helps people to know, “OK, take advantage of this while you can. “ Well, that’s true. articles.title: ‘One Night Only’ Director Will Gluck Cut Out ‘So Much Nudity’ Because People Dislike Sex on Screen: ‘It Takes You Out of the Movie’
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 4:00pm PT ‘One Night Only’ Director Will Gluck Cut Out ‘So Much Nudity’ Because People Dislike Sex on Screen: ‘It Takes You Out of the Movie’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest ‘One Night Only’ Director Will Gluck Cut Out ‘So Much Nudity’ Because People Dislike Sex on Screen: ‘It Takes You Out of the Movie’ 10 hours ago ‘The Odyssey’ Surpasses $1 Billion, Christopher Nolan’s First Movie Since ‘Dark Knight Rises’ to Reach Coveted Box Office Milestone 16 hours ago Natalie Portman, Jenna Ortega Satire ‘The Gallerist’ Lands at Roadside, Vertical 18 hours ago See All ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection “ One Night Only ” director Will Gluck doesn’t want you to overthink it. The filmmaker has been fielding a lot of inquiries about the premise, logic and loopholes of his new movie, a raucous romantic comedy about the one night a year where premarital sex is legal. (Think “The Purge,” but for banging instead of murder.) Monica Barbaro (“A Complete Unknown”) plays Allie, an aspiring singer who channels her talent through embarrassing jingles in drug commercials. Callum Turner (“Eternity”) portrays Owen, a pizza shop owner whose long-term girlfriend decides she wants to sleep with other people on this holy night. The two strangers keep running into each other during 12 hours of messy mayhem in New York City. Related Stories Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Gluck is aware the movie’s setup is sparking more questions — Why does the ban exist in the first place? What happens to people who break the law? How, exactly, is the government even tracking who’s getting it on? — than answers. But he maintains the particulars of this reality aren’t really the point. Popular on Variety “You can’t really describe this movie,” Gluck says. “[The cast] goes on talk shows and spends 80% of the time explaining the rules of the world, and that’s not what the movie is about. We have to just let people see it. That’s the best tool we have, especially for something that’s this crazy.” Gluck, best known for directing 2010s teen classic “Easy A” with Emma Stone, knows all that matters is that people are talking about the film in the first place. Word-of-mouth fueled the success of his last rom-com, 2023’s box office sleeper hit “Anyone But You,” starring Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell. “I learned from my last movie that people are going to discover this and say, ‘Wow, that’s not what I thought it was going to be,’” Gluck says. “You know how the acronym for word-of-mouth is WOM? I’m calling it a WOM-com.” Ahead of opening weekend, the director spoke to Variety about why audiences have become prudish about on-screen sex, his love of putting “cringe” songs in his movies, and why the theatrical rom-com isn’t dead, after all. How did you decide how much backstory to include to set up your premise? I did a lot of thinking about it, a lot of world building. These characters are living this little alternative world that could easily happen. We have to talk about it. But I really wanted the world to live in the background. I didn’t want the movie to be about that. It’s more about how our characters navigate life. What conversations did you have about the origin of the no-sex mandate? Someone asked me “why don’t people just get divorced?” Well, there’s municipal signage very prominently in the movie that says you cannot get divorced unless you were married for one year, plus one day. It’s like when COVID [started], there were rules, and then people started to do other stuff, so then more rules came out, right? That’s what I imagine when this mandate was passed. They had to keep doing amendments to these rules because, yes, the obvious idea would be just get married and divorce. Recent studies have found that Gen Z and Gen Alpha don’t want to see sex on screen . Was that a concern while making this movie? The answer is 100% yes. I went through this on two movies. I have long pages of empirical data about it. The only thing is I don’t think it’s just Gen Z and Gen Alpha. I believe it’s been a societal shift from taking nudity in adult situations and putting them on your phones at home for everybody. Now it’s more of a private, intimate thing that people don’t want to see when they’re in a shared experience. Whenever people now see nudity or very adult situations in a big theater, they get uncomfortable. How does that change your approach as a filmmaker? Once I’ve learned that, which was all through the editing process for my last movie, I applied it to this movie. But even so, I didn’t apply it enough. I cut out so much. There was so much nudity in this movie that we shot on the streets. I felt we needed to show the world that way. As we started to show it to audiences, we felt it takes you out of the movie. You’re engaged in the characters and what’s going on, and then you pan over and there’s two naked people having sex, and you watch the audience … it’s a physical thing. They turn to who they’re with and … the benefits do not nearly outweigh the negatives of it. So we just kept editing it out until we got a balance, and those comments went away. Did you use an intimacy coordinator? So many scenes had extras having sex in the background. Yes, we had an incredible intimacy coordinator. And we cast real-life couples in various stages of relationships. It was never like we met an extra and were like, “you guys are kissing.” It was fun because there were married couples, people who broke up during the movie and people who became couples so they could do that. There are a lot of fun and funny posters and advertisements about “the mandate” and “one night” all around the city. Were those actual props, or were they edited in later? This is all practical. That was the fun part of the world building. We had a huge document with every scene, not only what signage was there, but what graffiti was there and who would be in the background kissing. And the funny thing about the products, I’ve gotta stop reading the internet, but everyone says, “It’s a product placement fiasco. How much money did they make on that?” It was the opposite. We had to beg products to allow us to take them and twist it to the “one night.” Because, as you can imagine, not every corporate America consumer product was into this idea. So when I read stuff, like, “How much money did they get from Dunkin or Durex?” I’m like “Nothing!” So you had to get permission to make the fake ads? Of course. You can photograph anything that’s in the real world, but you can’t take something like Coke ad and say “there’s dirt in it.” We had a big list and it was “no, no, no, no.” And then we were surprised — well, the condom companies didn’t surprise us that they said yes — but Duolingo sure did. That was a shock. I was like, “Really?” So that’s why you have products like Duolingo, Red Bull, Dunkin and Equinox. Every time they would say “yes,” I’m like, “They did?” And then they would have to approve our take on it. What are some of the challenges of filming in New York City? Many times, we had actors in a car, half naked, and you’d have people just walking and staring. We’d say, “Hey, do you mind moving on?” A couple of people said, “No, we’re not going to move.” We were like, “Well, if this really did happen in real life, people would be staring.” So there are a couple scenes where people are looking in the windows. How much of Monica’s character was built around her actually being able to sing? I always rewrite the script completely once I have the actors. Once I cast Monica, I was like, “She has to be a singer.” We talked for a long time, and she does have some stage fright, which is crazy, because she has the best voice. So I just wrote that for her. And I’ve always been obsessed with drug commercials, so it was this great confluence. Did Callum actually learn how to make pizza? Yes, he spent five days at that pizza place being taught how to make pizza. He was really good at it. The one bummer about pizza is it doesn’t look great on film. It’s impossible because pizza gets cold so quickly. During that scene, we were constantly putting out a new fresh pizza. That’s a lesson for me. From now on, I’ll choose a different food that does not congeal that quickly. How quickly did everyone get sick of pizza? You can tell during that scene but Monica and Callum, they ate. They didn’t chew and spit. Because I don’t cut. I just keep rolling. They were both at the end like, “Oh my god.” Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell, your stars from “Anyone But You,” don’t exactly have cameos, but they pop up in funny, unexpected ways. Did you get their permission to include them in the movie? Yes, I did. They were both trying to do cameos, but their schedules didn’t work out. So this was great. Music plays a big part in many of your films. I can’t hear “Pocket Full of Sunshine” without thinking of “Easy A,” and “Unwritten” went viral on TikTok after the release of “Anyone But You.” How do you choose which songs to feature? For the drug commercials, I have a pretty good take on songs that were really popular that people think they hate, but they can’t stop singing. I’m kind of obsessed with those songs, and a lot of my movies have them in it. You’ve mentioned some of them, and I think it’s because people don’t want to admit they like popular music, so they call it cringe or lame. But they’re bangers. After my last movie, if you ever go to any bar or club all over the world, when “Unwritten” comes on, it’s like the biggest banger in the world. It always was, but now for some reason, it’s now OK to be a banger. I love those songs. People often say the theatrical rom-com is dead. What were your takeaways from the box office success of “Anyone But You”? If you’re not a superhero movie or gigantic IP, it’s really hard to cut through. The only way you really can cut through, if at all, is letting the audience do it. No matter how much you market it or tell people what it is, you have to let them see it and tell their friends and family about it, which is scary. If you’re spending all this money on something, you can’t just hope people talk about it. But the key is telling people it’s going to be in theaters for a while. And I think this one is going to be in theaters for a while. articles.title: ‘The Last House’ Ending Breakdown: Why Is the Family Trapped Inside Their Home?
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 5:00pm PT ‘The Last House’ Ending Breakdown: Why Is the Family Trapped Inside Their Home? By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest Dwayne Johnson Defends ‘Moana’ After Bad Reviews: ‘Just the Way It Goes’ 12 hours ago ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ Director on Their Kinky Rom-Com and Soundtracking the Year’s Bloodiest Scene to Counting Crows 15 hours ago ‘Bridgette Wrona and the Whisper Creek Murders’ Wraps From Little Spark Films; YA Mystery Follows Podcaster Hunting a Serial Killer (EXCLUSIVE) 17 hours ago See All Courtesy Netflix SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “ The Last House ,” out now on Netflix. “The Last House” is a new sci-fi feature that just dropped on Netflix that’s built around a central mystery: What if you and all of your neighbors were locked inside your houses with no option for escape and had no idea why? That’s what Ann (Greta Lee) and Jason (Wagner Moura), along with their two kids, Graham and Ruth (Noah Alexander Sosnowski and Riley Chung), face in this new dystopian tale from screenwriter Matthew Robinson and veteran blockbuster director Louis Leterrier (“Fast X,” “The Incredible Hulk”). Related Stories Samara Weaving to Play Emma Frost in Marvel's 'X-Men' Reboot 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day': Sadie Sink Is [SPOILER]. How Her Role Sets Up Marvel's Next Reboot The film starts on an unexpectedly rainy day, when the family realizes they’re sealed into their house with no way of opening or smashing through the doors or windows. Any attempt is thwarted by a seal seemingly made of rainwater. Popular on Variety Thanks to a well-stocked pantry, the family is able to survive handily as weeks crawl by. Christmas comes and goes, and at points the crew is happy to live the simple life together. But things grow more tense, especially as neighbors that are also sealed in struggle to survive. Although the film doles out answers, there is some economical hand-waving about why the neighborhood has power and running water for so long. And also there’s literally a Chekhov’s Gun, but more on that later. Things hit a tipping point when a neighbor who had been out jogging when everything was sealed runs up to the family’s windows and starts pounding, screaming things “Everyone is dead,” “Don’t let them see you!” and “They’re here, and no help is coming!” She also looks crazed and is carrying a big butcher knife, but is pulled away by wet-looking tentacles which burn bright after they capture the jogger. Things get increasingly bleak, as the family dog’s heart medicine runs out and Jason has to put him out of his misery, and then — in doomsday prepper mode — carves up the body and puts it in the freezer just in case food gets dire. As time goes by, rainfalls grow more sinister, as big monsters claw against the windows if they spot anybody inside, forcing the family to quickly close the curtains. Meanwhile the family is growing increasingly hungry and grumpy with each other, as food runs low with no new signs of escape. But just when it seems like all is lost, Jason comes up with an idea of how to trap animals outside and drag them through the open chimney, while Ann removes the flooring to turn the house into a garden. Unfortunately, the power finally goes out. We jump ahead five years and the house is a full-on farm. The kids are now older and played by different actors (Emma Ho and Gabriel Barbosa). The neighborhood is overgrown, looking like a full-blown forest. While there is plenty of food, everyone looks pretty depressed. Meanwhile, the soil surrounding the house is eroding and the structure is sinking. One day during a big rain, a creature uses water powers to open the door to the house. The family hides from the beast, which looks like a mix between a Cthulhu, an octopus and a big, beefy guy. Beyond causing distress, it appears as if some fluid dripping off the creature instantly deep freezes anything it touches. The alien leaves before it can do much damage, but when it departs the family is still trapped inside. Ruth accidentally tastes saltwater coming from one of the beasts, and they realize that all of the plants and drinking water were poisoned by said saltwater. It also solidifies a theory that perhaps the beasts come from the darkest depths of the sea, instead of the stars. Ruth gets bitten by a ferret that accidentally gets stuck in their food trap, which makes her sick and in need of antibiotics. Jason freaks out and tries to ram his car through the garage door, but it knocks him out and exposes some deeper cracks in the house’s foundation. He then lifts some tile out of the bathroom and realizes it opens up into the sewer drain, which connects the whole neighborhood — including the house of their dentist neighbor who has antibiotics. Ann has to go down into the sewer as she’s small enough to fit, and makes it to the dentist’s house. The inhabitants are long dead, and she grabs the antibiotics, but she’s chased out by a monster, who then realizes that there are humans in their house. The family then works to booby-trap the house “Home Alone”-style, confident that if they can defeat incoming aliens, they can escape out the doors that were opened in the process. The rain starts up again, paired with some nasty-looking cyclones. Water starts rapidly flooding the house, with a creature swimming through, clearly adept at moving underwater as had been predicted. Frantic skirmishes between the family and the beast take place as the house floods, and eventually the invading creature is tangled up in a trap. Jason frees it, hoping it will show the same mercy to them, and it does, letting them into the wilderness. They’re initially surrounded by more creatures, but the beast they helped shooed them away. Their house disintegrates and falls into the ground, and then Ruth — whose kindness to animals ultimately saved them, as it encouraged her father to free that beast — runs to the shoreline. It’s clear that Seattle is now underwater, given that the Space Needle is nearly fully submerged, but the family starts laughing as they go to grab their fishing gear and sail across the now elevated water. The movie ends with Ruth’s narration: “We never saw them again, but we think they’re still out there. After all, it’s their home too.” They finally ask over their boat’s radio if there are any survivors, and get an inquisitive “Hello?” back as the credits roll. Watch the trailer below. articles.title: Stanley Tucci on Why His Emmy-Nominated ‘Tucci In Italy’ Is Moving to the United Kingdom Next Season
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 5:41pm PT Stanley Tucci on Why His Emmy-Nominated ‘Tucci In Italy’ Is Moving to the United Kingdom Next Season Awards Circuit Podcast: Also on this episode, how 'Widow's Bay' continues to gain momentum — impacting the comedy race. By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Variety Editor at Large franklinavenue Latest Stanley Tucci on Why His Emmy-Nominated ‘Tucci In Italy’ Is Moving to the United Kingdom Next Season 9 hours ago ‘Baywatch’ Honors Hero 16-Year-Old Lifeguard Ryder Williams During Set Visit (EXCLUSIVE) 14 hours ago ‘Ted Lasso’ Stars on How Women’s Sports Was the Perfect Storyline to Bring Back the Hit Apple TV Show for Season 4 16 hours ago See All Getty Images Italy remains Stanley Tucci ‘s first love. But a man can travel, right? After winning three Emmys for CNN’s “Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy,” followed by two nominations (including this year) for Nat Geo’s “ Tucci in Italy ,” the star is on the move. Tucci tells Variety ‘s Awards Circuit Podcast that he’s currently filming his new season in the United Kingdom, where he lives full time. “I wanted to do the U.K. because I just feel like there’s so much here,” he says. “I’ve been here for almost 15 years now, and London was just voted the best food destination in the world. But I’m not just talking about fancy restaurants and all that. I’m talking about the U.K. as a whole. I think that the produce that’s here — the seafood that’s here, the meat that’s here, the devoted people like these fishermen or lobstermen, or a guy who raises pigs that will be like the best pork you’ll ever eat — that kind of stuff is amazing. And then, really amazing chefs that are devoted to farm to table or farm to fork, I guess is the new expression.” Related Stories Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Having now done travel shows for a while, Tucci says he considers it “a great honor to meet so many of these people, because they’re just extraordinary. Their devotion to what they do. Amazing chefs and home cooks alike, farmers, cheese makers. I mean, their whole life is invested into this one thing. This singular focus is really so impressive to me.” Popular on Variety Tucci is once again nominated as executive producer and host of “Tucci in Italy,” nominated for outstanding hosted nonfiction series or special. He talks to the Awards Circuit Podcast about what it was like to become a host, the skills he has developed in interviewing everyday people, and whether he’s OK with us calling him “The Tooch.” He also takes our 10 Questions quiz, and looks back at his first time in the pages of Variety. But first, on the Roundtable, Gold Derby editor-in-chief Debra Birnbaum joins us to give her takes on the Emmy race, including how “Widow’s Bay” has become the comedy front-runner. Listen below! “Tucci in Italy” comes at an interesting time for Tucci, who remains busy in front of the camera as well — including this year’s “The Devil Wears Prada 2.” “I’m really happy about having a lot to do, and yet at the same time, at the age of almost 66, I think, ‘how long can I do this?’” he says. “There’s a part of me that wants to spend more time at home, and so I’m trying to orchestrate things so that I can do that without compromising my career. Because there are still things I want to do, stories I want to tell, movies I want to make, plays I want to direct. It’s finding that correct balance.” Hosting a travel show didn’t seem like part of the plan, but Tucci notes that he first came up with the idea of traveling through Italy and breaking it down by region about 20 years ago. “I’d never seen a show like that,” he says. “I brought it up to a few people, and everyone looked at me like I was crazy. And then six or seven years ago, CNN came to me and said, ‘Do you have any ideas for a show?’ And I did. I had two other ideas: One was about refugees and food, and the other was about cancer, finding a balance between standard of care and alternative treatments. No one seemed very keen on either of those. So, and then I said, ‘Oh, I want to go through Italy and break it down region by region.’ And they went, ‘OK!’” So here’s the big question: What’s the most underrated region of Italy that we should check out? “I think Le Marche is a really beautiful region, which is right next to Tuscany. I shouldn’t even be saying this because I know that people will go to it. But it’s a really beautiful region, and it’s not packed with a huge number of tourists. The seaside is really pretty. The food is absolutely wonderful, and it’s not crazy expensive. But it’s gorgeous.” As for hosting, Tucci says there was a learning curve at first. “I was very nervous when I first did it. I thought, ‘What am I doing? I don’t know how to do this.’ I know how to memorize lines, or I know how to improvise, but with an actor, not with a normal person. But now I’m much better at it, and I feel more comfortable.” The secret, he says, is to listen. “If you’re not listening in the scene and responding truthfully, it’s not going to work,” he says. For Tucci’s first time in Variety, it was Oct. 6, 1982, in a review of Broadway’s “The Queen and the Rebels.” Tucci was listed as one of the travelers/soldiers, alongside his pal Campbell Scott. “I had just graduated from college,” he says. “I felt very lucky. I grew up with Campbell, and his mom was doing the play, and she cast us. He had one more year of university to do, I think. We were doing the play in the summer, so it was amazing for me. I understudied a role, and we were cast as extras for all practical purposes, and it was great because it got me my equity card and health insurance. That made a big difference. I was paid $550 a week, and I was in heaven. I thought this is the greatest thing ever. I got an agent, so I had all those things right out of college, SUNY Purchase. That’s a huge thing for an actor starting their career.” 10 QUESTIONS WITH STANLEY TUCCI: 1. Childhood nickname: “Tooch.” 2. Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into it now: “Velveeta.” 3. Go-to karaoke or sing-in-the-shower song: “You don’t want to hear me sing. If you’ll notice in those reviews you spoke of, there’s not a single musical in them, and in a 40-45 year long career, and there’s not a musical. But I sing in the shower, thinking I’m brilliant. Something like ‘Our Love is Here to Stay,’ which is a song that I always sang to my kids when they go to sleep.” 4. Give me an alternate title for your show: “Oh God, you don’t know how long it took us to come up with the simplest title in the book. ‘Tucci Eats Italy’? Just bad.” 5. What’s your secret talent? : “I would say drawing and painting.” 6. Favorite ice cream flavor : “I don’t really eat ice cream. If I had to say, it would be chocolate. It’s so boring. I’m so sorry.” 7. The one item you couldn’t live without : “A knife that I have. That sounds scary, doesn’t it? But no, it’s a chef’s knife.” 8. What TV show in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of? : “Wild Wild West.” 9. Fictional character you most admire : “I really loved doing ‘Captain America.’ I did it like 15,16, years ago, and it was one of the best work experiences I’ve ever had. And I absolutely loved playing that role, even though when I was sent the script, it said, ‘German scientist in his 70s,’ and I was 50. I was like, ‘Oh man, come on!’ But it was so well written, and I just loved it. I just watched it again with my kids the other day.” 10. Your favorite piece of advice : “My acting teacher George Morrison, who passed away a number of years ago, said, ‘go beyond what’s comfortable.’ And the second one is that ‘the undoing of something is as important as the doing of it.’ That was from my father who told me that. And Alberto Giacometti.” Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines, and much more. articles.title: ‘Power Book III: Raising Kanan’ Creator Sascha Penn and Stars Patina Miller and Mekai Curtis on the Deadly Series Finale and ‘Power: Origins’
articles.full_text: Cara Howe SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from the series finale of “Raising Kanan” now streaming on Starz . The final curtain has closed on the hit 1990s-set crime series “ Power Book III: Raising Kanan .” The show has been the origin story of Kanan Stark ( Mekai Curtis ), who, by embracing the very business his drug-queenpin mother, Raquel Thomas (an incomparable Patina Miller ), desperately wanted to keep him away from, becomes the monster who rips his entire family apart. The fifth and final season has not only depicted a young man at odds with his mother, but also his willingness to decimate his own family. Fans of “Power” — Courtney Kemp’s original series — have always known how Kanan’s story ends, but his background has been somewhat of a mystery until now. His story is one rife with terror, pain and a sweltering rage that has usurped everything around him. In “Power,” adult Kanan (Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson) viciously murders his cousin Laverne “Jukebox” Thomas (Anika Noni Rose). Viewers could never reconcile this ending, considering how close the cousins appeared to be. However, series creator Sascha Penn has always promised “a full and complete answer to that question.” “One of the things that’s so interesting about ‘Power’ is the notion of reliable narrators and people’s recollections and how they differ from the fact,” Penn tells Variety . “Something we played with quite a bit across the series is who told the truth. For Ghost [Omari Hardwick] in the original ‘Power,’ the story is always shifting with him in terms of who killed Breeze [Shameik Moore] and who was there, who wasn’t there, who knew?​” Related Stories ‘Obsession’ Star Inde Navarrette Confirms Meeting With ‘X-Men’ Director Jake Schreier and Would Love to Play Mystique Samara Weaving to Play Emma Frost in Marvel's 'X-Men' Reboot In the final moments of the series finale, “Unconditional Love,” that nagging question has finally been answered. In retaliation for Kanan murdering her father Marvin (London Brown), Jukebox (Hailey Kilgrove) kills Raq, the woman who raised her. “Watch until the end of the credits,” Penn says. Popular on Variety ​With this chapter of the “Power” Universe officially over, Variety chats with Penn, Miller and Curtis about the series finale, Raq’s shocking death and how the story will continue in Penn’s upcoming Starz series, “Power: Origins.” Cara Howe Sascha, did you know that this is how the chips would fall for the Thomas family? Sascha Penn : I kind of did. I mean, I didn’t know exactly when all this stuff would happen. I always knew Raq would most likely die in the final episode. That I knew. But I will say this: I did go back and forth quite a bit about that over the years. I think people forget we are telling the origin story of perhaps the most diabolically evil character in the history of the “Power” Universe. So when people are up in arms about Kanan killing Uncle Marvin, I mean, I’m always sort of surprised because it’s like, did you see the character I saw on “Power”? Because that guy was a monster. What was the alternative ending for Raq? Penn: I thought for a little while she could get away like Unique [Joey Bada$$]. I thought that was a possibility. But I’m going to be honest with you, I don’t know that I felt like she deserved that ending, both in terms of the story that we set out to tell, but also in terms of the character. One of the most amazing things about this experience is entirely because of Patina Miller. People have really gravitated toward Raq in the same way they gravitated toward Tony Soprano. Both characters are monstrous in their own ways. Mekai, killing Lou (Malcolm Mays) was an accident for Kanan, but when he kills Marvin, that’s very deliberate. Do you think that’s a pivotal moment of change for him? Mekai Curtis: Absolutely. I think they both are, because one doesn’t necessarily happen without the other. Kanan’s becoming a man. I think everything that he’s run into, everything that he’s been exposed to, everything that he’s learned has led him to this moment. Again, we’re talking about the pursuit of power. We’re talking about the pursuit of being great in this world. And that’s simply what sacrificing Uncle Marv is about for Kanan in that moment. It’s nothing more, nothing less. Kanan, more so than ever, is about his business. He understands all of the seeds that he has sown. After Lou’s death and then again after Marvin is killed, we begin to see glimmers of Raq’s humanity for the first time in a long time. Patina, how did you navigate showcasing this as the walls are closing in on her? Patina Miller: I think her having her little family, which she’s a matriarch of, really meant so much to her. So having the pieces start to fall around her is devastating. She’s been able to work and survive in this world because of the family unit she helped create and protect. To have her brothers, whom she desperately loved — and I know sometimes it might look like she didn’t, but everything she’s done shows that she loved her brothers — to have them gone, the only people she has are her niece and her son. Navigating that was exciting for me. There’s never really time or space for Raq to be vulnerable because of the world she’s in. Raq never gets the opportunity to sit with her feelings because it all comes at a cost. For the first time, you get to see her actually deal with herself, her humanity and the people around her. Cara Howe We have to talk about Shameik Moore’s performance as Breeze, because he’s a wild boy. What was it like working with Shameik? Does Kanan admire him, especially because Breeze is under the impression that they’re actual blood brothers? Curtis: It’s Kanan doing what Kanan does. He’s applying what he’s learned from Raq early on: Get what you can from who you can, hold your information until you very much need it, and just let the cards play out. Kanan is a very observant person, and I know it becomes a topic of discussion for people, especially given how emotionally charged and almost impulsive Kanan seems a lot of the time. But he’s a bit more calculated in why he does those things. One of the quotes that sticks out this season is when Joaquin (Goya Robles) tells Raq that her issue is that she has no boundaries. Do you think that’s true of the character? Miller: Oh, absolutely. I think she’s willing to do whatever, whenever, however. I think she’s so focused that she loses sight of what’s in front of her. In the beginning of this journey, it’s like, “Yeah, Raquel, there’s this woman. She’s in a man’s world, and she’s doing all this for legacy, legacy, legacy.” But then it starts to get a little iffy in the way she uses her power and manipulates the people she loves. She does lose sight of it, but I don’t think it’s because she wants to. I think she still thinks that she’s doing this for a purpose. She’s doing this because she has to. But Joaquin was 100% right about that for sure. Speaking of manipulation, do you think that Raq ever anticipated telling Marvin the truth about who killed Lou? Or was it something she just did as a reaction? Miller: I think it was a reaction. I think that one thing you can know about her is she’s good at keeping a secret. I think she would’ve protected that secret the entire time. But as the stakes grew even higher and she knew Kanan was in a dangerous space and had become an enemy, she needed her brother on her side. She’s always so good at having a card to play. She knows that she can’t do this really, truly without her brother. I don’t think she means to pull it out, but in that moment she saw an opening, and she took it. Before he dies, Marvin accuses Raq of never really caring about him in Lou. How do you think that affects Raq in the final days of her life? Miller: Raq has always been so good at keeping the traumas and all of the hurt at bay. It’s not because she doesn’t want to feel; she knows she doesn’t have the space to feel. I think that it’s a hurtful thing for Marvin to say that because, for her and in my own opinion, it’s like, “I have shown you so many times that I love you. Yes, I’m hard on you, but I went to war twice for you.” There have been so many opportunities where you could have seen if she really hated her brothers. With Lou, she loved him. She really did love him. Obviously, she loves the game, and she loves that they’re in it with her, but she raised [Marvin’s] daughter for him. That’s the ultimate act of love for me. So I think she’s feeling the words, and I think she’s realizing that even though she does love them, they feel this way. And it’s a lot. She’s just trying to put the pieces together and coming to terms with that. It’s devastating. It’s heartbreaking for her in the end, and then to lose him. I think she knows her time is coming. I think she’s ready for it. I think she’s not going to back down from it, which makes it even more devastating. Cara Howe In the penultimate episode, just before Kanan kills Marvin, Marvin tells him that he will eventually meet a lonely, tragic end. It’s something that Juke reiterates when she reveals that she’s killed Raq. Do you think that disturbs him at all? Curtis: A little bit. But at the end of the day, this story is about a mother and son. By the time Juke and Marvin are telling him the things that they’re saying, he already knows it. It’s more of a catharsis for them because they’ve been holding on to it. They’ve been just cleaning up his mess this entire time. London Brown’s performance as Marvin this season is phenomenal; the character development is astounding. Did you always know that Marvin would get this sort of redemption story? Penn: London is an unbelievable talent. I’ve been screaming this for as long as I’ve been doing this: all these actors deserve Emmy nominations. What people don’t really remember at this point is that in Episode 8 of Season 1, Marvin put his hands on his daughter because she’s a lesbian. London and I had many conversations about it, because he really felt like Marvin was irredeemable. He’s like, “Anyone who puts their hands on their daughter for that, how can anyone ever like him again?” And I said to him, “We can do it. I’m telling you we can do it, because here’s the thing about people in general: they have an incredible capacity for forgiveness.” I think that’s what’s happened with the audience: They forgave Marvin. He’s flawed, but he acknowledges his flaws, which, by the way, there aren’t many characters in this show that do that. Sascha, do you think Raq is a good mother? Penn: I’m always sort of intrigued when people talk about Raq as a mother. She’s not a good mother in any way. She uses her son to justify so many awful things. “I’m doing this for you” is the ultimate form of manipulation. During their final conversation, she still needs [Kanan] to say, “I love you.” She still is trying to get that. You see Kanan’s maturation in that moment where he says to her, “No, we’re past all that. That doesn’t matter anymore.” And Raq can’t get past it. She’s a narcissist, and she needs that, and she can’t get it. Patina, do you think Raq anticipated that Juke would take her out? Miller: I don’t think she ever would’ve thought in a million years, just like Marvin would’ve never thought in a million years that Kanan would ever do that to family. That would’ve never crossed her mind, especially for someone she raised, accepted, was there for and loved. I know it’s devastating for her. But even in that split second where she realizes this is happening, there’s nothing she can do about it. And again, she never backs down. Those last few seconds of her going for her gun. I don’t even know if she would’ve ever used it had she gotten to it, but that’s just that thing in her that is never willing to back down. Cara Howe Mekai, when Kanan goes to Raq’s house and sees her body on the floor, what was that like for you? Curtis: It’s devastating, but it is poetic; Raq’s not super innocent. We all love to root for her. She’s the ultimate antihero, but she’s also done her own wrongs. I think as Mekai, I went into that last episode trying to play an overhanging grief, knowing that that was going to happen. Not necessarily having control of it, but understanding what Kanan did and how this was going to come back to him. Raq is one of the most iconic characters I’ve ever seen on television, and her journey has been phenomenal to watch. What have you learned from her these last five seasons? Miller: I think what I’ve learned from her is, honestly, her perseverance. I’ve learned to own my voice. I’ve learned how to walk in my power. I’ve learned to trust myself more, honestly. I gained so much confidence from the very first season through the last episode of season five. I’ve learned to trust my gut, trust my instincts. I’ve learned, even through the craziness and messiness of her relationship, what it truly means to be bonded to someone. Loving my child the way that I do. When I first started the show, I was a new mom, and I just desperately wanted to be a good mother. Raquel’s battling that same thing of just not really knowing how, but wanting to be in her version of being a good mom. I’ve learned to give myself grace, but I think the biggest thing is the confidence to walk into spaces, own them and be yourself. As the narration says, as this series closes, this is in many ways just the beginning for Kanan. We’re going to see him again in “Power: Origins,” the Tommy and Ghost origin story. Can you share anything about what we can expect to see of the character and how this will continue for you? Curtis: Just buckle up. I had a lot of fun putting those 18 episodes together. I said it about “Raising Kanan,” but literal blood, sweat and tears stretched me in ways that I didn’t know were possible. But I’m extremely proud. I feel accomplished and ready for the world to see it. Not just my performance, but the entire show. There’s something different to it. I think with every spinoff that we’ve gotten to do and every spinoff that Sascha’s been a part of, he continues to up the ante. “Origins” is very much up there. We’re constantly pushing the boundary. We’re just trying shit, but I think it all worked out. I’m excited for people to go on that ride with us. Penn: It’s a true privilege to be able to continue the story. First and foremost, tonally the show is very different than “Kanan.” “Kanan,” I think we can agree, is pretty dark. “Origins” is a lot more fun. I sort of crafted it as much more of a two-hander like “48 Hours.” It has a real levity. Not to say there isn’t any darkness, and there is obviously violence and action. We do see Kanan more as the 50 Cent version than the “Raising Kanan” version. But the heart and soul of the show is the relationship between Ghost [Spence Moore] and Tommy [Charlie Mann]. I think this is what the “Power” fan base has really been clamoring for. This is their story. The access point to “Origins” is like, just flip it on. You’re along for the ride. You don’t have to have watched “Power” before. It’s just another incredible ensemble cast we’ve assembled. Again, it is not dark like “Raising Kanan,” and it’s not as glitzy and glamorous as “Power.” It’s somewhere in between. We’re still in South Jamaica. This interview has been edited and condensed. articles.title: Behind the Scenes of Obama’s Acting Cameo in ‘Life, Larry’: Blaming Larry David for His Tan Suit Debacle, Improvising Lines and Ranting About Ketchup
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 6:35pm PT Behind the Scenes of Obama’s Acting Cameo in ‘Life, Larry’: Blaming Larry David for His Tan Suit Debacle, Improvising Lines and Ranting About Ketchup By Ethan Shanfeld Plus Icon Ethan Shanfeld @ethanshanfeld Latest Behind the Scenes of Obama’s Acting Cameo in ‘Life, Larry’: Blaming Larry David for His Tan Suit Debacle, Improvising Lines and Ranting About Ketchup 8 hours ago Jake T. Austin Opens Up About ‘Wizards of Waverly Place’ Revival Snub: I’m ‘Disappointed’ to Have ‘Not Been Included’ 19 hours ago Lala Sadii Disney Channel Series in Development 2 days ago See All Art Streiber / HBO In his HBO sketch series “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness,” Larry David travels throughout history, inserting his stubborn and curmudgeonly self into America’s most pivotal moments. “Lawrence,” as he’s often called, fights in the trenches of World War I, heckles George Washington during his Farewell Address and defends Rosa Parks on a Montgomery bus (for all the wrong reasons, of course). The show is produced by Barack Obama through his and Michelle Obama’s Higher Ground banner. So it’s only right that, in the series finale, Obama stepped in to reexamine the most historically important moment in his presidency. Not the killing of Osama bin Laden, the Iran Nuclear Deal or the legalization of same-sex marriage. No, something far more momentous and presidency-defining: the time he ignited a media firestorm by wearing a tan-colored suit to a 2014 press conference about ISIS. (The sartorial choice, which has its own Wikipedia page, saw Obama lambasted as “unpresidential,” was criticized by news outlets ranging from the New York Times to GQ to Fox News.) Related Stories Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Obama appeared in the first episode of “Life, Larry” to help introduce the show. But when David and co-creator Jeff Schaffer told the former president they wanted him to act in a sketch, he and Higher Ground executive producer Ethan Lewis came up with the idea to relitigate the tan suit debacle. “From the very beginning, my dream was to close the book on the tan suit once and for all,” Lewis says. Popular on Variety Schaffer and David then devised a “Curb Your Enthusiasm”-like revisionist history in which David (appearing to play himself) is the one to blame for the fashion crime. In the sketch, Obama is preparing for the press conference while a mango smoothie sits on the Resolute Desk. When David asks for a sip, Obama turns him down to avoid “old lips” on his straw. When the president finally leaves the Oval Office, David goes to steal a sip of the smoothie, and he ends up spilling it all over the navy blue suit Obama planned to wear. When POTUS returns, David frantically tries to divert his attention away from the mess. “I think you should wear the tan suit to the press conference,” he says, insisting it’s “casual Friday.” Obama obliges, and tries on the lighter suit, causing David to deliver his classic, “prettay good… prettay… prettay… prettay… prettay good.” He assures Obama, “People are going to be talking about this for a long, long time.” Art Streiber / HBO Schaffer tells Variety that directing Obama was “one of the coolest things I’ve ever gotten the chance to do.” “It’s so cool being around him. You feel smarter and better, somehow, by just being in the area,” Schaffer says. “He had some great improv stuff. His comic timing was impeccable. He was a good actor, not just as a former president, but, like, as an actor.” Schaffer, who has worked with David since the “Seinfeld” days, was amused by watching Obama give the septuagenarian comedian notes. “The funny thing was watching him go, ‘Larry, you’re coming in late!’ He was the president, so he’s used to telling people what to do. Larry was in the odd position of being told what to do, which never happens on a Larry set.” The most nerve-wracking part of directing a former president? “The first thing was: What do I call this man?” Schaffer says. “I’m directing and things are moving fast, and I have to remember, ‘Sir, let’s do that one more time.’ Or, ‘Hold on, Mr. President.’ I didn’t want to screw things up and go, ‘Hey, Barack.’” The Oval Office stage was crafted by the Obamas’ interior designer Michael S. Smith, who led the 2010 makeover of the real White House room. Smith perfected the layout and furniture of the space, so much so that when Obama walked in, he said, “This is unbelievable. It looks just like it was when I was here,” Schaffer remembers. The attention to detail extended even to Obama’s on-screen aide, played by his real-life Director of Oval Office Operations Brian Mosteller. According to Schaffer, just as surreal as directing the former president was chatting with him during the downtime of the four-hour shoot. “You’re just sitting in the Oval Office with President Obama, hearing him talk about stuff,” he says. “He’s got some funny theories.” He relays one of Obama’s most memorable takes: “No one should be using ketchup after age 12. That’s a child’s condiment. It’s just sugar. Use mustard! Use an adult condiment!” Lewis, who joined Higher Ground in 2022 and serves as its head of non-fiction and sports, concurs: “The banter was phenomenal. Being a fly on the wall in that room was incredible.” Despite Schaffer’s praise of his acting chops, Lewis doesn’t think the ex-POTUS will be rushing to add more credits to his IMDb page. “President Obama doesn’t have a great desire to make that career pivot, but it was very fun [to watch him act] and I’m glad it worked out for the show,” Lewis says. “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness” was billed as a seven-episode limited series celebrating the 250th anniversary of America. Still, Lewis and Schaffer would love to extend the show. “I think it’s done well, and we all have a lot of fun making it,” Lewis says. “Ultimately, that’ll land at the feet of Larry and HBO to keep going, but I’d love to do it.” Though, for Obama’s own good, perhaps he should spend some time away from David. “The president said, ‘I have fun being annoyed by Larry, and when we get together, I realize I start sounding like him,’” Schaffer says. “Larry is sucking him into his black hole of negativity.” Magnus Ferrell on His Viral Hit ‘Asleep Talking’ and Dad Will Ferrell Showing Michelle Obama His Music: ‘I Finally Felt Ready to Have a Spotlight on It’ Paramount’s U.K. Concessions Give ‘Powerful Credibility’ to State AGs’ Lawsuit, Block the Merger Coalition Says: ‘The Dangers’ in U.S. Market ‘Are Unmistakable’ ‘Power Book III: Raising Kanan’ Creator Sascha Penn and Stars Patina Miller and Mekai Curtis on the Deadly Series Finale and ‘Power: Origins’ Virginie Efira – a ‘Showgirls’ Fan – Enjoyed the ‘Benedetta’ Controversy: ‘When Verhoeven Said There Would Be Lesbian Sex Scenes, I Just Replied: ‘No Problem’ Luca Guadagnino to Receive Cartier Glory to the Filmmaker Award at Venice Film Festival William Orbit, Grammy-Winning Producer for Madonna and Blur, Dies at 69 Loading comments... articles.title: ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine
articles.full_text: Aug 8, 2026 12:19am PT ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine German director Isabelle Stever brings sensitivity and visual ingenuity to this story of a young queer couple whose life together is upended by the Russian invasion. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine 2 hours ago ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller 1 day ago ‘Super Troopers 3’ Review: A Cult Comedy Franchise Seeks No Converts in Instantly Forgettable Third Go-Round 3 days ago See All 'I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming' Courtesy of X Filme Creative Pool GmbH Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine has prompted a wealth of urgent nonfiction filmmaking documenting the harsh realities of life under siege, but comparatively little dramatic storytelling — a space that the new German-Ukrainian production “ I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming ” occupies with bold formal imagination and a commitment to illuminating lives neglected in wider views of the conflict. A timely collaboration between German director Isabelle Stever and her wife, Ukrainian screenwriter Anna Melikova, the film is an intimate, bracingly intersectional relationship drama centered on a queer Kyiv couple whose attempts to flee to safety are complicated by local prejudice: a reminder that selective discrimination can still endure within a collectively persecuted population. Related Stories Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Premiering in the main competition at Locarno, this is a warmer, more humane work than Stever’s last film, the coolly provocative 2022 incest drama “Grand Jeté.” If that film could travel, even securing U.S. distribution with Altered Innocence, there’s no reason to think “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” — with its topical subject matter and emotional accessibility, plus the imprimatur of producer Tom Tykwer — won’t gain wider exposure still. Paris-based outfit Outplay Films, which specializes in LGBTQ-themed titles, picked up the film for international sales shortly before its Locarno premiere; queer-oriented distributors and programmers will take particular interest in a work that would stand out for its candid depiction of transgender marriage even without its complicating wartime context. Popular on Variety What Stever’s latest shares with “Grand Jeté” is a crisp aesthetic rigor that some viewers may find distancing despite the immediacy of the drama, though it has ample sensory rewards. The director and DP Volodymyr Usyk (who shot the celebrated 2024 wartime doc “Songs of Slow Burning Earth”) rarely permit us a close, unobstructed view of their principal characters, Olya (Tania Myronyshena) and Oleh (Markus Bright), often shooting them from afar in slivered, reflective surfaces, over another person’s shoulder or through staggered doorways. Actually seeing these lives takes patience and some concentration; in the unforgiving world of the film, many choose not to. It opens on a conversation — viewed through a boxy apartment window at night, and later revisited on the other side of the glass — that finds Olya and Oleh’s longtime relationship at breaking point. “I entered a heterosexual relationship against my will,” Olya seethes to her partner. “You promised me you’d stay the same person.” Gradually, their history emerges: They met and got together as women in Kyiv’s small but throbbing queer scene, before Oleh came out as a trans man. That hasn’t weakened their bond; indeed, Olya even proposed marriage to him, to the surprise and delight of her conservative suburban family, who take it as given that their new in-law is cisgender. (Children are expected in short order; Olya tends to swerve the subject.) But Oleh’s transition did more or less coincide with the Russian invasion, which has severely hindered his ability to live freely and openly at a time when men are expected to serve their country in the armed forces. Medical certification of Oleh’s gender dysphoria cuts little ice with the military, who exercise institutional transphobia while taking him at his word regarding his identity. The couple’s plans to cross the border are thus mired in an absurdist tangle of administrative contradictions, and through the prism of Oleh’s impossible bind — in the eyes of the law, he’s at once recognized and rejected as the man he’s fought to be — Melikova’s script thoughtfully addresses how masculinity is defined and confined in the national psyche. Both non-professionals who bring a degree of lived experience to their characterizations, Myronyshena and Bright underplay effectively, communicating through finely expressive gestures and mirrored body language, and bringing an in-the-moment rawness to their frankly intimate, occasionally confrontational dialogue. “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” isn’t fashioned as a performance showcase, however: The actors often feel another dynamic element in Stever’s complex mise-en-scène, sometimes tellingly cramped in Usyk’s tight, stylized compositions, or muted in Andreas Hildebrandt’s hauntingly sparse sound design, which is given no score to contend with. There are passages of bravura technique here: One dazzling tracking shot spans the crowded, kinetic turmoil of the border in wartime, flooded with the red and blue lights of state authorities — visually redolent of neon-streaked queer club nights from the couple’s recent past, but a whole life away. A third-act development that again redefines the couple’s place in heteronormative society is somewhat rushed, leaning too heavily into melodrama to be wholly convincing. But it’s moving just the same, underlining the filmmakers’ interest in unorthodox found-family structures, and their foregrounding of minorities whose rights are often the first to be disregarded in times of national crisis. As the conflict in Ukraine trudges on, Stever’s stark, surprising film is a reminder that we’ve barely skimmed the surface of the country’s war stories. ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine Reviewed at Locarno Film Festival (Competition), Aug. 7, 2026. Running time: 100 MIN. Production: (Ukraine-Germany) An X Filme Creative Pool production in co-production with Westdeutscher Rundfunk. (World sales: Outplay Films, Paris.) Producers: Uwe Schott, Tom Tykwer. Executive producers: Anna Melikova, Josef Reidinger. Co-producers: Natalia Libet, Olha Bregman. Crew: Director: Isabelle Stever. Screenplay: Anna Melikova. Camera: Volodymyr Usyk. Editors: Paul Groebel, Laura Lauzemis. With: Tania Myronyshena, Markus Bright, Iryna Mak, Viktor Zhdanov, Maiia Sobolevska, Maria Myronyshena, Oleksandr Rudynskyi. articles.title: Satyajit Ray’s ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne’ Making to be Chronicled in Srijit Mukherji’s ‘Maharaja Tomare Selam’
articles.full_text: Aug 8, 2026 2:13am PT Satyajit Ray’s ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne’ Making to be Chronicled in Srijit Mukherji’s ‘Maharaja Tomare Selam’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Male Contraceptive Doc ‘Give It a Shot’ From ‘Ask the Sexpert’ Director Vaishali Sinha Sets North American Theatrical Release, Unveils Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Vietnamese Boy Band Uprize Wants to Take Over the World: ‘We Won’t Set Limits for Ourselves’ 19 hours ago Danny DeVito-Produced Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Boards Blue Finch Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago See All Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Indian National Award-winning filmmaker Srijit Mukherji is bringing to screen the making of Satyajit Ray ‘s “ Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne ,” one of Indian cinema’s most celebrated classics, in a new film titled “ Maharaja Tomare Selam .” Jeetu Kamal, Ritwik Bhowmik, Rudranil Ghosh, Satakshi Nandy, Sairity Banerjee and Arijit Dutta star in the film, produced by Hoichoi Studios and Friends Communication in association with Piyali Films Pvt. Ltd, the original producer of “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne.” Related Stories Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale “Maharaja Tomare Selam,” which is also the title of a song in “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,” centers on Ray himself – the pressures he faced and the choices he made against the backdrop of a politically charged Kolkata – as he willed “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne” into existence. Principal photography will commence in January 2027. Popular on Variety Released on May 8, 1969, “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne” followed two inept village musicians, played by Tapen Chatterjee and Rabi Ghosh, who are banished from their homes and granted magical powers by the King of Ghosts, which they use to avert a war between two rival kingdoms. Beneath the fantasy, the film carried social and political undertones around class and the role of art, a thread Ray sharpened into direct satire of authoritarian rule with his 1980 sequel, “Hirak Rajar Deshe.” His son, Sandip Ray, closed out the trilogy with “Goopy Bagha Phire Elo” in 1992. Ray built a body of work over more than three decades that includes “Pather Panchali” and “Charulata” among its landmarks. In 1992, weeks before his death, he received an honorary Academy Award for lifetime achievement, becoming the first Indian filmmaker so honored. “I am just trying to tell the incredible true story of how one of the greatest classics of Indian cinema, ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,’ was conceived and made,” Mukherji said. Mukherji’s own credits include “Chotushkone,” for which he won the Indian National Film Award for best director, along with “Jaatishwar” and “Baishe Srabon.” He is known for his engagement with Bengali culture and storytelling, and with “Maharaja Tomare Selam,” he takes on a pivotal episode in the country’s film history. “Maharaja Tomare Selam” joins a run of Bengali films that have turned the camera on Ray’s own legacy. Anik Dutta’s “Aparajito” dramatized the making of “Pather Panchali,” with Kamal playing a character modeled on Ray, while Kaushik Ganguly’s “Apur Panchali” traced the later life of Subir Banerjee, the child actor who played Apu in that film. articles.full_text: Florence “Flo” Anthony, the pioneering celebrity journalist who broke barriers at the New York Post’s Page Six and became a defining voice in African American entertainment journalism, has died. She was 74. Jack Hirsch, biographer for her husband, boxing legend Michael Spinks, confirmed that she died early Thursday, Aug. 6. The two had worked together on Michael “Jinx” Spinks: An Authorized Biography , which was released in March. He said that she recently disclosed to him that she was battling cancer. Her weekly “ Go With The Flo ” column became a fixture in The New York Amsterdam News dating back to 2001, as well as in publications including the Philadelphia Sunday Sun and the Columbus Times . She also contributed entertainment news to the New York Daily News , served as publisher and editor-in-chief of Black Noir magazine, and acted as editor-in-chief of Black Elegance magazine. CNN entertainment journalist Lisa Respers France posted her reaction on social media upon learning of Anthony’s passing, saying in part: “As a Black woman who covers pop culture, I am deeply indebted to Florence ‘Flo’ Anthony, a syndicated columnist and author who did more than just cover gossip. She was so important to the culture.” A woman of firsts Anthony was known to walk into newsrooms and departments whose doors had once been barricaded against people of color—and particularly against African American women. She entered spaces where few people looked like her, where her presence alone challenged entrenched ideas about who could report the news, break a story, command a television screen, or become a trusted voice on celebrity culture. She became the first woman to work in the sports department of the New York Post and the first African American to work in the newspaper’s entertainment and world‑renowned Page Six departments, according to her own account of her career. She also made history as the first African American woman to write a column for a supermarket tabloid, penning “Eye on the Stars” for the National Examiner . For an African American woman rising through the overwhelmingly white, male, and notoriously insular world of tabloid journalism, these achievements were not merely promotions, but breaches in a wall. Before becoming one of America’s most recognizable celebrity journalists and media personalities, Flo worked in public relations as a publicist for some of boxing’s most formidable figures, including Spinks, whom she began dating in 1987 and married in January 2026; Muhammad Ali; Larry Holmes; Butch Lewis; Mike McCallum; Matthew Saad Muhammad; Saoul Mamby; and Eddie Mustafa Muhammad. Her publicity work gave her a deep understanding of the relationship between journalists, publicists, and public figures, allowing her to fight for a client’s visibility long before she sat on the other side of the desk. Many publicists owe some portion of their careers to Anthony, with a number of young representatives securing an early placement because she answered their call, opened their email, or recognized the potential in a story. A graduate of Howard University, Anthony initially came to New York with dreams of becoming an actress and also worked as a teacher. Her work with talent manager Tobe Gibson eventually expanded into publicity, sportswriting, and a position as an agate clerk in the New York Post’s sports department. From there, she began a historic ascent through sports, entertainment, and celebrity journalism. Legendary journalist Over the course of her career, she reported hundreds of exclusives, including the marriages of Mike Tyson and Robin Givens, Alec Baldwin and Kim Basinger, and John McEnroe and Tatum O’Neal, as well as the news that Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman were adopting. Flo did not regard gossip journalism as the careless recycling of rumors. To her, a gossip columnist was a reporter who broke stories—and she took the responsibility of getting those stories right seriously. Her influence expanded far beyond print. During the 1990s, she became a familiar and authoritative presence on daytime television, appearing on shows hosted by Joan Rivers, Ricki Lake, Rolonda Watts, Geraldo Rivera, Sally Jessy Raphael, Maury Povich, Leeza Gibbons, Tempestt Bledsoe, Bertice Berry, Vicki Lawrence, and others. She appeared on Court TV, CNN, MSNBC, Fox News Channel, and HLN, and contributed to entertainment‑news programs including “Inside Edition,” “The Insider,” and “Entertainment Tonight.” For six seasons, she appeared as a contributor and later a co‑host on E! Entertainment Television’s “The Gossip Show,” and was featured in numerous installments of “E! True Hollywood Story.” She became a regular contributor to TV One’s “Unsung,” “Unsung Hollywood,” and “Life After.” Her television work placed an authoritative African American woman at the center of national conversations about celebrity, scandal, and popular culture at a time when such visibility remained far too rare. Through her company, Dottie Media Group LLC, Flo extended her voice into syndicated radio with “Gossip on the Go With Flo” and “Flo Anthony’s Big Apple Buzz,” which aired in approximately 20 markets and introduced millions of listeners to her combination of insider knowledge, brisk reporting, and unmistakable personality. At the Amsterdam News, she was more than a byline. She was family. Flo was also the author of four novels: “Keeping Secrets, Telling Lies,” “Deadly Stuff Players,” “One Last Deadly Play,” and “Last Call for a Deadly Diva.” The books transformed decades of observing fame, ambition, deception, and power into fiction, bringing the practiced instincts of a journalist to the suspense and intrigue of a novelist. “I’ve broken in roads that will never be broken in again,” Anthony said in a 2013 interview with Urbanbridgez.com . “So if I never wrote another sentence or got on radio again in life or got on TV, I would miss it yes but I feel I’ve done a lot of what God put me on this earth to do.” — with reporting from AmNews contributor Jason Gonzalez.
