articles.title: Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 12:01am PT Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review By Alison Herman Plus Icon Alison Herman TV Critic aherman2006 Latest Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review 3 hours ago FX’s Adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ ‘The Shards’ Can’t Be Saved by a Strong Lead Performance: TV Review 2 days ago ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Netflix To kick off the third episode of the Netflix animated comedy “ Alley Cats ,” protagonist Gus — an overweight orange tabby voiced by writer, creator and frequent director Ricky Gervais (think Garfield with a distinctly working class British accent) — describes his plan for the day. It starts with an achievable goal. Then: “Get distracted immediately. Do loads of weird, pointless shit that somehow makes stuff worse. Kill something. Eat bits of it. Give up our mission. Come home here. Sleep for 14 hours.” Related Stories Locarno’s Match Me! Projects Push New Voices, Timely Relevance and Authenticity as a Younger Generation Moves Center Stage Gareth Edwards Exits 'Jurassic World Rebirth' Sequel Over Creative Differences “Home,” in this case, is a derelict London rowhouse where Gus and his mates Puke (David Earl), Fang (Andrew Brooke) and Olive (Diane Morgan, better known as daft presenter Philomena Cunk ) have taken to squatting. There, the cats watch TV, from a “Love Island” knockoff called “Thick and Single” to news footage of looting to nature documentaries, chat about nothing and generally do as Gus describes. “Alley Cats” ambles along as such for half a dozen sub-20-minute chapters — though the show is tinged throughout with a melancholy that’s a little surprising from the typically acerbic Gervais. Popular on Variety Given the other series’ swift cancellation , it’s unlikely many viewers will have watched both “Alley Cats” and “Kevin,” the Amazon Prime Video series with a similar premise co-created by Aubrey Plaza. But comparing the two, as is inevitable for a critic commissioned to review each in turn, proves instructive. Both are cartoons for adults distributed via streaming, centered on feline protagonists in major cities. Yet “Kevin” is louder, wackier and more joke-dense — one might even say more American — than “Alley Cats,” which is more downbeat and droll by comparison. “Alley Cats” also organizes itself around social caste, as befits its country of origin. The titular crew also hang around with a housecat they nickname Ponce (Tom Basden), who’s more genteel in every sense of the term than his friends. He sounds posh; he’s spoiled with pudding; he’s neutered and thus immune to baser urges, including Olive’s unrequited crush. The rest of the crew are more base, volleying the c-word — rhymes with “runt” — around freely as they debate useless topics like whether four cats could take down “one fat kid” or if bees are edible. (Most laughs come from these mumbled, mundane exchanges rather than conventional setups and punchlines.) Puke, the mangiest of the group, admits his private parts are “smashed up” because “I gave a hedgehog anal.” But “Alley Cats” doesn’t just revel in the nastiness of feral life. The show also depicts its hardships with disarming frankness, even verging on despondency. An associate of the crew is introduced and then fatally run over in seconds. A deadbeat dad is reassured that, since his kittens were adopted and grew into well-adjusted triplets, “maybe you not being around was their best chance.” The last line of the season — not really a spoiler, since there’s not much context necessary — is “we’re all gonna die soon.” Sometimes, this undercurrent of gloom tips over into outright nihilism. (“Fuck people,” Gus proclaims in one of his many rants at the television. “I can’t wait for people to wipe people off the face of the Earth.”) More often, though, the mood is more one of resignation to a hardscrabble existence that also has its pleasures. The serialized plot of “Alley Cats” comes from a lost kitten (Jo Hartley) the strays resolve to help find her way back home. Gervais isn’t overtly sentimental in depicting Gus’ growing affection for his young, quite cutely drawn (her eyes are enormous) young charge; in fact, the story resolves on a fittingly bittersweet note for the overall tone. But there is a real tenderness that’s thrown into the mix with the lewd banter and glass-half-empty outlook. “Alley Cats” is so compressed that it ends up stopping short of real heft. A subplot about Gus’ ailing mother is introduced so hastily it almost bewilders; on a broader level, this is fundamentally a hangout sitcom about free-range felines. The show nonetheless takes an unexpected direction that makes for an enjoyably low-key binge. Even bullshitting cats have feelings. All six episodes of “Alley Cats” are now streaming on Netflix. articles.title: Vishal Bhardwaj Sets ‘Rashomon’-Style Film on Tarun Tejpal Rape Case After Bombay High Court Conviction (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 12:15am PT Vishal Bhardwaj Sets ‘Rashomon’-Style Film on Tarun Tejpal Rape Case After Bombay High Court Conviction (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Danny DeVito-Produced Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Boards Blue Finch Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 12 minutes ago Vishal Bhardwaj Sets ‘Rashomon’-Style Film on Tarun Tejpal Rape Case After Bombay High Court Conviction (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago ‘The Traitors’ India Season 2 Unveils Trailer With Karan Johar and 21-Celebrity Cast (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago See All Getty Images/Humans of Cinema Indian auteur Vishal Bhardwaj is developing a film based on the Tarun Tejpal rape case, the director confirmed with Variety , hours after the Bombay High Court overturned a Goa sessions court acquittal and convicted the former Tehelka editor of rape, sentencing him to 10 years’ rigorous imprisonment. Bhardwaj, whose adaptations of Shakespeare – “Maqbool,” “Omkara,” “Haider” – have established him as one of Hindi cinema’s foremost interpreters of moral complexity, said he has read the Goa trial court’s 527-page judgment multiple times and described the divergence between the two rulings as the creative catalyst. He was in Goa for the hearing of the case. Related Stories France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets Cannes Critics’ Week Film 'Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building' Sells to Strand Releasing for North America (EXCLUSIVE) “The contradiction between the two judgments makes it a perfect case for a ‘Rashomon’-style narrative,” Bhardwaj tells Variety . “There are a lot of facts and incidents in this case that nobody knows about, and people will be amused and surprised to discover them on screen.” Popular on Variety He said the density of the legal record is precisely what drew him in. “As they say, the devil lies in the detail,” Bhardwaj says. “How do you expect people to go through the tiring, dry legal language of a 500-plus-page court judgment? I have gone through the minutest details. I have read the judgment many times and am still grappling with it. It’s a very important case for society.” Bhardwaj was careful to stress that his approach has not yet hardened into a fixed point of view. “It’s too early for me to make up my mind on what the film is about,” he says, “but I’m very clear that the approach must be that of a dispassionate observer, like a true film journalist, if I may say so.” That neutrality, he added, is structural as much as ethical. “Any crime of this nature, one with many points of view beyond reasonable doubt, must be approached without preconceived ideas or a biased starting point,” he says. “No story is complete without all the different points of view, especially in a “Rashomon” structure, because half a glass of water is also half empty at the same time – the only difference is perspective.” On casting, Bhardwaj set an unusual brief. “I want the actor to be unaware of the crime, if possible, and to set the judgments aside,” Bhardwaj says. “I would love for him to approach it as fiction.” The project is being produced by Bhardwaj alongside a major Bollywood studio, which he declined to name. He deflects a question about his authority on Shakespeare with characteristic self-deprecation. “I’m blessed by the almighty himself, otherwise how could an average student from a small town become an authority on Shakespearean adaptations?” He was equally expansive on what the film ultimately represents. “It’s not about India in 2026,” he says. “It’s about the truth, which must come out at any cost, at any 26th year of any century.” The Tejpal case has had one of the longest legal arcs in recent Indian criminal history. The former editor was arrested in 2013 after a junior colleague accused him of sexual assault. A Goa sessions court acquitted him in 2021, a verdict the state challenged. The Bombay High Court’s ruling on Aug. 6 called the trial court judgment “perverse” and relied on the complainant’s testimony, CCTV footage, and Tejpal’s own apology emails as evidence of guilt. Tejpal has said he will appeal to the Supreme Court. articles.title: Thomas Heise’s Final Documentary ‘Übergang,’ a Potential Locarno Highlight, Reflects on Time and Transience
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 12:47am PT Thomas Heise’s Final Documentary ‘Übergang,’ a Potential Locarno Highlight, Reflects on Time and Transience By JD Linville Plus Icon JD Linville Latest Low Light Films Boards Locarno Competition Thriller ‘O Jacaré,’ Basil Da Cunha Celebration of Lisbon’s Vibrant Reboleira District (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago Annecy Young Audience Award Winner ‘Into the Forest’ Finds Freedom Through Imagination 1 month ago Konstantina Kotzamani’s Debut Feature ‘Titanic Ocean’ Weaves Greek Myth Into Mermaid School at Cannes Un Certain Regard 3 months ago See All 'Übergang' Courtesy of Peter Badel, Chris Wright Thomas Heise ‘s final film, “ Übergang ,” arrives at the Locarno Film Festival as both a portrait of one of Germany’s most influential documentary filmmakers and the completion of a project left unfinished by his death. Premiering in the festival’s out of competition section, the film traces Heise’s life through newly shot footage, archival material and photographs, sewing together a meditation on time and transition. Related Stories NFL Hall of Fame Game 2026: How to Watch Carolina Panthers vs. Arizona Cardinals Live Online 'Michael 2' Eyes Filming Start 'Towards the End of This Year' or Early 2027 as Lionsgate Teases Release Date Heise, whose body of work chronicled the lives of ordinary people across East Germany during reunification and the decades that followed, began developing “Übergang” as a portrait of Berlin’s Schönhauser Allee before his death in 2024. Longtime collaborators Peter Badel and Chris Wright ultimately completed the documentary, shaping a film that explores the filmmaker’s life and enduring relationship with German history. Popular on Variety Produced by Ma.ja.de . Filmproduktion, “Übergang” at once imports you to Schönhauser Allee through patient, black and white street-level scenes of normal life: commuters boarding a tram, quiet revelers at a carnival, a couple in conversation. Voice over paints the picture of the man behind the camera, and through carefully placed interview vignettes of Heise, the observer becomes the observed. “Übergang” draws together contemporary observations set against Heise’s experiences growing up in East Berlin to shed light on the political and social transformations that defined both his life and art. Variety spoke with co-directors Peter Badel and Chris Wright ahead of the film’s world premiere at Locarno. The title “Übergang” suggests a transition or a passage. When did this emerge as the central theme of the film? Peter Badel : Here we are referring to a draft text that Thomas Heise wrote during the preparatory phase of the project. He was drawn to the dual meaning of the term “Übergang.” The film is largely shot around the station on Berlin’s Schönhauser Allee, a busy interchange between public transport lines, but the title also hints at the idea of change in society. Our film covers the period of transition from East Germany to the fall of the Wall and beyond. That includes the current climate of war and rearmament, and the shift away from the traditional politics of the left and right toward a direction that seeks to make us forget the lessons learned from two world wars and a Europe destroyed by the Nazis. For Chris and me, there was never any other title for the film than the one Thomas had chosen. Was it difficult to preserve Thomas’s artistic voice and vision while creating a new work after his death? Chris Wright: Thomas wanted work on the film to continue unchanged after his death. But of course, that was an impossible task, because his death changed everything. We decided it was vital that it become our own film, and that we make our own decisions about how to shape it. But at the same time, everyone working on the film had a long history of collaborating with Thomas. For me personally, that meant I could often almost hear his voice in the edit, saying, “Let’s try a scene like this. Let’s put that in. Let’s leave that out.” His aesthetic had become almost second nature. Badel: Another big factor was Thomas’ personal archive, which his husband Michael gave us full access to. Going through all that material, Thomas remained a critical and productive partner for us even after his sudden death. Of course, we missed his proven ability to cut things and, in doing so, amplify the fragmentary nature of his work. But I believe we remained true to his playful spirit. How did you bring the various elements of the film (new footage, archival material, photos and text) together into a single narrative? Badel: First we explored approaches that proved to be dead ends. I shot lots of interviews with friends and collaborators, for example. We also tried to incorporate too many aspects of Thomas’ work. Then Chris had the idea to take a break and go through all the original archive recordings of Thomas we could find to see how they worked cinematically. Wright: I wanted the film to incorporate as much unseen, or hardly seen, material as possible. So there are lots of outtakes (particularly from Thomas’ last film, “Heimat is a Space in Time”), VHS footage we found on tapes and hard drives, diary excerpts, unpublished texts and archive interviews. As much of the film as possible is told through new combinations of his own words and images. The fragmentary montage remains true to his approach. We don’t explain exactly where the materials come from. What is important is the dialogue they enter into with each other. At the same time, it was vital not to make a homage or an anecdotal work. We wanted the film to take a similar approach to Thomas as a character as “Heimat” took toward his own family. We tell a story of lived history, the way the emotions and experiences of a life can be shaped by the politics and society it takes place in. Courtesy of Peter Badel, Chris Wright The film’s final scene condenses a great deal of meaning into a single moment. Can you describe how you came across this interview and this quote? Badel: During the many days of filming at Schönhauser Allee station, we frequently encountered Michael, whom we observed (sometimes up close, sometimes from a greater distance among all the passers-by) as he waited for spare change at his spot by the subway stairs. We talked with him about the social divide around the station and discovered that he knew Thomas Heise by sight. He had also heard about Thomas’ death. Wright: Time and transience were two of Thomas’ biggest concerns in his filmmaking. And here, it is this homeless man, begging for change, who names them. Thomas often put unnoticed lives at the center of his films. So it only seemed fitting that Michael should have the last words in this film about Thomas. What do you hope the audience will learn about Thomas Heise through “Übergang?” Badel: I would be very pleased if Thomas’ remark about this film: “The author is a character in the film,” has become tangible and vivid through our work. And I hope that even people who don’t know much about him will find his fascinating way of thinking about and presenting time inspiring. Wright: I think that, with Thomas, we’ve lost an important critical voice for our times. I hope the film will remind people that it’s vital to keep questioning the status quo. Otherwise, as Thomas says, things can easily change for the worse, and you won’t notice until it’s too late. articles.title: Locarno Open Doors Buzz Title ‘Chapa 100,’ From Ique Langa, Adds Luminalia, Mo Harare, Mostafa El Kasha (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 1:22am PT Locarno Open Doors Buzz Title ‘Chapa 100,’ From Ique Langa, Adds Luminalia, Mo Harare, Mostafa El Kasha (EXCLUSIVE) In a drive into sub-Saharan African cinema, Luminalia is also representing Langa’s ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Atcha Atcha,’ the new doc by award winning Senegalese director Mamadou Dia By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Locarno’s Match Me! Projects Push New Voices, Timely Relevance and Authenticity as a Younger Generation Moves Center Stage 35 minutes ago Locarno Open Doors Buzz Title ‘Chapa 100,’ From Ique Langa, Adds Luminalia, Mo Harare, Mostafa El Kasha (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘La Koreana,’ a Banner New Talent Title From Spain, Brought to Market at Locarno by Producers Lazona Zinema and Estibaliz Urresola’s Sirimiri (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago See All 'Chapa 100' Courtesy of Ique Langa “Chapa 100,” the 2025 Atlas Workshops Development Award winner, now a potential highlight at Locarno’s Africa-focused strand Open Doors , has been boarded by Italy-based sales agent Luminalia . Written and directed by Mozambique’s Ique Langa , “Chapa 100” has also added as an associate producer Mo Harawe , whose “The Village Next to Paradise” screened in Cannes Festival’s 2024 Un Certain Regard to enthusiastic reviews, Variety hailing it as a “quietly powerful film.” Related Stories Cannes Critics’ Week Film 'Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building' Sells to Strand Releasing for North America (EXCLUSIVE) France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets Also on board are Egyptian cinematographer Mostafa El Kashef, and a third production partner, Mozambique’s Better Films – signs of a building production in which talent and industry wants in. Popular on Variety Also penned by Langa, “Chapa 100” marks the filmmaker’s follow-up to feature debut “The Prophet” (“O Profeta”), which world premiered in main competition this year at the IFF Rotterdam and now forms part of Locarno’s Open Doors Screenings. In advanced development, “Chapa 100” is lead produced by filmmaker Lara Sousa at Kulunga Filmes, based out of Mozambique capital Maputo, behind “Nós, Povo das Ilhas,” directed by Elson Santos and Sousa. Pedro Borges at Portugal’s Midas Filmes, a past Kulunga partner, co-produces. Shot with an observational style, priming social realism and emotional insight, “Chapo 100” lifts off into a magical realist style which, along the lines of Gabriel García Márquez’s “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” says much about the collective mindset and heart of Maputo dwellers and the illusions of individual characters, “celebrating the resilience, tenderness, and humanity found in the city’s everyday rhythms,” Langa and Sousa said in a statement. In it, Sitoé, an 80-year-old flower vendor meets Valentina, a vegetable seller in her seventies. A simple flower sparks a quiet romance. When a thief steals Valentina’s rented wig, Sitóe runs after him and is struck dead by a speeding chapa, a local minibus. His spirit becomes tied to the vehicle that killed him, however, and flowers begin to bloom within it. “‘Chapa 100’ is my love letter to Maputo. I wanted to portray the city not simply through its streets, but through the people who give it its heartbeat. By bringing together professional actors and non-professional performers from the city itself, the film seeks to capture something truthful and deeply human,” Langa told Variety. “Blending realism with magical poetry, ‘Chapa 100’ is ultimately a story about love, memory, and the invisible bonds that connect us and to the places we call home,” he adds. Langa has completed a seven-week residency at MacDowell, where, he told Variety , he had the “opportunity to deepen the screenplay and refine the emotional core of the story.” “Chapa 100” recently received the Cultiv’Art / Expertise France Development Grant, one of the largest international development grants ever awarded to a Mozambican feature film project. Together with the Atlas Workshop Development Prize , this marks an important step in the film’s international journey, noted Luminalia’s head of sales and festivals, Tommaso Priante. In a drive into sub-Saharan African cinema, Luminalia is also representing “The Prophet” and “ Atcha Atcha ,” the new doc by award winning Senegalese director Mamadou Dia . Dia’s debut, “Nafi’s Father,” won the award for best first feature at the 2019 Locarno Film Festival as well as the Golden Leopard in its Filmmakers of the Present section. Screening out of competition at this year’s Locarno Festival, “Atcha, Atcha” follows students in their third and final year at the École des Sables, founded by legendary Senegalese dancer and choreographer Germaine Acogny and described by Dia as “the Ivy League of dance schools in sub-Saharan Africa.” Dia and Harawe will deliver a masterclass at this year’s Open Doors. Screening at Open Doors and a Mozambique-South Africa-Qatar, “The Prophet” begins with evangelical Pastor Hélder preaching in the village of Manjacaze. His inspiration and congregation dwindling, he turns to black magic to fire up his oratory and heal his parishioners, but his powers come at ever larger sacrifice, literally. Pointedly framed, even in vertical box aspect, bringing sense and sensitivity to shots, “The Prophet” builds as a black and white film parable about overweening ambition, becoming as well “an expression of the community [Manjacaze] that inspired it,” Luque told Variety . “The Prophet” also marked out Luque as a director to track. “Distributing African films, for us, means accepting a challenge that is not only operational but also theoretical and positional. Luminalia was founded precisely on this idea: to question our own ethnocentrism and bring a more conscious approach while working with non-Western titles,” Priante told Variety . He added: ”We’re very happy to see that around 50% of this year’s line-up consists of African titles. This was our goal from the moment we launched the company last year, and it’s rewarding to see that established directors understand our approach, which seeks to question ethnocentrism and promote a form of distribution that involved a more theoretical and anthropological framework, not just a business model.” Savannah Guthrie Posts New Video Urging Mother’s Kidnappers to ‘Do the Right Thing’: ‘Tell Us Where to Look for Her’ Pima County Sheriff’s Department Made Several Mistakes During Search for Nancy Guthrie, New Report Claims Second Note Sent to Media Said Nancy Guthrie Was Dead Savannah Guthrie Fights Back Tears While Responding to Note Claiming Her Mom Nancy Is Dead: ‘We’ll Never Stop Looking for Her, Ever’ Savannah Guthrie Says ‘I Cry Every Morning on the Way to Work’ While Her Mom Is Still Missing Loading comments... articles.title: Locarno’s Match Me! Projects Push New Voices, Timely Relevance and Authenticity as a Younger Generation Moves Center Stage
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 1:55am PT Locarno’s Match Me! Projects Push New Voices, Timely Relevance and Authenticity as a Younger Generation Moves Center Stage Multiple titles turn on Millennial or Gen Z angst, uncertainty, the search for belonging and the damage dealt by old-school elites and their legacies By John Hopewell , Ed Meza 'The Queen of England Stole My Parents' Courtesy of Dansu Films Arthouse movies are increasingly made for younger audiences who are replacing ageing stay-at-home baby boomers at Europe’s upscale cinema theaters. That impact is now working its way through new arthouse projects, seen at Locarno’s 2026 Match Me! , its vibrant co-production meet this year welcoming projects from Europe and Latin America, where a younger generation move center stage or featue at least as co-protagonists. Later this Festival, a comment on market trends. For the moment, a close look at the producers attending Match Me! and a top project they are brining to market: Related Stories Cannes' Critics' Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) Cannes Critics’ Week Film 'Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building' Sells to Strand Releasing for North America (EXCLUSIVE) Brazil Amadeu Alban, Movioca Behind “Drag Me as a Queen” (NBCUniversal/E!), the first Brazilian reality show exported globally with formats in the Netherlands and Germany, Alban notes, and doc feature “Anatomy of Chaos,” a current Brazilian box office hit. Popular on Variety At Match Me! with “The Girl Who Bled Woman” where Dinha, 13, is forced to marry her older sister’s widower, the marriage only being consummated after her first menstruation. Dinha battles to hide her body changes. A coming-of-age drama/survival thriller. Amina Sophia Nogueira, Capivara Movies With a 20-year career, taking in a decade as Globo’s talent manager, now developing her first features at Capicara, founded 2024, including “The She-Devil.” Set in working-class Rio de Janeiro during the booming ‘90s, Araí, 11, develops an obsession with an imaginary killer who attacks girls in their neighborhood, while adoring Iara, an aunt who offers guidance and inspiration through her transgressive way of living. Emerging voices Clara Ferrer and Tainá Bevilacqua direct. Chile Francisco Gallardo Soto , Equeco Behind “Designation of Origin,” a 2025 B.O. phenom in Chile from Tomás Alzamora (“Little White Lie”) and now “The Chilean,“ playing Locarno’s Piazza Grande, a sign of its perceived broad audience appeal. At Match Me! with “Falling Waves,” set in a remote southern Chile fishing community where a teen girl’s secret entwines with environmental catastrophe. Suggesting “how guilt, faith, and reality begin to blur as the sea rots under the weight of an environmental collapse,” Reyes tells Variety . Catalina Miles, Villano Producer of “The Red Hangar,”a Malaga and Guadalajara top winner and sales hit , now at Locarno with “Champ,” from Pelayo Lira, behind Ventana Sur/Sanfic WIP “Kingdoms,” a millennial generation portrait. “Champ” is set in Chile, 2000. Samuel, 11, battles to enter an elite school after moving to a wealthy area. But in the race for success, he soon learns, every victory demands a sacrifice of identity. Denmark Mikkel Smidt, Napkin Productions Founded in 2025 by six producers from the same The National Film School of Denmark’s graduation class, pooling experience from Zentropa, Nordisk Film and Danish Documentary. Moving at Match Me! Its first feature film, Mone Frogg’s intriguing mystery drama “Glossy Pictures”: When a son brings his volatile, gambling-addicted mother to an isolated hotel, a casino jackpot and a sudden death pull him into an investigation that unravels everything he thought he knew about his mother. Giulia Triolo, Snowglobe A key European producer and co-producer involved in a dazzling lost of films from top filmmakers in Scandinavia, Latin America and beyond, such as Hlynur Pálmason (“Godland”), Joachim Trier (“The Worst Person in the World”), Gabriel Mascaro (“Divine Love”) and Christian Mungui’s 2026 Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord”). At Locarno with “Grasshoper,” turning on isfit Luka (15, she/they), a summer intern who finds in the blackberry-stained lips of curly-haired Frida — a tentative first love — a sense of belonging and path to their future. Dominican Republic Pablo Lozano, Sky Films ‘Gagá’ Courtesy of Sky Films Sky Films, founded by Pedro García and Rafael Llaneza, counts among its highlights the award-winning Berlinale screener “Ramona” and “The Godfather Part II” documentary “From Sicily to Santo Domingo.” At Locarno with “Gagá,” a documentary currently in post that follows Geo, a white Dominican, and Britis, a Black Haitian-Dominican — spiritual leaders, brothers of the road and keepers of sacred knowledge. “[B]ound since youth by an initiation the state doesn’t recognize, [they] embody the kinship that nationalist politics is working to erase,” says Lozano. Isaac Morantus, El Güeso Films ‘Camina Ven’ Courtesy of El Güeso Films Headed by Isaac Morantus and by Viviana Sánchez, El Güeso Films focuses on stories deeply rooted in Dominican culture but characterized by emotionally universal narratives. Recent works include Sánchez’s award-winning “Nueva Forma” and Morantus’ short “Camina Ven,” which he is now adapting into a feature film. The buddy road trip movie follows a young man seeking to confess his love to a girl before it’s too late. “‘Camina Ven’ is about finding the courage to speak before regret becomes permanent,” Morantus says. Estonia Inger Põder, Homeless Bob Production ‘Beyond the Visible Flowers’ Credit: Gabriela Urm Known for bold artistic choices, original stories, and auteur cinema, it says, such as Rainer Sarnet’s Tribeca title “November” and Locarno splash, the “zany” “ The Invisible Fight .” One of her Match Me! Projects: “Beyond The Visible Flowers,” where Anna investigates Paradise, a closed community where her mother shelters from her father, a PTSD victim during the Soviet-Afghan war. “The film examines how what happened in the war 35 years ago has affected one family today,” says writer-director Jaanika Arum. Laura Raud, Nafta Films ‘Think of Something Nice’ Courtesy of Nafta Films Founded in Tallinn in 2009, one of the Baltics’ biggest production companies, producing and providing services from offices in all three Baltic countries. Behind “Melchior the Apothecary.” At Locarno with “Think of Something Nice” (aka “The Bicycle Thief”), about Sigrit, 10, living in a small town. She receives a new bicycle for her birthday, only for it to be stolen the next day. The film’s central bilingual family is tender, funny, damaged and morally ambiguous, often all at once,” says Raud. Finland Hadi Nikzad, Lumina Films Helsinki-based Lumina Films, founded by Hadi Nikzad, focuses on character-driven, socially resonant arthouse cinema with international potential while also moving into genre. Recent titles include “The Lightning Rod,” selected for Cannes La Cinef, and Jussi Award winner “My Name Is Hope.” At Match Me! with “DOR,” a paranoid thriller about an Iranian-Finnish novelist in Helsinki who suspects she is being surveilled. “[W]hat interests me in ‘DOR’ is not the machinery of surveillance but what it does to intimacy,” Nikzad tells Variety . Pilvi Waltzer, Bufo Described as an “ambitious and thrill-seeking company” and headed by Misha Jaari and Mark Lwoff, Helsinki-based Bufo is behind such works as Aki Kaurismäki’s Berlinale Silver Bear Winner “The Other Side of Hope” and Cannes competition entry “Eagles of the Republic.” It’s moving “Something Rotten,” about a mixed-race Finnish man who believes his Libyan father abandoned him — until a video reveals the truth and unleashes a ghost, forcing him to face trauma and his own internalized racism. France Alice Perrault, Alabama Production Aiming to move from shorts to full-length titles, such as Miriam Fürniss-Yacoubi’s “The Peter Principle,” her feature follow up to the 17-minute English-language “After The Very End,” a Carte Blanche Canal+ Clermont Ferrand winner. It turns on a couple of thirty-year-olds facing an existential crisis through the ironic prism of the Peter Principle: the higher people climb, the less competent they become. This “is the next step in our shared ambition to create bold, internationally driven auteur cinema,” says Perrault. Anne-Laure Berteau, Because the Night Productions ‘Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance’ Courtesy of Because the Night Productions Founded by Berteau in 2018, its credits taking in Isidore Bethel’s debut “Liam” (Tënk) and Louise Groult’s “Gertrude and Yvan Party Hard” (France Télévisions). Now moving “Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance,” a doc feature remembering Arthur Douglas Thayer, who spent a lifetime crocheting creatures, shot by his wife, son and Daniel Hymanson as they organise an exhibition at the world’s busiest airport in Atlanta. “Shooting and editing become ways of rewriting their lives – of transforming sorrow into a story that transcends reality,” says Berteau. Gabriel Jumel, Belladone Films Normandy-based, behind auteur-driven fiction and documentary projects with strong social and political dimensions, such as Yannick Kergoat’s 2025 “Sarkozy-Gaddafi: The Scandal of All Scandals.” Now developing François-Xavier Rouyer’s “Half of the World,” about a fallen YouTube star who moves into an abandoned gated community in Switzerland and discovers she’s being watched by a mysterious intruder. A “contemporary genre film with elements of comedy, exploring surveillance, social media obsession, and the constant search for online validation,” says Juhel. Germany Alec Barth, Counterintuitive Film Behind 2023 Locarno winner “Critical Zone” and 2026 Visions du Reel screener “Opera of Horror and Salvation,” the company aims for “artistically uncompromising feature films.” At Locarno with Sina Ataeian Dena’s “Foxperson,” about an animal rights activist who, after rescuing an injured fox in Paris, is compelled to cross a moral line that transforms both himself and the city. “‘Foxperson’ explores how binary thinking can polarize a society until extreme decisions become acceptable — both politically and personally,” Barth tells Variety . Jasper Wiedhöft, Reynard Films ‘Jo of Montreal’ Courtesy of CMS Producer of Venice Days award-recipient “A Sad and Beautiful World” and the acclaimed “The Miserable Mother,” Reynard Films is partnering with Tabi360 and Creative Media Solutions on Ameen Nayfeh’s “Jo of Montreal,” about a spoiled 12-year-old gamer stranded in a remote Jordanian village. After meeting a shepherd, he rediscovers his roots and a passion for the village’s ancient heritage. The film offers a “universal theme of mentorship with a unique Levantine flavor,” says Nayfeh. It’s “Oscar-nominated ‘Theeb’ meets ‘Karate Kid,’ but without karate.” Melissa Byrne, Allergikerfilm, Nordpolaris ‘The West Was Never Waiting’ Courtesy of Allergikerfilm Repping Munich shingles Allergikerfilm and Nordpolaris, Melissa Byrne’s credits include Venice Critics’ Week opener “ Life is Not a Competition, But I’m Winning ” and Cannes Critics Week prize winner “‘Vaterland’ or a Bule Named Yanto.” At Match Me! she presents Justina Jürgensen’s “The West Was Never Waiting,” a female-led Western. Set amidst the greed of the 1860s gold rush, “the landscape becomes a state of mind and the action-packed journey into the Colorado wilderness unfolds as a descent into the human soul,” Jürgensen says. Italy Bruno Cristaldi, Eutropia Film Rome-based company Eutropia, headed by Bruno Cristaldi and Antonio Marzotto, aims to produce works that “inspire, provoke thought, and leave a lasting impact.” Current productions include upcoming docs “Reality is an Invitation” and “The Last Winner.” At Locarno, Eutropia presents “Manu e Vincenzina,” from Alessandro Borrelli, which follows two sisters who dream of snow-capped mountains while on the run from a Naples juvenile center. “A road movie about survival, sisterhood, and the fragile border between danger and hope,” they say. Camilla Gazzola, Amartia Film ‘Reborn’ Courtesy of Amartia Film Rome and Naples-based and behind Leone Balduzzi’s 2024 feature doc “Sting Like a Bee,” Amartia is moving “Reborn,” Francesco Pascucci’s doc feature made with Belgium’s Harald House and winner of a MIA Development Award and Italy’s 2025 Doc/it Women Award. It depicts a community of women forming deep emotional bonds with hyper-realistic silicone dolls resembling newborns. It asks a difficult question, Gazzola says. “What happens when our need for connection finds its answer in something that cannot respond?” Salvatore Lizzio, Revok Specializing in auteurist international co-productions, Revok’s recent productions include Giovanni C. Lorusso’s “Homo Sive Natura” and Marcello Di Noto’s “Pazzo & Bella.” At Locarno with Lorusso’s “Despite Evil” (“Malgré le mal”), about an elderly couple in La Reunión’s remote mountains waiting for a doctor impeded by an approaching cyclone. Facing their final farewell, they look back on their shared life. It’s an “intimate portrayal of love, loss, and mortality, told through visually powerful and emotionally restrained cinematic language,” says Lizzio. Latvia Grēta Grebže, Tasse Film Riga-based Tasse Film, best known for Berlinale Crystal Bear winner “ Mellow Mud ” and hit series “Soviet Jeans,” arrives in Locarno with Alise Zarina’s “Not My War.” It follows Lote, a young woman preparing for motherhood, but when war breaks out across the border, her carefully planned life is suddenly disrupted. “The main themes are the uncertainty we learn to live with, women in war as sort of outcasts and the future my generation faces in these turbulent times,” says Zarina. Līva Vernere, VFS Films ‘In The Truth’ Credit: Toms Harjo VFS Films boasts an award-winning slate of titles and international co-productions, including acclaimed docs “Bridges of Time” and “Redlight to Limelight.” At Locarno with Toms Harjo’s “In The Truth,” co-produced by Les Films d’Antoine. It follows 17-year-old Tom as he struggles to satisfy both his strict Jehovah’s Witness family and his own emerging sexual desires. Drawing from Harjo’s own experiences, it examines “a rarely seen religious community with intimacy and nuance” while “revealing the profoundly human desire to belong,” says Vernere. Lithuania Viktorija Rimkutė, Dansu Films ‘The Queen Of England Stole My Parents’ Courtesy of Dansu Films One of Lithuania’s biggest producers, co-producing “Agent Hamilton” and “Solomamma” and producing “Troll Farm,” at 2025’s Berlinale Series Market Selects. Now priming Ernestas Jankauskas’ “The Queen Of England Stole My Parents,” a semi fantasy fable exploring the challenges faced by foster parents when adopting Smiltė, a 10-year-old rebel with a vivid imagination. A Tallinn Co-Production Market favorite pitch award winner. Akvilė Žilionytė, Artišokai Developing documentary and fiction films rooted in personal stories with international relevance. Its first doc-feature, “In Passing,” premiered in 2025. Teaming with Poland’s MX35 on Nuruzzaman Khan’s “Where It Rains,” co-written by Žilionytė, about a Bangladeshi father living in Lithuania writing letters to his son, trying to bridge the distance between two cultures and two homes. “At first, I thought I was making a film to preserve my son’s childhood. Somewhere along the way, I realised I was also trying to preserve my own,” says Khan. Montenegro Ivan Marinović, Adriatic Western Nikola Đuričko stars in ‘The Educator’ Credit: Milan Josipović/Adriatic Western Founded by Ivan Marinović, Adriatic Western is behind award-winning films “The Black Pin” and “Forever Hold Your Peace.” At Locarno with “The Educator,” produced with Sense Production, a body-horror comedy about a teacher who remains drunk to suppress his inner monster. Chaos ensures when his pupil discovers the truth. It’s “a fresh take on the Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde myth,” exploring “what childhood feels like when the people meant to educate and protect you become the source of fear,” Marinović says. Miljan Vučelić, Protos Film Protos Film, headed by Miljan Vučelić, focuses on author-driven works, supports emerging filmmakers and develops projects with strong international potential. Recent features include “Comedown,” currently in post, and doc “About a Brother.” At Locarno with Đorđe Vojvodić’s development prize-winning “Nothing Will Be Named After Me,” produced with Bitter Frames, about a once powerful state official recovering from a stroke in his luxury hotel but trying desperately to retain power. It “moves from darkly comic character drama into psychological thriller,” Vučelić teases. Poland Julia Jendrysik, Rizz Films ‘Mother Daughter’ Courtesy of Rizz Films Warsaw-based Rizz Films, headed by Julia Jendrysik and Anna Majek, develops local works and international co-productions, including Tomasz Wróbel’s Fantasia short “The Noise of Waves.” It presents at Match Me! “Mother Daughter,” co-produced with WFDiF. Based on Mira Marcinów’s acclaimed novel, the film follows Rita, who’s forced to confront memories and trauma when her mother suddenly falls ill. While it explores difficult family themes “and the complexity of the mother-daughter relationship, it never loses its sense of humor,” Jendrysik tells Variety . Richard Karpala, Latarka Studio Latarka Studio, launched by Richard Karpala, saw debut film “Falling Stars” premiere at Locarno, where it’s now moving “Lektor.” About a foreign film voice-over narrator who, after the fall of communism, begins hearing his own voice in every foreigner he encounters. Now jobless, he discovers it’s an unexpected asset abroad. Focusing on a dubber was ideal “for a story set in the early ’90s” about a man who “has to adapt to the cultural and economic changes happening around him,” Karbala says. Korek Bojanowski, Amondo A Warsaw-based collective producing films and international co-productions,” Amondo is behind Warsaw screener “Hel” and Venice entry “The Hole in the Fence.” At Locarno with Bojanowski’s “The Art of Spitting.” Warsaw’s only superhero, Julek can fly but has never saved a single life. When a disastrous encounter is mistaken for a heroic rescue, he decides to expose the truth and the charade that is his life. “A portrait of millennial disappointment, wounded masculinity and the need to feel exceptional,” says Bojanowski. Portugal Ana Sofia Nunes, Jângal Studios “Focusing on emerging directors, with particular attention to new forms of storytelling and a commitment to diverse and distinctive voices,” says Nunes. Now developing “Capricorn Syndrome,” (“Síndrome de Capricórnio”), one of its first international co-productions, with Portugal’s David & Golias and Finland’s Films Films Films, “framing mental illness within a dystopian yet familiar reality, the film reflects on our growing search for certainty in an increasingly unstable world,” says director Miguel Munhá. Ana Almeida, Matiné Behind “Terra Vil,” its debut feature, a Tallinn Black Nights competition contender which closed distribution deals for Spain and The Netherlands, besides the production countries Portugal and Italy. Now backing murder mystery “Sacrifice Hill,” adapting Antonio Muñoz Molina’s same-titled short story, “a tense, serene and mysterious film noir,” says its director Luis Filipe Rocha, a 2017 Portuguese Academy Award original screenplay winner for “Grey and Black.” Spain David Aymerich, Ayhe Productions Tarragona-based, founded in 2020, behind divorce drama “March 14,” and making ambitious strong-identity auteur-driven films from a new generation of filmmakers. At Match Me! with “Cara Sucia,” about Bruno, a Black teenager, marked by skin vitiligo, sentenced to work at a residential home for minors with functional diversity. Unexpectedly, he finds a safe place where he can accept himself by embracing others. “A special coming-of-age story portraying a reality rarely seen on screen,” Aymerich says. Eva Bodas, Entre las Piedras One of Variety’s 2024 10 Emerging Spanish Producers, founding Madrid-based Entre las Piedras in 2022, “to produce bold, political films and giving voice to new filmmaker generations.” She hits Match Me! with “Laguna The Minister,” Antonio Llamas’ follow-up to DocumentaMadrid Audience Award winner “A Suburban Mythology.” An Atlántida – Mallorca Talents Lab laureate turning on a government minister who suddenly stops taking orders and disappear, it “addresses the visceral dissatisfaction with those who make decisions,” says Llamas. Jesús Chora Zataraín, Lazona Zinema Heading up Lazona Zinema, the Basque division of Lazona (“Spanish Affair,” “Gigantes”), which aims to “produce bold, risk-taking projects from emerging Basque voices and also large-scale productions and international co-productions,” he says. At Locarno with a banner new talent project, Ikusmira Berriak winner “La Koreana,” Basque writer-director Joana Moya feature debut, produced with Sirimiri Films, founded by Estibaliz Urresola, director of Berlinale winner “20,000 Species of Bees.” Another of Variety’s 2024 10 Emerging Spanish Producers. articles.title: Claes Bang Plays a Masseur of Nazi Leader Heinrich Himmler in ‘I Is Another’ — but John Paul in ‘Bad Sisters’ Is Still One of His ‘Worst Characters’
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 2:02am PT Claes Bang Plays a Masseur of Nazi Leader Heinrich Himmler in ‘I Is Another’ — but John Paul in ‘Bad Sisters’ Is Still One of His ‘Worst Characters’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Claes Bang Plays a Masseur of Nazi Leader Heinrich Himmler in ‘I Is Another’ — but John Paul in ‘Bad Sisters’ Is Still One of His ‘Worst Characters’ 54 minutes ago Locarno’s Alliance 4 Development Welcomes Queer Musical, Eco Body Horror and Bruce LaBruce’s Melodrama With Monica Bellucci and Béatrice Dalle 3 hours ago James Gray Says AI Is ‘Worthless’ and Young People Won’t Stand for It: They ‘Have a Real Hunger for Interesting, Honest Stuff’ 22 hours ago See All Claes Bang in ‘I Is Another’ (c) Anke Neugebauer_ostlicht Filmproduktion_Wega Filmproduktion Claes Bang plays Heinrich Himmler’s personal physical therapist in Locarno premiere “ I Is Another .” Directed by Felix Randau, it focuses on the true story of Felix Kersten. Kersten, who passed away in 1960, claimed to have saved numerous lives during the war due to his influence over the Nazi leader. However, many have disputed his claims. “It’s quite a wild story and for some reason it’s never been told,” Bang tells Variety . Related Stories Bella Thorne Is Also Directing and Writing the 'Spring Breakers' Sequel She's Starring In: 'From Start to Finish, It's Lit as F---’ Netflix Plans Week-Long 'Beef' Free Wellness-Centered FYC Events Throughout Los Angeles (EXCLUSIVE) “One of the worst characters I have embodied is probably John Paul in ‘Bad Sisters’ [the Apple TV+ series created by Sharon Horgan]. But I will always try to find something in there that I can relate to. With John Paul, it was his desire to protect his family and his belief that the other sisters were out to get him.” Popular on Variety With Kersten, it’s his search for validation. “He was trying to get the Nobel Peace Prize! He wanted people to say: ‘You were a good guy.’ It’s something I recognize, because I want people to like my work. I want people to go: ‘Wow, Claes, what you did in that play or that movie was really great.’ To some degree, we all want that. But it became his downfall.” In the film – sold by Beta Cinema and produced by Ostlicht Filmproduktion – an ambitious journalist (Valerie Pachner) wants to expose his lies. But she’s also hiding a few secrets of her own. “There were definitely people who were alive at the end of the war that would not have been alive had it not been for him. The problem is, he thought he hadn’t received enough credit for his actions, so he exaggerated them.” “I like it when a character’s actions don’t match what they present to the world. ‘The Square’ was a perfect example of that.” In Ruben Östlund Palme d’Or winner – and his breakout role – Bang played a respected curator whose perfect life starts to unravel after his phone is stolen. “He saw himself as a really good guy. He’s trying to put on this exhibition that’s supposed to say something about humanity, and then he goes and sends threatening letters to people. It makes me wonder: Why do we need that kind of validation? Why do we want fame, or for everyone to applaud us?” Kersten’s story and his ties to the Nazis made him a complicated historical figure. But Bang calls for compassion, not judgement. “I don’t think anyone can understand the terror you felt when you got a call to show up at the SS headquarters,” he notes. “If you didn’t obey, your whole family would be dragged out into the street and executed. He didn’t ask for this. Up until this point, he wasn’t a member of the Nazi party or had anything to do with the Nazis when he was summoned to meet Himmler.” Kersten became valuable when he was able to help Himmler with the severe stomach pains that had plagued him all his life. “What goes through your heart and your mind when you get a call to go and be part of it? In [another Apple series] ‘ The New Look ,’ I played a man who was the intermediary between the Nazi party and Coco Chanel. It’s a dark chapter in her story,” he adds. “Chanel is a French icon and Juliette Binoche [who played her] wanted to do her justice – she didn’t want to just hang her out to dry. That was one of the things we talked about: What did people know about the Nazi party’s atrocities when they were also keeping them a secret? People were just trying to survive while their country was at war.” He says: “It’s easy to say: ‘When Himmler offered him the job of being his masseur, why didn’t he just say no?’ But we can’t possibly fathom being in that situation.” “There’s evidence that Kersten helped people escape, but he was unhappy that, for example, he wasn’t mentioned in Count Bernadotte’s book [about the war]. He wanted to correct it and that got him into trouble.” It also confirmed his official affiliation to the SS. “It’s quite interesting when in the film, he realizes he’s now a part of it. O.K, I’m Heinrich Himmler’s masseur. Can I make something out of this that will actually do some good? I like when he asks: ‘How many human lives is a membership of the SS worth?’ Even though it’s impossible to answer.” Pima County Sheriff’s Department Made Several Mistakes During Search for Nancy Guthrie, New Report Claims Savannah Guthrie Posts New Video Urging Mother’s Kidnappers to ‘Do the Right Thing’: ‘Tell Us Where to Look for Her’ Savannah Guthrie Fights Back Tears While Responding to Note Claiming Her Mom Nancy Is Dead: ‘We’ll Never Stop Looking for Her, Ever’ Second Note Sent to Media Said Nancy Guthrie Was Dead Savannah Guthrie Says ‘I Cry Every Morning on the Way to Work’ While Her Mom Is Still Missing Loading comments... articles.title: Danny DeVito-Produced Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Boards Blue Finch Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 2:18am PT Danny DeVito-Produced Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Boards Blue Finch Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Vishal Bhardwaj Sets ‘Rashomon’-Style Film on Tarun Tejpal Rape Case After Bombay High Court Conviction (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago ‘The Traitors’ India Season 2 Unveils Trailer With Karan Johar and 21-Celebrity Cast (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Farhan Akhtar and Ritesh Sidhwani’s Excel Entertainment, AA Films Board Toronto Midnight Madness Malayalam Vampire Thriller ‘Half’ (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago See All Blue Finch Films Blue Finch Films has taken on international sales rights, outside North America, for the heist thriller comedy “ Drag ” from directors Greg Yagolnitzer and Raviv Ullman. The U.K. sales and distribution company plans to launch the title at the market during the Toronto Film Festival. Danny DeVito , Lucy DeVito and Jake DeVito produced the film, which premiered at SXSW 2026 to critical acclaim. Briarcliff Entertainment picked up North American distribution rights and is scheduled to open the film in U.S. theaters on Jan. 29, 2027. Related Stories 'The Batman 2' and 'The Batman 3' Are Not Filming Back-to-Back, Says James Gunn: 'I Can Deny' That Online Rumor Autlook Boards Barbara Kopple's ‘Union Town’ Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) The film stars Lizzy Caplan, Lucy DeVito, John Stamos and Christine Ko. Since its SXSW debut, “Drag” has continued its festival run with screenings at BiFan, Fantasia and Tubi FrightFest London. Popular on Variety The story follows two sisters with a strained relationship who target a house in rural upstate New York for a burglary. The heist goes wrong when one sister injures her back and ends up trapped on the second floor, setting off an increasingly frantic bid to get out before the homeowner comes home. “Drag” represents the first independent feature to come out of Jersey Films 2nd Avenue, the DeVito-founded production banner behind the animated FXX series “Little Demon” and the Prime Video sports docuseries “Game 7.” The label’s mission emphasizes distinctive creative voices and stories that defy genre convention. Blue Finch Films’ current sales slate also includes the Toronto Midnight Madness selection “Kick On,” the Fantasia titles “Attack On Paradise” and “Unholy Night,” and “Mission,” which is backed by BBC Film and Screen Scotland and stars George MacKay. articles.title: Bella Thorne Is Also Directing and Writing the ‘Spring Breakers’ Sequel She’s Starring In: ‘From Start to Finish, It’s Lit as F—’
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 2:23am PT Bella Thorne Is Also Directing and Writing the ‘Spring Breakers’ Sequel She’s Starring In: ‘From Start to Finish, It’s Lit as F—’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Minnie Driver Suffers Neck Injury in ‘Really Bad Car Accident’ and Says ‘I Am So Grateful to Be Alive’ 18 hours ago Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s ‘Rein Me In’ Becomes the U.K.’s Longest-Running No. 1 Single of All Time 7 days ago Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Raye Make Mercury Prize Shortlist 1 week ago See All Getty Images Bella Thorne is about to go full “ Spring Breakers .” The former Disney star has revealed that in addition to starring in an upcoming sequel to Harmony Korine’s 2012 cult classic, she’s also directing and writing the film. Variety exclusively announced the sequel and its cast in May 2025, which also includes “Stranger Things” breakout Grace Van Dien, Ariel Martin (“Zombies 2”) and True Whitaker (“I Love L.A.”). At the time, “Freeway” helmer Matthew Bright was attached to direct, but Thorne said in an interview on Alex Cooper’s “Call Her Daddy” podcast that she has now stepped into the director’s chair. Related Stories Cannes' Critics' Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets “The producers watched ‘Color Your Hurt,’ which is the movie that I just wrapped, an early cut of it. And they asked me to write something to see if they would like it,” Thorne said. “And they loved it! And now I’m writing and directing ‘Spring Breakers 2.'” Popular on Variety “Color Your Hurt” is Thorne’s directorial debut, described as a coming-of-age thriller that follows a young gay man seeking acceptance in a hostile community. Production wrapped on the film in October. Asked how her sequel will differ from the original, Thorne said that 2012 was “such an exploitative time and everyone was going through it,” adding that herself and fellow Disney kids Miley Cyrus, Zendaya and Selena Gomez — the last of which starred in the original “Spring Breakers” alongside Vanessa Hudgens, Ashley Benson and James Franco — were all “being compared of who was going to be that next bad girl.” “This time, things are different,” Thorne said. “They are crazy. There’s a lot of craziness, there’s a lot of litness. There is so much litness in this movie.” She added that “Spring Breakers 2” involves some of the original team, including Muse Productions’ Chris Hanley (“American Psycho,” “The Virgin Suicides”) and Jordan Gertner (“Bully”). Korine is not involved, and has previously said he has “no interest” in the sequel. “I don’t want to get in trouble, but what I can say is it is so litty, litty McTitties,” Thorne teased. “From start to finish, it’s lit as fuck. We are having fun. If you want to go to the theater and have fun, you’re going to have fun with this movie, that’s for sure.” Watch Thorne’s full “Call Her Daddy” interview below. articles.title: Werner Herzog to Be Honored at San Sebastián Film Festival
articles.full_text: Aug 7, 2026 2:59am PT Werner Herzog to Be Honored at San Sebastián Film Festival By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Bella Thorne Is Also Directing and Writing the ‘Spring Breakers’ Sequel She’s Starring In: ‘From Start to Finish, It’s Lit as F—’ 37 minutes ago Minnie Driver Suffers Neck Injury in ‘Really Bad Car Accident’ and Says ‘I Am So Grateful to Be Alive’ 18 hours ago Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s ‘Rein Me In’ Becomes the U.K.’s Longest-Running No. 1 Single of All Time 7 days ago See All Getty Images Prolific filmmaker Werner Herzog will receive the San Sebastián Film Festival’s prestigious Donostia Award during its 74th edition in September. The German director will be honored at the Spanish festival’s opening gala and will screen his latest film “Bucking Fastard,” following its world premiere at Venice Film Festival. “Over a career spanning six decades, Werner Herzog has become one of the most influential figures in contemporary cinema, building an extraordinary body of work ―around 80 films― shaped by obsession, extreme situations and the contradictions of human nature,” San Sebastián Film Festival said in a statement. “His films, both fiction and non-fiction, are populated by dreamers and conquerors confronted with extreme landscapes and forces beyond their control. Guided by his concept of ‘Ecstatic Truth,’ Herzog advocates a cinema that transcends the mere observation of facts to reveal a deeper, more poetic dimension of reality.” Related Stories Autlook Boards Barbara Kopple's ‘Union Town’ Ahead of Venice Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) After U.K. Approval of Paramount-WBD Deal, European Media Leaders Rally Behind David Ellison: 'The Industry Will Be Stronger' Regarded as a pioneer of New German Cinema, Herzog’s credits include “Aguirre, the Wrath of God” (1972), “Fitzcarraldo” (1982), “Grizzly Man” (2005) and “Cave of Forgotten Dreams” (2010). He was nominated for a best documentary Oscar in 2008 for “Encounters at the End of the World” and has won prizes at the Cannes, Berlin and Venice film festivals. Popular on Variety Starring sisters Rooney and Kate Mara, “Bucking Fastard” tells the “unusual story of twins whose extraordinary bond leads them to speak in unison, love the same man and share the same dreams,” according to its official synopsis. The San Sebastián Film Festival will take place from Sept. 18 to 26. articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Becomes Fastest Pic To Hit Half-Billion Mark At Domestic Box Office Read the full story By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Nielsen Set To Acquire Ad-Tech Firm DoubleVerify For $2.5 Billion Paramount-WBD Deal Endorsed By Lionsgate CEO Jon Feltheimer: “Uncertainty Is The Worst” Roku Posts Strong Q2 In Wake Of Fox Deal As Platform Revenue Jump Pushes It Past Wall Street Forecasts View All August 6, 2026 4:42pm Nielsen is paying $2.15 billion to acquire DoubleVerify, a provider of software that measures advertising performance. The all-cash acquisition will deliver shareholders of DoubleVerify $13.60 per share. Shares in the publicly traded company jumped nearly 14% in after-hours trading Thursday on the acquisition news. Nielsen has been privately held since 2022. Related Stories News Disney Closes $1.2 Billion Deal To Sell A+E Global Media Stake To Hearst News Lionsgate Sees Revenue Surge From ‘Michael’, ‘The Housemaid’ In June Quarter Nielsen was attracted to the deal as it looks to improve its ability to track streaming and work with programmers and advertisers reckoning with the ongoing shift from linear TV to streaming. While networks since the rabbit-ears days have complained about Nielsen’s methods, the company has been in the crosshairs numerous times during the streaming boom as its capabilities have faced scrutiny. The deal is expected to close by the first quarter of 2027, subject to approval by DoubleVerify shareholders and regulatory approval. Private equity firm Providence Equity Partners, which owns 12% of DoubleVerify, has agreed to vote in favor of the deal and plans to exit the investment after it closes. Watch on Deadline Nielsen CEO said in a statement that the transaction is in line with the “fundamental transformation” Nielsen has undergone in recent years. The company now aims to track “the full media lifecycle, from discovery and planning through measurement and outcomes; and strengthening our financial foundation. The result is a stronger, more agile Nielsen that has earned its place as a leading media intelligence platform for the modern advertising ecosystem.” DoubleVerify CEO Mark Zagorski called the acquisition “an exciting milestone.” The company will become “a private entity with the support of Nielsen,” gaining resources and opportunities to keep growing. articles.title: ‘Stuart’ Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Becomes Fastest Pic To Hit Half-Billion Mark At Domestic Box Office Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’ OG Return For WGA Strike Roast In Magic-Themed Episode 3 Where Wizards Seek “Residuals For Eternal Spells” ‘Stuart’ Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death Prime Video’s ‘Ride Or Die’ To Be Submitted As Comedy With Stars Hannah Waddingham & Octavia Spencer In Lead Actress Consideration For TV Awards View All August 6, 2026 6:30pm Story Arc (L-R): Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman, Brian Posehn and John Ross Bowie in Episode 3 of 'Stuart Fails To Save the Universe' HBO Max SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 3 of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe . Three episodes in, Stuart Fails To Save the Universe has brought back seven actors from the original show in addition to the spinoff’s leading quartet of Stuart (Kevin Sussman), Brian Posehn (Bert), Lauren Lapkus (Denise) and John Ross Bowie (Kripke), and has killed off two OG characters in two different universes. First, it was Kunal Nayyar’s opening episode who was shot dead by Kripke . In Episode 3, it is Wil Wheaton , killed with magic by another Stuart Fails To Save the Universe lead character, Bert. Related Stories News 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' Creators On Episode 2 Surprise OG Star Return & "Breaking Up" Beloved 'Big Bang Theory' Couple News 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' Stars On Stuart's Bold Move In Episode 2 As His Relationship With Denise Takes Off... What About Gary? Set in a world where magic is real and where, per the opening credits spoiler, “Bert is magic,” Wheaton is a representative of the Wizards Guild of America. He comes after Stuart for unwittingly enabling Bernadette (Melissa Rauch) to resume her demon form after she had been expelled from the guild and stripped of her magic powers. (You can read about Rauch’s return and Bernadette’s beef with the WGA here .) Bert shields Stuart from Wil’s deadly fireball, which leads to a magic fight to the death between the two that destroys most of the comic book shop and ends with Wil’s demise. (You can watch most of the scene below.) “I remember when the script was sent to me, and I was reading through it and not getting most of it because I hadn’t seen anything else,” Wheaton told Deadline. “We get to the magic shop, and I knew that I was going to be a wizard because I’d had a costume fitting, but I didn’t know anything about what it was going to be. What I see in the script is Wil Wheaton and Bert have an epic fireball fight, and I took a picture of it and I texted that picture to Bill and I just said ‘thank you.'” Wheaton spoke about the logistics of filming the fight, in which the Star Trek: The Next Generation alum also got to flash the Vulcan salute. “We had so much fun. Tom [Mahoney], the visual effects supervisor, and Brian and I really went through blocking and coordinating this entire fight sequence, and it was about like, well, how do you tease the fireball up in your hand, and how do you shape the fireballs in your hand?,” he said. “And for a particular kind of nerd, it’s a really big deal to be a wizard throwing a fireball, and to see that, like, I look so much cooler than I’ve ever looked ever in my entire life.” Wheaton revealed an Easter egg he had asked the show’s costume designer Valerie Klarich to incorporate into his costume — which she did. “The character that I play in Felicia Day’s series, The Guild , is Fawkes, he’s the leader of their rival guild. Felicia and I wrote a comic book together about him, and on the cover, there’s this really cool artwork that is Fawkes in a wizard’s robe with all these glowing runes on it. So Val said, ‘Do you have any requests for your costume?’ And I said, ‘If you could put some runes down the sides of the cloak, that would be really cool.’ And she said, ‘Yeah, we know a 3D printing guy who prints on fabric.’ So I got it.” He shared his reaction to the Fawkes-inspired cloak. “When I saw that, I was just like, there’s this great moment in Almost Famous where Lester Bangs says to the kid, ‘Oh no, they made you feel cool, and you’re not cool, so you’re trapped. They made me feel cool, and I’m not cool, and I was like, ‘This is an entirely fine place to be trapped.'” ‘Bert is magic” Posehn spoke of the cool and dark side of Episode 3 where Bert can do magic but he also is almost burnt at the stake for being a scientist. “People here think science is evil,” Kripke said about the magic-ruled alternate reality, to which Stuart responds in a rare topical comment on the show, “How is this different from our world?” “That was a funny episode, and then also that we play off it, where somebody goes, ‘In this world, science is forbidden,’ and Stuart goes, ‘Isn’t that kind of like our world?’ That joke I loved,” Posehn said. “But getting to be burned at a stake as a metalhead — it wasn’t a bucket list thing but getting to do it was super fun.” Posehn is known for his lifelong love for heavy metal which he has blended with stand-up comedy in his novelty comedy-metal tracks. There was another big draw for him in the episode. “I’m the biggest dog nerd you’re gonna meet, so having magic powers where I could make a puppy just transform out of nowhere — that was so fun to shoot,” he said. In the episode, Bert is asked by his acolytes to manifest life and he does it by conjuring up a puppy. “He was so excited about the dog, it was so cute,” Bowie said. “He was so, so pumped about the doggie they gave him.” Added Posehn, “Every time I had to be joyful when I said ‘Abracadabra puppy,’ it was like the easiest acting job I’d ever done because there was a puppy on my lap. So I’m like, ‘Hehehe, look at him! He’s adorable!’ That was super fun to play.” March of the Penguin In the episode, Bert also takes revenge on Kripke for not helping him when he was at the stake by turning him into a penguin sporting Kripke’s hair. Bowie spoke about the method acting involved in playing a penguin. “I went back to the the time in my life that I was a flightless waterfowl, and really went through a lot of sense memory on that,” he joked. “No, it was incredibly fun because I’ve never done mo-cap, I’ve never had one of those suits with the little buttons on them and the camera right in front of your face.” (L-R): Kevin Sussman, Brian Posehn and John Ross Bowie in Episode 3 of ‘Stuart Fails To Save the Universe’ There was some VFX wizardry involved in the transformation but also old-fashion practical special effects. “They built a mock-up of the comic book shop that was proportionally larger, and they put an elastic band around my knees so I had to waddle,” Bowie said. “It was really fun, and then the finished product looks amazing, and I love that he’s a penguin with my hair. I thought that was a really good choice to keep this magnificent coif on the penguin. Yeah, I enjoyed that a lot.” Q2 Revenue Surges With ‘Michael’; News On Sequel; CEO Backs Par-WBD Deal Sam Neill Filmed ‘Legend Of Zelda’ Role Before Death; Two Others Also In Cast Kit Connor Eyed For Cyclops Role In Disney/Marvel’s ‘X-Men’ Pic WBD Q2 Stumbles On ‘Supergirl’; Fox Corp Surges Thanks To World Cup Ads More from this Story Arc Stuart Fails To Save The Universe August 6, 2026 ‘Stuart Fails’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’ OG Return For WGA Strike Roast In Magic-Themed Episode 3 Where Wizards Seek “Residuals For Eternal Spells” July 30, 2026 ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Episode 2 Surprise OG Star Return & “Breaking Up” Beloved ‘Big Bang Theory’ Couple View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Stuart Fails’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’ OG Return For WGA Strike Roast In Magic-Themed Episode 3 Where Wizards Seek “Residuals For Eternal Spells”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Becomes Fastest Pic To Hit Half-Billion Mark At Domestic Box Office Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’ OG Return For WGA Strike Roast In Magic-Themed Episode 3 Where Wizards Seek “Residuals For Eternal Spells” ‘Stuart’ Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death Prime Video’s ‘Ride Or Die’ To Be Submitted As Comedy With Stars Hannah Waddingham & Octavia Spencer In Lead Actress Consideration For TV Awards View All August 6, 2026 6:30pm Story Arc (L-R): Kripke (John Ross Bowie) and Stuart (Kevin Sussman) visit 'Big Bang's Bernadette in Episode 3 of 'Stuart Fails To Save the Universe' HBO Max SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 3 of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe . Another episode of Stuart Fails To Save the Universe , another surprise — and dark — OG return. In Episode 3, it was Melissa Rauch reprising her role as Bernadette Rostenkowski. Like in Episode 2, where Penny, in an alternate universe, is with her former boyfriend Zack with no trace of her Big Bang husband Leonard, Bernadette does not have Howard’s last name and appears very much single. She is the focal point of a scene that skewers the 2023 WGA strike with “inside jokes that will be amusing to only 4,000 people in the world,” said Zak Penn , co-creator of the spinoff alongside Big Bang creators Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady . Related Stories News 'Stuart' Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Director Destin Daniel Cretton Talks Sadie Sink, That Ending & What Might Be Next The Episode 3 world is ruled by magic , so, to fix their broken alternate reality-hopping machine, Stuart (Kevin Sussman) and Kripke (John Ross Bowie) seek out Bernadette, a renowned local sorcerer. Turns out she is “all out of abracadabra.” What happened? “The Wizards Guild of America claimed I used my powers while we were on strike,” she explained. “What were you on stwike for?,” Kripke asked in his signature speech pattern where “r”s and “l” are replaced by “w”s. “Better dental, residuals for eternal spells. It’s ridiculous, we were out for six months, and basically everyone got a handful of magic beans,” Bernadette said. (You can watch the entire scene below.) For the uninitiated, the Wizards Guild of America shares the same moniker, WGA, with the Writers Guild of America, which Stuart Fails to Save the Universe creators are all members of. The 2023 WGA strike lasted five months with a minimum wage increase, viewership-based streaming residuals and AI protections among the gains in the new agreement with the studios. Melissa Rauch in Episode 3 of ‘Stuart Fails To Save the Universe’ Bernadette tells Stuart and Kripke that she was expelled from the guild for using her powers during the strike to bring her neighbor’s son’s adorable rescue dog Chocolate Chip back to life after he was hit by several cars. “I don’t see how that’s bweaking a stwike,” Kripke said. “Exactly,” Bernadette said, adding, “Let me tell you something about Wizards Guild of America. 90% of them don’t even work, and yet they get to vote.” While the percentage is not that high, non-working writers are the majority, representing more than 50% of the full WGA membership that gets to vote to authorize a strike and then to ratify a deal. That has been an ongoing gripe for some established writers and a cause of divide within the union. There was some difference of opinions among the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe creators too during a lively — and funny — interview with Deadline about the WGA strike jabs, which you can (and should) watch below. WGA members caught performing writing services during the strike get expelled, which happened again in 2023. Claiming that an appeal is not an option, Bernadette floats a reversal spell that would give her her powers back that requires “blood of an innocent,” which Stuart qualifies for and provides. Later in the episode, Big Bang ‘s Wil Wheaton shows up to reveal to Stuart that Bernadette is in fact a demon and is killed by Bert (Posehn) in a magic power duel. The episode ends with Bernadette, in a full-on demon form, terrorizing Pasadena and hunting for Stuart & Co. Lorre, Prady and Penn all participated in the 2023 strike and were on the picket lines. Penn has been the most active and public in his pro-WGA stance, having previously served on the WGA West Board of Directors and the union’s Negotiating Committee. (L-R): Bill Prady & Chuck Lorre during the 2023 WGA strike in front of a ‘Big Bang’ banner outside the Warner Bros. TV lot. DEADLINE: This seemed to me like I could hear Chuck’s voice, all the stuff about Wizards Guild of America. Chuck, you write that speech? And is this what you really think about this writers strike? LORRE : (laughing). PRADY : Oh, this is the Wizards Guild of America, an entirely different organization of wizards. LORRE : Of wizards, yes. The wizards are striking for all the good reasons, and strike breaking is… PRADY : It’s possible that section may include some inside jokes that will be amusing to only 4,000 people in the world. PENN : Also, we have different opinions on this issue, I’d like to say. There’s a continuum of opinions about those issues, but the joke, it can’t be pro-WGA and still be funny. Although let me point out, the WGA rep is right because she is a demon. PRADY : That’s right, Zak is right. The Wizards Guild of America is entirely correct in this episode. LORRE : She broke the strike by bringing Chocolate Chip back to life. PRADY : That’s a lie, that whole chocolate chip story is a lie. PENN : Yeah, she’s a demon. PRADY : She’s a demon. LORRE : Well, yes, but she was also using her powers, and she was supposed to not use her powers during the strike, right? PRADY : Well, we have a different understanding of the episode. I think that entire story is made up. LORRE : Oh, I don’t. PRADY : She makes up that story to get them to give her the blood. I think she made up the whole thing. PENN : You’re getting a little taste of the writers room. With her Demonic transformation, Rauch added a whole new shade of dark to Big Bang alums’ returns for the spinoff, following Kaley Cuoco’s ruthless Penny in Episode 2 and Kunal Nayyar’s deeply depressed Raj in Episode 1. The series’ creators spoke about Big Bang OGs relishing going dark in the spinoff. “Beyond,” Prady said. Added Lorre, “Beyond. It was fun to do something different, that was part of the promise, come and play with us, and we’ll make sure that you’re playing a version of your character you never got to play before, an entirely different approach to the character, and that was fun for the actors.” Q2 Revenue Surges With ‘Michael’; News On Sequel; CEO Backs Par-WBD Deal Sam Neill Filmed ‘Legend Of Zelda’ Role Before Death; Two Others Also In Cast Kit Connor Eyed For Cyclops Role In Disney/Marvel’s ‘X-Men’ Pic WBD Q2 Stumbles On ‘Supergirl’; Fox Corp Surges Thanks To World Cup Ads More from this Story Arc Stuart Fails To Save The Universe August 6, 2026 ‘Stuart’ Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death July 30, 2026 ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Episode 2 Surprise OG Star Return & “Breaking Up” Beloved ‘Big Bang Theory’ Couple View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments
