articles.title: Isabella Rossellini Talks Lynch, ‘Green Porno’ and How Animals Became Her Favorite ‘Muses’: ‘They Fascinate Me’
articles.full_text: Aug 6, 2026 2:26am PT Isabella Rossellini Talks Lynch, ‘Green Porno’ and How Animals Became Her Favorite ‘Muses’: ‘They Fascinate Me’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Isabella Rossellini Talks Lynch, ‘Green Porno’ and How Animals Became Her Favorite ‘Muses’: ‘They Fascinate Me’ 2 hours ago ‘Gagarine’ Directors Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh Talk ‘The Green Eyes’ as Kinology Announces First Sales: ‘Dreamers Know No Borders’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Locarno’s StepIn Focuses on ‘Power, People, Data and the Future of Film’: ‘The Counter-Algorithm Is a Human Being Who Gives a Damn’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago See All Credit: Edoardo Nerboni Isabella Rossellini has received the Excellence Award at Locarno. “The prize I’m receiving tonight is for excellence, which is something I haven’t heard very often,” she said during the opening ceremony. “I’m very proud of it and, above all, so moved because my father received this back in 1948 for his film ‘Germany, Year Zero.’ And then, four years ago, my brother Renzo [Rossellini], who was a great producer of Fellini and Scola. Being on par with my father and my brother fills me with so much emotion.” Related Stories Cannes' Critics' Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets During her masterclass at the fest, Rossellini – who holds a master’s degree in Animal Behavior and Conservation – also opened up about her popular web series “Green Porno” and “Seduce Me,” about animal mating rituals. Popular on Variety “I know nothing about computers. I don’t speak that language, so I made these films the way I knew how: super low-tech. I watched a lot of [Georges] Méliès. It was a no-tech technique. Animals, to me, they fascinate me. I have a farm and when I decided to make films myself, they became my muses,” she said. She is now developing a new series of shorts about the evolution of domestic animals. “It’s called ‘The Survival of the Friendliest.’ We always focus on the survival of the fittest, but this one is so important.” She will play all the roles. But she would like to concentrate on directing more in the future. “I am just fascinated by biology and diversity. When someone says: ‘It’s against nature to be gay or trans’ — it’s not! I don’t sit down to write something political or poetic, but I discover that earthworms are hermaphrodites. I am just always so surprised. That’s my inspiration – not politics.” She can’t ignore the ongoing political situation in the U.S., however. “It’s difficult right now and we are thinking of going back, but I have sheep, chickens, I have land. Should I abandon everything? For now, I’m staying. I just hope things will improve,” she said, answering a question from the audience. “My first passion was animals. Even when I was a kid, I would take stray dogs and take them home.” Still, she had to follow her second passion first – for a while, she worked on her father’s films as a costume designer. When her mother, Ingrid Bergman, was offered a film in Rome, “A Matter of Time,” she ended up playing a small role in it, too. “Just to spend some time with my mum! I didn’t think I would become an actress.” Discouraged by early critics, she pursued modeling and journalism, too. “When you are criticized publicly, as it happened with ‘The Meadow,’ it’s really hard. Being successful in the fashion world really reassured me. I worked with Avedon, and he told me: ‘Models are like silent movie stars. You have no lines, but I shoot the emotion.’ I was asked to be in films, maybe because I was Ingrid Bergman’s daughter, and I said: ‘Why not’?” She recalled meeting David Lynch for the first time to discuss her role in “Blue Velvet,” released in 1986. “I met David at a restaurant. We were both there with members of the De Laurentis family, and we joined the tables. He said: ‘You look like Ingrid Bergman.’ They said: ‘You idiot, she is her daughter!’ When I got the script, there was a note: ‘Why don’t you read it and tell me if you want to play this character. I loved it, but it was so controversial. I asked him if I could rehearse the scenes to see if my interpretation matches his [vision]. He said: ‘You got it right.’” “David was not so famous back then, and he really showed his mysterious world there. The plot was not so important. Some hated it and some loved it.” Composer Angelo Badalamenti helped her as well. “It sounds like I sing very well, but that’s movie magic.” Later, she went on to work with Robert Zemeckis, David O. Russell, Taylor Hackford and James Gray on “Two Lovers.” Gray is also celebrated at Locarno this year. “He was very nice. Joaquin Phoenix was more difficult, because he followed method acting back then. I come from neorealist cinema, where you always hurry and worry about money – and James didn’t have any. And Joaquin, when there was a scene where he had to sleep, said: ‘I have to sleep for real.’ I was so worried.” she laughed. She also praised “magical” Alice Rohrwacher – she worked with her on “La Chimera” – and was nominated for an Academy Award as Best Supporting Actress for Edward Berger’s “Conclave.” “I never think about someone’s ‘style.’ I think about what I want to say.” “When I turned 42, Lancôme didn’t renew my contract because I was ‘too old’. They took me back 20 years later, but it was a difficult moment. I wasn’t working that much as an actor, either. It just stopped. I was told that middle-aged women had no audience. I started making my films and then things have changed – maybe our society has changed its opinion on middle-aged women. I overcame that moment thanks to my curiosity. I also have to credit Robert Redford, who told me: ‘You can be a director’.” Redford was the one who asked her to create something for Sundance Channel. She added: “The thing is, I did everything late. Maybe because my parents were so well-known? I became a model when I was 27 years old, 22 when I started acting, I earned my master’s degree when I was 55 and I became a director in my 50s. I would have liked to start everything earlier, because I’m always 10 years too late!” NBCU’s Peacock Limited-Ads Tier Launches on YouTube Primetime Channels Jesse Eisenberg on Why It Would Be ‘Silly’ to Leave U.S. Because of Trump, Says ‘The Debut’ Is ‘The Opposite of AI’ Following A24 DeepMind Partnership Peacock to Be Included in YouTube Premium Subscription Bundle Starting in 2027 Olivia Wilde’s ‘The Invite’ Nears $40 Million Globally, Becoming a Rare Hit Summer Comedy ‘Ponies’ Canceled After One Season at Peacock ‘Backrooms’ Extended Version Coming to Theaters With 15 Minutes of Bonus Footage Loading comments... articles.full_text: Aug 6, 2026 4:02am PT Warner Bros. Discovery Q2 Profit Slumps on NBA Ads, Movie Schedule, Write-Downs By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Disney Says Commercials for Super Bowl LXI Have Sold Out 22 hours ago Disney, TikTok Strike Content-Sharing Deal Aimed at Boosting Short-Form Programming on Disney+ 1 day ago Paramount Q2 Profit Dips, With Streaming Boost Offset by TV Declines 2 days ago See All Getty Images Warner Bros. Discovery has a great story to tell about its streaming business –if only its other operations didn’t get in the way. The parent of HBO, TNT and the Warner Bros. movie studio said net income in the second quarter fell significantly as growth at its new-tech streaming operations was more than offset by the continued erosion of its cable-TV networks and a weaker studio lineup than in the year-earlier period. TV ad sales fell 22% due to Warner’s loss of NBA games after the 2025 season, and TV distribution revenue fell due in part to a 10% decrease in the number of subscribers to its networks. Related Stories Cannes Critics’ Week Film 'Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building' Sells to Strand Releasing for North America (EXCLUSIVE) France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets Total revenue fell 11% to $8.7 billion, compared with $9.8 billion in the year-earlier period. Net income attributable to the company fell to $149 million from $1.58 billion, partially the result of $1.1 billion of pre-tax acquisition-related amortization of intangibles, content fair value step-up, and restructuring expenses. Popular on Variety Warner is in a difficult spot. It needs to continue to manage its operations even though it has agreed to be purchased by Paramount Skydance. While the proposed deal has won approval in multiple countries, it has been held up in federal court by a coalition of 12 attorneys general who are making the case that the combination of the two media companies would create an entity that would be in violation of antitrust law in areas such as movie production and the operation of cable television properties. The case will not come to trial until next year. Even so, Warner had some bright spots to show off. Streaming revenue rose above $3 billion for the first time, thanks to an increase of 10% that was aided by expansion of HBO Max in various markets around the globe. In a move that counters conditions at its TV networks, Warner said advertising and distribution revenue increased noticeably at its streaming venues, with distribution fees up 11% and ad revenue up 8%. The owner of MS NOW , CNBC and USA said net income fell to $211 million from $302 million in the year-earlier quarter, a decline of $91 million. The company cited lower revenue, the costs of operating as a public company, interest expense following its separation from Comcast, and increased tax expense tied mostly to the divestiture of SportsEngine, an online sports management software company that was sold in May. In recent weeks, it has expanded Fandango into a broader consumer entertainment platform, and made progress on new subscription projects at both CNBC and MS NOW. “Together, we believe these initiatives build on the foundation of our portfolio, deepen consumer engagement, and position Versant for long-term growth,” said Mark Lazarus , the company’s CEO. Popular on Variety Revenue in the second quarter fell 3.8% to $1.64 billion. Distribution fees fell 6.3% in the second quarter, largely due to subscriber declines. Ad revenue was off 0.6%, compared with a decline of 13% in the year-earlier quarter, reflecting improvements in ratings at some of its networks. Revenue from platforms, which include many of Versant’s direct to consumer businesses, rose 0.8%, due to higher revenue at Fandango and GolfNow. Versant said it was confident in its near-term future, raising revenue and cash-flow projections for the second half of the year. articles.title: Festival In Focus: Edinburgh Chief Paul Ridd On How The Event Is Becoming A “Legitimate Launchpad” For New & Established Filmmakers
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Edinburgh’s Industry Programme Returns With High-Profile Names & UK Indie Focus Festival In Focus: Edinburgh Chief Paul Ridd On How The Event Is Becoming A “Legitimate Launchpad” For New & Established Filmmakers Haile Gerima Dissects His 10 Hour Documentary Feature ‘Black Lions – Roman Wolves’ & Teases His Next Project On America’s Black Maroons View All August 5, 2026 11:47pm Mission. Edinburgh International Film Festival. This year, the Edinburgh International Film Festival will debut 21 feature films, 10 of which will screen as part of the festival’s official competition strand, which is set to run from August 13 to 19. Titles competing for the festival’s Sean Connery Prize include Mission , the latest feature from Scottish filmmaker Paul Wright ( For Those In Peril ), starring George MacKay and Rosy McEwen (Blue Jean ). The film has been described as the “punk exploration” of an alienated young man who throws off the shackles of his solitary life in an attempt to experience the highs and lows of existence at its most extreme. Also screening in competition is The Mad World of Harvey Kurtzman, a documentary feature about the American cartoonist and editor Harvey Kurtzman. The film includes contributions from Terry Gilliam, the late Stan Lee and Robert Crumb. And Little Miss Sunshine producer Marc Turtletaub returns to feature filmmaking with Borges and Me , his first feature as a director since 2023’s Jules . The film is an adaptation of Jay Parini’s bestselling memoir. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Revealed: The Early-Stage Plans For A New TV Festival In Edinburgh Festivals Christine Vachon, Ewan McGregor & Sarah Brocklehurst Among Names Set For Edinburgh Film Festival's 2026 Industry Programme This year’s edition also marks Festival Director Paul Ridd ’s third at the helm. Ridd joined Edinburgh from Picturehouse in 2023, where he last served as head of acquisitions. “In these two past editions, we’ve created a festival with the competition strands at its core. They really have an identity now,” Ridd tells Deadline, adding that this year the festival has a record number of world premiere titles. The increase, he explains, best illustrates how Edinburgh has carved out a position for itself on the busy festival calendar. “We’re a legitimate launchpad for new and emerging filmmakers as well as established voices,” Ridd explains. “We have 10 films in competition each year, and last year seven of those 10 films went on to get distribution in the UK, U.S., or both.” One of those titles was Elliot Tuttle’s much-talked-about feature Blue Film , which debuted at last year’s festival before landing in UK cinemas via Peccadillo Pictures and the U.S. with Obscured Releasing. The film follows a fetish camboy (Kieron Moore) who accepts a private house call, only to discover his masked client is his former middle-school teacher and a convicted sex offender. Blue Film landed positive notices from critics out of Edinburgh and upon its theatrical release. Deadline’s critic Damon Wise described the film as a “very deftly played two-hander.” But shortly after the Edinburgh screening, Tuttle revealed the film had been turned down by every major festival it had been submitted to because of its subject matter. So why did Ridd and Edinburgh take a chance on the feature? “It was just a film that embodied in many ways the things we value and think are important,” Ridd says. “It was made on a micro budget outside of traditional systems. It was made on a controversial subject and was beautifully acted. We saw it in those terms when we watched it.” The Incomer, the debut feature from Edinburgh-born filmmaker Louis Paxton, will open this year’s festival. Set on a remote Scottish island and starring Domhnall Gleeson ( Ex Machina ), the film follows siblings Isla (Rankin) and Sandy (O’Rourke), who have lived in peaceful isolation for decades, hunting seabirds, chatting to mythic creatures, and defending their isle from dreaded Incomers. The official synopsis reads: “Their world is upended with the arrival of Daniel (Gleeson), an awkward council worker, tasked with uprooting them to the mainland.” Louise Lockwood’s debut documentary feature Bel will close the festival. The film tells the story of Beldina Odenyo, the Kenyan-Scottish musician who performed under the stage name Heir of the Cursed. After Since Yesterday: The Untold Story of Scotland’s Girl Bands , a documentary feature on Scottish girl bands from the 1960s to the present in 2024, and Paul Sng’s Irvine Welsh doc Reality Is Not Enough , in 2025, Bel will be the third documentary on Scottish artistry to close Edinburgh in as many years. Ridd says the trend is “completely unintentional.” “We’re always looking for something to close the festival with the right spirit behind it, and it’s always a very difficult process,” he says. “It’s just very nice that in the last three years we’ve done three films which, in different ways, talk about artistic integrity and creation in ways that feel kind of interesting and innovative.” With a smile, he adds: “But that is not to say that next year we’re absolutely guaranteeing that we’re going to close with a film about a Scottish artist.” Elsewhere, Iranian filmmaker Abdolreza Kahani returns to Edinburgh with his latest feature Empty Heaven . The filmmaker was in competition last year with Mortician , which won the Sean Connery Prize. He used the £50,000 cash prize to fund Empty Heaven. In the Out of Competition strand, films screening include Carlos Conceição’s Bodyhackers , Molly Manners’ Extra Geography, Nicolas Winding Refn’s latest Her Private Hell , and Gregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex . This year, Edinburgh also launches its honorary Outstanding Contribution to Cinema Award, which will be handed to actor and director Kenneth Branagh. The festival’s midnight madness strand continues with Chee Keong Cheung’s Bad Day at the Office , starring John Hannah, opening and Daniel Goldhaber’s latest feature, Faces Of Death , starring Barbie Ferreira ( Euphoria ) and Charli xcx, closing the strand. The EIFF lineup also features seven retrospective screenings, including a 30th-anniversary celebration of Trainspotting at Leith Theatre, with live cast and crew commentary, followed by DJ sets by Irvine Welsh and Darren Emerson. “This is the first time something like this has been done on this scale, certainly in terms of the number of people who will be in the room watching it,” Ridd says of the live commentary event. “It’s really designed to emulate the format that was so popular with DVD commentaries, providing an opportunity for cast and crew to reflect on memories of making the film, or to just banter with one another.” Edinburgh has yet to confirm which members of the film’s cast and crew will participate in the live commentary session; however, the film’s lead Ewan McGregor is confirmed for one of the festival’s industry in conversation sessions, so it is safe to speculate he will be present at the Leith Theatre. When asked whether director Danny Boyle might be present, Ridd smiles and deflects: “We’ve got some great people lined up,” he says. “I think it’s going to be beautiful.” Kelley & Reeves’ ‘Bonfire Of The Vanities’ Series Scrapped At Apple TV, Will Be Shopped Regal CEO Backs Par-WBD Merger; Trial “Creates More Uncertainty & Distraction” Swings To $42M Tuesday Record, Now Biggest Pic Globally Of 2026 Scribes Aren’t Spinning A Tale This Time: Jobs Really Have Plummeted In Past Decade Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Edinburgh’s Industry Programme Returns With High-Profile Names & UK Indie Focus
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Festival In Focus: Edinburgh Chief Paul Ridd On How The Event Is Becoming A “Legitimate Launchpad” For New & Established Filmmakers Haile Gerima Dissects His 10 Hour Documentary Feature ‘Black Lions – Roman Wolves’ & Teases His Next Project On America’s Black Maroons ‘West Side Familia’: Taylor Hosking On Crafting A New West Side Story With Her Feature Debut About Puerto Rican Biker Gang View All August 5, 2026 11:47pm EIFF CEO Paul Ridd and Festival Producer Emma Boa. Credit: Eamonn McCormack. The Edinburgh Film Festival’s industry programme returns this year in an expanded format, centered around a new symposium on the state of independent filmmaking in the UK, aptly titled the UK Film Conference. The festival launched the conference earlier this summer and tapped BFI CEO Ben Roberts as the inaugural keynote speaker. Roberts will take part in an onstage In Conversation session with Picturehouse Creative Director Clare Binns. The conference will run for one day, Saturday, August 15, and was born, Edinburgh director Paul Ridd explains, out of the increasing strength of the festival’s competition strands. “We’re showing work that’s not been seen anywhere else in the world before, which is the driver for industry and press,” Ridd explains, “and if you’ve got those people in town, having a really good moment during the festival to build something where people can talk about the current state and future of independent cinema felt like an opportune moment.” Related Stories News Revealed: The Early-Stage Plans For A New TV Festival In Edinburgh Festivals Christine Vachon, Ewan McGregor & Sarah Brocklehurst Among Names Set For Edinburgh Film Festival's 2026 Industry Programme Alongside the conversation between Roberts and Binns, the UK Film Conference will feature ‘Low Budget, High Ambition’, a session focused on low-budget filmmaking and how UK producers are adapting to an ever-changing landscape. That session will be followed by ‘Would This Get Made?’, an innovative concept that will feature industry professionals being quizzed on how they would approach the production of a range of projects from the past if they came across their desks in 2026. Watch on Deadline “We’ll be asking the speakers, would you make Trainspotting today? Or Four Weddings and a Funeral ?” Ridd says of the unique concept. “It will be a really fun way to look at how these different individuals and organizations think about what their purpose is and what kind of things they’re making now.” Speakers on the panel, hosted by Wendy Mitchell, will include producer Christine Vachon, Stefanie Fahrion (Film4), Alice Ojha (BBC Film), Laura Wilson (Altitude) and Simon Renshaw (Casarotto Ramsay & Associates). The EIFF Industry Talk session ‘New Nightmares’, hosted by horror content creator Chris Mayo (Big Fat Cult ), will conclude the UK Film Conference with speakers discussing the current state of genre filmmaking. Speakers include actor and filmmaker Max Minghella ( The Handmaid’s Tale ) and filmmakers Prano Bailey- Bond ( Censor ), Chee Keong Cheung ( Bad Day at the Office ) and Joby Stephens ( Abandoned ). “In the long term we’re hoping to sort of grow out and build something that potentially feels more open to works in progress or more market premieres,” Ridd says of Edinburgh’s industry offering, which has expanded rapidly since he took the helm in 2023. Ridd is a former acquisitions head at Picturehouse and well-liked among industry folk, which has undoubtedly been useful in attracting high-profile names to the festival. Recent visitors and EIFF industry program participants have included Andrea Arnold, Nia DaCosta, David Hinojosa, and Ken Loach. Beyond the UK Film Conference, high-profile industry guests this year include Ewan McGregor, Bruce Dern, and veteran documentary filmmaker Ken Burns, who will take part in career Q&A sessions, while Kenneth Branagh will be handed the inaugural EIFF Outstanding Contribution to Cinema Award. Burns will arrive in Edinburgh following the UK broadcast of his American Revolution docuseries. The series screened on PBS in the U.S. last November. “We were fortunate in that Ken had already been invited to Edinburgh by the wider International Festival to take part in another event earlier in the month,” Ridd explains. “When we heard that was happening, we jumped at the opportunity to have him at our festival too.” Another early addition Ridd made to the Edinburgh industry lineup was the NFTS Sean Connery Talent Lab. The scheme features 25 filmmakers who are chosen to work on a short project with support from BBC Film. Each team received a £25,000 production budget. The first set of shorts created from the Lab debuted at last year’s festival. This year’s shorts are Bubbles (writer/director Jagoda Tlok); Shutterbug (writer/director Fin Bain); My Little Blue Heart (writer/director Iqbal Mohammed); PANG (writer/director Lara Delmage); St Anthony (writer/director Declan Dineen) and The Angel in the House (writer/director Missy McNaught). Elsewhere, filmmaker Paul Sng will chair an industry talk titled ‘Unmaking the Colonial Gaze in Cinema’ on the generational impacts of colonialism on the moving image. Outgoing BFI Filmmaking Fund Director Mia Bays will chair EIFF’s ‘Business of Film Roadshow’, a session on the filmmaking business, featuring speakers from film financier Head Gear and the law firm Lee & Thompson. EIFF will also once again host its annual session on navigating early career filmmaking with BIFA Springboard. The panel will feature BIFA Springboard alumni, who will discuss their journeys graduating from their first to second feature. The EIFF and the wider Edinburgh Fringe Festival, the Scottish capital’s historic performing arts event, have also continued their partnership for another year. “We’re a completely independent entity, so we run our own business, but we are very invested in partnering and collaborating with Edinburgh institutions like the Fringe,” Ridd says. “We sell tickets through the Fringe app. We work through their channels to promote events, and we find ways to incorporate elements from other programs like hosts from other festivals presenting at our events.” With the EIFF, Fringe Festival, Edinburgh Book, Art and International Festivals, the Scottish capital’s population more than doubles to over one million during the month of August. This year, city officials are prepping for widespread disruptions as Princes Street, the city’s main thoroughfare, will be partially closed following a fire at a former department store. City officials have said their safety and preservation works are expected to take several weeks to complete. Ridd expects minor disruptions to EIFF’s work. “Obviously, these are all things that are outside our control, and when it comes to putting on a large-scale event in the middle of a very busy city at the height of its busyness of the year, everybody’s kind of aware of the challenges that we’re going to face,” he says. “Fortunately, being part of an organization like Festivals Edinburgh, we’re able to get a head start on the plans, but it’s just something people are going to have to factor in as well.” He adds: “I have confidence that we’re going to be able to run an effective and beautiful festival. The 2026 Edinburgh Film Festival will run from August 13 to 19. articles.title: Michelle Yeoh Named As Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Filmmaker Of The Year
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ReelShort On Course To Reach $1BN Revenue & First Profit In 2026 – MPA Report Michelle Yeoh Named As Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Filmmaker Of The Year Warner Bros Korea Sets September Release For ‘The Intern’ Remake, Starring Choi Min-sik & Han So-hee View All August 6, 2026 12:41am Michelle Yeoh Busan International Film Festival Michelle Yeoh has been named ‘Asian Filmmaker of the Year’ at the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF). The annual award honors an Asian film professional or organization for exceptional contributions to the advancement of Asian cinema. The festival commented: “Versatile, commanding, and fiercely resolute – Michelle Yeoh’s performances are transcendent in every aspect: technique, style, and presence. Yeoh revolutionized the representation of women in action cinema, establishing herself as one of Hong Kong cinema’s defining stars. “As the first Asian to win the Academy Award for Best Actress, she continues to move boldly between Asia and Hollywood, captivating global audiences with her magnetic screen presence and profound emotional depth.” Related Stories News Mouly Surya, Reza Rahadian & Prasanna Vithanage Among Filmmakers Selected For Busan's Asian Project Market News Award-Winning Kyrgyz Drama 'Kurak' Denied Censor Certificate On Eve Of Bishkek Film Festival Screening Born in Malaysia, Yeoh started her career in Hong Kong cinema with Yes, Madam! (1985), followed by iconic titles such as Police Story 3: Supercop (1992) and Wing Chun (1994), challenging the patriarchal conventions of the action genre along the way. Watch on Deadline She gained international recognition through Bond movie Tomorrow Never Dies (1997) and Ang Lee’s Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000), a rare non-English-language film to achieve both global box-office success and widespread critical acclaim. Her international career further developed with roles in Crazy Rich Asians (2018), Shang-Chi And The Legend Of The Ten Rings (2021), Wicked (2024), and Everything Everywhere All At Once (2022), which earned her the Academy Award for Best Actress as well as top honors at the SAG Awards and Golden Globes. She was also recently the first Asian woman to receive the Honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival. “With exceptional charisma, Yeoh forged a new image of the action heroine while continually exploring works ranging from genre films and arthouse cinema to musical comedies,” Busan said in a statement. “Transitioning seamlessly from grounded, relatable everyday characters to a powerful, timeless persona, Yeoh possesses a remarkable versatility, delivering performances with delicacy but never fragility. Her dynamic and memorable characters continue to inspire new generations of actors and filmmakers. Through consistently nuanced performances that defy boundaries of age and convention, her singular body of work proves how an actor can expand the very imaginative horizons of cinema.” Yeoh’s connections with BIFF date back to 2002 when she visited the festival for the Pusan Promotion Plan (PPP, now known as the Asian Project Market). Many of her films have screened at the festival, including Far North (2007), Reign Of Assassins (2010), The Lady (2011), Master Z: The Ip Man Legacy (2018) – which played as the closing film of the 23rd BIFF – and Everything Everywhere All At Once (2022). She last attended the festival and walked the red carpet in 2011 with Luc Besson’s The Lady , in which she played the Burmese leader Aung San Suu Kyi. At this year’s Busan (October 6-15), a Special Program in Focus will present three films personally handpicked by Yeoh: Reign Of Assassins , Everything Everywhere All At Once , and Sandiwara (2026). Her latest feature, It’s My Time (2026), will also be screened. ‘The Asian Filmmaker of the Year’ award will be presented at the festival’s Opening Ceremony at the Busan Cinema Center on October 6. Previous recipients of the award have included Jafar Panahi (2025), Kurosawa Kiyoshi (2024), Chow Yun Fat (2023), and Tony Chiu-Wai Leung (2022). articles.title: ReelShort On Course To Reach $1BN Revenue & First Profit In 2026 – MPA Report
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ReelShort On Course To Reach $1BN Revenue & First Profit In 2026 – MPA Report Michelle Yeoh Named As Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Filmmaker Of The Year Warner Bros Korea Sets September Release For ‘The Intern’ Remake, Starring Choi Min-sik & Han So-hee View All August 6, 2026 1:59am ReelShort Founder Joey Jia speaking at APOS Media Partners Asia Microdrama platform ReelShort is on track for a 34% increase in revenue to $1.05BN in 2026, according to a report from Asia-based analytics firm Media Partners Asia . The report, ‘ReelShort/Crazy Maple Studio: Inside the $1BN Micro Drama Machine’, found that ReelShort revenue grew from $97M in 2023 to $400M in 2024 and $785M in 2025. After the bump this year up to just over $1BN, MPA estimates revenue will grow to $1.4BN in 2027 and $1.7BN in 2028. After an estimated $12M net loss in 2025, MPA projects EBITDA of $63M and around $40M of net profit in 2026, rising to $306M of EBITDA at an 18% margin and $225M of net profit by 2028. Related Stories News ReelShort Adapts Cora Reilly's 'Bound By Duty' As Its Latest Mafia Romance Microdrama News Microdrama Audiences Getting Younger & More Male, Holywater Tech Report Finds Looking at the market as a whole, MPA is also predicting that microdrama revenue outside China will grow by 21% CAGR from $3.6BN in 2026 to $9.5BN by 2031. Within that, microdrama revenue in the US will grow from $1.5BN to $3.7BN, while in the Asia Pacific region outside of China it will triple to $2.4BN. Watch on Deadline One reason for ReelShort’s growing revenue and profits is the fact that marketing costs are falling, according to the MPA report. User acquisition and marketing costs are set to decline from 55% of revenue in 2025 to 44% by 2028, a shift worth around $10.5M of EBITDA for every percentage point. MPA said this was due to five factors: hit franchises and their sequels draw a growing share of demand without paid support, and supply much of the advertising creative used to acquire the rest; telco and strategic local market partnerships are adding subscribers at little acquisition cost; more billing is moving to ReelShort’s own web store and direct channels; faster creative testing and a hit rate MPA expects to improve raise the return on each dollar spent; and finally, the paid-social auction is maturing after several years of new entrants bidding up prices. The report also found that consumer payments and subscriptions account for the majority of ReelShort’s business, contribuing around 85-90% of revenue, with subscriptions already making up 60–70% of what viewers pay. Advertising, a small stream before 2024, is predicted to grow to around 15% of revenue by 2028 – and because it pays no app-store commission, roughly 65-70 cents of each advertising dollar flows through to earnings. At the same time, more consumer billing is moving to ReelShort’s own web store, reducing platform and payment fees. Together these two shifts account for close to half of the projected margin expansion. Asia is contributing around 12% of ReelShort revenue in 2026, and is the fastest-growing region in MPA’s forecast, reaching around $200M and 14% of revenue in 2027, with the AIS partnership in Thailand, live since April, delivering significant subscriber and engagement momentum. Latin America and Asia Pacific combined account for around 60% of an estimated 70 million global monthly users in 2026, but only 19% of revenue. North America contributes 59% of revenue with $620M. Narrowing that gap is the main source of upside in MPA’s forecast. MPA concluded the report by saying that microdrama is a five-player market, with ReelShort leading on an estimated 29% share, ahead of DramaBox on 21%, DramaWave on 13%, NetShort on 10% and GoodShort on 6%. The remainder is spread across some 300 smaller apps. “Microdrama has begun to be an earnings story rather than a growth story. Marketing costs are coming down as hit franchises bring audiences in without paid support, platform fees are falling as operators move billing onto their own web stores, and advertising is entering the mix at high margin. ReelShort is showing that the model can scale and make money at the same time. What decides the next phase is distribution and unit economics, not necessarily content volume,” said MPA CEO & Executive Director Vivek Couto. Nazzaro Talks Mission To Liberate Spectators In The Age Of The Algorithm As 79th Edition Kicks Off View All August 6, 2026 2:00am EXCLUSIVE: PiperPlay has boarded sales on Edoardo Gabbriellini ’s true crime drama The City of the Living ( La città dei vivi ) ahead of its world premiere in Venice’s Orizzonti competition and North American debut in Toronto’s Centrepiece , and also unveiled the trailer. The feature is freely inspired by Italian writer Nicola Lagioia’s award-winning, best-selling true-crime work delving into the circumstances around the senseless and sadistic murder of a much-loved young man in 2016 that shocked Rome and the wider world. Gabbriellini’s film frames the events from a tender and poetic perspective rather than reconstructing the crime, to shift the focus to its origins, exploring the human, cultural and emotional dynamics behind it. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Documentary TIFF Docs Lineup Revealed: Rapinoe, Said, Love, And A Scent Of Musk Festivals Toronto Unveils Wavelengths & TIFF Classics Lineups With Films By Angela Schanelec, Radu Jude, Denis Côté & Lisandro Alonso The synopsis reads: “Luca is twenty-three years old. He lives with the family that adopted him and loves him. He moves between the suburbs and the city center with his friends and has a girlfriend with whom he shares a young yet deeply significant love. Luca is searching for his path—at an age when everything seems both possible and already lost—and in this quest, he leads a double life. One night, following a seemingly chance encounter, the trajectory of Luca’s life is shattered, broken by an act of blind, senseless violence.” In his first starring role, rising young actor Emanuele Maria di Stefano plays Luca with the cast also featuring Gaia Merlonghi, Simona Senzacqua, Roberta Mattei, and Valerio Mastandrea ( There’s Still Tomorrow ). Director and actor Gabbriellini previously played in Toronto ’s Centrepiece sidebar with last film Holiday , which also revolved around the fallout and human consequences of a crime. One of the producers on the film was Luca Guadagnino. Gabbriellini had previously starred in Guadagnino’s I am Love , as well as served as second-unit director on Guadagnino’s TV miniseries We Are What We Are . The City Of The Living is produced by Eagle Pictures, Cinemaundici and Lungtafilm with the participation of HBO Max. Top distributor Eagle Pictures, which also handles Paramount and Sony Pictures releases in Italy, will bring the film to Italian cinemas. Rome-based PiperPlay is a joint venture formed in 2025 between Italian production and distribution powerhouse PiperFilm and Playtime, within the Vuelta Group. Its summer and fall festival slate also includes Locarno International Competition title Ketticè by Giovanni Tortotici, the Venice Orizzonti Competition title Children of the Monkey and Venice’s closing film God Laughs ( Dio Ride ) by Giovanni Veronesi. articles.title: Warner Bros. Discovery Stumbles In Q2 As ‘Supergirl,’ Lack Of NBA Drag Down Results
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Sinclair CEO Chris Ripley “Couldn’t Be Happier” About Expected FCC Repeal Of Federal Ownership Cap Disney Sells Out Super Bowl Ad Inventory, Wraps Upfront Sales Process ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Triumph “Bodes Well” For ‘Avengers: Doomsday’, Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro Says View All August 6, 2026 4:10am An aerial view of the Warner Bros. studio lot in Burbank, CA Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Warner Bros. Discovery fell short of Wall Street expectations in the second quarter, as Supergirl and the lack of the NBA dragged total revenue down 11% to $8.7 billion. Analysts had projected $9.2 billion in revenue. Diluted earnings per share of 6 cents topped estimates of a loss of 10 cents a share. The company reported the quarterly financials with its $110 billion merger with Paramount in legal limbo. The attorneys general of 12 states, as well as the Writers Guild of America, have filed a lawsuit seeking to block the deal on antitrust grounds. A trial has been scheduled for March 2027. Streaming proved a bright spot, with total revenue up 10% to $3.1B and EBITDA jumping 75% to $512 million. Flagship streamer HBO Max, which has recently expanded to key international territories, was paced by titles like Euphoria , House of the Dragon , Hacks and The Pitt . Related Stories Legal Judge Dismisses Consumer Lawsuit Challenging Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger News Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna Champions Paramount-WBD Merger, Says Antitrust Trial "Creates More Uncertainty And Distraction" The studio division faced tough comparisons with the year-ago period, which featured hits like A Minecraft Movie , Sinners , and Final Destination Bloodlines . Revenue tumbled 39% to $2.3 billion and EBITDA plummeted 89% to $96 million. Supergirl grossed just $126 million worldwide, the lowest for any DC release since Catwoman in 2004. Watch on Deadline Total advertising revenue plunged 22% from the year-ago period to settle at $1.7 billion. The main culprit was the absence of the NBA. After nearly 40 years of broadcasting the league’s games, WBD did not reach a deal to extend its rights, with NBCUniversal taking its place as a primary partner. The ad story marred the quarterly performance of the Global Linear Networks division, whose revenue slid 17% to $3.99 billion. Adjusted EBITDA was off 4% to $1.4 billion. The quarterly numbers followed Tuesday’s earnings report from Paramount, which featured some updated comments about the WBD merger. articles.title: ITV’s Zandland Doc ‘Inside Iran: War & Revolution’ Goes Undercover During Anti-Regime Protests & Conflict With The U.S.
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart ProSiebenSat.1 Ad Sales Dented By Weak TV Market & Rivals’ World Cup Rights Catherine Zeta-Jones Takes On The Seven Demons In Revenge Thriller ‘Kill Jackie’ BritBox & BBC’s Poirot Origin Series ‘Hercule’ Reveals Cast View All August 6, 2026 4:11am Inside Iran: War & Revolution ITV, Zandland EXCLUSIVE: ITV has greenlit Inside Iran : War & Revolution . The one-off doc goes undercover and inside Iran, with testimony from journalists and civilians during the 2025-2026 protests and, more recently, the conflict with the U.S. The film comes from UK-based doc studio Zandland . It marks another ITV-Zandland project following their BAFTA-nominated film Breaking Ranks: Inside Israel’s Army . Inside Iran: War & Revolution is told from the perspective of an anonymous Iranian journalist. It has access to people living inside Iran and under its authoritarian regime. The doc chronicles the struggles and suffering of protestors in the uprising and shows the brutal crackdown by the authorities, including footage from the mass protests, and inside the hospitals where the injured were being treated and also faced arrest. It goes on to give an inside-Iran account of the hostilities with the U.S. Related Stories News ITV Studios Bosses Bullish Despite U.S. & International Declines As 'Love Island' & 'The Gentlemen' Maker Prepares To Go Independent News ITV Reveals Early Share Buyback Of $140M Before Sky Deal Completes As Broadcaster Unveils First Set Of Results Since Confirming The Deal Capturing footage from inside Iran is perilous. The film spells out the risks the contributors took with an on-screen graphic that reads: “Almost all of the footage in this film was filmed inside Iran by citizens taking significant personal risks.” Given the risk of punishment or even execution, some contributions are anonymized or voices altered. Watch on Deadline Zandland is run by British-Iranian filmmaker Ben Zand . Based in London and Liverpool, the doc studio has harnessed YouTube and digital distribution , as well as working with traditional broadcasters. Zand directed Inside Iran: War & Revolution . “What this film captures is an impossible situation, and the full range of what it does to the people living through it,” Zand said. “Our contributors describe grief, fury, hope and heartbreak, often side by side, and rarely in the ways outside observers might expect. As a British-Iranian this is deeply personal to me, but the film belongs to the people inside Iran who risked everything to share their reality.” ITV’s Controller of Current Affairs, Tom Giles, commissioned Breaking Ranks: Inside Israel’s Army and also greenlit Inside Iran: War & Revolution . “This is a powerful and significant piece of work by people who have taken great risks to film and bear witness to events which have commanded the world’s attention all year, and which they themselves have directly experienced,” he said. “These are filmed voices we rarely hear from inside Iran: urgent, passionate, fearful and inspiring.” The film bows on ITV1 and streaming service ITVX on August 9. Maya Rostowska is the Producer, and Josh Reynolds and Ben Zand are the Executive Producers. articles.title: ‘Soulm8te’ Director Kate Dolan on Her Twisty Journey After ‘M3GAN 2.0’ and What That Ending Could Mean
articles.full_text: Skip to main content David Rysdahl and Kate Dolan behind the scenes of 'Soulm8te.' Universal Pictures Home Entertainment Logo text [This story contains spoilers from Soulm8te .] Four years ago, Blumhouse struck gold with M3GAN , the story of a roboticist who creates an AI-powered doll to serve as a companion for her niece after the child loses her parents. The horror-comedy became a breakout hit with critics and audiences, grossing $180 million worldwide on a $12 million budget. However, last year’s M3GAN 2.0 failed to replicate that success. The sequel followed M3GAN being rebuilt to help combat a humanoid military robot, but it ultimately underperformed, grossing $39.1 million worldwide. Related Stories Movies 'Soulm8te' Review: Erotic Fembot Thriller From the M3GAN-Verse Is Enjoyably Lurid Pulp That Comes Up Short on Satirical Bite Movies 'Other Mommy' Trailer: Jessica Chastain Returns to Horror as a Body-Twisting Doppelganger That changed the trajectory for Soulm8te , a spinoff set in the M3GAN universe starring Lily Sullivan as Sara, an AI-powered companion for a grieving widower, David, played by David Rysdahl. But Sara quickly becomes dangerously obsessed. Kate Dolan’s feature was originally expected to follow in the franchise’s footsteps and debut in theaters. But the film was removed from Universal’s theatrical calendar in December, leaving its release plans uncertain. It was a surprise for Dolan and those involved, but last month, the world learned the film would make its way to audiences, with Blumhouse Atomic Monster announcing Soulm8te would premiere as a home entertainment release on Aug. 1. In a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter , Dolan, who co-wrote the screenplay with Rafael Jordan from a story credited to James Wan , Ingrid Bisu and Jordan, discusses crafting an erotic thriller spin on the AI doll, her future with Blumhouse Atomic Monster, why she is glad the film is reaching audiences at home, and comparisons to horror hit Obsession and the film’s ending. *** How did you balance the erotic thriller tone of this film without losing what audiences love about the M3GAN universe? That tone was the big question of how to balance those things. The reason James and Ingrid wanted to make this was because they love erotic thrillers and they wanted to make something that was true to that era of of filmmaking. And when I first spoke to James, he was referencing a lot of the classic erotic thriller films. And then they were like, OK but it needs to work in the M3GAN universe. So that was my biggest task initially — what’s the tone of this film, and how do we balance that? I watched a lot of films for reference, and films of that era are quite campy and can be — now looking back — quite fun in some ways. So I was just like mining what worked in those films and how to balance those tones together. James Wan is, of course, a horror maestro. What was it like collaborating with him so closely? For sure. It was something that he really wanted to do, so it was sort of his brainchild on doing this as a film. He’s such a wealth of knowledge in terms of filmmaking. He’s worked at the highest levels, and he obviously knows his genre really well. So it was always great to have him there as someone to bounce things off. And he would always look at set pieces, and he even came to set for a few days at one point when we had quite a heavy week of set pieces and stunts. It was great to have his input and insights because he obviously has done this many times before. This film reminded me of the 2013 film Her at times, and particularly, Lily’s voice as Sara, which sounded reminiscent of Scarlett Johansson’s performance. Was that movie a touchstone as you were working on this? Definitely. There were a lot of films that me and the cast watched when we were prepping the movie and the HODs as well. We watched a whole host of erotic thrillers and AI-related robot movies, as well as tonal references like [Paul] Verhoeven’s RoboCop. But Her was definitely one that we watched again. It was interesting watching Her how much has evolved since then, and what we can do to try and tell this story in the now. But even when I was starting to write the film, to when we were shooting, to now, how much things progress so quickly is really crazy. Stuff that we were writing that felt like science fiction months ago suddenly is happening, really, and it’s quite bizarre to experience. ( Laughs. ) But yeah, Her is a great movie. I think it was really ahead of its time in terms of what it was saying. It’s so interesting to watch it now, because it just feels so strange that that’s real. This film went through several changes before ultimately landing as a home entertainment release. Do you feel like Soulm8te was impacted by the reception to M3GAN 2.0? What explanation were you given for the change in release strategy? Yeah, I think M3GAN 2.0 was a big surprise for everybody, and it definitely impacted how Soulm8te was going to go out into the world. M3GAN 2.0 underperformed, and I think that was the main reason. The market is just so unpredictable these days. You don’t really know what’s going to happen or how something’s going to land. It can be very surprising sometimes. M3GAN in M3GAN 2.0. Universal Pictures How did you find out that it was going straight to home entertainment, and did you ever worry that audiences wouldn’t get to see the film? There was definitely a moment where I was concerned that we wouldn’t get to finish the film or people wouldn’t get to see it. So, I was really glad when I knew that it would be released at home because, as a filmmaker, when you’re doing your Dolby Atmos mix, you’re listening to big speakers. You’re hearing all the great sounds that you’re trying to do, and you want that, obviously, to be experienced in a theatrical space. But the bottom line is: What audiences buy into is story and character. That’s always been the case. That’s something that can be enjoyed in a theatrical space, or at home. A lot of movies I grew up loving, I watched at home, and I grew up watching on VHS, late night movies that would be on TV. I think it really allows the film to be seen by a really wide audience as well. A lot of people watch movies at home now, and that’s just part of our world and our culture. I’m just delighted that people are going to get to see the movie. And what a time we’re in for horror too — Original films like Obsession and Backrooms have exceeded expectations at the box office this year. When the trailer came out for Soulm8te, a lot of people were like, “This is like Obsession mixed with Companion .” Given that it explores similar themes, do you think it could have found an audience theatrically, post- Obsession success? You never know. It’s hard to [tell] — So, I’m not sure. But it’s funny the comparisons to Obsession because obviously this is a film that we made a while ago now, so it’s been a long time. And it’s funny seeing the comments, people being like, “Oh, this is just being Obsession. ” It’s like, “Well, we made this movie a long time ago.” ( Laughs .) But it’s so amazing to see those movies do well, and I’m such a fan of those films — I think [ Curry Barker and Kane Parsons] are great filmmakers. It’s very exciting. Anything that brings attention to horror and the genre, and a more mainstream audience into that niche, is like a rising tide lifts all boats. It’s a great time for original horror. If people find something in Soulm8te that’s like Obsession that makes them want to watch it, that’s great.​ In previous interviews, Jason Blum has been coy about whether M3GAN would appear in Soulm8te, which led to speculation. Now that we know she doesn’t appear, what was the thinking behind that decision? I think it was always going to be standalone — from the very first conversation I had about it. The team at Blumhouse Atomic Monster wanted this film to be its own thing and not have too much crossover with M3GAN. Also, tonally, the team there wanted to make something that felt a little darker, where they could push for the R rating, be a little more violent, or include sexual content. I felt it was better to do that as its own story, and we could push things a little more. Are there any Easter eggs from films in the franchise that audiences should keep an eye out for? Yeah, definitely. It was always going to be a standalone movie, but M3GAN 2.0 was actually prepping while I was writing the script for Soulm8te, and they were going into production close to when we were prepping. It was very abreast of each other, and I was always reading the latest drafts of M3GAN 2.0 and finding little things that I could put in that a fan of M3GAN could find in the movie, and they could link things. So yeah, there’s definitely stuff in there for sure. Can you tell me what in case myself or anyone else missed it at first? No, you gotta look out for them. They’re very subtle. But we also have a lot of references to different erotic thrillers. There’s the pub in the movie where they do the karaoke at the bar called the White Rabbit, and that was like a Fatal Attraction reference. There’s a lot of little small things in there that blink, and you miss them, but they’re there. David Rysdahl and Lily Sullivan in Soulm8te . Courtesy of Universal Pictures Home Entertainment There’s a particularly brutal death scene in the film. Why does Sara to use her sexuality as part of how she manipulates and kills her victims? That was always a reference back to the heyday of erotic thrillers in the ’80s and ’90s. I think the quote-unquote villain was always a very sexually promiscuous woman who was morally bankrupt, and she would often be using her feminine wiles to trick these men who were these innocent, quote-unquote, victims in this scenario. So, it was always riffing off that. But I always found the sex scenes in the movie, particularly with Sara, to be an abstract symbolism for how we interact with AI and how we’re lured in and we’re seduced in. It’s all symbolizing that — any scenes where she’s doing that are a manifestation of that idea. Early in the film, Sara says she can survive with water on her for up to 30 minutes. After she’s driven off the cliff, should audiences believe she could have survived? It was always set up that there’s a potential for that, because the thing with AI and tech is that no matter how much you delete something, it always exists in the digital ether and it survives in some way. You don’t know where those things can live on — and it’s something that we can’t comprehend. It’s not like you can destroy something anymore. There is always a risk that those things exist in the digital space, so it was just playing with that idea as well. I think, as humans, we see things in a very black-and-white way, but I think when it comes to that tech, it’s amorphous and we can’t really get control over it. So, there is a chance that she will survive and live on, and there’s not much we can do about that, really. At the end, we see another Soulm8te who looks like Sara but with dark hair introduced to David. Is that the real Sara? I mean, that’s up to the audience to decide if they want to believe it or not. The cast often asks me that, and I was like, “It’s up to you to decide if it is or not.” So, I’m not gonna say any more on that. ( Laughs. ) Do David and Aubrey (Claudia Doumit) end up together? Yeah, I was always rooting for them. I know we don’t see a conclusive result for them at the very end. But I feel like they have survived through this situation together, and they have a deep connection, which is clear. So, I’m always rooting for David and Aubrey. I think they make it in the end. Have James and Jason Blum talk to you about potentially directing another film for Blumhouse Atomic Monster after Soulm8te? We haven’t had that conversation yet. At the moment, I have some original ideas that I was writing over the past while. So I’m focused on working on those projects for now. But yeah, I’m always open to the idea of working with those guys again for sure. If Soulm8te is a hit on VOD, could you imagine doing more with it? I hadn’t thought about it too much, but recently there was this story about the New York school system thinking about having support teachers who were androids. I’d love a movie where Sara’s pretending to be human or pretending to be a teacher at a school, and we could do something fun with that to riff off that news story. But no, I haven’t thought about it too much. I mean, Lily is amazing as Sara, and I would love to see her in that role again. How have you navigated building your career as a female director in the horror genre? I can only speak to my own experience. I tend not to think of myself too much as a female [director]. Because then you start to think about the hurdles that you might face. I’ve always been working on projects that I love and feel connected to; putting as much into them as I possibly can. I’ve been very lucky in my career so far in that I’ve got to do some amazing things — but it’s tough. There’s a lot of unconscious bias in the industry, and there have been times when I’ve come up against that. There’s more you have to think about as a female filmmaker — how you come across on set and all of those kinds of things, which can be tricky. It’s sad to see some of the statistics of when those studies come out, and you see how few women are directing studio films, or films that are released theatrically. It’s definitely something that still needs to be talked about and looked at. But there’s so many amazing female filmmakers out there as well, who are making really cool films and doing amazing work. So, I always feel optimistic that the tables will turn and there will be more people getting to make movies. *** Soulm8te is now streaming digitally. THR

articles.title: The Highest-Grossing Theater for ‘The Odyssey’ in 70MM Hadn’t Screened a New Movie in 35 Years
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Gary Baum Plus Icon Gary Baum Senior Writer garymbaum Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 4:03pm A 70mm screening of 'The Odyssey' at the Alex Theatre in Glendale, California. Photo by Erik Bakshi for Film Leader Co. Glendale’s century-old Alex Theatre installed its 70mm presentation system six weeks ago, just ahead of the July 17 premiere of The Odyssey . Now the venue, which hadn’t shown a first-run movie for 35 years, has announced it’s the highest grossing theatre in the country for Christopher Nolan’s mythological epic on the film format. “The response from audiences has been overwhelming and a wonderful reminder of how much people still value the shared experience of seeing a great film together,” Alex’s artistic director Miles Williams said in a statement which thanked Universal Pictures “for recognizing the important role historic theatres continue to play in Hollywood’s cinematic legacy.” The Odyssey ’s domestic box office total reached $395.5 million over the weekend. The film relinquished first place to Spider-Man: Brand New Day , Sony’s superhero sequel success story, which is sharing a portion of the Imax screens with Nolan’s movie. The 900-seat Alex, known for its mix of Classical Revival and Moderne architectural detailing, has been showing The Odyssey three times per day. The venue will be extending its run by at least two weeks. The marquee advertising The Odyssey at the Alex Theatre in Glendale, California. Photo by Erik Bakshi for Film Leader Co. Williams tells The Hollywood Reporter that the theatre — whose last first-run film was 1991’s Terminator 2: Judgment Day — is now scheduling eight to 10 nights of movie programming each month. (Its busy calendar is filled with live events, from ballet performances to rock concerts.) It intends to host periodic special engagements of other large-format releases, including Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three in December and Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew in February 2027. The Alex invested $500,000 in technical upgrades, including a new ground-floor projection booth. In-demand Los Angeles projectionist Taylor Umphenour, an Imax consultant who has worked with Nolan on his dailies, helped oversee the design and construction. “What you have at a cinema like the Alex is a true understanding of the in-person experience of shared narrative,” he says. “That’s why people are coming — and losing their minds.” A view from the open-air forecourt at the Alex Theatre. Photo by Erik Bakshi for Film Leader Co. THR
