articles.title: Police Respond to Perez Hilton’s Miami Home After He Appeared to Harm Himself on Livestream
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 7:47pm Perez Hilton Ethan Miller/Getty Images Police reportedly responded to Perez Hilton ‘s home in Miami after the celebrity gossip blogger appeared to be harming himself on a TikTok livestream. In graphic clips reposted on social media, Hilton, appearing manic, could be seen in the livestream covered in blood, using an object to cut himself repeatedly. The Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office told Newsweek in a statement that deputies responded to Hilton’s home after the office received “multiple calls” about a person livestreaming acts of self-harm. After authorities confirmed Hilton was alone inside the home and spoke with family members at the scene, deputies decided to “tactically disengage while continuing to monitor the situation.” Related Stories Lifestyle Perez Hilton Claims He Encountered God After Being Hospitalized for Three Weeks Lifestyle Kate Moss, Joan Collins, Jerry Hall Set for 'Absolutely Fabulous: The Movie' Cameos “In many incidents involving a person experiencing a mental health crisis or actively harming themselves, deputies prioritize de-escalation by creating time, distance, and opportunities for communication,” the statement continued. “Unless there is an immediate threat to others, slowing the situation and utilizing crisis intervention techniques can reduce the likelihood of a suicide-by-cop encounter and minimize the risk of injury to the individual, deputies, and the public.” Local news station NBC6 , which had reporters at the scene, later reported that a man, believed to be Hilton, was seen being taken away in an ambulance. The sheriff’s office also confirmed to TMZ that “the individual has been safely recovered and transported by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention.” The Hollywood Reporter has also reached out to the Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office for comment on the incident involving Hilton, in addition to his personal rep. Earlier this year, Hilton shared in a lengthy Instagram video that he was hospitalized for three weeks after initially battling the flu before developing “an ulcer, and then a perforation, and then Sepsis,” he said at the time. “The Sepsis just kept working and my body kept falling apart,” Hilton explained in the video in March. “Then one night with rapid response came ’cause my heart got out of control. They had to put me on heart medications. And then I developed another infection in the hospital.” He added, “It was just such a slow process. I mean, two weeks of just sickness and then another week of getting better before I was released. And that last week was hell because I had already been in the hospital two weeks by then. I was like, ‘I just wanna go home. I just want to be with my babies.’” Perez is a single father of three children. Once he was released from the hospital and sent back home, Hilton said he had time to reflect and came to the realization “that God presented Himself to me” during the challenging experience. “It was real and this has been life-changing. I’m so grateful,” he added at the time. “I’m excited to start taking the kids to church every week. And to just know that God is real. … I don’t have to hope to believe. I know now.” THR

articles.title: What David Ellison Is Really Up to
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All August 4, 2026 7:54pm David Ellison, CEO of Paramount, speaks onstage at the Paramount Pictures presentation at The Dolby Colosseum at Caesars Palace during CinemaCon on April 16, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. A raft of pro-merger pieces have appeared in news outlets in the past week. Gabe Ginsberg/Getty Images At first it just seemed like a happy coincidence — a Hollywood agency mogul supporting a Hollywood corporate merger. Ari Emanuel published an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal last Tuesday saying David Ellison buying Warner Bros. was a good idea and that those 12 Democratic AG’s who have sued to stop the deal were on the wrong warpath. “The attorneys general should drop this case and get back to enforcing the laws as they are written,” the WME chief wrote, as he extolled a Paramount -WB tie-up and said it would be good for the business. Sure, Ellison had committed last year to pay Emanuel’s TKO nearly $8 billion to broadcast UFC fights, a fact he conveniently neglected to mention. And the timing certainly benefited Ellison — earnings were coming, a time when Wall Street would be paying close attention and could express its worry financially about a deal falling through. But still, just a nice little stocking-stuffer under the mogul’s tree. Over the past week, though, the support has started to look a lot less like passive presents and a lot more like an active strategy. The play? Make it seem like a lot of Democrat-approved personalities have no problem with the merger, isolating as regulatory crazies Rob Bonta, Tish James and the rest of the dozen AGs suing to block the deal. Never mind that these are some of the country’s most decorated legal enforcers, with many decades of experience, from places as different as Arizona and Massachusetts. The maneuvers unfolded like a stunt pilot’s careful course-plotting. A few days after the Emanuel op-ed came an anonymously sourced story Friday in the Journal about how one of the preeminent national Democratic leaders, California governor Gavin Newsom, was behind the deal foursquare, according to “people close to the suit.” “Newsom’s office has encouraged Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office, which has independent authority to file such suits, to find a resolution out of court,” the paper said. Never mind that Newsom has a long history of deferring to giant corporations (remember his 11th-hour capitulation to Big Tech on Scott Wiener’s AI bill in 2024?) — this merger was going to create jobs! (“State employment would suffer” without a deal, the paper said Newsom has told colleagues, never mind that no credible economist has supplied such evidence.) Another happy coincidence. Or, given that the paper was pointedly not citing sources close to Newsom, perhaps part of an Ellison-led strategy. Then today, an op-ed of Ellison’s own in a redoubt of mainstream liberalism, The New York Times. The mogul trotted out all the usual arguments for legacy media mergers these days — if we don’t do this the tech companies win, movie theaters should survive, Hollywood should be employed. “What I can promise is the work, and more of it,” he wrote , using the noun four times, which is four times more than he used the noun Donald Trump. Los Angeles County researchers have concluded that the merger will likely lead to less work . Meanwhile, Ari has been hitting the hustings, appearing on CNBC Tuesday morning to rattle off a series of Ellison talking points and praising the mogul. “This is a guy who said ‘hey I’m going to make 30 movies a year, 45-day release,” Emanuel said. “He’s gonna spend he says 30 billion in content a year. We need that for the economy of Hollywood.” The comments wouldn’t have been out of place on the Paramount investor earnings-call Tuesday, where executives touted all these numbers and used words like “pro-competitive” to describe the deal. If there’s one thing we know about capitalism, it’s that combining two major companies leads to more competition. These media hits that aimed to buck the headwinds even involved a literal plane — the day Bonta and the AGs were suing, Ellison jetted to Washington to lobby for a federal tax credit, a news stunt meant as much to lobby support among Hollywood as to win over legislators. One story his coverage play overshadowed that week: ProPublica’s bombshell report that Paramount allegedly provided gifts to FCC commissioners reviewing the deal. More of these pieces are no doubt coming, perhaps even in my own outlet. More foot soldiers arguing for the merger’s value to the business, or the world, or the First Amendment. Never mind that the WGA — those fierce opponents of free expression! — have just sued to stop the deal. Doesn’t the world’s richest family have the right to own CNN? Isn’t that enshrined in the Constitution? All these enlisted authors are a shrewd flyer, and you need to give Ellison’s team credit for landing it so effectively. But you also don’t need an advanced radar beacon to see what’s happening. Having courted MAGA and Donald Trump to win the deal federal approval (how many Kennedy Center boxes and UFC ringside seats can one centibillionaire’s son fill?) Ellison is now pivoting to Dems to take care of the state challenge. Not regulatory-minded Dems, as that group, from Elizabeth Warren to Cory Booker to Adam Schiff, have all been sharply critical of the deal and ask hard questions about combining the country’s third and fourth biggest pure-play entertainment companies. Not those decorated and often landslide-winning Democratic AGs, either. But if you get enough Dem-ish poobahs like Newsom and the Kamala-donating Ari on your side, maybe people won’t notice all the Democrats who aren’t. Or enough of their constituents will lose interest, causing AGs to do the same. Heck, maybe people will even magically forget that no fewer than 1,000 creatives, from Bryan Cranston to J.J. Abrams to Glenn Close to Lin-Manuel Miranda, all signed a letter this spring opposing the deal, noting how a merger “would further consolidate an already concentrated media landscape, reducing competition at a moment when our industries — and the audiences we serve — can least afford it” and lead to “fewer opportunities for creators, fewer jobs across the production ecosystem, higher costs, and less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.” Who can remember any of those beloved entertainers’ warnings when an agent is telling us something is good for creativity? There’s a reason Paramount needs the deal to happen. Warner Bros. Discovery turned a profit of $1.2 billion this past quarter once you strip out all the money they had to pay as part of the acquisition (like severance costs). That’s a lot of profit for a company like Paramount, which revealed Tuesday that in the same quarter it netted $41 million . And there’s a reason Paramount needs the deal to happen soon. Starting Oct. 1, Paramount must pay Warners shareholders $7 million every day until the deal closes. By the second week, they’ll have wiped out all the profits they earned this quarter. By the spring, they’ll have wiped out the profits of the company they’re buying. One can’t imagine a lot of joy on Melrose, then, when the word came down Tuesday that the trial won’t start until March . Also, the deal is partly bankrolled by Larry Ellison and his significant AI investments. And can that boom go on forever? The reality is the AGs may not just have the law on their side — they have the leverage. And with every week that passes they have more of it. (With even more come potential Democrat victories in November.) Could they extract a major settlement — possibly even forcing a carve-out of CNN? Don’t rule it out, no matter how many UFC fights Ellison attends with the president. “Winning comes down to having the best stories,” Paramount CFO Dennis Cinelli told investors on the earnings call Tuesday. Ellison and his allies will keep telling them. That doesn’t mean it will result in victory. THR

articles.title: Maria Bäck on ‘Brave New Love,’ Her Provocative Take on Motherhood, Desire and Modern Romance
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 4, 2026 11:00pm 'Brave New Love' Courtesy of Snowglobe Swedish-Danish writer-director Maria Bäck ( I Remember When I Die , Psychosis in Stockholm ) likes to push the envelope. With her new feature, Brave New Love , she invites us to talk about love, relationships and desire — but not within the tidy bounds of what’s considered “normal” or “right.” The film centers on Kate, a mother torn between her husband, Orla, and a secret relationship with another man, Andreas. A triangle of madness? Of sadness? Of badness? Something else entirely? Watch and decide for yourself. Brave New Love stars Kathrine Thorborg Johansen ( Post Mortem: No One Dies in Skarnes ) as Kate, Simon Sears ( Shadow and Bone ) as Orla, young Noemi Carbone Mannov as their daughter Athena, Anders Danielsen Lie ( Sentimental Value , Everybody Digs Bill Evans ) as Andreas and Angeliki Papoulia ( Dogtooth , The Lobster ). The film world premieres Sunday, Aug. 9, in the main international competition at the 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland. Related Stories Lifestyle Ariana Grande's Decision to Withdraw From 'Sunday in the Park' Came as Surprise to Key Production Members Lifestyle Fashion Keeps Debating John Galliano. It's Ignoring Its Jewish History. Produced by Anna-Maria Kantariusand and featuring cinematography by Maria Von Hausswolff, Brave New Love was edited by Julius Krebs Damsbo. Reinvent Yellow is handling international sales. Ahead of the Locarno premiere of the film, Bäck talked to THR about the inspiration for Brave New Love , why she enjoys asking tough questions, working with a cast of actors who have made names for themselves and why the film’s title reminds you of that famous Aldous Huxley novel. What was the inspiration for Brave New Love ? My interest in all kinds of normative questions has been something that’s been following me forever. I have, for the last 30 years or so, been either in or out of relationships, and my friends have been in or out of relationships. So it’s this huge collection of dilemmas and problems with love life, which has always been something that interests me. I’m also fascinated by how hard it is for people to confront habits. That doesn’t only apply to love, but when you study something like love, which is so present in our lives, many of these things become very clear because we always struggle with love. And not so much has changed regarding the rules of love in modern times. When I think about what drove me to make the film, I keep returning to this want and need to share a loneliness and the feeling of “being fundamentally wrong.” It is so human to fuck up; we all do it all the time! And you can feel empathy with — almost — anyone if you understand their inner world. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe The film doesn’t come across as a recommendation though… Yes, the film is not trying to say that you should have an open relationship. I don’t have an open relationship. I live very conventionally in many ways, but it’s just interesting how we can feel like we are very liberal and open, but when we are confronted with reality, things turn out to be different. When you hear of a woman like Kate, a mother who falls in love with another man, most people will have a strong opinion. Even though we might consider ourselves liberal, we all have these [ingrained] ideas, and there is shame — so much is about shame. I think all these ideas and feelings are deeply rooted in us. We just have all these predefined and automatic reactions, and we tend not to question them much or update our worldview. This human contradiction is just fascinating and amusing to watch in a way. It’s stimulating to explore that with a story and characters, because there’s a lot to dig into. The only thing I really didn’t want with the film was to create something convenient about love that we’ve already seen before. A love triangle is one of the oldest themes, and I really wanted to challenge that narrative, both story-wise and conceptually in terms of the film’s language. For me, it’s always about questions rather than answers. I feel I know nothing. I just question and doubt everything. I found myself going from laughing to cringing and thinking, “No, don’t do this!” It was a rollercoaster of emotions. How did you write and “build” the movie and its world? I worked on this project for six years, so it’s been a long, long process. Like with all my films, usually it starts with an emotion and an abstract universe that tries to become more concrete. In my head, these themes and this character kept circling around. I write a lot and there was a poem I wrote where I pictured this woman. So she came to me. I didn’t know it was Kate back then. But the first picture I had was this naked woman in a cave watching a man, and I didn’t know who she was. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe So then you connected her to the themes you were pondering? Yes, it becomes an investigation, kind of. Of course, I am in charge because I write, but I also feel a lot that I’m following something that I’m trying to understand. Who is she? Where does she come from? So, things usually come to me in the form of different images, different situations. And I also always collect things from my own life that I find fascinating or provocative or just beautiful, and they make it into the film. Such as a balloon scene, for example, in Brave New Love . My son was playing with this balloon when I was hoovering, and all of a sudden the balloon did something I had never seen. That became a little note and then a scene. Some things come from really concrete stuff like that, and other things come from more abstract feelings that I need to translate. Did you get any help in the writing stage? What I want to mention about the writing process is my collaboration with Eskil Vogt ( Sentimental Value , The Worst Person in the World ), who was my script consultant both on Psychosis in Stockholm and Brave New Love . His humorous and generous mind has meant a great deal for the process in terms of asking me disturbing and provocative questions that helped me shape the film. I work a lot with different methods for different stages of writing — sometimes very open and flowy, and then periods with lots of lists and dots and arrows and stuff that I translate into pretty basic, traditional storytelling. But a guide for me is always a strong desire to surprise and do what you don’t expect. I think that is important. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe You mentioned shame. I also want to ask you about guilt. There are scenes where I can imagine viewers saying, “Kate is a bad mother. How dare she?!” How difficult is it to write something so different from the traditional all-loving, all-caring mother? That’s one of the biggest challenges. I didn’t want to make a film that I had seen before. And I didn’t want to make a film that was convenient. Kate was pretty obvious to me as a character from the beginning, and I knew that I had to defend her. You always apply for money, and from the start, it was very clear that it was provoking to people that she was a mother, and she still insisted on her desire, instead of just putting a lid on everything. People asked me why I even wanted to tell this story because, “She’s so egoistic, and the audience wants somebody they can sympathize with.” So it comes back to me in the sense that I have to work with my own shame, and I have to work with my own willingness to be vulnerable in these kinds of situations. Luckily, this is also something that triggers me in a creative way. I get provoked by the people who get so provoked. If they have this idea that a mother should be a very specific way, that makes me angry. So then it’s easier for me to find the energy to stand up for Kate. And people like Kate exist in real life… Yes, I think this idea that you should change as a person just because you become a parent is so ridiculous. Of course, you change a lot of your values. But why would you stop having the same kind of desire and emotions just because you have kids? It’s easy to say about Kate that she should say goodbye to one of the men, or she should get a divorce, blah blah. Or people would also say she has to be honest and tell her husband. But she knows that her husband doesn’t want to know, so then what? Or if she has to get a divorce, that would mean even more pain for everyone. But I have no good answers. And I wanted to make a film where there were no good answers. It’s not a proposal or recommendation — like, “please come and live your life the way Kate does.” She’s struggling a lot. It’s not something I would suggest. But these things and situations happen. I know a lot of Kates, and I know a lot of Orlas, and I know a lot of Andreas. All these perspectives are all around us all the time. So why wouldn’t we see them in a film? Maria Bäck, courtesy of Leo Bäck Geertsen What’s up with all the Greek references and themes in the film? The daughter is named Athena, there is a Greek island, and there seem to be some references to Greek mythology. That’s a good question. I absolutely love Greece, and I’ve done so all my life. I was a very strange, lonely kid in many ways. And Greek mythology really meant a lot to me. Through cassette tapes, I listened a lot to Greek mythology on my Walkman. Even as a kid, my interest in mythology started. It’s just an interest in stories, basically. And then on top of that, I’ve been to Greece a lot in my life, both as a kid on holidays and also later, and I have always felt at home in Greece. I cannot explain why. Even though the film is not about me at all, I use a lot of my own fascinations, so it just came naturally to me to include it in Kate’s character. I’m not romanticizing ancient Greece, but it’s interesting to see how they built Christianity and other cultures on top of it. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe When Locarno unveiled Brave New Love for its lineup, I immediately wondered if it was a reference to Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World . And when I watched the film, I did notice that this title was indeed not a coincidence, right? How early did you know the title? The title I actually had pretty early. I think it was in the first or second draft of the script. I read the book as a teenager, and it made a huge impression on me. I haven’t read it again, actually, but I still have a strong feeling from it. This whole idea of how much society forms our ways of acting and our desires is the core element, of course, of Brave New Love . Of course, it’s a very loose reference. The book works with this very dystopian world where desires are controlled. So I thought what would happen if you had a protagonist who just follows her desire without any restrictions? There is also a scene where Orla is reading that book. Do you know what you will work on next? I’m very early in developing my fourth feature. In parallel, I’m actually expanding Brand New Love as a novel. THR

articles.title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Review: Season 4 of Apple’s Hit Soccer Dramedy Struggles to Find Anywhere Interesting Left to Go
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All August 5, 2026 12:00am 'Ted Lasso' Apple TV It would surely take a real a-hole to hate on Apple’s Ted Lasso . As of the latest season — the fourth, following a third that played coy to the very end about whether it might be the last — it remains perhaps the most insistently warmhearted series on television, full of kindly heroes who are open of mind and generous of spirit. Every new person is just a new friend waiting to happen. Every new challenge is an exciting opportunity to extend oneself or someone else a bit of grace. In a world where cruelty so often seems to be the point, it should be a balm for the soul, a fortifying reminder that common decency still matters and always will. Related Stories TV 'Ted Lasso' Makes Long-Awaited Return: When and Where to Watch Season 4 Online TV Meet Coach Alice, the New Face of 'Ted Lasso' Ted Lasso The Bottom Line Sweet but empty. Airdate: Wednesday, Aug. 5 (Apple) Cast: Jason Sudeikis, Hannah Waddingham, Juno Temple, Tanya Reynolds, Jeremy Swift, Brett Goldstein, Abbie Hern, Faye Marsay, Jude Mack, Aisling Sharkey, Rex Hayes Creators: Jason Sudekis, Bill Lawrence, Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly And yet, I must confess, what this latest outing brought up in me was not my better angels but my inner grump, growing ever more impatient with the whole endeavor. Unimpeachably well-intentioned but frustratingly hollow, the long-delayed new season mostly serves to confirm that the Richmond way may have run its course. Perhaps I’m being harsh on a season that, in fairness, I did not actively despise. (I did warn you I was a jerk.) Where season three frustrated with its aimless pacing, its unruly plotting, its self-congratulatory strain of goodness, new showrunner Jack Burditt ( 30 Rock , Modern Family ) dials back the worst of the show’s excesses. The five (of 10) episodes sent to critics average a still-kinda-long-but-basically-reasonable 45 minutes. Our hero’s general vibe has been scaled back from nigh-saintly to merely very nice. All the male players — save Brett Goldstein’s Roy Kent, now Richmond’s coach — have been jettisoned from the show, taking their many half-baked storylines along with them. The problem is that, having rid itself of its messier elements, Ted Lasso has replaced them with…well, not much of anything, really. The season follows Ted ( Jason Sudeikis ) as he takes charge of their inaugural women’s team, none of whose members at this point have gotten ample or interesting enough screen time to leave a real impression. (I’d keep an eye on Jude Mack’s cheerfully unhinged goalie Boots, Faye Marsay’s maternal Lizzie and Abbie Hern’s prickly Gemma, though.) The only new face that does demand a lot of attention so far is a prickly new assistant coach, Alice (an excellent Tanya Reynolds). Seeing as she’s the single most interesting part of the new season — not least because she’s the only lead who’s yet to succumb to the Pluribus -ian hive mind of Lasso-style positivity — it’s easy to want to lend it to her. The challenge to be overcome this time is not some scheming villain or a more talented rival team, but the dully abstract concept of an unjust system: In the face of sexist male fans, skeptical executives, an indifferent sports media and a shameful lack of resources, can Rebecca ( Hannah Waddingham ) and Keeley’s ( Juno Temple ) new passion project of a team possibly prevail? It’s a timely plot, what with the recent surge of interest in established organizations like the WNBA and the NWSL as well as nascent ones like the PWHL and the WPBL , and undeniably a noble one. Ted Lasso knows it, sprinkling in speeches about how much it matters not just for little girls but little boys, older women and really people of all ages and genders to see that women can play, too. (And if you think it strange that such a proudly feminist endeavor has put a man in charge, there’s a whole episode-two subplot explaining, not very convincingly, why in this specific case it’s actually fine.) But it’s one thing to label a thing important. It’s another to make it interesting. Ted Lasso succeeds at the former, but falters at the latter. In keeping the players and fans at arm’s length, at least for now, the show misses a shot to make the stakes feel personal — to show us what makes them so passionate about this sport, to reflect on the paths that have brought them here, to take stock of their own private hopes now that they’ve arrived. It might yet, and I hope it does; for my money, the most fun I had this season was watching these women bond or butt heads with equal raucousness. Mostly, the series’ focus remains on its core cast. But rather than use the in-universe three-year gap to flip to a new chapter in the characters’ lives, it simply returns them to a familiar status quo. Assistant coach Beard (Brendan Hunt) remains trapped in a toxic on-off dynamic with Jane (Phoebe Walsh), despite having married her in the previous finale. Keeley and Roy are “really really good friends” who want to be more, but are kept apart by mechanisms that have only ever existed in the minds of screenwriters desperate to stretch out a will-they-won’t-they. Rebecca’s dragging her feet on a commitment to her hot pilot, Matthijs (Matteo van der Grijn), again seemingly just so the series can milk this storyline as long as it can. As for Ted, Sudeikis still shines most in the moments when we see sadness or worry peeking through his relentlessly upbeat façade. But the creaky pacing of this season — it takes a full episode for Ted to even begin to consider taking the job, all the better to deliver on what I can only assume is a lucrative partnership with Kansas City’s tourism board, and then two more before he’s assembled a full coaching staff and team — can’t hide the fact that the show doesn’t seem to know what to do with him when he’s not giving inspirational, metaphor-laden speeches. Because really, where is there even left for Ted to go? In the first season, he was met with resistance on all fronts to his unorthodox methods of coaching, his ignorance of the sport, his sheer Americanness. By the end of the third, he’d so fully converted everyone to his brand of empathetic leadership that even Trent Crimm (James Lance), his toughest media critic, has written a book touting his wisdom. The Ted that knocks on Rebecca’s door this season is not a fish out of water but a legendary hero returning to a kingdom he’s remade entirely in his image. Ted himself would never say so, of course — he’d aw-shucks the notion via some convoluted reference to a beloved ’80s movie. But he might as well let himself weep, for there are no more naysayers left for him to conquer. THR

articles.title: Inside ‘I Is Another’: The True(ish) Story of the Man Who Massaged a Nazi and Maybe Saved Lives
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 5, 2026 1:00am 'I Is Another' Courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega A few years ago German writer-director Felix Randau ( Iceman ) got what sounded like an interesting proposal from France: to direct episodes of a miniseries about Felix Kersten, the former massage therapist of Nazi SS leader Heinrich Himmler. “When I got back to Berlin and read their concept, I really liked it,” he recalls. “But there was this one special sentence in it that said, ‘If Steven Spielberg had known about Felix Kersten, he would have shot a film about Felix Kersten and not about Oskar Schindler.’ I knew that Steven Spielberg struggled for, I don’t know, about 10 years before he started shooting Schindler’s List , and he’s a smart guy who has a lot of assistance. So I became suspicious and started my own research, going to the archives and reading a lot of books and stuff.” Related Stories Movies Maria Bäck on 'Brave New Love,' Her Provocative Take on Motherhood, Desire and Modern Romance Lifestyle Ariana Grande's Decision to Withdraw From 'Sunday in the Park' Came as Surprise to Key Production Members In the process, he realized that Kersten’s legacy is much less clear-cut. “I figured out that the story the French guys wanted to shoot was a hero story, a superhero story,” Randau tells THR . “But I felt you simply cannot do it.” He soon started focusing his work energy elsewhere. The result is his new film, I Is Another ( Ich Ist ein Anderer ), which world premieres on Friday, Aug. 7 in the Piazza Grande program of the 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland. Set in 1952, the film sees a journalist ambush Kersten and his wife on a train because she has doubts about the heroic narrative that he has been presenting about himself — one that might even get him the Nobel Peace Prize. What starts as a normal interview quickly turns into a psychological cat-and-mouse game. Is Kersten a hero or an impostor? Or could he maybe be both? “Every story has three sides,” Randau says in a director’s note. “Yours. Mine. And the truth…” To explore all these complex themes, I Is Another features a cast of big European names, led by Danish star Claes Bang ( The Square , Bad Sisters , Home ) as Felix Kersten, Austria’s Valerie Pachner ( The Stories , Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore , Four Minus Three ) as journalist Hedda, fellow Austrian Susanne Wuest ( Sound of Falling ) as Kersten’s wife Irmgard, German actor Timocin Ziegler as Hedda’s husband Winfried, and Germany’s Martin Müller as Himmler. Felix Randau, courtesy of Felix Randau The film, whose cinematographer was Sebastian Thaler, was edited by Joana Scrinzi. Beta Cinema is handling international sales. For writer-director Randau, I Is Another is much more than a post-war film — and much more timely. “Of course, it’s a period movie, but it has a lot to do with our present time,” he tells THR . “It’s about truth and the question: what is truth? Nowadays, there are no more fundamental agreements about anything, so truth has become quite a flexible thing. And that’s very dangerous, as we all can see. So, I Is Another is a movie about that.” Indeed, the themes of truth and image that the movie explores seem tailor-made for the social media age. “If Felix Kersten was alive today, he would be deep into all this social media shit, I’m pretty sure,” Randau acknowledges. But he highlights the ambiguities and shades of gray that he sees in Kersten that the writer-director wanted to also showcase in I Is Another . “He was a narcissist. He was an opportunist,” says Randau. “But I think he also was a hero somehow because he saved some lives. Not thousands, as he said, but he saved some lives. And I think he saved lives not for good reasons. He wanted to save his own ass, I think.” Where in the film’s facts turn to fiction doesn’t really matter much, according to the filmmaker, because much of how people feel about Kersten depends on whether they focus on his autobiography or facts and stories told by others. “All the scenes with Himmler and Kersten are from Kersten’s autobiography,” Randau explains. “So they are, I think, all fake, but it is his truth. All the other stuff, the journalist and the train ride and stuff like that, is invented. It’s fiction. But somehow it’s also true.” Director Felix Randau and stars Claes Bang and Valerie Pachner during the shoot for ‘I Is Another,’ courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega Of course, to bring the story of Kersten and the themes that I Is Another explores to life, Randau needed a strong cast. “I’m really proud of our casting,” he tells THR . “They all were great and added so much.” Randau reached out to Bang first to cast him as Kersten. The Danish star had never heard about the massage therapist. “I did not know about any of this until Felix brought it to me, and it’s quite interesting because it seems to be a story that everybody’s quite fascinated by when you retell it,” the star tells THR in a Zoom chat during a break from filming the Netflix series Assassin’s Creed . “It’s a story that’s really gone under the radar, even if it’s a quite crazy one.” The team may have spent quite a few years getting the financing for the movie together, but the actor remained up for it throughout. “Ever since he brought it to me, I’ve been really into it and really wanted to do it,” Bang recalls. “I really felt strongly about this. So I stayed with it, and we managed to make it last summer. We had to do it quite fast because there wasn’t a massive budget. I think we had 24 shooting days altogether, which is a stretch for something like this. Everybody really put in a massive effort. Everybody was so devoted to it, and that is something that I will carry with me.” How did he think about Kersten and what was key for portraying the character? “It’s really hard to find out what is actually the truth here,” Bang observes. “But what’s interesting is that if this guy hadn’t been so preoccupied with his legacy, then we would have had no story to tell. It’s only because it seems that after the war, he was not quite content with the credit he was given for what he had done, and therefore he started perhaps exaggerating.” For the Danish star, Kersten’s story is about the human need for validation: “Ultimately, Kersten wants the Nobel Peace Prize because that would validate him. That whole thing of not being able to just trust yourself and knowing that you have done your bit seems weird and wild.” Claes Bang as Felix Kersten and Martin Müller as Heinrich Himmler in ‘I Is Another,’ courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega Courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/Ostlicht Filmproduktion/Wega Filmproduktion The fact that a prominent world leader has been desperately hoping (some might say whining) for a Nobel Peace Prize is not lost on Bang. “Obviously, we have Trump at the moment who is seeking the exact same validation. I mean, he also so desperately wants the Nobel Peace Prize. I know that the parallel is too much. But actually it’s more about … when can we just trust ourselves and know in our hearts ‘I have done my bit.’ Why can’t we just find our inner peace?” Adds Bang: “What intrigued me, and that’s probably also something that I can really relate to and recognize in myself because I really very often wonder, ‘Why do I need that bloody validation from everywhere else? Why do I need the reviews to say that I’m great? Why do I need people to come up to me and say, Wow, that was a great movie.’ Why isn’t it just enough for me just to be whatever I am?” In case you wonder: Bang and his director on I Is Another weren’t at all concerned with him trying to look like the real-life Kersten, which he doesn’t — at all. “That is not the story we’re trying to tell here. We’re trying to tell a story of the journey of a soul,” the star emphasizes. “This is not the wax museum of Madame Tussauds. So that was never important.” Pachner was game for the role of the journalist immediately. “I loved the title, and the film’s themes were something I felt I could really connect with,” she tells THR . “It’s this idea of what you tell yourself and others about yourself, and how that can be very far from the truth. And what is the truth? Felix Randau also plays with our own idea of what’s true and right. And there is this autobiography that Felix Kersten wrote and how people took it as fact just because he wrote it. So, yes, the film is set after the Second World War, but with talk about fake news, it also feels very modern.” Valerie Pachner as journalist Hedda and Claes Bang as Felix Kersten in ‘I Is Another’ Courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/Ostlicht Filmproduktion/Wega Filmproduktion She adds that the character of Hedda is more complex than she may appear. “I was really happy to explore that because it felt so rich,” says Pachner. “It’s not this young journalist who is just this good girl who wants to get to the bad guy. She has her own very twisted and dark story. I’m so happy when I get to play a woman where not everyone says, ‘Oh, she’s so nice.'” In fact, Pachner enjoyed teasing that her character isn’t sure who she is or wants to project to be either, very much like Kersten. “As Hedda, I didn’t know who I was,” she shares. “Is me another? Who is I? Or maybe I just want to be different. And I think she really wants to be. That struggle tells us that maybe she and Kersten are not that different.” Pachner had never met any of the other cast members, but she felt a natural chemistry with them once shooting got underway. “We all enjoyed doing the scenes with the four of us, the two couples,” she says. “It just flowed. These weird relationships were kind of there, and there was such a rich history behind Hedda’s relationship with her husband. The Kerstens play these weird mind games with the younger people. I enjoyed working with all of them so much. They’re all really, really great actors.” Wuest was also fascinated by the themes explored by the film, and couldn’t help but notice parallels to our current moment. “I feel that the timing of the film is so spot on for so many reasons,” she says. “First of all, it’s all about the image you create of yourself, and how manipulative that is. It’s like on social media where it’s not only about the ego; it’s about selling something all the time. And the film is about the questions of who do we want to be and how do we want to be perceived from the outside. That has become more important than creating a community, which I think is very toxic. I think it is a dead end.” Director Felix Randau and stars Claes Bang and Valerie Pachner during the shoot for ‘I Is Another,’ courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega She adds that the movie also ties in with a troubling political trend that’s been on the rise throughout the world: “The second thing is the rise of all the right-wing radical politicians and ideologies again, which I think go hand-in-hand with this me, me, me culture. The film tells a story about that and perspective. You have at least three, if not four or five, different perspectives. You have the perspective of Felix Kersten. You have the perspective of the journalist who’s trying to get to him. You have the perspective of his wife. You have the perspective of the poor journalist’s husband. And then you have the perspective of the audience who also has a take on it. Plus, then you have the perspective of the person who tells the story, which is the director. So there are a lot of layers.” Wuest concludes that I Is Another is much more timely than audiences may at first expect: “We live in very strange times, and I think the film covers and mirrors that.” As mentioned before, the Kerstens of I Is Another look nothing like the real-life couple, and Wuest lauds director Randau for “allowing different ideas to happen.” Such as when they were trying out different looks for Irmgard. Says Wuest: “I was putting on makeup, and we were discussing what she could look like. I thought her prime was in the 1930s, maybe in the 1940s even. And people tend not to change hairstyles every decade. We keep the hairstyles we grow up with. And because this story is being told by Felix Karsten, we get to see his memory and his idea of everything. So, Felix Karsten and his wife don’t see each other the way they really look, but more like this Hollywood couple. I really love that the film twists these things and ideas.” THR

articles.title: Disney and TikTok Ink Wide-Ranging Deal, Videos From Tech Platform Will Be Added to Disney+
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All August 5, 2026 3:00am Dan Kitwood/Getty Images TikTok videos will be coming to Disney +. The tech giant and the entertainment giant have inked what they are calling a “first-of-its-kind” content sharing deal, which will allow TikTok videos from Disney fans to live on both of their streaming platforms. The deal bears a striking similarity to last year’s short-lived announcement with OpenAI to fold videos from Sora into Disney+ … but without the whole AI-generated angle. Creators who opt-in to the program will gain access to Disney assets (think photos and videos featuring Disney characters and IP). A “thoughtfully curated” selection of videos will live on both TikTok and in Verts on Disney+. The companies also say that they “will enable best-in-class creators to unlock special rewards and provide them with increased visibility, access to exclusive events and career development pathways,” making it a two-way street of engagement. The partnership will launch in the U.S. in the next couple months, with plans to eventually bring it to other markets. “The best storytellers are fans first,” said Asad Ayaz, chief marketing and brand officer for Disney. “That has always been true at Disney, and today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways. This collaboration creates a new bridge between the stories we tell and the creativity they inspire, giving creators a bigger stage to share what they’ve made, and audiences more to discover on Disney+ every day.” “Creators are at the heart of everything we do at TikTok. Their creativity extends the life of films and shows into conversations that fans discover and share,” added Dawn Yang, global head of entertainment for TikTok. “Together with Disney, we’re bringing the authentic creator expression of the TikTok community to Disney+, inviting audiences to experience the shared creativity that makes fandom so powerful.” The deal will inevitably turbocharge Disney’s Verts offering, with the company teasing the possibility of creator content there when it launched in March. Vertical video has become a top priority for streamers, recognizing that consumers who watch videos on their phones are just not likely to turn it sideways in most use cases. Peacock, HBO Max, and Netflix have all also rolled out enhanced vertical video offerings in recent months. But the Disney-TikTok tie-up also recognizes the role that creators are playing in fandom, with fand of characters and IP, be it Marvel Star Wars or Moana, often turning to social video platforms to dissect, discuss and celebrate those characters and worlds. THR

articles.title: ‘Toy Story 5’ and Theme Parks Power Disney in Latest Quarter, as Company Teases Big Changes Ahead
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All August 5, 2026 3:39am (L-R): Bullseye, Jessie, and Lilypad in Disney and Pixar's Toy Story 5 Disney/Pixar The Walt Disney Co. reported its fiscal Q3 earnings early Wednesday, with films like Toy Story 5 , streaming, and its lucrative experiences division powering its results. The company missed Wall Street expectations for revenue, but beat them in operating income and earnings per share, with stronger-than-expected theme park performance helping to bolster its bottom line. The company also teed up some big changes coming to its divisions, teasing a plan to turn Disney+ into “a comprehensive membership ecosystem,” with the first elements of that vision rolling out early next year. Related Stories Business Disney and TikTok Ink Wide-Ranging Deal, Videos From Tech Platform Will Be Added to Disney+ Movies 'Toy Story 5' Has Given Away 18,000 Toys to Sick Kids Meanwhile, the company’s lucrative consumer products segment will move from being part of Disney’s experiences division and into its entertainment division: “We believe this shift will have strategic and operational benefits by bringing the monetization of our IP through consumer products closer to the studios that create that IP,” the company writes. Disney reported revenue of $25.2 billion, up 7 percent from a year ago, with segment operating income of $5.5 billion, up 21 percent from a year ago. In entertainment, revenues were $11.3 billion with operating income of $1.68 billion. In streaming, SVOD entertainment revenue (Disney+ and Hulu minus ESPN) was $712 million, a sharp increase from a year ago, and a signal that streaming is becoming more reliably profitable. The company did note that The Mandalorian and Grogu and the live action Moana “underperformed” at the box office, but argued that “these franchise investments contributed to value creation beyond their theatrical releases.” Toy Story , for example, has generated more than $16 billion for Disney as a franchise, it said. In experiences, revenues were $10 billion, up 10% from a year ago, with operating income of $3 billion, up 20%. That was despite market concerns around theme parks, especially with Universal recently reporting lower than expected results. The company said that international visitors are still down at its park, but they made up for it with domestic attendance and annual passholders. In sports, the NBA Finals helped power ESPN, with revenues of $4.5 billion, up 4 percent, though operating income fell 17 percent to $858 million due to higher NBA rights costs. Disney also said that it would use the cash from the $1.2 billion sale of its A+E stake to do stock buybacks, and elaborated a bit on how it expects to use artificial intelligence: “With AI, it isn’t simply about efficiency. We use it first and foremost to enhance a creative process that will always be human-centered, artist-driven, and creator-led,” the company writes. “We’ve cultivated the world’s richest portfolio of IP and production experience across a century of filmmaking, giving us an advantage that our peers and no new entrant can quickly replicate.” THR

articles.title: Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation
articles.full_text: Aug 4, 2026 8:48pm PT Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation By Jack Dunn Plus Icon Jack Dunn Latest Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation 7 hours ago Geno Segers Apologizes For Transgender Comments After ‘Hadestown’ Exit: ‘I Recognize the Impact of My Statements’ 1 day ago Mary Rivera, ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home’ Actress, Dies at 82 1 day ago See All Getty Images Local police were dispatched to the Miami home of Hollywood gossip journalist Perez Hilton after receiving reports about a disturbing livestream during which Hilton, covered in blood, appeared to be cutting himself, Variety has confirmed. The Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office received multiple calls about Hilton’s livestream on Tuesday night and sent deputies to respond. Once on scene, officers spoke with several of Hilton’s family members. Authorities confirmed that Hilton was alone in his home during the time of the live stream. Deputies have since been ordered to “tactically disengage,” but continue to keep an eye on the situation. At this time, we have not been able to make direct contact with him, despite our ongoing efforts to reach him. Our primary concern is Perez’s health and well being, as well as the well being of his family. Until we have confirmed information, we will not speculate or comment further,” Golden Artists Entertainment CoCEO’s Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan said in a statement when Variety reached out for comment. “We appreciate everyone’s concern and ask that his privacy be respected during this time.” Hilton launched his career in the early 2000s, operating a popular celebrity gossip blog that offered a biting, unfiltered look at some of Hollywood’s most unsavory moments. In a 2012 sit-down with The New York Times , Hilton said that he was no longer aligned with his provocative reporting. “What’s important for me is not being liked, but it is that people think I am no longer toxic to the world,” he said. articles.title: How Genesis Is Using Korean Hospitality and the Power of Sports to Build a New Kind of Luxury Brand
articles.full_text: Aug 4, 2026 10:23pm PT How Genesis Is Using Korean Hospitality and the Power of Sports to Build a New Kind of Luxury Brand By Katie Ann Lehman Plus Icon Katie Ann Lehman Latest ‘Bluey’ Fans Can Now Bring the Heeler Family Home With Tonies’ New Collection – Here’s Where to Shop 1 week ago Who Will Take Home the Claret Jug? Here’s How to Watch The Open Championship 2026 3 weeks ago From ‘Happy Gilmore’ to ‘Top Gun,’ Golf Apparel Brand Pins & Aces Taps Into Pop Culture Favorites for Bestselling Golf Gear 3 weeks ago See All Genesis If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. A few months ago, crowds lined the 18th green at The Riviera Country Club in Pacific Palisades, California, as 26-year-old American golfer Jacob Bridgeman secured his first PGA Tour victory at the 2026 Genesis Invitational. But the tournament wasn’t just drawing golf fans. Around the course, guests wandered through hospitality lounges, sampled Korean-inspired food and beverages, explored the latest Genesis vehicles and settled in to watch the action from premium viewing areas. Related Stories Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Genesis may have cornered the golfing market, but their activation at recent events is the kind of experience that’s becoming increasingly common across sports. Today’s biggest sponsorships are about far more than logos on a leaderboard or a name on a tournament. Brands are creating experiences that bring consumers into the action, turning fans into customers long before they ever make a purchase. Popular on Variety T-Mobile , for example, has expanded its sports strategy well beyond traditional sponsorships. The company helps power everything from broadcasting to on-site operations at sporting events. But for fans, the partnership is experienced in more tangible ways: discounted tickets, access to exclusive Club Magenta lounges at events like the PGA Championship and other member-only perks that make for long-term Luxury automakers are taking a similar approach. Mercedes-Benz, for example, has built a strong connection with consumers through Formula 1, where the sport’s focus on performance, engineering and innovation naturally aligns with the brand’s identity. For newer luxury brands, sports sponsorships can serve as a powerful way to start building the recognition that legacy brands already have. Genesis entered that same competitive space in 2015 as a new luxury automaker. Without the history of its established rivals, the brand looked to sports—particularly golf—as a way to create deeper connections with consumers. Why golf? The sport offered a natural overlap with the audience Genesis wanted to reach, their executives tell Variety, from business leaders and global travelers, to luxury consumers who value premium experiences. As the first Official Vehicle and Mobility Sponsor of the PGA Tour, Genesis has embedded itself into events including the Genesis Invitational, Genesis Scottish Open and as well as emerging made-for-TV formats like TGL. The strategy has coincided with rapid growth, with the brand surpassing 1 million global vehicle sales and reaching a record 82,331 U.S. vehicles sold in 2025. The decision to commit to golf early in the brand’s journey was intentional, according to Jose Munoz, President and CEO of Hyundai and Genesis Motor North America. “At the beginning, partnering with the PGA Tour and with Tiger—and committing to golf consistently—was a big decision for us,” Munoz tells Variety. “Back then, we were selling just a few thousand vehicles, and today we’ve achieved record sales and significant growth. We cannot be happier with everything we’ve done together, and the partnership has become not just strategic, but also personal.” That long-term approach is perhaps most evident in the experience Genesis has built around its tournaments. Drawing from the Korean concept of sonnim , or treating guests as honored visitors rather than customers, the brand has reimagined hospitality as more than traditional VIP access. At events like the Genesis Invitational, that philosophy comes to life through thoughtfully designed lounges, elevated food and beverage offerings and welcoming spaces that encourage guests to linger rather than simply pass through. That philosophy carries into the vehicle itself. I spent a week behind the wheel of the Genesis GV70 SUV, and those same priorities showed up in the details. On a long drive from Savannah to Augusta, the driver’s seat massage function became a small but memorable touch that made hours on the road feel effortless. Combined with customizable mood lighting, a quiet cabin and technology that felt intuitive rather than distracting, the experience reflected the same attention to comfort and hospitality I’d seen throughout the tournament. It reinforced something I hadn’t considered before: the sponsorship isn’t just about putting Genesis in front of consumers—it’s about creating a consistent brand experience wherever someone encounters it. Whether that’s relaxing in a hospitality lounge overlooking the 18th green or settling in for a four-hour drive, the feeling is intentionally the same. Across industries, more brands are recognizing that familiarity is one of the most valuable assets they can build. The companies that stand out aren’t always the ones with the longest history—they’re the ones that consistently create experiences people remember. Genesis Fan Shop Genesis is not just showing up at events — the brand is also partnering with brands on must-have merch and apparel that’s become as coveted as a seat behind the wheel. articles.title: Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes
articles.full_text: Aug 4, 2026 11:00pm PT Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes The second year of Open Doors’ Africa focus takes in new projects and emerging directors and producers from fest and lab winners to new propositions By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes 5 hours ago San Sebastián New Directors: Billy Lumby, Marlene Emilie Lyngstad, ‘Money Heist’ Star Jaime Lorente and More 6 days ago Mubi to Release ‘La Mesías,’ From ‘La Bola Negra’ Cannes Best Director Winners, in the U.K., Germany, Canada, Australia and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE) 6 days ago See All 'A Vineyard for a Lobster' Courtesy of Talemwa Pius Magic realist love story “Chapa 100,” absurdist political allegory “A Vineyard for a Lobster” and cross-continental queer drama “Hibiscus by the River” look like some of the potential standouts at Locarno’s talent-deep, wide-ranging 2026 Africa-focused Open Doors , unspooling on-site at Locarno over Aug. 5-10. Winner of a 2025 Atlas Workshops Development Award no less, moving from observational social realism to – literally – flowering magical realism, love story “Chapa 100” is set in Mozambique capital Maputo. It marks scribe-helmer Ique Langa ’s follow-up to “The Prophet,” a 2026 IFF Rotterdam main competition entry. Related Stories Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Beginning with an impossible snowfall blanketing a drought-ridden Ugandan village, “A Vineyard for a Lobster” signals the feature debut of Ugandan Talemwa Pius, a New York Film Academy alum. Popular on Variety Now in advanced development, “Hibiscus in the River” is one of five projects brought to market at Locarno by David Ikeata at Vox Cinematic Films, a burgeoning force on Nigeria’s new film scene. Screenings this year at Open Doors pack a particularly powerful punch taking in, for example, Suzannah Mirghani ’s Venice Critics’ Week premiere “Cotton Queen,” a Thessaloniki’s best film and Doha Audience Award winner and the first feature-length fiction film from Sudan that is written and directed by a woman. Also on show is “Crocodile,” a doc-feature best film, Viewpoints laureate at Tribeca Film Festival, New York and Youth Jury Prize at the U.K.’s Sheffield DocFest, and “Diya,” a 2025 TIFF Centerpiece title praised by those who caught it. Aymar Esse’s touching “My Father’s Kora” world premieres at Locarno. A Snapshot of Africa’s Upscale Film Scene Carefully curated, Open Doors 2026 provides a telling take of the range of current upscale titles coming out of Africa plus their artistic and industrial trends. Though light years from parity in Africa at large, women cineastes feature prominently at Open Doors, dominating its producers, new Open Doors Connect and directors sections. Also, “the cohort of Open Doors 2026 is made up of projects and filmmakers that don’t compromise with authenticity,” says Suzsi Bankuti, head of Open Doors. Many titles are indeed redolently and proudly local. “I Live in V.I’s” “character ensemble and dramatic situations are colored with different aspects of the Nigerian collective psyche,” promises director Ugochukwu Azuya. In “Crocodile,” Nigeria’s The Critics collective, though achieving increasing global renown, debate what it takes to be a Nigerian filmmaker. Directly or indirectly, most films deal with the state of Africa today. That includes a critique of post-colonial dynamics. Formally, the British Empire et al. has gone. But their legacy lingers. In “Cotton Queen,” set on a Sudanese cotton farm, teen Nafisa, raised on her grandmother’s heroic tales of battling British colonizers, sets out to save the cotton fields – and herself when a British businessman arrives planning to introduce genetically engineered cotton. “‘A Vineyard for a Lobster’ grows out of my interest in how colonial structures continue to shape authority, belief and communal life in Uganda decades after independence,” explains director Talemwa Pius. Facing Africa’s Challenges It Takes a Village, a panel at Locarno Pro on Aug. 8, will examine new investment cinema models. Africa desperately needs them, crippled by a fundamental lack of traditional national film funding incentives. Open Doors does hint, however, at some ways African cinema can go and indeed is going. One is the full international co-production and sales agent route, empowering a production with top technical talent. One case in point: Produced by Caroline Daube’s Strange Bird in Germany and Didar Maneki’s Maneki Films in France and co-produced by Annemarie Jacir’s Philistine Films in Palestine and Jordan, “Cotton Queen” was set up as a Germany, France, Palestine, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Sudan production, supported by 10 institutions in those countries and Netherlands’ Hubert Bals Fund. African companies are not just looking towards Europe, however. At Locarno’s mass networking encounter Match Me!, Amadeu Alban at Brazil’s Movioca is currently in development on two Brazil-Nigeria projects, “Trapped” and “La Pyramide,” reflecting his strategy of building co-productions across the Global South. Or filmmakers are turning to genre, with its ingrained entertainment drive. Brought to Open Doors by producer Tapiwa Chipfupa, “Life On the Other Side of the Sun” has supernatural elements; “Diya” weighs in as a blood money crime thriller. Pius uses genre storytelling “to reclaim African narratives and expand how the continent is represented on screen,” he says. Open Doors producer David Ikeata’s slate at Vox Cinematic Films spans “fiction and genre-driven storytelling,” he notes. Rather than a market ploy, however, that passion can come from the filmmakers themselves. “Crocodile” charts how Godwin and Raymond, not yet 11, create a homemade collective with siblings and cousins, shooting ever more ambitious sci-fi films on one of their dad’s iPhones. Or companies can seek out larger same-territory entities, galvanized by global streamer deals. Nemsia Studios, one of Nigeria’s leading film production-financing companies which signed a slate deal with Prime Video in 2022, has boarded Ikeata’s “Hibiscus by the River” as a financing partner. Such deals may be for the lucky few. Their tenor is clear, however. A new initiative, Open Doors Connect, bringing together producers from Africa, Latin America and Asia, aims “to move co-production, circulation and long-term collaboration beyond traditional industry schemes,” Bankuti says. Larger collaboration, now being essayed by film industries as established as France and the Nordic States , is the bigger major way Africa’s film industries can also go. Open Doors 2026 Selection Open Doors 2026 is focused on African projects, producers and directors from outside the northern Maghreb and Egypt and South Africa. Open Doors Projects “Accept My Plea for Burial” (“Baryo Aas Iga Gudoon,” Mohammed Sheikh, Djibouti, Somalia, Qatar) After Warmooge, 12, falls to his death while playing with Waasuge, a fellow goatherd, the village elder fails to resolve the case via customary law and religious counsel. From Minnesota-based U.S.-Somali filmmaker Sheik’s follow-up to “Barni,” screening at Locarno, “a morally complex story where there is no clear truth, told through a rarely seen Somali cultural framework,” he says. ‘Chapa 100’ Ique Langa “Chapa 100” (Ique Langa, Mozambique, Portugal) Sitóe, 80, a Maputo flower vendor, and Valentina, a widowed vegetable seller, fall in love. When he is killed by a speeding minibus when trying to help her, flowers begin to bloom within the vehicle. “My love letter to Maputo, ‘Chapa 100’ is ultimately a story about love, memory, and the invisible bonds that connect us and to the places we call home,” Langa tells Variety. ‘I Live in V.I’ “I Live in V.I” (Ugochukwu Azuya, Nigeria) One of the first titles from Lagos-based Ensemble, launched by Azuya and O.O. Ogunsola last year, a social class satire from Azuya, whose short ghost story “Swimming in a Sea of Trauma,” played IFF Rotterdam. Florence, 23, to avoid a tough commute to her job in luxurious Victoria Island, squats in an abandoned high-rise, a relic from an ‘80s government building project. “A film about grief, urban alienation and gentrification in the city of Lagos exploring the lost hope of the Nigerian dream,” say Azuya and O.O. Ogunsola. “The Ones With the Tempered Flowers” (Neema Ngelime, Tanzania) Ngelime’s debut feature, a diary-like essay, she says, using constructed archives, cinema verité performances with her family and stop motion to explore, respectively, Neema’s 1990s childhood, today and imagined future. An auto doc feature about “a journey I am taking,” “exploring identity and the expectations of womanhood,” says Ngelime. Produced by LBx Africa, run by creative producer Bramwel Iro and director-producer Sam Soko. “Too Much Music” (Aseye Fiagbe, Ghana) A music doc bio, about Kiki Gyan, a Ghanaian keyboard prodigy catapulted to international fame as a teen with Afro-rock pioneers Osibisa, which he left over conflict over credit and ownership. Shaping African disco and funk, but unrecognised, he became famed for addiction and an early death. “Kiki’s story is about memory and erasure, about who gets remembered for their work and who is remembered only for how they fell,” says Fiagbe. ‘A Vineyard for a Lobster’ “A Vineyard for a Lobster” (Talemwa Pius. Uganda) Billed as absurdist political allegory, after mysterious snowfall blankets a drought-stricken Ugandan village, a desperate trader, a disgraced priest and a reluctant chairman exploit the “miracle.” Their escalating ambitions threaten to tear the community apart. From Kampala-based Gripmagic, “in the film, an impossible snowfall in a Ugandan village becomes a political allegory, echoing colonial intrusion,” says Pius. Producers Tapiwa Chipfupa , Ambidextrous Pictures, Zimbabwe, “Life on the Other Side of the Sun” Heading Ambidextrous, founder of AVEL and Girls Making Films training programs and a producer exploring “implications of tradition, culture and custom within modern-day Zimbabwe and on the continent, particularly in the life of women,” says Chipfupa. One case in point:“Life On the Other Side of the Sun, ” a supernatural thriller set in a men-ruled mountain hamlet which slides into desperation and witch hunts – until the free-spirited girl Sungano emerges as the village heroine. Natasha Craveiro , Korikaxoru Films, Cabo Verde, White Mask (“dja branku dja”) “In a market dominated by advertising, we established an auteur cinema production house as an act of resistance and cultural affirmation,” Craveiro says of Korikaxoru Films, set up in 2017. Following on multi-prized docu-fiction fest fave Pirinha (2024), she is now developing hybrid feature “White Mask” which plumbs what she calls her father’s “identity denial:” “a Black man from Cabo Verde who served as a soldier in the Portuguese army and, after the war, erased his Cabo Verdean life to settle in Portugal as a judge.” David Ikeata , Vox Cinematic Films, Nigeria, “Hibiscus by the River” Set up in 2024 by Nigerian actor Chimezie Imo and producer David Ikeata, Vox Cinematic Films slate includes “Hibiscus by the River,” the tale of a young Nigerian man who moves to England to pursue an education, only to find himself pulled back into the currents of his past. Holmes Awa, behind Prime Video’s “Soft Love,” directs. South African producer-screenwriter Paballo Molingoane, and Bulgaria’s U.K.-based Teodora Shaleva also produce. Mamounata Nikièma , Pilumpiku Production, Burkina Faso General secretary of the Africadoc Association Burkina over 2009-2014 and honored at the Pan-African Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou, Africa’s largest cinema festival, in 2021. Behind multiple doc-features, such as “Djeliya, Memory of Mandingo,” an ambitious, five-county co-pro. “Our vision is to become a national and continental reference in film production, digital marketing, and promotion, championing impactful African storytelling, creating jobs for professionals, and nurturing emerging talent,” Nikièma has said. Rua Osman , Helomur Picture, Sudan, “Manageable Matter” Osman’s Helomur focuses on stories that explore memory, identity and social transformation, while fostering meaningful South–South and international co-productions. At Locarno with her “Manageable Matter,” a film take on Berlin-based Emma Waltraud Howes’ installation, staging a procession of the Paradox Crew as an Artichoke Brigade, feature nine performances. These build a “meditation on repetition, collective endurance and the search for humility and grace within seemingly unresolvable cycles,” the synopsis reads. Adja Soro (Studio KÄ, Ivory Coast, “Unchosen”) Behind Abidjan’s animation Studio KÄ and now Studi KÄ France and editor-in-chief of Spark Anim and developing African stories such as YA animated thriller series “Unchosen.” It turns on Esmel, an Olympic taekwondo silver medal winner who returns home a national hero, but, linked to his father’s unsolved murder, risks everything in a live TV interview, to help him find his missing sister. “Through Esmel’s journey, ‘Unchosen’ explores the violence of public exposure in a world where the line between good and evil grows thinner every day,” says Soro. Open Doors Feature Screenings “Barni” (Mohammed Sheik, U.S., Somalia) Sheik’s debut feature, a 2025 Red Sea Fest competition world premiere line-produced by Kadir Harbi at Minneapolis-based Aleel, now behind “Accept My Plea for Burial.” Sheik’s passion to depict Somalia through a Somali lens plus older generation fecklessness shines through as Amini leaves her somnolent village to find sis Barni, 9, in a big city. Arrestingly shot – whether ochre scrub-desert or a big city scrap yard beach – speaking well of Sheik/Harbi’s larger production ambitions. “Catcher” (aka “Wrestlers,” Derhwa Kasunzu, Burkina Faso, France, Democratic Republic of Congo, Saudi Arabia) When Kelekele Lituka, a wrestler who became world champion in 1974, dies in 2021, he’s buried with little fanfare. To honor him, the New Generation wrestling club announces one last catch event in his honor, despite a war-torn Kisangani and the fact its members are getting on in years…. A “lovingly made film,” said an IDFA description. ‘Cotton Queen’ “Cotton Queen” (Suzannah Mirghani, Germany, France, Palestine, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan) An undoubted Open Doors standout, sparking some rave reviews – “a beguiling mix of magic-realist fable, coming-of-age drama and post-colonial critique,” says Eye for Eye – scoring top plaudits at a slew of festivals labs such as Cannes’ Cinéfondation L’Atelier and sales from Totem Films to MAD Solutions/Film Clinic Indie Distribution (Arab-speaking countries), TAPE Collective (U.K./Ireland) and Jip Film (Germany). Cotton Queen “highlights how Sudanese girls must navigate authority in all its forms, whether patriarchal or matriarchal – from the specter of colonialism, to familial authoritarianism to the needs of contemporary capitalism,” Mirghani has said. “Crocodile” (The Critics, Pietra Brettkelly, New Zealand, Nigeria) Built on footage collected by The Critics, a kids’ collective filmed over 13 years through 2025 as Godwin, Raymond, not yet 11, launch The Critics, a filmmaking collective based out of a hardscrabble part of Kaduna, Nigeria, making sci-fi and super-hero films. Now, still determined to make Nigerian genre, they’ve received a digital camera from J.J. Abrams and Morgan Freeman’s narrated Ogun Ola: War Is Coming.” “Crocodile” The Critics and New Zealand’s Brettkelly, whose “A “Flickering Truth” played Venice and TIFF and “Yellow Is Forbidden” Tribeca, chronicle together that journey. “Diya” (Achille Ronaïmou, Chad, France, Germany, Ivory Coast) Rated by critics who have caught it – TIFF’s in-house review calls it “a relentless thriller” – “Diya” sees Dane, an NGO driver, accidentally knock down and kills a child, whose family demands an exorbitant blood debt – a diya – driving Dane ever deeper into crime. Ronaïmou’s feature debut, a critique of diya, still widely extended in Chad, in a film praised for its moral complexity, engrossing tension and sense of place. Bought by Canal+ and a triple winner at the Brussels Intl. Film Festival. ‘My Father’s Kora’ “My Father’s Kora” (“La Kora de mon père,”Aymar Esse, Benin, Switzerland, Germany) A Locarno world premiere. Souleymane, an Afro-German trans man, talented fashion designer and increasingly less timid figure on Berlin’s ballroom scene, travels to Dakar to repair his father’s kora. In doing so, he repairs himself, building his new identity rooted in part in his origins, his griot family in Dakar. Souleymane’s journey’s is sluiced by simple but touching scenes such as his bonding with his brother sewing and with grandfather praying and metaphorical shots of the wash of the ocean on Dakar’s beaches. “The Prophet” (“O Profeta,” Ique Langa, Mozambique, South Africa, Qatar) Preaching in the village of Manjacaze, his inspiration and congregation dwindling, evangelical Pastor Hélder turns to black magic to fire up his oratory and heal his parishioners. His powers come at ever larger sacrifice, literally. Pointedly framed, even in vertical box aspect, bringing sense and sensitivity to shots, a black and white film parable becoming “an expression of the community [Manjacaze] that inspired it,” marking out Luque as a director to track. “Katanga: the Dance of the Scorpions” (“Katanga la danse des scorpions, Dani Kouyaté, Burkina Faso) Last caught by Variety at Abidjan’s SICA, debating African cinema’s future , here vet Kouyaté (“Sia, the Dream of the Python”) re-imagines “Macbeth” in Africa, shot in bold black and white and placed in a broadly modern setting. A Fespaco Yennega Etalon d’Or winner, creating many new scenes, but key plot beats and the broad parable of overweening ambition remain.
